### `k6/websockets` Stable Module — Multi-Connection VU Pattern

The `k6/websockets` module (stable since v0.52, migrated from `k6/experimental/websockets`)
uses a **global event loop** rather than a session-scoped local loop. This enables a single VU
to maintain multiple concurrent WebSocket connections simultaneously — a pattern impossible
with the legacy `k6/ws` module.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/ws-multi-connection.js
import { WebSocket } from "k6/websockets";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ws_load: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 20,
      duration: "2m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "websocket_connecting":   ["p(95)<200"],   // connection establishment latency
    "websocket_msgs_sent":    ["count>1000"],  // total messages across run
    "websocket_session_duration": ["p(95)<120000"], // session < 2 min
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Each VU manages two concurrent WebSocket connections
  const ws1 = new WebSocket("wss://api.example.com/ws/feed");
  const ws2 = new WebSocket("wss://api.example.com/ws/alerts");

  let feed_received = 0;
  let alert_received = 0;

  ws1.onopen = () => {
    ws1.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "subscribe", channel: "prices" }));
  };

  ws1.onmessage = (e) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(e.data);
    feed_received++;
    check(msg, { "feed has price field": (m) => m.price !== undefined });
  };

  ws2.onopen = () => {
    ws2.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "subscribe", channel: "system-alerts" }));
  };

  ws2.onmessage = (e) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(e.data);
    alert_received++;
    check(msg, { "alert has severity": (m) => ["low", "med", "high"].includes(m.severity) });
  };

  // Close after session duration
  setTimeout(() => {
    ws1.close(1000, "normal closure");
    ws2.close(1000, "normal closure");
  }, 60_000);  // 60-second session

  // Block VU until both sockets close
  ws1.addEventListener("close", (e) => {
    check(e, {
      "ws1 clean close": (ev) => ev.code === 1000,
      "ws1 received messages": () => feed_received > 0,
    });
  });

  ws2.addEventListener("close", (e) => {
    check(e, {
      "ws2 clean close": (ev) => ev.code === 1000,
      "ws2 received alerts": () => alert_received >= 0,   // alerts may be empty
    });
  });
}
```

> **Key difference from `k6/ws`:** The legacy `k6/ws` module blocked the VU inside a
> `ws.connect()` callback — you could not run other code while the socket was open. The
> `k6/websockets` module is event-driven: the VU proceeds and the sockets run concurrently
> via the global event loop. Always migrate away from `k6/ws` (removed in v2.0.0).

---

### gRPC Bidirectional Streaming with Clean Teardown

gRPC bidirectional streaming requires careful stream lifecycle management. Streams not closed
explicitly before VU iteration ends leak server-side goroutines and can exhaust the server's
connection limit under sustained load.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/grpc-bidi-stream.js
import { Client, Stream } from "k6/net/grpc";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    bidi_load: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 10,
      duration: "3m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "grpc_req_duration": ["p(95)<500"],
  },
};

// Per-VU client — NEVER share across VUs (race condition on gRPC channel)
export default function () {
  const client = new Client();
  client.connect("grpc-service.internal:50051", {
    plaintext: false,           // TLS in production
    reflect: true,              // use server reflection to load protos dynamically
    timeout: "10s",
  });

  // Bidirectional streaming: both sides send and receive multiple messages
  const stream = new Stream(client, "chat.ChatService/Chat", {
    metadata: { "authorization": `Bearer ${__ENV.GRPC_TOKEN}` },
  });

  let responses = 0;
  let streamError = null;

  stream.on("data", (msg) => {
    responses++;
    check(msg, { "chat reply has text": (m) => typeof m.text === "string" });
  });

  stream.on("error", (e) => {
    streamError = e;
    console.error(`[VU ${__VU}] gRPC stream error: ${JSON.stringify(e)}`);
  });

  stream.on("end", () => {
    console.log(`[VU ${__VU}] stream ended after ${responses} responses`);
  });

  // Send 3 messages then signal half-close (client done sending)
  const messages = ["Hello", "How are you?", "Goodbye"];
  for (const text of messages) {
    stream.write({ text, sender: `vu-${__VU}` });
    sleep(0.1);
  }

  // Half-close: signal end of client writes; server continues until it sends end
  stream.end();

  // Wait for server to finish — in practice, poll with a timeout
  sleep(2);

  // Always close the client connection, even if stream errored
  client.close();

  check(streamError, { "no stream errors": (e) => e === null });
}
```

> **[community]:** Calling `stream.end()` only closes the client's write direction (half-close).
> The server may continue to send messages. If the VU iteration ends before the server sends
> its final `end` event, the stream is forcibly closed and the server may log `"stream reset
> by client"` errors. Add a `sleep()` after `stream.end()` or listen for the `end` event
> with a timeout to allow graceful server-side shutdown. (Gotcha #34 details the `finally`
> block pattern.)

---

### `per-vu-iterations` Executor for Batch / Migration Testing

The `per-vu-iterations` executor guarantees each VU runs **exactly N iterations**. Unlike
`shared-iterations`, there is no contention between VUs. This is ideal for:
- Data migration tests (each VU processes its own shard)
- Smoke testing a fixed set of API endpoints
- Ensuring all VUs exercise the same workflow count

```javascript
// k6/scripts/migration-verification.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

// Each row = one record to migrate; distribute across VUs
const records = new SharedArray("records", () =>
  JSON.parse(open("./data/migration-records.json"))
);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    migration_verify: {
      executor: "per-vu-iterations",
      vus: 20,
      iterations: 50,          // each VU processes 50 records = 1000 total verifications
      maxDuration: "10m",      // safety stop if processing hangs
      tags: { phase: "migration-verify" },
      env: { API_URL: __ENV.API_URL || "https://api.example.com" },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_failed{phase:migration-verify}": ["rate<0.001"],  // <0.1% error
    "http_req_duration{phase:migration-verify}": ["p(99)<2000"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Deterministic record selection: VU N handles records N, N+20, N+40, ...
  // __VU is 1-based; __ITER is 0-based per VU
  const idx = (__VU - 1) + (__ITER * __ENV.VUS || 20);
  if (idx >= records.length) return;   // guard for uneven distribution

  const record = records[idx];
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/records/${record.id}`, {
    tags: { phase: "migration-verify", record_type: record.type },
  });

  check(res, {
    "record found after migration": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "record checksum matches": (r) => {
      const body = r.json();
      return body && body.checksum === record.expected_checksum;
    },
  });
}
```

---

### Multi-Scenario Composition — Sequential Phases with Shared Auth

Combining sequential scenarios with `startTime` offsets models realistic user journeys:
warm-up → ramp → sustained → ramp-down. Using `exec` to point to named exported functions
keeps each phase isolated with its own metric tags.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/full-journey.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

// Auth token shared via setup() return value (copy per VU)
export function setup() {
  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.API_URL}/auth/token`, JSON.stringify({
    client_id: __ENV.CLIENT_ID,
    client_secret: __ENV.CLIENT_SECRET,
    grant_type: "client_credentials",
  }), { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } });

  if (res.status !== 200) throw new Error(`Auth failed: ${res.status}`);
  return { token: res.json("access_token"), expires_in: res.json("expires_in") };
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    // Phase 1: warm-up — 0 to 30s
    smoke: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 2,
      duration: "30s",
      startTime: "0s",
      exec: "smokeTest",
      tags: { phase: "smoke" },
    },
    // Phase 2: ramp — starts after smoke (30s)
    ramp_up: {
      executor: "ramping-vus",
      startVUs: 5,
      stages: [
        { duration: "1m", target: 50 },
        { duration: "2m", target: 50 },
      ],
      startTime: "30s",
      exec: "loadTest",
      tags: { phase: "load" },
    },
    // Phase 3: soak at peak — starts after ramp reaches plateau (30s + 1m ramp = 1m30s)
    soak: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 50,
      duration: "5m",
      startTime: "3m30s",   // 30s + 3m (ramp total)
      exec: "loadTest",
      tags: { phase: "soak" },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_duration{phase:load}":  ["p(95)<500", "p(99)<1000"],
    "http_req_duration{phase:soak}":  ["p(95)<600"],   // slightly relaxed for soak
    "http_req_failed":                ["rate<0.01"],
    "checks":                         ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

export function smokeTest(data) {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/health`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${data.token}` },
  });
  check(res, { "health OK": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}

export function loadTest(data) {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/products?page=1&limit=20`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${data.token}` },
  });
  check(res, {
    "products 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "products has items": (r) => r.json("items") && r.json("items").length > 0,
  });
  sleep(Math.random() * 2 + 0.5);  // 0.5–2.5s think time
}
```

> **[community]:** `startTime` is **relative to the test start**, not the end of the previous
> scenario. If your `setup()` takes 30 seconds, all scenario `startTime` values are shifted by
> that 30 seconds automatically — but only for VU execution. Plan your `startTime` offsets
> by accounting for the actual setup duration visible in test logs. See Gotcha #67.

### Prometheus Remote Write — Native Histograms CI Pattern

Native histograms remove the approximation error of pre-aggregated percentile gauges and
enable accurate post-hoc percentile queries at any granularity via `histogram_quantile()`.

```bash
# docker-compose.yml snippet — Prometheus with native histogram support
services:
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v2.45.0   # requires 2.40+ for native histogram ingestion
    command:
      - --storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus
      - --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - --enable-feature=native-histograms   # REQUIRED: feature flag
      - --web.enable-remote-write-receiver    # accept k6 remote-write pushes
    ports:
      - "9090:9090"
```

```bash
# CI run with native histogram output
K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_SERVER_URL=http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/write \
K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true \
K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_STATS=p(95),p(99),min,max,avg \
K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_PUSH_INTERVAL=5s \
K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_STALE_MARKERS=true \
k6 run --tag testid=${CI_RUN_ID} -o experimental-prometheus-rw script.js
```

```promql
# PromQL queries for Grafana dashboards (native histogram)
# P95 response time across all requests
histogram_quantile(0.95, k6_http_req_duration)

# P99 for a specific scenario tag
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  k6_http_req_duration{scenario="checkout"})

# Error rate per scenario
rate(k6_http_reqs_total{status=~"5.."}[1m])
  / rate(k6_http_reqs_total[1m])

# Stale marker alert — detect when k6 stops sending (CI hang or crash)
absent_over_time(k6_http_reqs_total[2m])
```

> **Important:** After a test completes, k6 sends Prometheus stale markers so that Grafana
> graphs show a gap rather than a flat line at the last value. Enable with
> `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_STALE_MARKERS=true`. Without stale markers, dashboards appear to show
> metrics continuing after the test ends, misleading on-call engineers reviewing historical runs.

### Large-Scale Distributed Testing — 3-Node Coordination Pattern

When a single k6 instance cannot generate sufficient load (typically when generating
>300,000 req/s or when the load generator's network becomes the bottleneck), split the
test across multiple machines using `--execution-segment`.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# distributed-run.sh — launch 3 k6 instances in parallel

SCRIPT="k6/scripts/peak-load.js"
SEQ="0,1/3,2/3,1"        # partition sequence — must be identical on all instances
COMMON_FLAGS="--execution-segment-sequence $SEQ \
  -e API_URL=$API_URL \
  -e K6_TEST_ID=$CI_RUN_ID \
  --out experimental-prometheus-rw"

# Each instance targets the same Prometheus endpoint — metrics are merged by label
K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_SERVER_URL=$PROM_URL \
  k6 run --execution-segment "0:1/3"   $COMMON_FLAGS $SCRIPT &

K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_SERVER_URL=$PROM_URL \
  ssh k6-node-2 "k6 run --execution-segment '1/3:2/3' $COMMON_FLAGS $SCRIPT" &

K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_SERVER_URL=$PROM_URL \
  ssh k6-node-3 "k6 run --execution-segment '2/3:1'   $COMMON_FLAGS $SCRIPT" &

wait   # block until all 3 instances complete
echo "All k6 instances finished: $?"
```

**Important constraints in distributed mode:**
- Each instance evaluates thresholds **independently** — there is no built-in coordinator.
  Use Prometheus alerting rules (or `histogram_quantile()` across all instances) for aggregate pass/fail.
- VU counts are split proportionally: 300 VUs with `"0:1/3"` = 100 VUs on that machine.
- All instances must use identical `--execution-segment-sequence` or they will partition
  the VU space incorrectly and you'll run duplicate or missing iterations.
- Combine with `--paused` + k6 REST API (`k6 resume`) to synchronize start times across
  nodes — otherwise clock skew causes one instance to start 5-10 seconds before others.

```javascript
// Script hint: tag each instance in its metrics for segmentation in Grafana
export const options = {
  tags: {
    node: __ENV.K6_NODE_ID || "unknown",  // set via -e K6_NODE_ID=node-1 per instance
    test_id: __ENV.K6_TEST_ID,
  },
  // ... scenarios, thresholds
};
```

### k6 v2.0.0 — Go Module Path Migration for Extension Authors

Extension authors building with `xk6` must update their Go import path when targeting k6 v2.x.

```go
// Before (k6 v1.x)
import (
  "go.k6.io/k6/js/modules"
  "go.k6.io/k6/lib"
  "go.k6.io/k6/metrics"
)

// After (k6 v2.x) — mechanical find-and-replace
import (
  "go.k6.io/k6/v2/js/modules"
  "go.k6.io/k6/v2/lib"
  "go.k6.io/k6/v2/metrics"
)
```

```bash
# Migrate extension source with sed (macOS/Linux)
find . -name "*.go" -exec sed -i '' \
  's|go\.k6\.io/k6/|go.k6.io/k6/v2/|g' {} \;

# Rebuild with xk6 targeting k6 v2.0.0
xk6 build v2.0.0 --with github.com/myorg/xk6-myextension=.

# Verify: k6 v2 reports extension in --version output
./k6 version
# k6 v2.0.0 (go1.23.x, linux/amd64)
# Extensions:
#   github.com/myorg/xk6-myextension v0.2.0, k6/x/myextension [JavaScript]
```

> **[community]:** If you forget to update the Go module path and attempt to compile against k6 v2
> with v1 imports, you'll see cryptic linker errors like `undefined: modules.Instance` rather than
> a clear "wrong module path" message. The find-and-replace is mechanical but must cover all
> `*.go` files in your extension, including test files.

### Streams API — Incremental CSV Processing at Scale

`k6/experimental/streams` with `k6/experimental/fs` enables memory-efficient processing
of very large test-data files. Rather than loading all rows into `SharedArray` (which buffers
the entire file in each VU's heap), the stream approach reads the file incrementally.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/stream-csv-load.js
import { open } from "k6/experimental/fs";
import { ReadableStream } from "k6/experimental/streams";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

// Open file once at init context; the file handle is shared but cursor is per-VU
let dataFile;

export async function setup() {
  // Warm-up: nothing to authenticate, just confirm connectivity
  const probe = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/health`);
  if (probe.status !== 200) throw new Error("API unreachable in setup()");
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    stream_test: {
      executor: "per-vu-iterations",
      vus: 5,
      iterations: 1,       // each VU reads the whole file once
      maxDuration: "10m",
    },
  },
};

// Factory: create a line-reading stream over an open fs.File
function createLineStream(file) {
  let buffer = "";

  return new ReadableStream({
    async pull(controller) {
      const chunk = new Uint8Array(4096);
      const n = await file.read(chunk);
      if (n === null) {
        // End of file — flush remaining buffer as last line
        if (buffer.length > 0) {
          controller.enqueue(buffer);
          buffer = "";
        }
        controller.close();
        return;
      }
      buffer += new TextDecoder().decode(chunk.subarray(0, n));
      const lines = buffer.split("\n");
      buffer = lines.pop();   // keep incomplete last line
      for (const line of lines) {
        if (line.trim()) controller.enqueue(line);
      }
    },
  });
}

export default async function () {
  const file = await open("./data/large-dataset.csv");
  const stream = createLineStream(file);
  const reader = stream.getReader();

  let lineNum = 0;
  while (true) {
    const { done, value } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;

    lineNum++;
    if (lineNum === 1) continue;  // skip CSV header row

    const [id, email, tier] = value.split(",");
    const res = http.post(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/users/sync`, JSON.stringify({ id, email, tier }), {
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    });
    check(res, { "sync OK": (r) => r.status === 200 || r.status === 204 });
  }

  console.log(`[VU ${__VU}] processed ${lineNum - 1} records`);
}
```

> **[community]:** `k6/experimental/streams` is still experimental — its API may have breaking
> changes in future k6 versions. However, for processing files >50 MB in test scripts, it is the
> only viable approach; loading the entire file into `SharedArray` with `JSON.parse(open(...))` at
> that size will exceed VU heap budgets and cause OOM errors on k6 instances with <4 GB RAM.
> Monitor with `--out json` and inspect `data_received`/`data_sent` to verify you're not
> buffering unexpectedly.

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 20)

### 77. `k6/websockets` `binaryType` defaults to `"blob"` — binary frames are unreadable as Uint8Array without explicit override  [community]

**What:** The `WebSocket` class from `k6/websockets` sets `binaryType` to `"blob"` by default,
matching the browser WebSocket spec. When the server sends binary frames, `e.data` in `onmessage`
is a Blob object, not a `Uint8Array`. Trying to call `.byteLength` or iterate over it directly fails silently (returns `undefined`).

**WHY:** k6 follows the browser WebSocket API for compatibility, but the `Blob` type in k6 is a
limited shim — it does not support `.arrayBuffer()` or `.text()` methods the way a browser does.
For binary protocols (MessagePack, Protobuf over WebSocket, raw byte frames), you must explicitly
set `binaryType = "arraybuffer"` before the first message arrives.

```javascript
import { WebSocket } from "k6/websockets";

export default function () {
  const ws = new WebSocket("wss://api.example.com/ws/binary");
  ws.binaryType = "arraybuffer";   // MUST set before first message

  ws.onmessage = (e) => {
    const view = new DataView(e.data);          // now works
    const msgType = view.getUint8(0);
    console.log("Binary msg type:", msgType);
  };
  // ...
}
```

---

### 78. `per-vu-iterations` + `SharedArray` index calculation breaks when `vus` changes between runs  [community]

**What:** A common pattern indexes into `SharedArray` as `((__VU - 1) * iterations) + __ITER`.
This works when all VUs run the full configured `iterations`. However, if you tune VU count
between CI runs without also recalculating the shard boundaries, VUs at the high end start
reading out-of-bounds indices and silently process `undefined` records.

**WHY:** `__VU` is 1-based and goes up to the configured `vus` value, but `SharedArray.length`
is fixed at load time. If `vus * iterations > array.length`, the high-VU iterations will
receive `undefined` without an error.

```javascript
// SAFE PATTERN — always bounds-check before using the record
const idx = (__VU - 1) * __ENV.ITERATIONS_PER_VU + __ITER;
if (idx >= records.length) {
  console.warn(`VU ${__VU} iter ${__ITER}: no record at idx ${idx}, skipping`);
  return;
}
const record = records[idx];
```

---

### 79. `client.connect()` in gRPC must be called before `new Stream()` — calling inside `if (__ITER == 0)` causes race on first `Stream` of subsequent iterations  [community]

**What:** The pattern `if (__ITER == 0) { client.connect(...) }` is correct for reusing a
connection across iterations. However, if the first iteration's stream ends before the second
iteration's `new Stream()` call but the client was closed and reconnected in-flight, the
stream constructor throws `"client not connected"`.

**WHY:** k6's gRPC client does not automatically reconnect. Once `client.close()` is called,
subsequent `new Stream()` calls fail. Only call `client.close()` in `teardown()` or after the
very last iteration.

```javascript
// WRONG — closes client per iteration, breaks next iteration's Stream
export default function () {
  const stream = new Stream(client, "svc/Method");
  stream.on("end", () => client.close());  // closes after iteration 0 — next iteration fails
}

// CORRECT — close only in teardown
export function teardown() {
  client.close();
}
```

---

### 80. `--execution-segment` does NOT split `setup()` and `teardown()` — they run on ALL nodes  [community]

**What:** When using `--execution-segment` for manual distributed testing across multiple
k6 instances, `setup()` runs independently on **each machine**. If `setup()` creates test
data (e.g., inserts records into a database), you end up with N times the expected test
data — one set per k6 instance.

**WHY:** k6 has no built-in coordinator for distributed runs. Each instance is a fully
independent k6 process. `setup()` and `teardown()` are not aware of other instances.

**Mitigation:** Use idempotent setup (e.g., upsert instead of insert), or designate one
instance as the "coordinator" that runs `setup()`/`teardown()` and have others skip it
via an env var:

```javascript
export function setup() {
  if (__ENV.K6_NODE_ROLE === "worker") return {};  // skip on worker nodes
  // Only coordinator node creates test data
  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/test-sessions`, JSON.stringify({ testId: __ENV.TEST_ID }));
  return { sessionId: res.json("id") };
}
```

---

### 81. `options.cloud` migration from `options.ext.loadimpact` — both keys accepted in v1.x but `options.ext` silently ignored in v2.0.0  [community]

**What:** In k6 v1.x, both `options.ext.loadimpact` and `options.cloud` were accepted for
Grafana Cloud configuration. In v2.0.0, `options.ext.loadimpact` is silently removed — the
cloud executor uses only `options.cloud`. Scripts that still use `options.ext.loadimpact` in
v2.0.0 will run but the project ID, name, and distribution settings will be ignored.

**WHY:** The `ext` namespace was deprecated in v0.46 when `options.cloud` was introduced,
but the old key was kept for backward compatibility through v1.x. v2.0.0 removed the shim.

```javascript
// BEFORE (v1.x — works but deprecated)
export const options = {
  ext: {
    loadimpact: {
      projectID: 3456789,
      name: "Checkout API Load Test",
      distribution: { "amazon:us:ashburn": { loadZone: "amazon:us:ashburn", percent: 100 } },
    },
  },
};

// AFTER (v2.0.0+ — required)
export const options = {
  cloud: {
    projectID: 3456789,
    name: "Checkout API Load Test",
    distribution: { "amazon:us:ashburn": { loadZone: "amazon:us:ashburn", percent: 100 } },
  },
};
```

---

### 82. `http.batch()` does NOT parallelize across VUs — it only parallelizes within a single VU's iteration  [community]

**What:** Teams use `http.batch()` expecting it to coordinate parallel requests across all VUs
simultaneously. In reality, `http.batch()` sends multiple HTTP requests **within one VU's
single iteration** in parallel — it is per-VU concurrency, not cross-VU coordination.

**WHY:** k6's VU model is already parallel at the VU level. `http.batch()` is designed to
simulate a browser sending multiple sub-resources (JS, CSS, images) simultaneously. Each VU's
`http.batch()` call is independent of all other VUs. Total parallelism = VUs × batch size.

```javascript
// CORRECT use: simulate browser loading multiple assets in one page load
export default function () {
  const [html, css, js] = http.batch([
    ["GET", "https://example.com/"],
    ["GET", "https://example.com/style.css"],
    ["GET", "https://example.com/app.js"],
  ]);
  check(html, { "HTML 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  check(css,  { "CSS 200":  (r) => r.status === 200 });
  check(js,   { "JS 200":   (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

// WRONG expectation: "I'll use batch() to send 100 requests at once from one VU"
// → just use 100 VUs with a single request each for accurate load modeling
```

---

### 83. `__ENV` variables injected via `-e` flag are always strings — numeric comparisons silently fail  [community]

**What:** All values injected via `-e MY_VAR=10` or from the environment are strings in k6.
Comparisons like `if (__ENV.CONCURRENCY > 5)` always evaluate to `true` (string `"10" > 5`
coerces the number to string for comparison, and `"10" > "5"` is `false` — but `"10" > 5`
uses JS coercion rules that may surprise).

**WHY:** JavaScript coercion: `"10" > 5` is `true` (string is coerced to number) but
`"10" === 10` is `false`. The subtle failure is when you use the value in arithmetic:
`sleep(__ENV.THINK_TIME)` where `THINK_TIME="2.5"` — `sleep("2.5")` actually works because
k6 internally coerces, but `__ENV.THINK_TIME * 2` would yield `"2.52.5"` via string
concatenation rather than `5`.

```javascript
// SAFE PATTERN — always parse env vars before numeric use
const THINK_TIME = parseFloat(__ENV.THINK_TIME || "1");
const MAX_VUS    = parseInt(__ENV.MAX_VUS    || "50", 10);

export default function () {
  // ...
  sleep(THINK_TIME);          // number, not string
}
```

---

### 84. `discardResponseBodies: true` prevents `check()` on body content — combine with selective `responseType`  [community]

**What:** Setting `options.discardResponseBodies = true` globally reduces memory by not
allocating response body strings, but it also makes all `r.body`, `r.json()`, and
`r.html()` calls return `null`. Teams set this globally for performance, then wonder why
their body-content checks silently pass (check against `null` often matches `(r) => r.body === null`).

**WHY:** `discardResponseBodies` is a global setting. There is no per-request `discardBody`
parameter in `http.get()`/`http.post()`. To selectively keep bodies for specific requests,
override `responseType` on those requests.

```javascript
export const options = {
  discardResponseBodies: true,    // global: discard bodies for performance
};

export default function () {
  // Status-only check — body not needed (global discard applies)
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/health`);

  // Body check needed for this endpoint — override per-request
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/products/123`, {
    responseType: "text",   // "text" | "binary" | "none" — overrides global discard
  });
  check(res, {
    "product has title": (r) => r.json("title") !== undefined,
  });
}
```

---

### 85. Prometheus `--tag testid=` is not automatically unique per CI run — use `$GITHUB_RUN_ID` or timestamp  [community]

**What:** The `--tag testid=ci-run` approach from documentation examples is frequently
copy-pasted verbatim into CI pipelines. Every run uses the same static `testid` tag value,
making it impossible to filter individual test runs in Grafana dashboards — all runs merge
into one time-series segment.

**WHY:** Tags are label values in Prometheus. If every run uses `testid="ci-run"`, Grafana
can only show an aggregated view across all runs. To isolate a specific run (e.g., for
post-incident analysis), each run needs a unique tag value.

```bash
# GitHub Actions — use run ID for unique test identification
k6 run \
  --tag testid=ci-${GITHUB_RUN_ID} \
  --tag branch=${GITHUB_REF_NAME} \
  --tag commit=${GITHUB_SHA:0:7} \
  -o experimental-prometheus-rw \
  k6/scripts/api-load.js
```

```promql
# Then in Grafana: filter by specific run
k6_http_req_duration{testid="ci-12345678"}

# Or compare two runs
histogram_quantile(0.95, k6_http_req_duration{testid=~"ci-12345.*|ci-12346.*"})
```

### `page.waitForEvent()` — Console, Dialog, and Download Event Interception (k6 v1.5+)

`page.waitForEvent(event, optionsOrPredicate?)` blocks the VU until the specified browser
event fires. Unlike `page.waitForResponse()` (network-level), it intercepts page-level
events: `"console"`, `"dialog"`, `"download"`, `"frameattached"`, `"framenavigated"`, etc.
This is the only way to assert on `console.log` output or intercept browser dialogs in k6.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-events.js — console message capture + dialog handling
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    event_tests: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      vus: 1,
      iterations: 2,
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: { checks: ["rate==1.0"] },
};

const APP = __ENV.APP_URL || "http://localhost:3001";

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();

  try {
    await page.goto(`${APP}/`);

    // ── Pattern 1: capture console.log output ────────────────────────────
    // Set up the listener BEFORE triggering the action that causes the log
    const [consoleMsg] = await Promise.all([
      page.waitForEvent("console", (msg) => msg.text().includes("analytics")),
      page.getByRole("button", { name: "Track Event" }).click(),
    ]);
    check(consoleMsg, {
      "analytics log fired":  (m) => m.text().includes("analytics"),
      "log level is log/info": (m) => ["log", "info"].includes(m.type()),
    });

    // ── Pattern 2: intercept and dismiss a browser confirm() dialog ──────
    // waitForEvent("dialog") resolves when the dialog opens
    const [dialog] = await Promise.all([
      page.waitForEvent("dialog"),
      page.getByRole("button", { name: "Delete Account" }).click(),
    ]);
    check(dialog, {
      "confirm dialog shows": (d) => d.type() === "confirm",
      "message has account text": (d) => d.message().toLowerCase().includes("account"),
    });
    await dialog.dismiss();  // or .accept() / .accept("input text")

    // ── Pattern 3: wait for a download event ────────────────────────────
    // Download events carry metadata — check filename and MIME type
    const [download] = await Promise.all([
      page.waitForEvent("download"),
      page.getByRole("link", { name: "Export CSV" }).click(),
    ]);
    check(download, {
      "download filename correct": (d) => d.suggestedFilename().endsWith(".csv"),
    });

    // ── Pattern 4: waitForEvent with a timeout override ──────────────────
    // Default timeout is the page's defaultTimeout (usually 30s in k6 browser)
    try {
      const [rarEvent] = await Promise.all([
        page.waitForEvent("console", { timeout: 2000 }),  // 2 s max
        page.getByRole("button", { name: "Optional Feature" }).click(),
      ]);
      console.log("Optional console event received:", rarEvent.text());
    } catch {
      // Timeout is expected for optional features — not a test failure
    }

  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**`waitForEvent` event reference for k6 browser:**

| Event | Fires when | Predicate receives |
|-------|------------|-------------------|
| `"console"` | `console.log/warn/error` is called in the page | `ConsoleMessage` — `.text()`, `.type()`, `.args()` |
| `"dialog"` | `alert()`, `confirm()`, `prompt()` open | `Dialog` — `.type()`, `.message()`, `.accept()`, `.dismiss()` |
| `"download"` | A file download starts | `Download` — `.suggestedFilename()`, `.path()` |
| `"frameattached"` | An iframe is added to the page | `Frame` |
| `"framenavigated"` | A frame navigates to a new URL | `Frame` |

> **[community]:** Always combine `waitForEvent` with `Promise.all()` alongside the action
> that triggers the event. Setting up the listener after the action is a race condition — the
> event may fire between the action and the listener registration, causing the test to hang
> until timeout. This is the same pattern required for `waitForResponse` (Gotcha #57).

---

### `locator.pressSequentially()` — Character-by-Character Input (k6 v1.5+)

`pressSequentially(text, options?)` types each character individually with an optional
`delay` between keystrokes. This is the correct approach for:
- Inputs with autocomplete that fires on each character (not just on `fill()`)
- Rate-limited typing tests
- Simulating slow user input for flakiness investigation

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-sequential-type.js
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";
import { Trend } from "k6/metrics";

const autocompleteLatency = new Trend("autocomplete_response_ms", true);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    search_test: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      vus: 2,
      iterations: 5,
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    autocomplete_response_ms: ["p(95)<500"],
    checks: ["rate>0.95"],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();

  try {
    await page.goto(`${__ENV.APP_URL || "http://localhost:3001"}/search`);

    const searchInput = page.getByRole("combobox", { name: "Search" });
    await searchInput.waitFor({ state: "visible" });

    // pressSequentially: fires keyboard events for each character
    // delay: 50ms between chars simulates real typing speed (~240 WPM)
    const start = Date.now();
    await searchInput.pressSequentially("laptop", { delay: 50 });

    // Wait for the autocomplete dropdown to appear
    const dropdown = page.getByRole("listbox");
    await dropdown.waitFor({ state: "visible" });
    autocompleteLatency.add(Date.now() - start);

    // Verify suggestions appeared
    const suggestions = dropdown.getByRole("option");
    const count = await suggestions.count();
    check(count, { "autocomplete suggestions shown": (n) => n > 0 });

    // Select first suggestion
    if (count > 0) {
      await suggestions.first().click();
      check(page.url(), {
        "navigated to search results": (url) => url.includes("/search"),
      });
    }

    // Contrast: fill() vs pressSequentially() — when to use each:
    // fill("text") — fastest; replaces entire value atomically; no keyboard events
    // pressSequentially("text", {delay}) — fires keydown/keypress/keyup per char; triggers onChange per char
    // type("text", {delay}) — legacy alias for pressSequentially; prefer pressSequentially in v1.5+

  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**`fill()` vs `pressSequentially()` decision table:**

| Scenario | Use |
|----------|-----|
| Standard form input without autocomplete | `fill()` — faster, atomic |
| Autocomplete / live-search inputs | `pressSequentially()` — triggers per-char events |
| Inputs with `onKeyDown` validation | `pressSequentially()` |
| Password fields with strength meter | `pressSequentially()` |
| Bulk form fill (no JS listeners) | `fill()` — avoid synthetic key overhead |

> **[community]:** `locator.type()` was the legacy name before `pressSequentially()` was
> added in k6 browser v1.5. Both methods are currently available but `pressSequentially()`
> is the preferred name going forward. Do not confuse with `locator.press("Enter")` which
> sends a single named key event (not character sequences).

### PBKDF2 WebCrypto Key Derivation (k6 v1.6+)

k6 v1.6 added PBKDF2 support to the built-in `crypto` module, enabling password-based key
derivation without external extensions. Use it to test APIs that require client-side
key derivation before authentication (e.g., E2E encrypted apps where the server never sees
the raw password).

```javascript
// k6/scripts/pbkdf2-auth.js — PBKDF2 key derivation + HMAC-signed API requests
import { crypto } from "k6/experimental/webcrypto";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

// Load test users — each has a password; we derive a key per-VU
const users = new SharedArray("users", () => JSON.parse(open("./data/test-users.json")));

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    auth_load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 20,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 30,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<800"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

/**
 * Derive a 256-bit AES key from a password + salt using PBKDF2.
 * Returns the raw key bytes as a Uint8Array.
 */
async function deriveKey(password, saltHex, iterations = 100_000) {
  const encoder = new TextEncoder();
  const salt = hexToBytes(saltHex);

  // Import the password as a PBKDF2 key
  const baseKey = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
    "raw",
    encoder.encode(password),
    { name: "PBKDF2" },
    false,                        // not extractable
    ["deriveBits", "deriveKey"]
  );

  // Derive 256 bits using SHA-256
  const derivedBits = await crypto.subtle.deriveBits(
    {
      name:       "PBKDF2",
      hash:       "SHA-256",
      salt:       salt,
      iterations: iterations,
    },
    baseKey,
    256
  );

  return new Uint8Array(derivedBits);
}

/** Sign a message with HMAC-SHA256, return hex digest */
async function hmacSign(keyBytes, message) {
  const hmacKey = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
    "raw",
    keyBytes,
    { name: "HMAC", hash: "SHA-256" },
    false,
    ["sign"]
  );

  const encoder  = new TextEncoder();
  const sigBuf   = await crypto.subtle.sign("HMAC", hmacKey, encoder.encode(message));
  return bytesToHex(new Uint8Array(sigBuf));
}

function hexToBytes(hex) {
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(hex.length / 2);
  for (let i = 0; i < bytes.length; i++) {
    bytes[i] = parseInt(hex.substr(i * 2, 2), 16);
  }
  return bytes;
}

function bytesToHex(bytes) {
  return Array.from(bytes).map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join("");
}

export default async function () {
  const user = users[__VU % users.length];

  // Step 1: Get the user's salt from the server (stored per-user)
  const saltRes = http.get(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/auth/salt?email=${encodeURIComponent(user.email)}`
  );
  if (!check(saltRes, { "salt 200": (r) => r.status === 200 })) return;

  const { salt, challenge } = saltRes.json();

  // Step 2: Derive key client-side (never sends raw password to server)
  const keyBytes = await deriveKey(user.password, salt);

  // Step 3: Sign the challenge with the derived key
  const signature = await hmacSign(keyBytes, challenge);

  // Step 4: Authenticate with the signed challenge
  const authRes = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/auth/verify`,
    JSON.stringify({ email: user.email, challenge, signature }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } }
  );

  check(authRes, {
    "auth 200":       (r) => r.status === 200,
    "token received": (r) => Boolean(r.json("access_token")),
  });
}
```

> **[community]:** PBKDF2 with `iterations: 100_000` takes ~80–200 ms per call depending on
> k6's single-threaded Go runtime. In a load test with 50 VUs each deriving a key at the
> start of every iteration, this adds 4–10 seconds of pure CPU overhead before the first
> HTTP request fires. Cache the derived key in a module-level variable keyed by user email
> if the same user runs multiple iterations, or pre-derive all keys in `setup()` and pass
> them via the return value.

### `k6 deps` CLI — Extension Dependency Auditing (k6 v1.6+)

`k6 deps` analyzes a k6 script and emits a list of all required extensions (xk6 modules).
Use it in CI to detect when a script imports an extension that isn't in the compiled binary
before the test starts.

```bash
# Analyze script dependencies
k6 deps k6/scripts/load-with-extensions.js

# Output (plain text):
# k6/x/faker     >=v0.4.0
# k6/x/sql       >=v0.3.1
# k6/x/kafka     >=v2.0.0

# JSON output — machine-readable for CI parsing
k6 deps --json k6/scripts/load-with-extensions.js
# [
#   { "module": "k6/x/faker", "constraint": ">=v0.4.0" },
#   { "module": "k6/x/sql",   "constraint": ">=v0.3.1" }
# ]

# Version constraint manifest (K6_DEPENDENCIES_MANIFEST env var)
# Use to enforce minimum extension versions across all CI runs:
export K6_DEPENDENCIES_MANIFEST='{"k6/x/faker": ">=v0.4.4", "k6/x/sql": ">=v0.3.2"}'
k6 run k6/scripts/load.js
# k6 validates that the compiled-in extension versions satisfy the manifest constraints
# and fails at startup if any constraint is violated
```

```javascript
// k6/scripts/load-with-extensions.js — script that requires xk6 modules
import { Faker } from "k6/x/faker";        // requires: xk6-faker >= v0.4.0
import { Client } from "k6/x/kafka";        // requires: xk6-kafka >= v2.0.0
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

const faker  = new Faker(42 /* seed */);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    api_load: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 10, duration: "1m" },
  },
  thresholds: { http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"] },
};

export default function () {
  // Generate realistic test data using xk6-faker
  const user = {
    name:  faker.person.fullName(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
    phone: faker.phone.number(),
  };

  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/users`,
    JSON.stringify(user),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } }
  );
  check(res, { "user created 201": (r) => r.status === 201 });
}
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/k6-ext-check.yml
# Validate extension dependencies before building the custom k6 binary
name: k6 Extension Check

on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  deps-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install k6 (base binary)
        run: |
          curl -fsSL https://github.com/grafana/k6/releases/latest/download/k6-linux-amd64.tar.gz \
            | tar -xz --strip-components=1 -C /usr/local/bin

      - name: Check script extension requirements
        run: |
          # Verify script does not require extensions beyond what the stock binary provides
          DEPS=$(k6 deps --json k6/scripts/basic.js)
          echo "Script requires: $DEPS"
          # If DEPS is non-empty, a custom xk6 build is needed
          if [ "$DEPS" != "[]" ] && [ "$DEPS" != "null" ]; then
            echo "ERROR: Script requires extensions — build a custom xk6 binary"
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Build custom binary if extensions required
        if: failure()
        run: |
          go install go.k6.io/xk6/cmd/xk6@latest
          xk6 build \
            --with github.com/szkiba/xk6-faker \
            --with github.com/mostafa/xk6-kafka@v2.0.0
```

> **[community]:** `k6 deps` only inspects **ES module `import` statements**, not dynamic
> `require()` calls. Scripts that use conditional dynamic imports (`require("k6/x/foo")`)
> will not have those extensions listed in the deps output. This is an intentional design
> decision (v1.4.0 change) — wrap all extension imports as top-level `import` statements
> so `k6 deps` can detect them. This also improves tree-shaking in bundled scripts.

### WebSocket Close Codes — Precise Session Lifecycle Tracking (k6 v1.5+)

k6 v1.5 added structured access to WebSocket close codes and reasons via the `close` event
data. Before v1.5, the close handler received no structured data. Now you can distinguish
normal closure (1000) from server-initiated drops (1001), protocol errors (1002), and
application-defined codes (4000–4999).

```javascript
// k6/scripts/ws-close-codes.js — WebSocket session lifecycle with close code tracking
import { WebSocket } from "k6/websockets";
import { check } from "k6";
import { Counter, Trend } from "k6/metrics";

// Track closure reasons as custom metrics
const normalClosures   = new Counter("ws_normal_closures");
const abnormalClosures = new Counter("ws_abnormal_closures");
const sessionDuration  = new Trend("ws_session_duration_ms", true);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ws_lifecycle: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 30,
      duration: "3m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    ws_normal_closures:   ["count>0"],           // at least some clean closures
    ws_session_duration:  ["p(95)<120000"],       // sessions < 2 min
    // Ratio guard: abnormal closures < 5% of total
    ws_abnormal_closures: ["count<30"],           // for 30 VUs × 2 min
  },
};

export default function () {
  const sessionStart = Date.now();
  const ws = new WebSocket(`${__ENV.WS_URL || "wss://api.example.com"}/ws/session`);

  ws.binaryType = "arraybuffer";  // explicit — avoids Gotcha #77 (blob default)

  ws.onopen = () => {
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "auth", token: __ENV.WS_TOKEN || "test-token" }));
  };

  ws.onmessage = (e) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(e.data);
    if (msg.type === "session_ready") {
      // Send heartbeat every 5s to keep the connection alive
      const interval = setInterval(() => {
        if (ws.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
          ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "ping", ts: Date.now() }));
        } else {
          clearInterval(interval);
        }
      }, 5000);

      // Auto-close after 30s
      setTimeout(() => {
        clearInterval(interval);
        ws.close(1000, "session complete");  // normal closure
      }, 30_000);
    }
  };

  ws.onclose = (e) => {
    const duration = Date.now() - sessionStart;
    sessionDuration.add(duration);

    // Close code reference:
    // 1000 — Normal closure (clean, expected)
    // 1001 — Going Away (server restarting / navigating away)
    // 1002 — Protocol Error
    // 1003 — Unsupported Data (server cannot handle message type)
    // 1006 — Abnormal Closure (connection dropped without close frame)
    // 1011 — Internal Error (server-side error)
    // 4000-4999 — Application-defined codes

    if (e.code === 1000) {
      normalClosures.add(1);
    } else {
      abnormalClosures.add(1);
      console.warn(
        `[VU ${__VU}] Abnormal WS close: code=${e.code}, reason="${e.reason}", duration=${duration}ms`
      );
    }

    check(e, {
      "ws closed cleanly": (ev) => ev.code === 1000,
      "close has reason":  (ev) => typeof ev.reason === "string",
    });
  };

  ws.onerror = (e) => {
    console.error(`[VU ${__VU}] WS error:`, e.message || e);
    abnormalClosures.add(1);
  };
}
```

**WebSocket close code reference:**

| Code | Name | Cause | k6 Action |
|------|------|-------|-----------|
| `1000` | Normal Closure | Client/server agreed to close | Track as success |
| `1001` | Going Away | Server restarting; browser navigating away | Investigate server health |
| `1002` | Protocol Error | Malformed frame | Fix client message format |
| `1006` | Abnormal Closure | TCP dropped without close frame | Network instability |
| `1011` | Internal Error | Server threw unhandled exception | Investigate server logs |
| `4001`–`4999` | Application-defined | Custom app-level codes | App-specific handling |

> **[community]:** Code `1006` (Abnormal Closure) is emitted when the TCP connection is
> dropped without a WebSocket close handshake — it is NOT sent by the remote; it is
> synthesized locally by the WebSocket stack. You will never receive `1006` from a `send()`
> — it only appears in `onclose`. An `1006` rate spike under load usually indicates the
> server is dropping connections due to resource exhaustion (connection pool full, OOM kill,
> or network throttling), not a client-side bug.

### OpenTelemetry Stable Output — Production Integration (k6 v1.4+)

The OpenTelemetry output graduated from experimental in k6 v1.4 and is now available
as `--out opentelemetry`. It exports k6 metrics as OTLP (gRPC or HTTP) to any OTel-compatible
backend: Grafana Tempo, Jaeger, Honeycomb, Datadog, New Relic.

```bash
# Send to local OTel Collector (gRPC, port 4317)
k6 run \
  --out opentelemetry \
  k6/scripts/load.js
# Defaults: gRPC, localhost:4317, no TLS

# Full configuration via env vars
K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_PROTOCOL=grpc \          # or "http/protobuf"
K6_OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=k6-load-test \
K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_ENDPOINT=otel-collector:4317 \
K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_INSECURE=true \          # disable TLS for local collector
K6_OTEL_METRIC_PREFIX=k6_ \              # prefix all metric names
K6_OTEL_FLUSH_INTERVAL=5s \
  k6 run --out opentelemetry k6/scripts/load.js

# HTTP/protobuf (e.g., Honeycomb, Datadog OTLP endpoint)
K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf \
K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_ENDPOINT=https://api.honeycomb.io \
K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_HEADERS="x-honeycomb-team=${HONEYCOMB_API_KEY}" \
  k6 run --out opentelemetry k6/scripts/load.js
```

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml — OTel Collector + Grafana Tempo for local development
version: "3.9"
services:
  otel-collector:
    image: otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:latest
    volumes:
      - ./otel-collector-config.yml:/etc/otel/config.yml
    command: ["--config", "/etc/otel/config.yml"]
    ports:
      - "4317:4317"    # gRPC OTLP receiver
      - "4318:4318"    # HTTP OTLP receiver

  tempo:
    image: grafana/tempo:latest
    ports:
      - "3200:3200"    # Tempo HTTP API

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:latest
    environment:
      - GF_FEATURE_TOGGLES_ENABLE=traceqlEditor
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
```

```yaml
# otel-collector-config.yml — route k6 metrics from gRPC to Tempo
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317

exporters:
  otlp:
    endpoint: tempo:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true

service:
  pipelines:
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlp]
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlp]
```

```javascript
// k6/scripts/otel-correlated.js — emit custom OTel-compatible metrics with trace context
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { Trend, Counter } from "k6/metrics";

const apiDuration = new Trend("api_request_duration_ms", true);
const apiErrors   = new Counter("api_error_total");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    correlated_load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 50,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "3m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 30,
    },
  },
  // Add trace context headers to correlate k6 load with distributed traces
  // in Tempo / Jaeger — use x-k6-vu and x-k6-iter as synthetic trace IDs
};

const BASE = __ENV.API_URL || "http://localhost:3001";

export default function () {
  const traceId = `${__VU.toString(16).padStart(8, "0")}${__ITER.toString(16).padStart(8, "0")}`;

  const start = Date.now();
  const res = http.get(`${BASE}/api/products`, {
    headers: {
      "x-trace-id": traceId,       // correlate k6 VU/iteration with app traces
      "x-k6-scenario": "correlated_load",
    },
    tags: { endpoint: "products-list" },
  });
  apiDuration.add(Date.now() - start);

  if (!check(res, { "products 200": (r) => r.status === 200 })) {
    apiErrors.add(1);
  }
}
```

> **[community]:** The `K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_TYPE` env var was deprecated in k6 v1.4.0 in
> favour of `K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_PROTOCOL`. Using the old name (`K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_TYPE=grpc`)
> still works through v1.x but triggers a deprecation warning. In v2.0.0+ environments,
> always use `K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_PROTOCOL` to avoid surprises when the old alias is removed
> in a future major version.

### `k6/experimental/fs` + `csv.parse` — Fast Init-Context Data Loading

For structured CSV test data that fits in memory (< ~100 MB), `csv.parse()` with
`k6/experimental/csv` at init context is significantly faster than streaming because k6
can initialise once and distribute the parsed array to all VUs via `SharedArray`.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/csv-init-pattern.js — recommended init-context CSV loading pattern
import { open }   from "k6/experimental/fs";
import { parse }  from "k6/experimental/csv";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

// Parse CSV once at init time — result is an immutable SharedArray shared across VUs
// Much faster than streaming: no per-iteration seek() or Parser construction overhead
const users = new SharedArray("users", async () => {
  const file = await open("./data/test-users.csv");
  const rows = await parse(file, { header: true, skipFirstLine: true });
  return rows;  // [ { email: "...", role: "admin", tier: "premium" }, ... ]
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    user_load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 100,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "3m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 40,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Deterministic round-robin: spread across all users
  const user = users[(__VU + __ITER * 100) % users.length];

  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/auth/login`,
    JSON.stringify({ email: user.email, role: user.role }),
    {
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      tags: { tier: user.tier },
    }
  );

  check(res, {
    "login 200":     (r) => r.status === 200,
    "token present": (r) => Boolean(r.json("access_token")),
  });

  sleep(0.2);
}
```

**`csv.parse` option reference:**

| Option | Default | Purpose |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `header` | `false` | First row is column names; rows returned as objects |
| `skipFirstLine` | `false` | Skip the very first row (useful with `header: true`) |
| `delimiter` | `","` | Column separator character |
| `comment` | `""` | Lines starting with this character are skipped |
| `asObjects` | `true` when `header: true` | Return rows as `{key: value}` maps |

> **[community]:** `csv.parse()` in the `SharedArray` init function is executed **once
> per k6 VU initialisation phase** — NOT once globally. For a test with 50 VUs, the
> parse runs once and the result is shared via the SharedArray's memory-mapped storage.
> The cost is O(1) parses, not O(VUs). However, the `await open(file)` and `await parse()`
> calls inside `SharedArray`'s init callback require an async wrapper — the standard
> pattern is to wrap in an `async` IIFE or use the `async () =>` form as shown above.
> Ensure your `k6` version supports top-level `await` in init context (v0.52+).

---

### Scenario `env` and `tags` — Per-Scenario Configuration Without Script Branching

Each scenario can inject its own environment variables and metric tags without any `if`
branching in the script body. This keeps the shared `default()` function generic while
allowing per-scenario behaviour through externally injected config.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/env-tags-config.js — clean scenario-per-environment setup
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

// Single generic test function — no scenario-specific branching
export function runApiTest() {
  const base     = __ENV.BASE_URL;           // injected by scenario env
  const endpoint = __ENV.TEST_ENDPOINT;      // injected per scenario
  const delay    = parseFloat(__ENV.THINK_TIME || "0.5");

  const res = http.get(`${base}${endpoint}`, {
    // tags added here merge with scenario-level tags automatically
    tags: { endpoint: endpoint.replace(/\//g, "_") },
  });

  check(res, {
    "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "latency ok": (r) => r.timings.duration < parseInt(__ENV.MAX_LATENCY_MS || "1000"),
  });

  sleep(delay);
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    // Scenario A: staging, read endpoints, relaxed SLO
    staging_read: {
      executor: "ramping-vus",
      stages: [
        { duration: "1m", target: 20 },
        { duration: "2m", target: 20 },
        { duration: "30s", target: 0 },
      ],
      exec: "runApiTest",
      env: {
        BASE_URL:      "https://staging.api.example.com",
        TEST_ENDPOINT: "/api/products",
        THINK_TIME:    "0.5",
        MAX_LATENCY_MS: "1000",
      },
      tags: { env: "staging", type: "read" },
    },

    // Scenario B: staging, write endpoints, stricter SLO
    staging_write: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 10,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "3m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 15,
      startTime: "30s",         // start after read scenario warms up
      exec: "runApiTest",
      env: {
        BASE_URL:       "https://staging.api.example.com",
        TEST_ENDPOINT:  "/api/orders",
        THINK_TIME:     "1.0",
        MAX_LATENCY_MS: "2000",
      },
      tags: { env: "staging", type: "write" },
    },
  },

  thresholds: {
    // Per-scenario SLOs using tag selectors
    "http_req_duration{type:read}":  ["p(95)<500"],
    "http_req_duration{type:write}": ["p(95)<2000"],
    "http_req_failed{env:staging}":  ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};
```

> **[community]:** Scenario `env` values are **strings only** — all values injected via
> the scenario `env` block are converted to strings, matching `-e` flag behaviour. If your
> test function needs numeric config (like `THINK_TIME` or `MAX_LATENCY_MS`), always parse
> with `parseFloat()` / `parseInt()` before use. Using them directly in arithmetic
> (`sleep(__ENV.THINK_TIME)` where THINK_TIME is a string) relies on k6's internal coercion
> which currently works but is fragile — it may break if k6 tightens type handling in
> future releases. (See also Gotcha #83.)

---

### `http.batch()` Parallel Assets — SPA Page-Load Simulation

`http.batch()` is the right tool for simulating a browser loading multiple sub-resources
simultaneously (HTML + CSS + JS + images). Each call fires all requests in parallel from a
single VU, matching real browser behaviour without the browser module overhead.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/spa-page-load.js — simulate full SPA page load with asset parallelism
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, group, sleep } from "k6";
import { Trend } from "k6/metrics";

const pageLoadTime = new Trend("spa_full_page_load_ms", true);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    page_loads: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 5,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "3m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    spa_full_page_load_ms: ["p(90)<3000"],   // full page load P90 < 3s
    http_req_failed:        ["rate<0.005"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.APP_URL || "https://staging.example.com";

export default function () {
  const loadStart = Date.now();

  group("initial page load", () => {
    // Step 1: HTML (sequential — needed to discover asset URLs)
    const htmlRes = http.get(`${BASE}/`, {
      tags: { asset_type: "html" },
    });
    check(htmlRes, { "HTML 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });

    // Step 2: Critical assets in parallel — simulates browser resource hints
    const [cssRes, mainJsRes, vendorJsRes] = http.batch([
      { method: "GET", url: `${BASE}/static/main.css`,     params: { tags: { asset_type: "css" } } },
      { method: "GET", url: `${BASE}/static/main.js`,      params: { tags: { asset_type: "js" } } },
      { method: "GET", url: `${BASE}/static/vendor.js`,    params: { tags: { asset_type: "js" } } },
    ]);
    check(cssRes,      { "CSS 200":       (r) => r.status === 200 });
    check(mainJsRes,   { "main.js 200":   (r) => r.status === 200 });
    check(vendorJsRes, { "vendor.js 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });

    // Step 3: Deferred API calls (SPA data hydration — after JS executes)
    sleep(0.1);  // synthetic JS parse/execute time
    const [configRes, userRes] = http.batch([
      { method: "GET", url: `${BASE}/api/config`,           params: { tags: { asset_type: "api" } } },
      { method: "GET", url: `${BASE}/api/session`,          params: { tags: { asset_type: "api" } } },
    ]);
    check(configRes, { "config 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
    check(userRes,   { "session 200 or 401": (r) => [200, 401].includes(r.status) });
  });

  pageLoadTime.add(Date.now() - loadStart);
  sleep(Math.random() * 3 + 2); // 2–5s between page loads (think time)
}
```

> **[community]:** `http.batch()` has a default concurrency cap of `http.batch.max` which
> defaults to `20` parallel requests per call. Batches larger than 20 requests are
> queued internally. Increase `options.batch` in your script options (`options.batch = 50`)
> if you need to simulate browsers that open more simultaneous connections. This is distinct
> from `options.batchPerHost` (default: `6`) which caps connections per hostname — matching
> browsers' per-host connection limit.

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 22)

### 86. `k6/experimental/webcrypto` module path — use `crypto` import alias, not `webcrypto`  [community]

**What:** The PBKDF2 and other WebCrypto APIs are exported from `"k6/experimental/webcrypto"`,
but the imported object should be aliased as `crypto` (not `webcrypto`) to match the
browser's `globalThis.crypto` API:

```javascript
// WRONG — confusing alias; .subtle is on the `crypto` object, not `webcrypto`
import { crypto as webcrypto } from "k6/experimental/webcrypto";
await webcrypto.subtle.importKey(...);  // works but misleading

// CORRECT — matches browser WebCrypto API shape
import { crypto } from "k6/experimental/webcrypto";
await crypto.subtle.importKey(...);
await crypto.subtle.deriveBits(...);
await crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(16));  // random bytes
```

**WHY:** `k6/experimental/webcrypto` exports a `crypto` named export that mirrors
`window.crypto` in browsers. The `subtle` property contains all asymmetric/symmetric
algorithms; `getRandomValues()` is on the `crypto` object directly. Aliasing to `webcrypto`
obscures this structure and breaks copy-paste from browser WebCrypto examples.

---

### 87. `page.waitForEvent("dialog")` does not suppress the dialog — you MUST call `dialog.accept()` or `dialog.dismiss()`  [community]

**What:** After `waitForEvent("dialog")` resolves, the dialog is still open and blocking
the browser page. If your test does not call `.accept()` or `.dismiss()` on the dialog
object, the page remains frozen and subsequent page interactions (clicks, navigations,
`waitForURL`) time out.

**WHY:** k6 browser does not auto-dismiss dialogs, unlike some Playwright configurations.
The `waitForEvent("dialog")` only _notifies_ your code — it does not handle the dialog.

```javascript
const [dialog] = await Promise.all([
  page.waitForEvent("dialog"),
  page.getByRole("button", { name: "Delete" }).click(),
]);
// REQUIRED — must call one of these or the page stays blocked:
await dialog.dismiss();   // clicks "Cancel" / "No"
// or
await dialog.accept();    // clicks "OK" / "Yes"
// or with input (for prompt() dialogs):
await dialog.accept("my text input");
```

---

### 88. `locator.pressSequentially()` fires `keydown`+`keypress`+`input`+`keyup` per character — don't use for password fields with paste-only restriction  [community]

**What:** Some password managers and security-conscious apps block `keydown` paste events
but allow `fill()` (which sets the input value via CDP `Runtime.callFunctionOn`). Conversely,
some form validators reject `fill()` because no keyboard events fired, and accept only
`pressSequentially()`. Test which your app requires.

**WHY:** `fill()` goes through the CDP Input API's `Input.insertText` path (no keyboard
events). `pressSequentially()` dispatches `keydown → keypress → input → keyup` for each
character. Apps that check for keyboard event order will reject `fill()`.

Diagnostic pattern:
```javascript
// Try fill() first; fall back to pressSequentially() if the field remains empty
await field.fill("test-value");
const afterFill = await field.inputValue();
if (afterFill !== "test-value") {
  await field.clear();
  await field.pressSequentially("test-value");
}
```

---

### 89. `options.summaryTrendStats` controls which percentiles appear in `handleSummary` JSON — missing from docs  [community]

**What:** By default, k6 only stores `avg`, `min`, `med`, `max`, `p(90)`, `p(95)`,
`p(99)` in the end-of-test summary JSON. If your `handleSummary` or CI regression script
needs `p(99.9)` or `p(50)` (median vs p50 distinction), you must explicitly configure
`summaryTrendStats`:

```javascript
export const options = {
  summaryTrendStats: [
    "avg", "min", "med", "max",
    "p(50)", "p(75)", "p(90)", "p(95)", "p(99)", "p(99.9)",
  ],
  // ...
};
```

**WHY:** Storing all possible percentiles by default would inflate the summary JSON
significantly for scripts with many custom Trend metrics. The default list covers
common SLO thresholds. Teams that define `p(99.9)` thresholds must also add `p(99.9)`
to `summaryTrendStats` or the threshold key `"p(99.9)"` will evaluate against `undefined`
(which k6 treats as `0`, causing silent false-positive passes).

---

### 90. `k6 deps` auto-resolution only fires for `import` at module scope — not for imports inside functions  [community]

**What:** `k6 deps` analyzes static `import` declarations at the top of the file. Extension
modules imported inside function bodies (dynamic imports) are not detected. Additionally,
k6's automatic subcommand extension resolution (`k6 x <ext>`) also only inspects top-level
ES module imports.

```javascript
// NOT detected by k6 deps — conditional dynamic import
export default function () {
  if (__ENV.USE_KAFKA === "true") {
    const { Client } = require("k6/x/kafka");  // NOT analyzed by k6 deps
    // ...
  }
}

// CORRECT — top-level import (always detected, tree-shaken if unused)
import { Client } from "k6/x/kafka";

export default function () {
  if (__ENV.USE_KAFKA !== "true") return;
  const client = new Client(...);
}
```

---

### 91. `--out opentelemetry` rate metrics changed format in v1.4.0 — breaking change for existing dashboards  [community]

**What:** In k6 v1.4.0, the OTel rate metric format changed. Previously, rate metrics
(like `http_req_failed`) emitted as a single gauge. After v1.4.0, they emit as a counter
with two label values: `zero` and `nonzero`. Existing Grafana dashboards that query the
old gauge format show no data after upgrading.

**Migration:**
```promql
# BEFORE (v1.3.x and earlier)
k6_http_req_failed   # single gauge, 0.0–1.0

# AFTER (v1.4.0+) — two counters
k6_http_req_failed_total{value="nonzero"}   # requests that were failures
k6_http_req_failed_total{value="zero"}      # requests that succeeded

# Compute rate:
rate(k6_http_req_failed_total{value="nonzero"}[1m]) /
(rate(k6_http_req_failed_total{value="nonzero"}[1m]) + rate(k6_http_req_failed_total{value="zero"}[1m]))
```

> Update all existing OTel-based Grafana dashboards after upgrading past k6 v1.4.0.
> The change applies to all `Rate` metrics (built-in and custom).

---

### 92. `k6/experimental/csv` `parse()` loads entire file into memory — chunked approach needed for > 50 MB  [community]

**What:** `csv.parse()` reads and parses the entire file at once. For CSV files
>50 MB, this inflates k6's memory usage significantly during initialization, potentially
causing OOM on `k6` instances with 2 GB RAM limits.

**Rule of thumb:** `csv.parse()` memory cost ≈ 3–5× raw file size (string allocation +
JSON object overhead + SharedArray copy). A 50 MB CSV may consume 150–250 MB at init.

**Fix for large files:** Use the streaming pattern (Cycle 20, `ReadableStream` over
`k6/experimental/fs`) to process the file incrementally rather than loading it fully.
For medium files (5–50 MB), `csv.parse()` into `SharedArray` is the recommended approach.

```javascript
// Decision table:
// File size  | Approach
// < 5 MB     | csv.parse() into SharedArray — fastest, no seek overhead
// 5–50 MB    | csv.parse() into SharedArray — acceptable; monitor k6 --mem-limit flag
// > 50 MB    | ReadableStream with k6/experimental/fs — incremental, O(chunk) memory
// > 500 MB   | Pre-split file by VU count outside k6; mount each shard as a separate file
```

---

### 93. `http.batch()` `params` is a top-level key, NOT nested inside the request object  [community]

**What:** The short-form `http.batch()` array syntax is `[method, url, body, params]`.
Teams that use the object form mix up where `params` goes:

```javascript
// WRONG — params nested inside method object (silently ignored)
http.batch([
  { method: "GET", url: "https://example.com/a", params: { tags: { t: "x" } } },
]);

// CORRECT — object form: params IS a top-level key in the request object
http.batch([
  { method: "GET", url: "https://example.com/a", params: { tags: { t: "x" }, headers: { "X-Req": "1" } } },
]);

// ALSO CORRECT — array tuple form: [method, url, body, params]
http.batch([
  ["GET", "https://example.com/a", null, { tags: { t: "x" } }],
]);
```

**WHY:** The object form of `http.batch()` entries mirrors `http.get(url, params)` where
`params` is the last argument. The `params` key in the object form IS the correct location
for tags, headers, and cookies — this is NOT wrong. The confusion arises because some
developers nest `params` inside a `config` or `options` subkey, which does nothing.

---

### 94. `group()` nesting adds metric tag prefix — affects threshold tag selectors for nested groups  [community]

**What:** k6 automatically tags metrics with `group:<path>` where `<path>` is the
`::` separated chain of nested group names. A nested `group()` produces tags like
`group::outer::inner`, which requires exact string matching in threshold tag selectors.

```javascript
group("checkout", () => {
  group("payment", () => {
    const res = http.post("/api/pay", payload);
    // This request is tagged: group=::checkout::payment
    // (note the leading "::" — k6 always prepends "::")
  });
});

// Threshold to target only the payment group:
thresholds: {
  "http_req_duration{group:::checkout::payment}": ["p(95)<2000"],
}
```

**WHY:** The `::` prefix is k6's convention to mark the top-level default group (which
has an empty name, hence the leading `::`). Even top-level groups are tagged
`::group-name` not `group-name`. Always verify the exact tag value by inspecting
the `--out json` output's `metric.tags.group` field before writing a threshold.

---

### 95. `page.route()` URL pattern matching is glob-only — regex patterns silently never match  [community]

**What:** k6 browser's `page.route(pattern, handler)` accepts URL patterns as:
- Exact URL strings: `"https://api.example.com/data"`
- Glob patterns: `"**/api/data"`, `"https://*.example.com/**"`

It does NOT accept regular expressions. Passing a regex literal (e.g., `/\/api\/data/`)
or a string that looks like a regex silently fails to match any URLs — the handler is
never called but no error is thrown.

```javascript
// WRONG — regex literal silently never matches
await page.route(/\/api\/data/, (route) => {
  route.fulfill({ body: JSON.stringify({ mocked: true }) });
});

// WRONG — regex string silently never matches
await page.route("/api/data", (route) => { ... });  // exact match only, not partial

// CORRECT — glob pattern
await page.route("**/api/data", (route) => {
  route.fulfill({
    status: 200,
    contentType: "application/json",
    body: JSON.stringify({ mocked: true }),
  });
});

// CORRECT — exact full URL
await page.route("https://api.example.com/data", (route) => { ... });
```

> Unlike Playwright (which accepts both glob and regex), k6 browser currently supports
> glob patterns and exact URL strings only. This is a known divergence from Playwright's
> API surface documented in k6 browser's compatibility matrix.

---

### 96. PBKDF2 iteration count of 100,000+ is CPU-bound — run in `setup()` + cache results to avoid per-iteration overhead  [community]

**What:** PBKDF2 with `iterations: 100_000` is deliberately slow by design (it is a
key-stretching algorithm). Running it inside `default()` on every VU iteration with 50 VUs
running for 5 minutes means ~15,000 PBKDF2 calls — each taking 50–200 ms on k6's CPU.
This creates artificial CPU-bound latency that inflates your load test's request duration
metrics and reduces actual RPS throughput.

**Fix:** Pre-derive all keys in `setup()` and pass them via the return value, or cache
derivation results per-user in a module-level `Map`:

```javascript
import { crypto }    from "k6/experimental/webcrypto";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

// Option A: derive all keys in setup() — safest, keys available to all VUs
export async function setup() {
  const users = JSON.parse(open("./data/test-users.json"));
  const keys  = {};

  for (const user of users) {
    const base = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
      "raw",
      new TextEncoder().encode(user.password),
      { name: "PBKDF2" }, false, ["deriveBits"]
    );
    const bits = await crypto.subtle.deriveBits(
      { name: "PBKDF2", hash: "SHA-256", salt: hexToBytes(user.salt), iterations: 100_000 },
      base, 256
    );
    keys[user.email] = Array.from(new Uint8Array(bits));  // serializable for VU transfer
  }

  return { keys };
}

export default async function (data) {
  const user    = users[__VU % users.length];
  const keyBits = new Uint8Array(data.keys[user.email]); // pre-derived
  // Use keyBits directly — no PBKDF2 on hot path
  const signature = await hmacSign(keyBits, __ENV.API_CHALLENGE);
  // ...
}
```

> **[community]:** The `data` returned by `setup()` is serialised to JSON and distributed
> to each VU. `Uint8Array` values must be converted to regular arrays before returning
> (as shown above with `Array.from(...)`) because `JSON.stringify(Uint8Array)` produces
> an object format (`{0: 32, 1: 45, ...}`) that does not deserialise back to a typed array.
> Reconstitute with `new Uint8Array(data.keys[email])` in `default()`.

### `execution.vu.metrics.tags` — Per-VU Dynamic Tag Injection for High-Cardinality Metrics

k6's `execution` module exposes `execution.vu.metrics.tags` and `execution.vu.metrics.metadata`,
allowing you to set VU-level metric tags and metadata at runtime without passing `params` to every
`http.*` call. Tags set here propagate automatically to **all metrics emitted by that VU** for
the rest of the iteration.

Use cases:
- Tagging all metrics with the logged-in user's role or tier
- Correlating metrics with a distributed trace ID set per-iteration
- A/B variant tagging without touching every request

```javascript
// k6/scripts/vu-dynamic-tags.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";
import { execution } from "k6";   // named import from built-in module

const USERS = new SharedArray("users", () => JSON.parse(open("./data/users.json")));

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mixed_users: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      stages: [
        { target: 50, duration: "2m" },
        { target: 50, duration: "5m" },
        { target: 0,  duration: "1m" },
      ],
      preAllocatedVUs: 60,
      maxVUs: 120,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // Separate SLOs per user tier
    "http_req_duration{tier:premium}": ["p(95)<300"],
    "http_req_duration{tier:free}":    ["p(95)<800"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const user = USERS[__VU % USERS.length];

  // ── Set VU-level tags once per iteration ───────────────────────────────────
  // These tags are applied to ALL metrics for the rest of this iteration
  execution.vu.metrics.tags["tier"]    = user.tier;          // "free" | "premium"
  execution.vu.metrics.tags["region"]  = user.region;        // "eu" | "us"
  // metadata is not exported to output but available for in-process correlation
  execution.vu.metrics.metadata["traceId"] = `${Date.now()}-${__VU}-${__ITER}`;

  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/orders`,
    JSON.stringify({ itemId: user.favoriteItem }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Authorization": `Bearer ${user.token}` } }
  );

  check(res, {
    "order created":   (r) => r.status === 201,
    "has order id":    (r) => !!r.json("orderId"),
  });

  sleep(Math.random() * 2 + 1);
}
```

**`metrics.tags` vs per-request `params.tags`:**

| Approach | Scope | Verbose? | Best for |
|----------|-------|----------|----------|
| `execution.vu.metrics.tags` | All metrics this iteration | No | User role, region, test variant |
| `params.tags` per request | Single request only | Yes | Per-endpoint classification |
| `tagWithCurrentStageProfile()` | Stage-level tagging (cloud) | No | Cloud ramp profile labels |

> **[community]:** Setting `execution.vu.metrics.tags` inside `setup()` or `teardown()` has no
> effect — those lifecycle functions run as VU 0 and their tags are reset before VU execution
> starts. Set tags at the top of `default()` on every iteration.
