### OpenTelemetry Output — Streaming k6 Metrics to OTLP Collectors

k6's `--out opentelemetry` output plugin converts all k6 metric types to OpenTelemetry
equivalents and emits them over gRPC or HTTP/protobuf to any OTLP-compatible collector
(Grafana Tempo, Jaeger, Honeycomb, Datadog, etc.).

```bash
# Start a local OpenTelemetry collector on default ports (4317 gRPC, 4318 HTTP)
# Then run k6 with OTLP export:

K6_OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=checkout-svc \
K6_OTEL_SERVICE_VERSION=v2.1.0 \
K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf \
K6_OTEL_HTTP_EXPORTER_URL=http://otel-collector:4318/v1/metrics \
K6_OTEL_EXPORT_INTERVAL=5s \
k6 run --out opentelemetry k6/scripts/checkout-load.js
```

```javascript
// k6/scripts/checkout-load.js — script with named service for OTEL correlation
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 50,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "5m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 60,
      // scenario-level tag flows into every OTEL attribute automatically
      tags: { scenario: "checkout" },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<400"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/checkout`,
    JSON.stringify({ cart_id: `cart-${__VU}`, promo: null }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } },
  );
  check(res, { "checkout 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.1);
}
```

**k6 to OTEL metric type mapping:**

| k6 type | OTEL type |
|---------|-----------|
| Counter | Int64Counter |
| Gauge | Float64Gauge |
| Rate | Int64Counter (with `condition` attribute: pass/fail) |
| Trend | Float64Histogram |

**Tradeoff:** OTEL output adds ~5–10% CPU overhead on the k6 side due to serialization.
For very high-rate tests (>50k reqs/s), benchmark with and without the output flag.

> **[official]** OTEL output does NOT carry distributed trace context into application
> spans — it exports k6 *metrics* in OTEL format. Correlating k6 load events with
> application traces requires injecting `traceparent` headers manually in the VU script.

> **[community] Gotcha #128:** Configuring both `--out opentelemetry` and
> `--out influxdb` simultaneously doubles the metric serialization path. On high-VU
> tests this has been observed to cause metric drops in the InfluxDB output because
> both outputs compete for the same goroutine pool. Run at most two outputs concurrently
> and prefer Prometheus remote-write for time-series storage alongside OTEL.

### `handleSummary()` with JUnit XML — CI-Native Test Reports

The `jUnit()` helper from `jslib.k6.io/k6-summary` converts the summary `data` object
into JUnit XML, enabling any CI system (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab) to parse k6
threshold results as test cases with pass/fail status.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/ci-junit-summary.js — emit JUnit XML for CI integration
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { jUnit, textSummary } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 5,
      duration: "30s",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
    checks:            ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

export function handleSummary(data) {
  return {
    // Human-readable summary to stdout
    stdout: textSummary(data, { indent: " ", enableColors: true }),
    // JUnit XML for CI test-results parser
    "k6-results.xml": jUnit(data),
    // Full raw metrics JSON for archiving
    "k6-summary.json": JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
  };
}

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/health`);
  check(res, {
    "status 200":     (r) => r.status === 200,
    "body not empty": (r) => (r.body?.length ?? 0) > 0,
  });
  sleep(1);
}
```

GitHub Actions integration:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/k6-perf.yml
- name: Run k6 smoke test
  run: k6 run --env API_URL=${{ secrets.API_URL }} k6/scripts/ci-junit-summary.js

- name: Publish k6 JUnit results
  uses: mikepenz/action-junit-report@v4
  if: always()
  with:
    report_paths: "k6-results.xml"
    check_name: "k6 Performance Thresholds"
```

**Tradeoff:** `jUnit()` maps *thresholds* to test cases — checks that don't have a
corresponding threshold are invisible in the JUnit output. Add a threshold on `checks`
(e.g., `rate>0.99`) to ensure check failures appear as CI test failures.

> **[community] Gotcha #129:** `handleSummary()` is called **after** the test finishes
> regardless of exit code. A threshold breach (exit code 99) still triggers
> `handleSummary()`. However, if k6 is **killed** mid-run (SIGKILL, OOM, ctrl-c without
> graceful-stop time), `handleSummary()` may **not** execute. Always use
> `if: always()` in CI upload steps to catch the exit-code-99 case.

### `k6/secrets` Multi-Source — Mixing Mock and Vault Secrets per Environment

The `k6/secrets` module (v2.0+) supports multiple named `--secret-source` providers
in a single run. One source can be marked as `default`; the others are accessed via
`secrets.source('name').get('key')`. This lets the same script run against mock secrets
in local dev and Vault/cloud secrets in CI without code changes.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/multi-source-secrets.js — environment-agnostic secret access
import secrets from "k6/secrets";
import http    from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    auth_flow: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      vus: 3,
      iterations: 9,
    },
  },
};

// Usage:
//   Local dev:
//     k6 run --secret-source=mock=default,api_key=dev-key-123 script.js
//   CI (Vault):
//     k6 run --secret-source=vault=default,addr=https://vault.corp:8200,token=$VAULT_TOKEN \
//             --secret-source=mock=name=fallback,api_key=fallback-key script.js

export default async function () {
  // get() targets the default source; throws if key absent
  const apiKey = await secrets.get("api_key");

  // source('fallback').get() targets a named non-default source
  // Useful for multi-tenant tests where each VU needs a different key
  const tenantKey = await secrets
    .source("fallback")
    .get(`tenant_key_${__VU}`);

  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/secure`, {
    headers: {
      "X-API-Key":    apiKey,
      "X-Tenant-Key": tenantKey ?? apiKey,
    },
  });

  check(res, { "authorized": (r) => r.status !== 401 });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `secrets.get()` is async — your `default` function must be declared
`async function` and every secret access requires `await`. This adds per-iteration
overhead versus reading from `__ENV`. Prefer `k6/secrets` when values must not appear
in logs or k6 cloud test reports.

> **[official]** Secrets are redacted in logs as `***SECRET_REDACTED***`. The actual
> value is available inside the script but never written to stdout, stderr, or the
> summary JSON by k6's runtime — though `handleSummary()` code that explicitly
> serializes HTTP response bodies could inadvertently expose secrets.

> **[community] Gotcha #130:** Accessing `secrets.source('name')` where `name` does not
> match any configured `--secret-source` throws at **runtime**, not at startup. Validate
> all source names in `setup()` before VU code runs so a misconfiguration fails fast
> rather than mid-iteration on a long-running test.

### `k6/experimental/fs` — Memory-Efficient File Streaming for Large Test Data

`k6/experimental/fs` loads files into a shared memory space across all VUs and exposes
a streaming read interface (`read()` + `seek()`). Unlike the top-level `open()` function,
which loads the entire file into each VU's copy, `fs.open()` loads once and all VUs share
the underlying buffer.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/fs-csv-stream.ts — streaming CSV line-by-line with k6/experimental/fs
import { open, SeekMode } from "k6/experimental/fs";
import { check }          from "k6";
import http               from "k6/http";

// File is opened once at init time; all VUs share the underlying buffer
const file = await open("./data/users.csv");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    bulk_create: {
      executor: "per-vu-iterations",
      vus: 5,
      iterations: 50,
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  // Read a fixed-size chunk per iteration
  const buf      = new Uint8Array(256);
  const bytesRead = await file.read(buf);

  if (bytesRead === null) {
    // EOF — rewind to start so VUs can cycle through the file
    await file.seek(0, SeekMode.Start);
    return;
  }

  const line = new TextDecoder().decode(buf.subarray(0, bytesRead)).trim();
  if (!line || line.startsWith("email")) return; // skip header row

  const [email, password] = line.split(",");
  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/users`,
    JSON.stringify({ email, password }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } },
  );

  check(res, { "user created": (r) => r.status === 201 || r.status === 409 });
}
```

**Memory comparison:**

| Approach | 100k-line CSV, 50 VUs |
|----------|-----------------------|
| `open()` + `SharedArray` | ~220 MB (one copy, shared) |
| `open()` per VU (anti-pattern) | ~11 GB |
| `k6/experimental/fs` | ~50 MB (streaming, no full load) |

**Tradeoff:** The streaming interface is lower-level than `SharedArray`. You manage byte
buffers and `seek()` manually. For random-access by VU index, `SharedArray` is simpler.
Use `fs` when files exceed ~500 MB or when you need to stream files too large to
deserialize fully in memory.

> **[community] Gotcha #131:** `k6/experimental/fs.open()` uses a **top-level `await`**
> which means the module init code must support top-level await (available in k6 v0.50+).
> Wrapping the `open()` in a regular synchronous init context causes a
> `"cannot await in sync context"` error. Always scaffold with the official `k6 new`
> template or the `async` IIFE pattern.

### `ramping-arrival-rate` — Avoiding VU Starvation with `preAllocatedVUs` Tuning

The `ramping-arrival-rate` executor injects iterations at a target rate regardless of
VU availability. If `preAllocatedVUs` is too low and the rate ramps faster than VUs can
complete iterations, k6 logs `"not enough available VUs"` and silently drops iterations.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/arrival-rate-tuned.js — correctly sized preAllocatedVUs
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check }        from "k6";

// Sizing formula:
//   preAllocatedVUs >= peak_rate_per_second × (avg_response_s + think_time_s)
//   e.g., 100 rps × (0.25 + 0.1) = 35 VUs minimum; use 1.5× headroom = ~53
//   maxVUs adds burst buffer for p99 latency spikes

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    api_ramp: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate: 0,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 60,   // sized for avg response time at peak rate
      maxVUs: 150,            // burst buffer for p99 latency
      stages: [
        { duration: "1m", target: 20  },  // warm-up to 20 rps
        { duration: "3m", target: 100 },  // ramp to 100 rps
        { duration: "2m", target: 100 },  // sustain peak
        { duration: "1m", target: 0   },  // cool-down
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration:  ["p(95)<300"],
    http_req_failed:    ["rate<0.01"],
    dropped_iterations: ["count<10"], // fail if k6 drops >10 iterations
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/catalog`);
  check(res, { "catalog 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  // NOTE: do NOT add sleep() here — ramping-arrival-rate manages pacing already
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Setting `maxVUs` very high avoids drop warnings but may overwhelm the
test machine. Use the `dropped_iterations` metric threshold as a canary — if it
triggers, the system under test is likely overloaded, not just k6 misconfigured.

> **[official]** Adding `sleep()` inside a `ramping-arrival-rate` iteration inflates
> the iteration duration and therefore the VU demand. The executor already handles
> pacing — `sleep()` is an anti-pattern here.

> **[community] Gotcha #132:** The `dropped_iterations` metric counts iterations k6
> *intended* to start but couldn't because no free VU was available. A non-zero value
> means `preAllocatedVUs`/`maxVUs` sizing is too tight for the configured rate. Monitor
> this metric in all arrival-rate tests; a threshold of `count<50` over a 5-minute run
> is a reasonable CI gate.

### `k6/websockets` (Stable) — Per-VU WebSocket Connections with Global Event Loop

The `k6/websockets` module (stable since v1.3) replaces `k6/ws` and runs on the **global
event loop**. Each VU can hold multiple active connections and must `await` events,
enabling cleaner `async/await` patterns versus the callback-heavy `k6/ws` API.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/ws-stable.js — per-VU WebSocket with k6/websockets stable module
import { WebSocket }    from "k6/websockets";
import { check }        from "k6";
import { Counter }      from "k6/metrics";

const msgReceived = new Counter("ws_messages_received");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    realtime_feed: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 20,
      duration: "3m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    ws_messages_received: ["count>100"],
    ws_connecting:        ["p(95)<500"],
    ws_msgs_sent:         ["count>0"],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const ws = new WebSocket(`${__ENV.WS_URL}/feed`);

  ws.addEventListener("open", () => {
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ action: "subscribe", channel: "prices" }));
  });

  ws.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
    msgReceived.add(1);
    const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
    check(data, { "has price field": (d) => "price" in d });
  });

  ws.addEventListener("error", (event) => {
    console.error(`WS error VU ${__VU}:`, event.error?.message);
  });

  // Keep connection open for 30 seconds per iteration
  await ws.waitForClose(30_000);
}
```

**`k6/ws` vs `k6/websockets` comparison:**

| Feature | `k6/ws` (legacy) | `k6/websockets` (stable) |
|---------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| API style | Callback (`socket.on`) | Event listener (`addEventListener`) |
| Event loop | Per-VU poll | Global async event loop |
| Multi-connection per VU | No | Yes |
| Binary messages | `sendBinary()` | `binaryType = "arraybuffer"` standard |
| Async/await | No | Yes |

> **[community] Gotcha #133:** In `k6/websockets`, the `"close"` event fires **after**
> `waitForClose()` resolves. Code placed inside the `"close"` event listener may run
> after the VU has already moved on to the next iteration. Use `waitForClose()` as the
> synchronization point and process teardown logic **after** the await, not inside the
> event listener callback.

### Custom `handleSummary()` with Remote POST — Pushing Results to Analytics Platforms

`handleSummary()` can HTTP-POST the summary data to an external service (Datadog,
Splunk, a custom webhook) by performing the request inside the function and returning
an empty `stdout` key. This enables post-test result ingestion without a separate output
plugin or shell scripting around k6.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/remote-summary.js — push test summary to analytics endpoint
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { textSummary }  from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js";

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<400"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
  scenarios: {
    load: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 10, duration: "1m" },
  },
};

export function handleSummary(data) {
  // Build a compact payload for the analytics platform
  const payload = {
    run_id:     __ENV.CI_RUN_ID ?? "local",
    timestamp:  new Date().toISOString(),
    p95_ms:     data.metrics.http_req_duration?.values?.["p(95)"] ?? null,
    error_rate: data.metrics.http_req_failed?.values?.rate ?? null,
    thresholds: Object.fromEntries(
      Object.entries(data.thresholds ?? {}).map(([k, v]) => [k, v.ok]),
    ),
  };

  // http is available inside handleSummary — synchronous call
  http.post(
    `${__ENV.ANALYTICS_URL}/perf-results`,
    JSON.stringify(payload),
    {
      headers: {
        "Content-Type":  "application/json",
        "Authorization": `Bearer ${__ENV.ANALYTICS_TOKEN}`,
      },
      timeout: "5s",
    },
  );

  return {
    stdout: textSummary(data, { indent: " ", enableColors: true }),
  };
}

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/v1/search?q=test`);
  check(res, { "search 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** HTTP calls inside `handleSummary()` are synchronous and block process
exit. A slow or unreachable analytics endpoint delays CI job completion. Always set an
explicit `timeout` and consider whether a fire-and-forget approach is acceptable.

> **[community] Gotcha #134:** `handleSummary()` receives `data.metrics` with values
> **only for metrics that recorded at least one data point**. Accessing
> `data.metrics.my_custom_trend?.values?.["p(95)"]` returns `undefined` for metrics
> never triggered (e.g., an error-path Trend on a test run with 0 errors). Guard every
> metric access with `?.` and null-coalesce defaults to prevent `JSON.stringify(undefined)`
> silently producing `null` payload fields.

### Environment Variable Precedence — `__ENV`, `K6_*` Options, and CLI Flags

k6 has three layers of configuration: script `options`, environment variables, and CLI
flags. Misunderstanding their precedence causes subtle misconfiguration bugs, especially
when parameterizing scenarios dynamically.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/env-precedence-demo.js — illustrating __ENV vs K6_ options
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

// CORRECT: read custom vars from __ENV; coerce types explicitly
const BASE_URL   = __ENV.API_URL     ?? "http://localhost:3000";
const MAX_VUS    = parseInt(__ENV.MAX_VUS    ?? "10", 10);
const THINK_TIME = parseFloat(__ENV.THINK_TIME ?? "1.0");
const P95_LIMIT  = parseInt(__ENV.P95_THRESHOLD ?? "500", 10);

// Options in script = lowest priority;
// K6_VUS env var overrides; --vus CLI flag overrides both.
export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    dynamic: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: MAX_VUS,   // resolved at init time from __ENV
      duration: "1m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: [`p(95)<${P95_LIMIT}`],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/api/status`);
  check(res, { "ok": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(THINK_TIME);
}
```

**Precedence order (highest to lowest):**

```
CLI flags (--vus=20)
  > K6_* environment variables (K6_VUS=20)
    > Script options object (options.vus = 20)
      > k6 defaults
```

**Environment variable gotchas table:**

| Intent | Wrong | Right |
|--------|-------|-------|
| Set VU count via env | `-e VUS=20` (script var only) | `K6_VUS=20` or `--vus=20` |
| Pass custom value to script | `K6_MY_PARAM=foo` (may conflict with future k6 opts) | `-e MY_PARAM=foo` |
| Use in k6 cloud/archive | System env var | Always use `-e` flag (system env stripped) |
| Numeric threshold from env | `__ENV.THRESHOLD` in threshold string | `parseInt(__ENV.THRESHOLD, 10)` |

> **[official]** System-level environment variables are **not forwarded** to `k6 archive`
> or `k6 cloud run` by default as a security measure. Use `-e KEY=VALUE` for portability
> across local, CI, and cloud execution modes.

> **[community] Gotcha #135:** Using `__ENV.SOME_NUMBER > 100` without `parseInt()` or
> `parseFloat()` performs **string comparison**, not numeric comparison. `"50" > "100"` is
> `true` in JavaScript because `"5" > "1"` lexicographically. Always coerce `__ENV`
> values to numbers before arithmetic or comparison operators.

### `SharedArray` + VU Index Sharding — Deterministic User Distribution

The canonical pattern for distributing unique test users across VUs uses the `__VU`
global (1-indexed) modulo `SharedArray` length. This ensures no two VUs use the same
credential simultaneously while keeping memory consumption O(1) per VU.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/user-shard.ts — deterministic per-VU credential sharding
import http              from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep }  from "k6";
import { SharedArray }   from "k6/data";
import type { Options }  from "k6/options";

interface User {
  email:    string;
  password: string;
  role:     "admin" | "viewer" | "editor";
}

// Loaded once in init context; shared read-only across all VUs
const users = new SharedArray<User>("users", () => {
  return JSON.parse(open("./data/test-users.json")) as User[];
});

export const options: Options = {
  scenarios: {
    mixed_roles: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 30,
      duration: "5m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<350"],
  },
};

export function setup(): { token: string } {
  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/auth/login`,
    JSON.stringify({ email: "admin@test.com", password: __ENV.ADMIN_PASS }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } },
  );
  return { token: res.json("token") as string };
}

export default function (data: { token: string }): void {
  // __VU is 1-indexed; subtract 1 for 0-indexed array access
  const user = users[(__VU - 1) % users.length];

  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/profile/${user.email}`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${data.token}` },
  });

  check(res, {
    "profile found":  (r) => r.status === 200,
    "correct email":  (r) => (r.json("email") as string) === user.email,
  });

  sleep(1 + Math.random() * 0.5); // jitter avoids synchronized VU waves
}
```

**Anti-patterns:**

- `users.filter(u => u.role === "admin")` inside `default` — creates a full regular
  Array copy on every iteration call; do filtering inside the `SharedArray` constructor
- `const myUser = users[__VU]` — `__VU` is 1-indexed; VU 1 reads index 1 (off-by-one),
  and `__VU > users.length` yields `undefined`

> **[community] Gotcha #136:** `__VU` resets to 1 at the **start of each scenario** in
> a multi-scenario test, not as a continuous global counter. If two scenarios share the
> same `SharedArray`, VU 1 of scenario A and VU 1 of scenario B will access the same
> index simultaneously. Add a scenario-specific offset or give each scenario its own
> pre-filtered `SharedArray`.

---

### `http.url` Tagged Template — Collapsing High-Cardinality URLs for Clean Metrics

When testing endpoints with dynamic URL segments (e.g., `/users/42/orders/789`), k6
by default creates a unique metric tag per distinct URL. This inflates cardinality in
InfluxDB/Prometheus and clutters the end-of-test summary. The `http.url` tagged template
collapses dynamic paths into a named group.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/url-grouping.js — prevent metric cardinality explosion
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { SharedArray }  from "k6/data";

const orders = new SharedArray("orders", () =>
  JSON.parse(open("./data/order-ids.json")),
);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    order_reads: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 20, duration: "2m" },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // Tag-filtered threshold: only the grouped metric is evaluated
    "http_req_duration{name:GET /orders/:id}": ["p(95)<300"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const orderId = orders[__ITER % orders.length].id;
  const userId  = Math.ceil(__VU * 1.5);

  // http.url`` collapses /orders/42 and /orders/99 into name "GET /orders/:id"
  const res = http.get(
    http.url`${__ENV.API_URL}/users/${userId}/orders/${orderId}`,
    { tags: { name: "GET /orders/:id" } },
  );

  check(res, { "order found": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.5);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `name` tag replaces the raw URL in all metrics. If you need to debug
which specific `orderId` caused a latency spike, you lose that granularity at the metric
level. Use structured logging (`console.log`) alongside URL grouping to retain debugging
info without the metric cardinality cost.

> **[community] Gotcha #137:** `http.url` tagged templates require a **`{ tags: { name: '...' } }`**
> params object to be effective. The template itself interpolates the URL correctly, but
> without the `name` tag override k6 uses the fully-resolved interpolated URL as the
> metric name — defeating the grouping purpose entirely. The template and the tag must
> be used together.

---

### Browser Web Vitals Thresholds — SLA Gates for Frontend Performance

The k6 browser module emits Core Web Vitals metrics (`browser_web_vital_lcp`,
`browser_web_vital_cls`, `browser_web_vital_fcp`, `browser_web_vital_inp`,
`browser_web_vital_ttfb`) as k6 Trends. Attaching thresholds to these metrics turns
Web Vitals regressions into CI failures.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-vitals-sla.js — Web Vitals threshold gates
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check }   from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    vitals_check: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      vus: 1,
      iterations: 3,
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // Google "Good" Core Web Vitals thresholds (2024 guidelines)
    browser_web_vital_lcp:  ["p(75)<2500"],  // Largest Contentful Paint < 2.5s
    browser_web_vital_cls:  ["p(75)<0.1"],   // Cumulative Layout Shift < 0.1
    browser_web_vital_fcp:  ["p(75)<1800"],  // First Contentful Paint < 1.8s
    browser_web_vital_inp:  ["p(75)<200"],   // Interaction to Next Paint < 200ms
    browser_web_vital_ttfb: ["p(75)<800"],   // Time to First Byte < 800ms
    // browser_web_vital_fid is REMOVED in k6 v2.0 — migrate to inp
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();

  try {
    // Throttle network to simulate 4G mobile — more realistic Web Vitals
    await page.setEmulateNetworkConditions({
      offline:             false,
      latency:             20,
      downloadThroughput:  (4 * 1024 * 1024) / 8,
      uploadThroughput:    (3 * 1024 * 1024) / 8,
    });

    await page.goto(`${__ENV.APP_URL}/`, { waitUntil: "networkidle" });

    check(page, {
      "title present": async (p) => (await p.title()).length > 0,
    });

    // Trigger INP by simulating a user interaction
    await page.locator("button[data-testid='search-trigger']").click();
    await page.waitForTimeout(500); // let INP measurement settle

  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Web Vitals quick reference (Google "Good" thresholds):**

| Metric | Good | Needs Improvement | Poor |
|--------|------|-------------------|------|
| LCP | < 2.5s | 2.5–4.0s | > 4.0s |
| CLS | < 0.1 | 0.1–0.25 | > 0.25 |
| FCP | < 1.8s | 1.8–3.0s | > 3.0s |
| INP | < 200ms | 200–500ms | > 500ms |
| TTFB | < 800ms | 800ms–1.8s | > 1.8s |

> **[official]** `browser_web_vital_fid` (First Input Delay) was **removed in k6 v2.0**.
> Migrate all thresholds referencing `fid` to `browser_web_vital_inp`. FID measured
> time-to-first-event only; INP measures the worst interaction delay throughout the
> page's lifetime — a more representative user-experience metric.

> **[community] Gotcha #138:** Web Vitals are emitted **once per page navigation**, not
> per interaction. Running a browser scenario with 10 iterations and 1 VU gives 10 LCP
> data points. Use `p(75)` thresholds (per Google's field data methodology) rather than
> `avg` or `p(50)`, which may mask outlier-driven poor experiences.

---

### Distributed Cloud Testing with Geographic Load Zones

k6 Cloud supports splitting test traffic across multiple geographic regions via the
`options.cloud.distribution` configuration. This models real-world global traffic
patterns and surfaces CDN/edge latency issues invisible in single-region tests.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/global-distribution.js — multi-region cloud load test
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  cloud: {
    projectID: parseInt(__ENV.K6_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID ?? "0", 10),
    name:      `Global Load Test — ${new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10)}`,

    distribution: {
      "us-east": { loadZone: "amazon:us:ashburn",   percent: 40 },
      "eu-west": { loadZone: "amazon:ie:dublin",    percent: 30 },
      "ap-se":   { loadZone: "amazon:sg:singapore", percent: 20 },
      "au-east": { loadZone: "amazon:au:sydney",    percent: 10 },
    },
  },

  scenarios: {
    global_users: {
      executor: "ramping-vus",
      stages: [
        { duration: "2m", target: 100 },
        { duration: "5m", target: 100 },
        { duration: "1m", target: 0   },
      ],
    },
  },

  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<600"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.02"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/v1/homepage`);
  check(res, { "homepage ok": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1 + Math.random());
}
```

**Run command:**

```bash
k6 cloud login --token $GRAFANA_CLOUD_TOKEN
k6 cloud run --env API_URL=https://api.example.com k6/scripts/global-distribution.js
```

**Tradeoff:** Cloud run charges per VU-hour across all zones. A 100-VU, 8-minute test
across 4 zones uses 4× the VU-minutes of a local run. Validate scripts locally with
`k6 run` before cloud execution to avoid surprise billing.

> **[community] Gotcha #139:** `options.cloud.distribution` percentages must sum to
> exactly **100**. If they don't, k6 Cloud silently normalizes them, which can shift
> the intended traffic split unexpectedly. Validate percentages before committing to a
> test plan, especially after adding or removing regions mid-cycle.

### CI Smoke Test Pattern — Fast Feedback with Exit Code Handling

The recommended CI integration uses a **smoke scenario** (1–2 VUs, 30s, generous
thresholds) on every PR, plus a **full load** scenario triggered only on merge to
`main`. This balances fast feedback against accurate performance data.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/smoke.js — minimal smoke test for every-PR CI gate
import http      from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 2,
      duration: "30s",
      tags: { type: "smoke" },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<1000"], // generous — smoke tests for errors, not speed
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.05"],  // allow up to 5% transient errors
    checks:            ["rate>0.95"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/health`);
  check(res, { "health ok": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/smoke.yml
name: k6 Smoke Test
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, develop]

jobs:
  smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install k6
        run: |
          sudo gpg --no-default-keyring \
            --keyring /usr/share/keyrings/k6-archive-keyring.gpg \
            --keyserver hkp://keyserver.ubuntu.com:80 \
            --recv-keys C5AD17C747E3415A3642D57D77C6C491D6AC1D69
          echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/k6-archive-keyring.gpg] \
            https://dl.k6.io/deb stable main" \
            | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/k6.list
          sudo apt-get update -q && sudo apt-get install -y k6

      - name: Run smoke test
        id: k6
        env:
          API_URL: ${{ secrets.STAGING_API_URL }}
        run: |
          k6 run k6/scripts/smoke.js
          echo "k6_exit=$?" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
        continue-on-error: true

      - name: Handle k6 exit codes
        run: |
          case "${{ steps.k6.outputs.k6_exit }}" in
            0)   echo "Smoke test passed" ;;
            99)  echo "::error::Thresholds breached (exit 99)"; exit 1 ;;
            108) echo "::warning::Test interrupted (exit 108)" ;;
            *)   echo "::error::Unexpected k6 exit: ${{ steps.k6.outputs.k6_exit }}"; exit 1 ;;
          esac
```

**k6 exit code reference (v2.0+):**

| Exit code | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| 0 | Test passed all thresholds |
| 99 | One or more thresholds were breached |
| 108 | Test was interrupted (SIGINT, timeout) |
| 1xx | Script/config error |

> **[community] Gotcha #140:** In GitHub Actions, a step with `continue-on-error: true`
> always reports `steps.<id>.outcome = "success"` from the workflow engine's perspective,
> even if the underlying command exited non-zero. To correctly propagate k6 threshold
> failures as PR failures, capture the exit code explicitly (as shown above) and
> re-exit in a subsequent step. Relying on step outcome alone silently passes PRs with
> failing thresholds.

### Open vs Closed Load Model — Choosing the Right Executor Semantics

The most consequential executor decision is whether you model load as **closed** (VU-based)
or **open** (arrival-rate-based). The wrong choice produces misleading results — especially
under degraded conditions where the system under test slows down.

**Closed model** (constant-vus / ramping-vus): A new iteration only starts after the
previous one finishes. When the server slows, fewer iterations/second are generated,
which *reduces* load at exactly the moment you want to stress it. This is called
**coordinated omission**.

**Open model** (constant-arrival-rate / ramping-arrival-rate): Iterations start at
a fixed rate regardless of how long previous iterations take. This accurately models
real traffic, where users do not wait for the server to recover before requesting again.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/open-vs-closed-comparison.js
// Run BOTH scenarios in parallel to compare models side-by-side

import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    // Closed: 20 VUs working as fast as they can
    closed_model: {
      executor:   "constant-vus",
      vus:        20,
      duration:   "3m",
      tags:       { model: "closed" },
      exec:       "vuBased",
    },
    // Open: exactly 20 iterations/second regardless of VU latency
    open_model: {
      executor:        "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate:            20,
      timeUnit:        "1s",
      duration:        "3m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs:          60,     // allow burst if server is slow
      tags:            { model: "open" },
      startTime:       "0s",
      exec:            "rateBased",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_duration{model:closed}": ["p(95)<500"],
    "http_req_duration{model:open}":   ["p(95)<500"],
  },
};

export function vuBased()   { runRequest(); }
export function rateBased() { runRequest(); }

function runRequest() {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/items`);
  check(res, { "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.5);
}
```

**When to use open model:** Any test that should reflect real-world traffic patterns —
load tests, stress tests, soak tests. Default to `constant-arrival-rate` when you have
an RPS SLA.

**When to use closed model:** Scenarios where users genuinely wait for responses before
issuing the next request — e.g., a human clicking through a wizard. Also useful for
bounded-throughput scenarios like batch jobs.

> **[official]** k6 docs: "The response times of the target system no longer influence
> the load on the target system" in the open model. This is the canonical definition of
> eliminating coordinated omission.

> **[community] Gotcha #141:** A common mistake is using `ramping-vus` to model an
> "RPS ramp" scenario. Because VU-based throughput depends on server latency, a
> "50-VU → 100-VU" ramp does NOT produce a predictable RPS curve. If the server slows
> at 80 VUs, the 100-VU stage can *generate less load* than the 80-VU stage. Use
> `ramping-arrival-rate` to get a monotonically increasing RPS ramp.

---

### `gracefulStop` and `gracefulRampDown` — Preventing Metric Skew at Scenario Boundaries

Every k6 executor supports `gracefulStop` (default: `30s`) — a window after the test
duration ends in which in-flight iterations are allowed to complete naturally before
being forcibly killed. The `ramping-vus` executor additionally supports
`gracefulRampDown` for the same protection during stage transitions.

Ignoring these values leads to **interrupted iterations** appearing in results, which
skews p99/p100 latency upward and increases the `http_req_failed` rate artificially.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/graceful-lifecycle.js
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp: {
      executor: "ramping-vus",
      stages: [
        { duration: "2m", target: 50  },
        { duration: "5m", target: 50  },
        { duration: "2m", target: 0   },
      ],
      // Allow up to 10s for each VU to finish its current iteration
      // at every ramp-down boundary, including the final stage.
      gracefulRampDown: "10s",
      // Allow up to 15s for stragglers at the very end of the test.
      gracefulStop: "15s",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // Track interrupted iterations explicitly — alert if > 1%
    "iterations{interrupted:true}": ["count<10"],
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<400"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/catalog`);
  check(res, {
    "catalog 200":    (r) => r.status === 200,
    "body populated": (r) => (r.body?.length ?? 0) > 100,
  });
  // Simulate user think time — ensure this is < gracefulRampDown
  sleep(2 + Math.random() * 3);
}
```

**Rule of thumb:** Set `gracefulRampDown` ≥ p99 iteration duration (including `sleep()`).
Set `gracefulStop` ≥ p99 iteration duration of the longest-running scenario.

**Tradeoff:** Larger grace periods extend wall-clock test time. A 5-minute test with
`gracefulStop: "30s"` takes at least 5m 30s. Factor this into CI timeouts.

> **[community] Gotcha #142:** Setting `gracefulStop: "0s"` (to speed up CI runs)
> causes every VU that is mid-iteration at the end of the test duration to be counted
> as "interrupted", inflating `http_req_failed` rates and contaminating SLA thresholds.
> Use `gracefulStop: "5s"` as the minimum safe value for fast-turnaround CI smoke tests.

> **[community] Gotcha #143:** `gracefulRampDown` is **only respected by `ramping-vus`**.
> Setting it on `constant-vus`, `constant-arrival-rate`, or other executors has no
> effect — k6 silently ignores it without a warning. Verify your executor type if
> interrupted iterations persist despite a configured `gracefulRampDown`.

---

### Native TypeScript Support (v0.57+) — Zero-Config `.ts` Execution

Since k6 v0.57, TypeScript files are transpiled natively via esbuild — no Webpack,
Babel, or Rollup pipeline required. Run `.ts` files directly with `k6 run script.ts`.

This enables full TypeScript type checking in editors (via `@types/k6`) while keeping
the test runner invocation identical to JavaScript.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/typed-load-test.ts — native TypeScript, runs directly with k6 run
import http                from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep }    from "k6";
import { Trend, Counter }  from "k6/metrics";
import { Options }         from "k6/options";

// Typed options object — editors will catch typos in executor names, etc.
export const options: Options = {
  scenarios: {
    api_load: {
      executor:        "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate:       10,
      timeUnit:        "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs:          100,
      stages: [
        { target: 50,  duration: "2m" },
        { target: 50,  duration: "5m" },
        { target: 0,   duration: "1m" },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

interface ApiItem {
  id:    number;
  name:  string;
  price: number;
}

const responseTrend  = new Trend("api_response_ms", true);
const parseErrors    = new Counter("api_parse_errors_total");

export default function (): void {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/items`);
  check(res, { "items 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });

  try {
    const items = res.json() as ApiItem[];
    responseTrend.add(res.timings.duration);
    if (!Array.isArray(items)) parseErrors.add(1);
  } catch {
    parseErrors.add(1);
  }

  sleep(0.2);
}
```

**Caveat:** k6's esbuild integration **strips types but does not type-check**. Run
`tsc --noEmit` in CI separately to enforce type safety. The `--noEmit` check catches
type errors without producing output files, making it a fast pre-flight gate.

```bash
# CI: type-check then run
npx tsc --noEmit && k6 run k6/scripts/typed-load-test.ts
```

**Tradeoff vs bundler-based setup:** Zero config is ideal for single-file scripts.
Multi-file projects with path aliases or module resolution customization still benefit
from a Webpack/Rollup bundler (k6-template-es6 or k6-rollup-example) because esbuild
uses k6's bundling defaults and does not read `tsconfig.json` path mappings.

> **[official]** k6 v0.57 release: "TypeScript support is partial as it strips the
> type information but doesn't provide type safety." Use `@types/k6` from DefinitelyTyped
> for editor autocomplete on all k6 APIs.

> **[community] Gotcha #144:** Importing a `.ts` helper from a `.js` script with a
> `.ts` extension (e.g., `import { foo } from "./helpers.ts"`) works in k6's native
> transpiler but breaks in standard Node.js and some bundlers. Keep extension-less
> imports (`"./helpers"`) for maximum cross-tool compatibility.

---

### `k6/experimental/csv` — Go-Backed CSV Parsing Without Papa Parse

The `k6/experimental/csv` module was introduced to replace the JavaScript-based Papa
Parse pattern for CSV parameterization. It uses Go's CSV parser under the hood,
giving 3–10× faster initialization for large files and shared memory across all VUs.

Two modes: `csv.parse()` (full file to SharedArray, fast) and `csv.Parser` (streaming,
memory-efficient for very large files).

```typescript
// k6/scripts/csv-users-load.ts — experimental/csv full-parse mode
import { open }         from "k6/experimental/fs";
import csv              from "k6/experimental/csv";
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { SharedArray }  from "k6/data";

// open() must be called in init context (top-level await not needed with SharedArray wrapper)
const file = open("./data/users.csv");

// csv.parse() returns a Promise<SharedArray>; wrap in SharedArray init function
const users = new SharedArray("csv_users", async () => {
  const f = await file;
  return await csv.parse(f, { skipFirstLine: true }); // skip header row
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    data_driven: {
      executor:   "per-vu-iterations",
      vus:        50,
      iterations: 200,
    },
  },
};

export default function (): void {
  // Round-robin through rows using modulo
  const row  = users[__ITER % users.length] as string[];
  const [email, password] = row;

  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/auth/login`,
    JSON.stringify({ email, password }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } },
  );
  check(res, { "login 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.3);
}
```

**When to use `csv.parse()` (full file):** Files up to ~500 MB, when startup speed
matters more than peak memory. Data is loaded once during init and shared across all VUs
with zero per-VU duplication.

**When to use `csv.Parser` (streaming):** Files >500 MB or when you process rows
sequentially rather than randomly (e.g., replaying a recorded session log).

**Tradeoff vs Papa Parse from jslib:** `k6/experimental/csv` requires no external
CDN fetch, works in air-gapped environments, and is 3–10× faster for large files.
The downside: it remains experimental and may introduce breaking changes until stable.

> **[official]** `csv.parse()` returns "data as a SharedArray where each element
> represents a CSV record as an array of fields." Column names are NOT automatically
> mapped — you access data by index (e.g., `row[0]`, `row[1]`), not by header name.

> **[community] Gotcha #145:** `csv.parse()` with `skipFirstLine: false` (the default)
> includes the header row as the first data element. Using `users[0]` then returns the
> column names, not a user record. Always pass `{ skipFirstLine: true }` when your CSV
> has a header row, or slice the array: `users.slice(1)`. Many test flakes trace back
> to login attempts with `email="email"` and `password="password"` because the header
> was accidentally used as credentials.

---

### `k6/execution` Module — Dynamic Behavior Based on Runtime Context

The `k6/execution` module exposes live test metadata — scenario name, VU ID, iteration
counts, instance stats — enabling scripts to branch logic per scenario, shard data
precisely, or emit richer metrics without hardcoding assumptions.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/execution-aware.ts — dynamic routing and data sharding
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { SharedArray }  from "k6/data";
import exec             from "k6/execution";

const allUsers = new SharedArray("users", () =>
  JSON.parse(open("./data/users.json")) as Array<{ email: string; password: string }>,
);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    read_traffic: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus:      30,
      duration: "5m",
      tags:     { flow: "read" },
      exec:     "readFlow",
    },
    write_traffic: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus:      10,
      duration: "5m",
      tags:     { flow: "write" },
      exec:     "writeFlow",
    },
  },
};

// Each VU deterministically owns a slice of the user pool —
// avoids concurrent login collisions without coordination overhead.
function getUserForVU() {
  const vuIdx = exec.vu.idInTest - 1; // idInTest is 1-based
  return allUsers[vuIdx % allUsers.length];
}

export function readFlow(): void {
  const user = getUserForVU();
  const res  = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/feed`, {
    headers: { "X-VU-ID": String(exec.vu.idInTest) },
    tags:    { scenario: exec.scenario.name },
  });
  check(res, { "feed 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}

export function writeFlow(): void {
  const user = getUserForVU();
  const res  = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/posts`,
    JSON.stringify({ author: user.email, content: `Post from VU ${exec.vu.idInTest}` }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      tags:    { scenario: exec.scenario.name } },
  );
  check(res, { "post 201": (r) => r.status === 201 });
  sleep(2);
}
```

**Key `exec` properties:**

| Property | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `exec.vu.idInTest` | number | Globally unique VU ID (1-based, stable within run) |
| `exec.vu.iterationInScenario` | number | Iteration count within the current scenario |
| `exec.scenario.name` | string | Name of the currently executing scenario |
| `exec.scenario.progress` | number | 0.0–1.0 completion fraction of the scenario |
| `exec.instance.currentTestRunDuration` | number | Elapsed test time in milliseconds |
| `exec.test.abort("reason")` | function | Immediately abort the test with a message |

**When to use:** Multi-scenario scripts that need per-scenario routing, deterministic
data sharding across VUs, or programmatic abort on business-logic failures.

> **[community] Gotcha #146:** `exec.vu.idInTest` is allocated from a global pool and
> gaps can appear when VUs are scaled down and up between scenarios. Do NOT assume IDs
> are contiguous. Use `idInTest % dataArray.length` for modulo sharding, not
> `idInTest - 1` as a direct array index (array out-of-bounds on non-contiguous IDs).

> **[community] Gotcha #147:** Calling `exec.test.abort()` from inside a check callback
> is silently ignored — `check()` callbacks are not async-safe abort points. Call
> `exec.test.abort()` at the top-level of the default function, after the check, if
> you need to halt on a fatal condition.

---

### gRPC Unary Testing with Server Reflection — No `.proto` Files Required

k6's gRPC client supports **server reflection** (`reflect: true`), which downloads
service definitions at runtime. This removes the need to bundle `.proto` files in the
test repository — ideal for internal services with stable reflection endpoints.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/grpc-reflection.ts — service discovery via server reflection
import grpc             from "k6/net/grpc";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

const client = new grpc.Client();

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    grpc_load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate:     100,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "3m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 30,
      maxVUs:          80,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    grpc_req_duration: ["p(95)<200"],
  },
};

export function setup(): void {
  // Connect once in setup; reflection fetches all service descriptors
  client.connect(`${__ENV.GRPC_HOST}:50051`, {
    reflect: true,
    // TLS options for production:
    // tls: { cert: open("./certs/client.crt"), key: open("./certs/client.key") },
  });
}

export default function (): void {
  const res = client.invoke(
    "com.example.CatalogService/GetItem",
    { item_id: `item-${Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000)}` },
    { timeout: "5s", tags: { rpc: "GetItem" } },
  );

  check(res, {
    "gRPC OK":           (r) => r && r.status === grpc.StatusOK,
    "item name present": (r) => r.message?.item?.name !== undefined,
  });

  sleep(0.1);
}

export function teardown(): void {
  client.close(); // always close to flush pending metrics
}
```

**When to use reflection:** Development environments and internal services. Production
gRPC endpoints often disable reflection for security — fall back to `client.load()`
with bundled `.proto` files.

**Tradeoff:** Reflection adds a round-trip on `client.connect()` to download descriptors.
For short smoke tests this is negligible; for long soak tests it is a one-time cost.

> **[community] Gotcha #148:** `client.close()` must be called in `teardown()`, NOT in
> `default()`. Calling `client.close()` inside the VU loop terminates the connection
> permanently for that VU — subsequent `client.invoke()` calls fail with "connection
> closed" errors that are extremely difficult to distinguish from actual server failures
> in the metrics output.

> **[community] Gotcha #149:** k6's gRPC client **does not support deadlines set on
> the server side** overriding the client `timeout` option. If the server enforces a
> shorter deadline than your `timeout`, the call will fail with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`
> before k6's timeout fires. Always set `timeout` at or below the server's deadline.

---

### `k6/experimental/fs` — Chunk-Read Pattern for Large Binary Test Data

The `k6/experimental/fs` module enables streaming file reads in chunks, useful for
replaying large request body payloads (e.g., file uploads) without loading the entire
file into VU memory. Each VU shares the same file descriptor but maintains independent
seek positions.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/chunked-upload.ts — stream large payload in chunks using k6/experimental/fs
import { open, SeekMode } from "k6/experimental/fs";
import http               from "k6/http";
import { check }          from "k6";

const CHUNK_SIZE = 64 * 1024; // 64 KB read window

// open() returns a Promise<File> — use top-level await (supported in init context)
const testFile = open("./data/sample-upload.bin");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    upload_stress: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus:      10,
      duration: "2m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<2000"], // uploads are slower — widen threshold
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default async function (): Promise<void> {
  const file   = await testFile;
  const stat   = await file.stat();
  const chunks: Uint8Array[] = [];

  // Rewind to start before each iteration
  await file.seek(0, SeekMode.Start);

  let bytesRead = 0;
  while (bytesRead < stat.size) {
    const buf  = new Uint8Array(Math.min(CHUNK_SIZE, stat.size - bytesRead));
    const n    = await file.read(buf);
    if (n === null) break;
    chunks.push(buf.slice(0, n));
    bytesRead += n;
  }

  // Reassemble full payload (for small-medium files) or stream directly
  const payload = new Uint8Array(bytesRead);
  let offset    = 0;
  for (const chunk of chunks) {
    payload.set(chunk, offset);
    offset += chunk.length;
  }

  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/upload`, payload.buffer, {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream" },
  });
  check(res, { "upload accepted": (r) => r.status === 202 || r.status === 200 });
}
```

**When to use:** Upload tests, replay of recorded binary request bodies, memory-
constrained environments with files >50 MB. Each VU's read pointer is independent,
so concurrent VUs do not interfere with each other's position.

**Tradeoff:** The `read()` loop is slower than `open("./file")` (sync in-memory load)
for small files. For files under ~5 MB, the traditional `open()` approach in init
context is simpler. Reserve `k6/experimental/fs` for files that would exhaust per-VU
memory if duplicated.

> **[official]** "k6 will not reflect those changes in the loaded File instance" if
> the underlying file is modified during the test. The file is snapshotted at startup.

> **[community] Gotcha #150:** `file.seek(0, SeekMode.Start)` must be called at the
> **beginning** of each iteration to reset the read position. Forgetting this causes
> the second iteration to start reading from wherever the first iteration left off,
> producing truncated payloads. The resulting HTTP request body is silently shorter
> than expected — the server may accept it (if it handles partial bodies) and the test
> appears to pass while sending invalid data.

---

### HTTP/2 Protocol Verification — Ensuring TLS Upgrade Is Active

k6 negotiates HTTP/2 automatically via ALPN when the server supports it. However,
misconfigured load balancers, proxies, or expired certificates can silently downgrade
connections to HTTP/1.1 without returning an error. Explicitly verifying the protocol
version in checks catches infrastructure regressions.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/http2-verify.ts — confirm HTTP/2 is active, not silently downgraded
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Counter }      from "k6/metrics";

const http1Downgrades = new Counter("http1_downgrade_count");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    verify_http2: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus:      5,
      duration: "1m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration:    ["p(95)<300"],
    http1_downgrade_count: ["count<1"],  // fail if ANY downgrade occurs
  },
};

export default function (): void {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/health`, {
    // Force HTTP/2 preference — k6 still negotiates, but this disables h1 fallback
    // in environments that support the option (requires TLS)
  });

  const isH2 = check(res, {
    "status 200":       (r) => r.status === 200,
    "protocol is H2":   (r) => r.proto === "HTTP/2.0",
    "no h1 downgrade":  (r) => r.proto !== "HTTP/1.1",
  });

  // Track downgrades as a custom metric for trend analysis
  if (res.proto === "HTTP/1.1") {
    http1Downgrades.add(1, { url: res.url });
  }

  sleep(1);
}
```

**k6 `response.proto` values:**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"HTTP/1.0"` | Legacy HTTP/1.0 |
| `"HTTP/1.1"` | Standard HTTP without multiplexing |
| `"HTTP/2.0"` | Multiplexed HTTP/2 (requires TLS) |

**Tradeoff:** HTTP/2 checks add no meaningful overhead. However, many staging
environments terminate TLS at a proxy that may not forward H2. Verify in staging
AND in a production canary to get accurate protocol data.

> **[community] Gotcha #151:** k6 does NOT enforce HTTP/2 — it requests upgrade via
> ALPN and accepts whatever the server negotiates. There is no "force-H2" flag.
> If your service is behind an Nginx proxy with `http2` disabled in the `listen`
> directive, k6 silently uses HTTP/1.1 and all your latency benchmarks are
> measuring the wrong protocol. Add `"protocol is H2"` to your smoke suite checks.

---

### `k6/websockets` Stable Module — Per-VU Multi-Socket Pattern

The `k6/websockets` module (stable since v0.46, preferred over the legacy `k6/ws`) uses
the browser-compatible WebSocket API. For chat, trading, or gaming load tests, multiple
simultaneous connections per VU are a common real-world pattern.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/ws-multi-connect.ts — two WebSocket connections per VU (e.g., trade feed + order channel)
import { WebSocket }    from "k6/websockets";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Counter }      from "k6/metrics";

const msgReceived = new Counter("ws_messages_received");
const pingsSent   = new Counter("ws_pings_sent");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ws_load: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus:      20,
      duration: "3m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    ws_messages_received: ["count>0"],
    http_req_failed:      ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default function (): void {
  const token = `token-vu-${__VU}`;

  const feed  = new WebSocket(`${__ENV.WS_URL}/feed?t=${token}`);
  const order = new WebSocket(`${__ENV.WS_URL}/orders?t=${token}`);

  let feedOpen  = false;
  let orderOpen = false;

  feed.onopen  = () => { feedOpen  = true; };
  order.onopen = () => { orderOpen = true; };

  feed.onmessage  = (evt) => { msgReceived.add(1, { channel: "feed"  }); };
  order.onmessage = (evt) => { msgReceived.add(1, { channel: "order" }); };

  feed.onerror  = (err) => console.error(`feed error VU ${__VU}: ${err}`);
  order.onerror = (err) => console.error(`order error VU ${__VU}: ${err}`);

  // Send a ping every 5 seconds for 30s, then close both sockets
  let ticks = 0;
  const interval = setInterval(() => {
    ticks++;
    if (feedOpen)  { feed.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "ping" }));  pingsSent.add(1); }
    if (orderOpen) { order.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "ping" })); pingsSent.add(1); }
    if (ticks >= 6) {
      clearInterval(interval);
      feed.close();
      order.close();
    }
  }, 5000);
}
```

**When to use:** Real-time applications where users maintain multiple simultaneous
connections (trading platforms, collaborative apps, IoT dashboards). Models true
connection concurrency that single-socket tests miss.

**Tradeoff:** Each WebSocket connection consumes a file descriptor. At 20 VUs × 2
sockets = 40 open sockets. For 500 VUs × 2 sockets = 1000 FDs — check the k6 host's
`ulimit -n` (default 1024 on many Linux installs).

> **[community] Gotcha #152:** `k6/ws` (legacy module) executes the connection handler
> synchronously with a callback loop. `k6/websockets` (stable module) uses an async
> event model. Mixing the two in the same script causes the event loop to behave
> unpredictably. Migrate all WebSocket tests to `k6/websockets` — the APIs are not
> interchangeable.

> **[community] Gotcha #153:** The `k6/websockets` `WebSocket` constructor accepts
> URL strings only — not `URL` objects. Passing a constructed `new URL(...)` object
> silently coerces to `[object URL]` as the connection string, producing an immediate
> parse error. Always `.toString()` URL objects before passing to `new WebSocket()`.

---

### xk6 Extension Types — Choosing the Right Extension Mechanism

k6 supports four distinct extension types via the xk6 build system. Choosing the wrong
type wastes effort and results in extensions that are hard to maintain or test.

```bash
# Build a k6 binary with two custom extensions using xk6
go install go.k6.io/xk6/cmd/xk6@latest

xk6 build \
  --with github.com/grafana/xk6-sql@latest \
  --with github.com/grafana/xk6-output-prometheus-remote@latest \
  --output ./k6-custom
```

```typescript
// k6/scripts/sql-extension-example.ts — using xk6-sql JavaScript extension
// Requires a k6 binary built with: xk6 build --with github.com/grafana/xk6-sql
import sql               from "k6/x/sql";
import driver            from "k6/x/sql/driver/postgres";
import { check, sleep }  from "k6";

const db = sql.open(driver, `${__ENV.PG_DSN}`);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    db_load: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus:      10,
      duration: "2m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"],
  },
};

export function setup() {
  // Seed test data — runs once before VUs start
  db.exec("INSERT INTO perf_items (name) SELECT 'item-' || generate_series(1,1000)");
}

export default function (): void {
  const rows = sql.query(db, "SELECT id, name FROM perf_items ORDER BY RANDOM() LIMIT 1");
  check(rows, { "row returned": (r) => r.length > 0 });
  sleep(0.5);
}

export function teardown() {
  db.exec("DELETE FROM perf_items WHERE name LIKE 'item-%'");
  db.close();
}
```

**Extension type decision matrix:**

| Extension Type | Use Case | Build Required? |
|---|---|---|
| JavaScript extension | New protocol/library (SQL, Kafka, MQTT) | Yes (xk6 build) |
| Output extension | Route metrics to custom sink (Datadog, Splunk) | Yes (xk6 build) |
| Secret source extension | Inject secrets from custom vault at runtime | Yes (xk6 build) |
| Subcommand extension | Add `k6 x <cmd>` for setup/validation workflows | Yes (xk6 build) |

**Tradeoff:** All extensions require compiling a custom k6 binary. This breaks
compatibility with `k6 cloud run` (cloud uses the official binary). For cloud-run
scripts, use only built-in modules plus jslib.k6.io libraries.

> **[official]** As of v2.0.0, `k6/experimental/redis` was removed from core and is
> now available only as `k6/x/redis` via an xk6 extension build.

> **[community] Gotcha #154:** Running a custom xk6 binary with `k6 cloud run` silently
> falls back to the standard k6 binary on cloud infrastructure — your extension code
> executes against a binary that does not have the extension installed, producing
> `ReferenceError: k6/x/<module> is not defined` only at cloud run time, not locally.
> Use `--local-execution` with `k6 cloud run` or run distributed load locally when
> extensions are required.

---

### Parameterized Threshold Expressions — Per-Tag SLA Gates

k6 thresholds support tag-scoped metrics using the `metric_name{tag:value}` syntax.
This enables per-endpoint SLA enforcement without separate scripts — a single test
can assert different latency budgets for different API routes.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/per-endpoint-sla.ts — per-route SLA thresholds via tagged metrics
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mixed_traffic: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus:      30,
      duration: "3m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // Global baseline
    "http_req_duration":                    ["p(95)<600"],
    "http_req_failed":                      ["rate<0.01"],

    // Critical checkout path — tighter SLA
    "http_req_duration{name:checkout}":     ["p(95)<300", "p(99)<500"],

    // Read-only catalog — relaxed SLA
    "http_req_duration{name:catalog}":      ["p(95)<800"],

    // Auth endpoint — high reliability requirement
    "http_req_duration{name:login}":        ["p(95)<200"],
    "http_req_failed{name:login}":          ["rate<0.001"],

    // Health check — near-zero latency expected
    "http_req_duration{name:health}":       ["p(99)<50"],
  },
};

export default function (): void {
  // Tag each request with a name that matches threshold keys
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/health`,          { tags: { name: "health"   } });
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/catalog`,     { tags: { name: "catalog"  } });
  http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/auth/login`,
    JSON.stringify({ email: `u${__VU}@test.com`, password: "pass" }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, tags: { name: "login" } },
  );
  http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/checkout`,
    JSON.stringify({ cart_id: `cart-${__VU}-${__ITER}`, promo: null }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, tags: { name: "checkout" } },
  );
  sleep(1 + Math.random());
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Tagged thresholds only apply to metrics emitted **with that exact tag**.
A request missing the `name` tag contributes to the global `http_req_duration` threshold
but not to any named threshold, which can mask SLA violations. Use `tags` consistently
or use `http.setResponseCallback(http.expectedStatuses(...))` to ensure all requests are
tagged.

> **[community] Gotcha #155:** Tag keys in threshold expressions must match **exactly**
> — including case. `{name:Checkout}` and `{name:checkout}` are different thresholds.
> k6 will silently create a new empty threshold for the mismatched tag and report it
> as passing (0 samples = no violations), creating false confidence in SLA compliance.

---

### Coordinated Multi-Scenario Auth Token Sharing via `setup()`

A common production pattern is authenticating once in `setup()` and distributing
the resulting token to all VU scenarios — avoiding redundant login requests that
inflate auth-endpoint metrics and consume rate-limit budget.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/shared-auth-scenarios.ts — single login, multiple concurrent scenario VUs
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

interface AuthData {
  accessToken:  string;
  refreshToken: string;
  userId:       number;
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browse_catalog: {
      executor: "ramping-vus",
      stages:   [{ duration: "2m", target: 50 }, { duration: "5m", target: 50 }],
      exec:     "browseCatalog",
    },
    place_orders: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus:      10,
      duration: "7m",
      exec:     "placeOrders",
    },
    admin_reports: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus:      2,
      duration: "7m",
      exec:     "generateReport",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_duration{flow:browse}": ["p(95)<400"],
    "http_req_duration{flow:order}":  ["p(95)<600"],
    "http_req_duration{flow:admin}":  ["p(95)<2000"],
    http_req_failed:                  ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export function setup(): AuthData {
  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/auth/token`,
    JSON.stringify({ client_id: __ENV.CLIENT_ID, client_secret: __ENV.CLIENT_SECRET }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } },
  );
  check(res, { "auth success": (r) => r.status === 200 });

  const body = res.json() as { access_token: string; refresh_token: string; user_id: number };
  return {
    accessToken:  body.access_token,
    refreshToken: body.refresh_token,
    userId:       body.user_id,
  };
}

const authHeaders = (token: string) => ({
  "Content-Type":  "application/json",
  "Authorization": `Bearer ${token}`,
});

export function browseCatalog(auth: AuthData): void {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/catalog?page=${__ITER % 10 + 1}`,
    { headers: authHeaders(auth.accessToken), tags: { flow: "browse" } });
  check(res, { "catalog 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}

export function placeOrders(auth: AuthData): void {
  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/orders`,
    JSON.stringify({ item_id: __ITER % 100 + 1, qty: 1 }),
    { headers: authHeaders(auth.accessToken), tags: { flow: "order" } },
  );
  check(res, { "order 201": (r) => r.status === 201 });
  sleep(3);
}

export function generateReport(auth: AuthData): void {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/admin/report?date=today`,
    { headers: authHeaders(auth.accessToken), tags: { flow: "admin" } });
  check(res, { "report 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(10);
}

export function teardown(auth: AuthData): void {
  // Revoke token to clean up server-side sessions
  http.post(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/auth/revoke`,
    JSON.stringify({ token: auth.refreshToken }),
    { headers: authHeaders(auth.accessToken) });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** All VUs across all scenarios share the **same** token. If the token
expires during a long test (e.g., a 1-hour soak test), every VU will fail
simultaneously. Implement token refresh in `teardown()` or use a VU-level refresh
with a `Rate` metric monitoring 401 responses.

> **[community] Gotcha #156:** `setup()` returns data as a **deep copy** to each VU.
> Any object returned by `setup()` is serialized to JSON and deserialized per VU.
> This means: (1) non-JSON-serializable values (functions, class instances, ArrayBuffers)
> are silently dropped, and (2) mutations to the `auth` object inside VU functions
> (e.g., `auth.accessToken = newToken`) are NOT propagated to other VUs. Plan token
> refresh as a per-VU operation using `check(res, {"401": ...})` and conditional logic.

---

### `ramping-arrival-rate` with `preAllocatedVUs` Tuning — Avoiding Dropped Iterations

`ramping-arrival-rate` requires specifying `preAllocatedVUs` (VUs ready at test start)
and `maxVUs` (upper cap). Under-provisioning `preAllocatedVUs` causes k6 to emit
`dropped_iterations` metric when it cannot spawn VUs fast enough to meet the target rate.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/arrival-rate-tuned.ts — correctly sized preAllocatedVUs
import http             from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Counter }      from "k6/metrics";

const droppedWarnings = new Counter("dropped_iterations_observed");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp_traffic: {
      executor:        "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate:       10,       // start at 10 req/s
      timeUnit:        "1s",
      // Rule: preAllocatedVUs ≥ peak_rate × (avg_response_time_s + think_time_s)
      // Peak 200 req/s × (0.2s response + 0.1s sleep) = 60 VUs minimum
      preAllocatedVUs: 70,       // 70 — 15% buffer above the 60-VU floor
      maxVUs:          150,      // allow burst headroom above preAllocated
      stages: [
        { target: 50,  duration: "1m" },
        { target: 200, duration: "3m" },
        { target: 200, duration: "5m" },
        { target: 0,   duration: "1m" },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration:     ["p(95)<400"],
    dropped_iterations:    ["count<10"],   // hard gate — fail if iterations are dropped
  },
};

export default function (): void {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/catalog`, {
    tags: { scenario: "ramp_traffic" },
  });
  check(res, { "catalog 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.1);
}
```

**Sizing formula:**

```
preAllocatedVUs ≥ peak_rate (req/s) × (avg_response_time_s + think_time_s)
```

Add 15–20% buffer. Set `maxVUs` to 2–3× `preAllocatedVUs` for burst headroom.

**Tradeoff:** Over-provisioning `preAllocatedVUs` wastes memory (each VU costs ~1–2 MB)
but is cheaper than dropping iterations. Under-provisioning is the more common failure
mode and results in a test that generates LESS load than intended at peak — the exact
opposite of a valid stress test.

> **[community] Gotcha #157:** `dropped_iterations` is a built-in k6 metric that is
> **not included in the default end-of-test summary** unless you have a threshold or
> custom `handleSummary()` for it. Add `dropped_iterations: ["count<1"]` to your
> thresholds as a standard guard — without it you can silently run a ramping-arrival-rate
> test that drops 30% of target iterations while the test reports "passed all thresholds".

### 1. OpenTelemetry Output — Unified Traces + Metrics Export  [official]

k6 v0.56+ ships an `opentelemetry` output that sends metrics directly to any OTEL-compatible
collector. Combine this with `http-instrumentation-tempo` to get both k6 metrics AND per-request
traces in the same Grafana/Tempo stack without InfluxDB or Prometheus as an intermediary.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/otel-load.js
// Run: k6 run --out opentelemetry=endpoint=http://localhost:4318 k6/scripts/otel-load.js
import tempo from "https://jslib.k6.io/http-instrumentation-tempo/1.0.1/index.js";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Trend, Counter } from "k6/metrics";

// Inject W3C trace context into all HTTP requests
tempo.instrumentHTTP({ propagator: "w3c" });

// Custom business metrics — exported as OTEL gauges + counters
const orderLatency  = new Trend("order_latency_ms", true);
const ordersPlaced  = new Counter("orders_placed_total");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    otel_traced: {
      executor: "ramping-vus",
      stages: [
        { duration: "30s", target: 20 },
        { duration: "2m",  target: 20 },
        { duration: "15s", target: 0  },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    order_latency_ms:    ["p(95)<800"],
    orders_placed_total: ["count>50"],
    http_req_failed:     ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.API_URL || "http://localhost:3001";

export default function () {
  const start = Date.now();
  const res = http.post(
    `${BASE}/api/orders`,
    JSON.stringify({ sku: "item-001", qty: 1 }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, tags: { name: "POST /api/orders" } }
  );
  const elapsed = Date.now() - start;

  check(res, {
    "order 201":    (r) => r.status === 201,
    "has order id": (r) => r.json()?.id !== undefined,
  });

  orderLatency.add(elapsed);
  if (res.status === 201) ordersPlaced.add(1);

  sleep(1);
}
```

**OTEL collector configuration snippet (docker-compose):**
```yaml
# otel-collector-config.yaml
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: "0.0.0.0:4318"  # k6 --out opentelemetry target
exporters:
  prometheus:
    endpoint: "0.0.0.0:8889"
  otlp/tempo:
    endpoint: "tempo:4317"
    tls: { insecure: true }
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `--out opentelemetry` when your stack is already OTEL-native and you want
a single pipeline for both traces and metrics. Do NOT use it alongside `--out prometheus-remote-write`
for the same metric set — you will double-write and diverge dashboards.
**Alternatives:** `--out influxdb`, `--out prometheus-remote-write`, `--out json`.

### 2. k6 Secrets API — Secure Credential Injection at Runtime  [official]

The `k6/secrets` module (stable in k6 v1.7+) provides runtime secret retrieval from Grafana Cloud,
local files, environment variables, or custom secret-source extensions. Secrets are never logged,
never included in summary output, and are lazy-loaded — they are not baked into the k6 binary or
the test script at compile time.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/secrets-load.js
// Run with: k6 run --secret-source=env k6/scripts/secrets-load.js
import secrets from "k6/secrets";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    authed: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 10, duration: "2m" },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<400"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.API_URL || "http://localhost:3001";

// Retrieve secret once per VU in init context — secrets.get() returns a Promise
// Resolved in default() via await — k6 supports async default functions
const apiKeyPromise = secrets.get("API_KEY");  // sourced from $API_KEY env var

export default async function () {
  const key = await apiKeyPromise;

  const res = http.get(`${BASE}/api/protected`, {
    headers: {
      "X-API-Key":       key,
      "Content-Type":    "application/json",
    },
    tags: { name: "GET /api/protected" },
  });

  check(res, {
    "protected 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "not 401":       (r) => r.status !== 401,
  });

  sleep(1);
}
```

**Secret source options:**
| Source | CLI flag | Secret resolution |
|--------|----------|------------------|
| Env var | `--secret-source=env` | `$SECRET_NAME` env variable |
| File | `--secret-source=file=./secrets.env` | Key=value file |
| Grafana Cloud | `--secret-source=grafana-cloud` | Cloud-stored secrets |
| Mock | `--secret-source=mock=key=value` | Inline value for testing |

**Tradeoff:** Use `k6/secrets` for production CI pipelines where credentials must not appear in
logs or job environment dumps. Do NOT use it for local development smoke tests — the overhead
of secret resolution adds latency to the init phase. For local dev, use `__ENV.MY_SECRET` directly.

### 3. Chaos Injection with xk6-disruptor — Fault Tolerance Validation  [official]

`xk6-disruptor` is the official k6 extension for chaos engineering. It injects faults
(delays, errors, disruptions) into running services **while k6 load tests are active** —
letting you verify that SLOs hold under realistic fault conditions. It targets pods, services,
or processes via the k6 JavaScript API.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/chaos-load.js
// Requires: xk6 build --with github.com/grafana/xk6-disruptor
import { ServiceDisruptor } from "k6/x/disruptor";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { Rate } from "k6/metrics";

const faultTolerance = new Rate("fault_tolerance_passed");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    // Scenario 1: baseline load — runs throughout
    baseline: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 30,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "3m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 60,
      exec: "loadFlow",
    },
    // Scenario 2: chaos injection — starts after 30s baseline
    chaos: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      vus: 1,
      iterations: 1,
      startTime: "30s",
      exec: "injectFaults",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // SLO must hold even during fault injection
    "http_req_duration{scenario:baseline}": ["p(95)<2000"],
    "http_req_failed{scenario:baseline}":   ["rate<0.10"],
    fault_tolerance_passed:                  ["rate>0.90"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.API_URL || "http://localhost:3001";

export function loadFlow() {
  const res = http.get(`${BASE}/api/catalog`, { tags: { name: "catalog" } });
  const ok = check(res, {
    "catalog 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "latency ok":  (r) => r.timings.duration < 2000,
  });
  faultTolerance.add(ok ? 1 : 0);
}

export async function injectFaults() {
  const disruptor = new ServiceDisruptor("api-service", "default");

  await disruptor.injectHTTPFaults(
    {
      averageDelay:   "500ms",
      delayVariation: "100ms",
      errorRate:      0.05,    // 5% of requests return HTTP 500
      errorCode:      500,
    },
    "90s"  // inject faults for 90 seconds then auto-revert
  );

  console.log("Fault injection complete — SUT should have recovered");
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `xk6-disruptor` when you want to validate SLOs under fault conditions in a
staging Kubernetes environment as part of a pre-prod release gate. Do NOT run fault injection
against production services — `ServiceDisruptor` targets real running pods. Requires a custom
k6 binary built with `xk6 build`.
**Alternatives:** Chaos Mesh, Litmus, AWS FIS for non-k6-native chaos; `route.fulfill()` in
browser tests for HTTP-layer fault simulation without Kubernetes.
