## Cycle 36 — 2026-05-14

### 76. `exec.test.fail()` Soft-Fail Pattern for Non-Blocking SLO Violations  [official]

Use `exec.test.fail()` to mark a test run as failed without aborting in-flight VU iterations. Unlike `exec.test.abort()`, which immediately kills all VUs, `exec.test.fail()` sets the test result to failed (exit code 110) while allowing every VU to finish its current iteration cleanly. This is the correct pattern when you detect a business-logic violation mid-test — for example, discovering that a critical API starts returning 503s for a subset of calls — and want to preserve partial results without polluting metrics with forceful teardown artifacts. The function is synchronous and idempotent: calling it multiple times from concurrent VUs produces a single failure record.

```javascript
import { check } from "k6";
import http from "k6/http";
import exec from "k6/execution";

const CRITICAL_ENDPOINTS = ["/api/checkout", "/api/payment"];

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 5, duration: "30s" },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  for (const endpoint of CRITICAL_ENDPOINTS) {
    const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}${endpoint}`);
    const ok = check(res, { [`${endpoint} 200`]: (r) => r.status === 200 });
    if (!ok && res.status >= 500) {
      // Mark failed but let all VUs complete their current iteration
      exec.test.fail();
      console.error(`Critical endpoint ${endpoint} returned ${res.status} — marking test failed`);
    }
  }
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `exec.test.fail()` exits with code 110, which is distinct from threshold failures (exit code 99) and aborts (exit code 97, k6 v2.0+). CI pipelines must handle all three codes. If you need to distinguish a "soft-fail from business logic" from a "hard threshold breach", check both exit code and the summary JSON's `metrics.checks.values.fails` count. [official]

---

### 77. `page.waitForRequest()` URL-Pattern Synchronization for SPA Navigation  [official]

Single-page applications (SPAs) trigger async API calls during navigation that are not visible to `page.waitForNavigation()`. The `page.waitForRequest(urlPattern)` method (k6 v1.4.0+) blocks the caller until the browser initiates an outgoing HTTP request whose URL matches a string or RegExp pattern. This enables reliable synchronization with AJAX-heavy flows: wait for the data-fetch request before asserting on rendered content, ensuring assertions are not racily evaluated against skeleton loaders. Pair it with `page.waitForResponse()` to bracket the request-response lifecycle when you need the response body for in-page assertions.

```javascript
import { browser } from "k6/experimental/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browser: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/dashboard`);

    // Wait for the async data-fetch before asserting on rendered content
    const [, response] = await Promise.all([
      page.waitForRequest(/\/api\/dashboard\/data/),
      page.waitForResponse(/\/api\/dashboard\/data/),
      page.getByRole("button", { name: "Refresh" }).click(),
    ]);

    check(response, {
      "dashboard data fetch 200": (r) => r.status() === 200,
    });

    // Now safe to assert on rendered content — data has loaded
    await page.getByTestId("revenue-total").waitFor({ state: "visible" });
    check(page, {
      "revenue total visible": () =>
        page.getByTestId("revenue-total").isVisible(),
    });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `page.waitForRequest()` fires on request initiation, not completion. If your assertion depends on the response body being rendered, chain with `page.waitForResponse()` as shown above. Long-polling or SSE endpoints that send the same URL pattern repeatedly will trigger the matcher on the first match — add a predicate function `page.waitForRequest(req => req.url().includes('/api/dashboard') && req.method() === 'GET')` to be more specific. [official]

---

### 78. OpenTelemetry Stable Output with Per-Run `test-id` Tag for Trace Correlation  [official]

The `opentelemetry` output (stable since k6 v1.4.0, graduated from `experimental-opentelemetry`) pushes k6 metrics to any OTEL-compatible collector. Tag every run with a unique `test-id` using `--tag test-id=$(date +%s)` so that k6 metrics and application traces share a common attribute. All k6 metric types map to OTEL instrument types: Counter → `Float64Counter`, Trend → `Float64Histogram`, Rate → `Int64Counter` with a `condition` attribute (`zero`/`nonzero`). Downstream dashboards must filter on `condition="nonzero"` to recover the rate numerator from the OTEL representation.

```javascript
// k6 run --tag test-id=run-20260514-001 -o opentelemetry script.js
// Environment: K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf
//              K6_OTEL_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4318
//              K6_OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=checkout-load-test

import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { Trend, Rate } from "k6/metrics";

const checkoutLatency = new Trend("checkout_latency_ms", true); // true = isTime
const checkoutErrors  = new Rate("checkout_error_rate");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    load: { executor: "constant-arrival-rate", rate: 50, timeUnit: "1s", duration: "5m", preAllocatedVUs: 60 },
  },
  thresholds: {
    checkout_latency_ms: ["p(95)<500"],
    checkout_error_rate: ["rate<0.02"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const start = Date.now();
  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/checkout`, JSON.stringify({ items: [{ sku: "ABC", qty: 1 }] }), {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    tags: { endpoint: "checkout" },
  });
  checkoutLatency.add(Date.now() - start, { endpoint: "checkout" });
  const ok = check(res, { "checkout 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  checkoutErrors.add(!ok, { endpoint: "checkout" });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** Rate metrics arrive at the OTEL backend as a pair of `Int64Counter` series differentiated by a `condition` label. Legacy Prometheus/Grafana dashboards built for the old experimental format (which used `.occurred` / `.total` suffixes) must be updated to use `condition` attribute filtering. The stable output name is `opentelemetry`; the legacy alias `experimental-opentelemetry` still works in v1.x but is not guaranteed beyond v2.x. [official]

---

### 79. `locator.evaluate()` and `locator.evaluateHandle()` for In-Page DOM Assertions  [official]

`locator.evaluate(pageFunction)` (k6 v1.4.0+) executes a JavaScript function within the browser page context, passing the matched DOM element as the first argument, and returns the result to the k6 script. This is the correct pattern for assertions that require DOM inspection not available through k6's high-level locator API — such as reading computed CSS properties, inspecting shadow DOM internals, or extracting data attributes. `locator.evaluateHandle()` is the async variant returning a `JSHandle`, which is required when the in-page function returns a DOM node or a non-serializable object that you need to pass to further page operations.

```javascript
import { browser } from "k6/experimental/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ui: { executor: "per-vu-iterations", vus: 1, iterations: 1,
          options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } } },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/product/123`);
    await page.getByTestId("price-badge").waitFor({ state: "visible" });

    // Read computed color to verify promotion styling is applied
    const badgeColor = await page
      .getByTestId("price-badge")
      .evaluate((el) => window.getComputedStyle(el).color);

    check(badgeColor, {
      "price badge is red for promotion": (c) => c === "rgb(220, 38, 38)",
    });

    // Extract data-sku attribute via evaluate — not exposed by locator API
    const sku = await page
      .getByTestId("price-badge")
      .evaluate((el) => el.dataset.sku);

    check(sku, { "SKU attribute populated": (s) => typeof s === "string" && s.length > 0 });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `locator.evaluate()` serializes the return value through the Chrome DevTools Protocol JSON serializer. DOM nodes, Promises, and non-cloneable objects cannot be returned directly — use `locator.evaluateHandle()` for those cases. The evaluation runs in the page's JS context, so closures from the k6 script cannot be referenced inside the `pageFunction` string; pass all required values via the optional `arg` parameter: `locator.evaluate((el, arg) => el.textContent === arg, expectedText)`. [official]

---

### 80. `options.cloud` Configuration Block for Grafana Cloud k6 Run Metadata  [official]

The `options.cloud` block (replacing the deprecated `options.ext.loadimpact`) centralizes Grafana Cloud k6 run configuration in the script itself, eliminating the need for CLI flags in CI pipelines. Set `projectID`, `name`, `note`, and `distribution` (load zone weights) inside `options.cloud`. This metadata is consumed both by `k6 cloud run` (fully managed) and `k6 cloud run --local-execution` (local execution with cloud results streaming). In k6 v2.0+, `options.cloud.stackId` or the `K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID` environment variable is mandatory; omitting it produces a non-zero exit code with the message "no default Grafana Cloud stack configured".

```javascript
export const options = {
  cloud: {
    // Grafana Cloud k6 project and run metadata
    projectID: 12345,
    name: "checkout-flow — regression gate",
    note: "Triggered by PR #789 — payment service refactor",
    // Distribute load across two zones: 70% US East, 30% EU West
    distribution: {
      "us-east":  { loadZone: "amazon:us:ashburn",    percent: 70 },
      "eu-west":  { loadZone: "amazon:ie:dublin",     percent: 30 },
    },
  },
  scenarios: {
    checkout: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      stages: [
        { duration: "2m", target: 50 },
        { duration: "5m", target: 50 },
        { duration: "1m", target: 0  },
      ],
      preAllocatedVUs: 100,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<400"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default function () { /* ... */ }
```

> **Tradeoff:** `distribution` load zone weights must sum to exactly 100 — non-integer percentages are rounded and k6 cloud will reject configurations that do not sum to 100 after rounding. The `name` field appears in the Grafana Cloud k6 run list and supports template variables like `${__ENV.GIT_SHA}` for traceability, but the interpolation is done by the k6 CLI, not JavaScript, so `${...}` syntax in the YAML/JSON config works while JS template literals do not. [official]

---

### 81. `k6 cloud run --local-execution` with Auto-Injected Cloud Secrets (k6 v2.0+)  [official]

`k6 cloud run --local-execution script.js` runs the test locally on the CI agent while streaming results to Grafana Cloud k6 for persistence and visualization. In k6 v2.0+, secrets configured in the Grafana Cloud k6 project are automatically injected into the local execution environment — you do not need `--secret-source` for cloud-managed secrets. Opt out with `--no-cloud-secrets` when you want to use only locally provisioned secrets and prevent the cloud from providing additional values. This pattern is the recommended migration path away from running `k6 run` with separate secret management: one command gives cloud reporting plus secret injection.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# CI pipeline step: cloud-streamed local execution with auto-injected secrets
export K6_CLOUD_TOKEN="${GRAFANA_CLOUD_TOKEN}"
export K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID="${GRAFANA_CLOUD_STACK_ID}"  # mandatory in v2.0+

k6 cloud run --local-execution \
  --out opentelemetry \
  --tag ci-run=true \
  --tag git-sha="${GIT_SHA}" \
  --tag branch="${BRANCH_NAME}" \
  script.js

EXIT_CODE=$?
# k6 v2.0+: exit 97 = cloud-aborted (budget/concurrency exceeded)
#           exit 99 = threshold failure
#           exit 110 = exec.test.fail() called
if [ $EXIT_CODE -eq 97 ]; then
  echo "Test aborted by Grafana Cloud (budget or concurrency limit)" >&2
  exit 1
fi
exit $EXIT_CODE
```

> **Tradeoff:** `--local-execution` streams metrics to the cloud over HTTPS in real time. In high-throughput tests (>5,000 iterations/s), the metric streaming overhead adds latency on the load generator. For latency-sensitive benchmarks, use `k6 run` without cloud streaming and push the summary JSON separately via `handleSummary()`. Cloud auto-injection of secrets requires the secrets to be pre-configured in the Grafana Cloud k6 project — there is no way to see or verify which secrets were injected without explicit `console.log("[secret check]", { key: key ? "[RESOLVED]" : "[MISSING]" })` guards in `setup()`. [official]

---

### 82. `handleSummary()` with Machine-Readable JSON and Remote POST for CI Analytics  [official]

`handleSummary(data)` (k6 v0.30+, enhanced in v1.5.0 with `--new-machine-readable-summary` format) receives the full aggregated metrics object after all VUs complete and returns a map of output destinations. Returning `{ "stdout": textSummary(data), "/tmp/summary.json": JSON.stringify(data, null, 2) }` writes both human and machine output. In v1.5.0+, the machine-readable format schema is versioned and documented in `grafana/k6-summary`. Use the `http.post()` pattern inside `handleSummary()` to push results to an analytics endpoint for cross-run trend tracking — the function runs after teardown, so side effects from HTTP calls do not affect test metrics.

```javascript
import { textSummary } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.1.0/index.js";
import http from "k6/http";

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default function () { /* ... */ }

export function handleSummary(data) {
  // Post result to internal analytics endpoint for cross-run trend analysis
  const payload = JSON.stringify({
    timestamp:   new Date().toISOString(),
    gitSha:      __ENV.GIT_SHA || "unknown",
    branch:      __ENV.BRANCH_NAME || "unknown",
    passed:      Object.values(data.metrics).every((m) => !m.thresholds || Object.values(m.thresholds).every((t) => t.ok)),
    p95Duration: data.metrics["http_req_duration"]?.values?.["p(95)"],
    errorRate:   data.metrics["http_req_failed"]?.values?.rate,
  });

  http.post(`${__ENV.ANALYTICS_URL}/api/k6-results`, payload, {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Authorization": `Bearer ${__ENV.ANALYTICS_TOKEN}` },
  });

  return {
    stdout:              textSummary(data, { indent: " ", enableColors: true }),
    "/tmp/summary.json": JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
  };
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** HTTP calls inside `handleSummary()` are NOT included in any k6 metrics — they run in a separate context after the test completes. Network errors in `handleSummary()` are logged to stderr but do not affect the test exit code. The `data` object structure changed between the legacy format and the v1.5.0+ machine-readable format — if you consume both in downstream tooling, version-detect using `data.root_group !== undefined` (legacy) vs. presence of `data.summary` (new format). [official]

---

### 83. `locator.pressSequentially()` for Realistic Keystroke Simulation with Debounce-Triggering  [official]

`locator.pressSequentially(text, { delay: N })` (k6 v1.5.0+) types a string character-by-character, firing `keydown`, `keypress`, `input`, and `keyup` events for each character with a configurable inter-keystroke delay in milliseconds. This is the correct pattern for testing search-as-you-type (SAC) inputs, form-validation debounce logic, and autocomplete widgets — behaviors that only activate after individual key events, not after a single `fill()` call that dispatches an `input` event only. Setting `delay: 100` replicates a 60 WPM typist, ensuring debounce timers (typically 300–500 ms) fire correctly and autocomplete dropdowns appear as they would for real users.

```javascript
import { browser } from "k6/experimental/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    search: { executor: "shared-iterations", iterations: 5,
              options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } } },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/search`);
    const searchBox = page.getByRole("searchbox");
    await searchBox.waitFor({ state: "visible" });

    // Type at ~60 WPM (100ms/char) to trigger debounce-based autocomplete
    await searchBox.pressSequentially("load test", { delay: 100 });

    // Wait for autocomplete dropdown to appear after debounce fires
    await page.getByRole("listbox").waitFor({ state: "visible", timeout: 3000 });

    const suggestions = await page.getByRole("option").all();
    check(suggestions, {
      "autocomplete returned results": (s) => s.length > 0,
    });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `pressSequentially()` is significantly slower than `fill()` because it generates N×4 CDP events for an N-character string. For high-iteration browser tests (>100 iterations/VU), prefer `fill()` for fields where debounce behavior is not being tested. The `delay` parameter accepts `0` for maximum speed, which may still trigger individual key events but at native CDP event dispatch rate — fast enough to miss some mobile-targeted debounce implementations with very tight timing windows. [official]

---

### 84. `page.unrouteAll()` Cleanup Pattern to Prevent Route Handler Leaks in Long Sessions  [official]

`page.route(url, handler)` (k6 browser module) intercepts matching network requests for the lifetime of the `Page` object unless explicitly removed. In multi-iteration browser tests where VUs reuse a `Page` or `BrowserContext` across iterations, route handlers accumulate: a handler registered in iteration 1 remains active during iterations 2–N. If the handler is a stub that returns mock data, real network calls for the same pattern are silently intercepted in subsequent iterations, producing misleading metrics. `page.unrouteAll()` (k6 v1.4.0+) removes all registered route handlers at once and should be called at the start of each iteration or in a `finally` block.

```javascript
import { browser } from "k6/experimental/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mock_test: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 3, duration: "1m",
                 options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } } },
  },
};

// Reuse context across iterations to reduce browser startup overhead
let context, page;

export async function setup() {}

export default async function () {
  if (!context) {
    context = await browser.newContext();
    page = await context.newPage();
  }

  // Remove all route handlers from the previous iteration — prevents accumulation
  await page.unrouteAll({ behavior: "ignoreErrors" });

  // Register route handler fresh each iteration
  await page.route("**/api/feature-flags", async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({ status: 200,
      body: JSON.stringify({ newCheckout: true }),
      contentType: "application/json" });
  });

  await page.goto(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/checkout`);
  const featureFlag = await page.evaluate(() => window.__featureFlags?.newCheckout);
  check(featureFlag, { "new checkout flag injected": (f) => f === true });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `page.unrouteAll()` accepts a `{ behavior: "ignoreErrors" }` option that silently ignores races where a handler is invoked during removal. Without this option, concurrent requests hitting a route being removed can throw. The `behavior: "wait"` option (block until active handlers complete) is safer but can deadlock if a route handler is awaiting a response that the route itself must fulfill. Default to `"ignoreErrors"` in load tests unless you need strict handler lifecycle control. [official]

---

### 85. Custom `Trend` Metric with Tagged `add()` for Per-Endpoint Latency Breakdown  [official]

A single `Trend` metric can collect latency samples from multiple endpoints when each `add()` call includes an `endpoint` tag. Downstream threshold expressions filter on the tag using the `{endpoint:"checkout"}` selector syntax, enabling per-endpoint SLOs in a single script without creating one `Trend` per endpoint. This pattern scales cleanly when endpoints are discovered dynamically (e.g., from a fixture file) — the tag value is a runtime string rather than a compile-time variable name. The `isTime: true` constructor flag marks the metric as a duration, enabling automatic millisecond-to-second conversion in Grafana dashboards.

```javascript
import http from "k6/http";
import { Trend, Rate } from "k6/metrics";
import { check } from "k6";

const apiLatency = new Trend("api_latency_ms", /* isTime= */ true);
const apiErrors  = new Rate("api_error_rate");

const ENDPOINTS = [
  { method: "GET",  path: "/api/products",  tag: "product-list"  },
  { method: "GET",  path: "/api/cart",       tag: "cart-get"      },
  { method: "POST", path: "/api/cart/add",   tag: "cart-add"      },
  { method: "POST", path: "/api/checkout",   tag: "checkout"      },
];

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    // Per-endpoint SLOs via tag-filtered threshold expressions
    "api_latency_ms{endpoint:product-list}": ["p(95)<200"],
    "api_latency_ms{endpoint:cart-get}":     ["p(95)<150"],
    "api_latency_ms{endpoint:cart-add}":     ["p(95)<300"],
    "api_latency_ms{endpoint:checkout}":     ["p(95)<500"],
    "api_error_rate{endpoint:checkout}":     ["rate<0.005"],
  },
  scenarios: {
    api_flow: { executor: "constant-arrival-rate", rate: 100, timeUnit: "1s", duration: "3m", preAllocatedVUs: 120 },
  },
};

export default function () {
  for (const ep of ENDPOINTS) {
    const start = Date.now();
    const res = ep.method === "GET"
      ? http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}${ep.path}`, { tags: { endpoint: ep.tag } })
      : http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}${ep.path}`, null, { tags: { endpoint: ep.tag } });
    const duration = Date.now() - start;

    apiLatency.add(duration, { endpoint: ep.tag });
    apiErrors.add(res.status >= 400 || res.status === 0, { endpoint: ep.tag });
    check(res, { [`${ep.tag} non-5xx`]: (r) => r.status < 500 });
  }
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** Tag-filtered thresholds increase cardinality in the k6 metrics engine. Each unique `{endpoint:value}` combination creates a separate time series. With many endpoints and many tags, memory pressure on the k6 process grows proportionally. For scripts exercising >50 distinct tag values, consider using `--system-tags` to control which built-in tags are emitted and reduce total cardinality. Tag-filtered thresholds are evaluated only at test end — they cannot be used with `abortOnFail` in their tag-filtered form. [official]

---

### 86. WebSocket `setInterval` Heartbeat with `setTimeout` Session Timeout Guard  [official]

Long-lived WebSocket connections (chat, notifications, live dashboards) require two concurrent timers: a periodic heartbeat `setInterval` to keep the connection alive through NAT/proxy idle-timeout rules, and a `setTimeout` session guard to terminate the VU after a maximum session duration. The `socket.setTimeout()` callback calls `socket.close()`, which triggers the `close` event and unblocks the VU's run function. Without the session timeout, VUs in `constant-vus` or `ramping-vus` executors may hold open connections indefinitely when the server does not send a close frame, preventing graceful test teardown within the `gracefulStop` window.

```javascript
import ws from "k6/ws";
import { check } from "k6";
import { Rate, Counter } from "k6/metrics";

const wsErrors    = new Rate("ws_error_rate");
const msgReceived = new Counter("ws_messages_received");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    live_feed: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 50, duration: "5m", gracefulStop: "15s" },
  },
  thresholds: {
    ws_error_rate:        ["rate<0.01"],
    ws_messages_received: ["count>100"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const url = `${__ENV.WS_URL}/live-feed`;
  const res = ws.connect(url, {}, function (socket) {
    socket.on("open", () => {
      // Heartbeat every 15s to prevent NAT/proxy idle-timeout (typically 30-60s)
      socket.setInterval(() => socket.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "ping" })), 15_000);
      // Session timeout guard: close after 55s so the VU re-loops within gracefulStop
      socket.setTimeout(() => socket.close(), 55_000);
    });

    socket.on("message", (data) => {
      const msg = JSON.parse(data);
      if (msg.type !== "pong") {
        msgReceived.add(1);
      }
    });

    socket.on("error", (err) => {
      wsErrors.add(1);
      console.error("WebSocket error:", err.error());
    });

    socket.on("close", (code) => {
      check(code, { "WS closed cleanly (1000 or 1001)": (c) => c === 1000 || c === 1001 });
    });
  });

  check(res, { "WS handshake 101": (r) => r && r.status === 101 });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `socket.setInterval()` and `socket.setTimeout()` run on the VU's event loop, not the Node.js event loop. k6's WebSocket event loop is single-threaded per VU — if a `message` handler is slow (e.g., JSON.parse of a large payload), heartbeat timers may fire late. For sub-second heartbeat precision on large payloads, move the heartbeat to a separate `scenarios` entry with its own VU pool rather than multiplexing it inside the message handler. [official]

---

### 87. `k6/net/grpc` `asyncInvoke()` for Non-Blocking gRPC Unary Calls in Arrival-Rate Tests  [official]

`client.asyncInvoke()` (k6 experimental gRPC module) returns a Promise that resolves when the gRPC response arrives, enabling concurrent in-flight RPCs within a single VU when combined with `Promise.all()`. In `constant-arrival-rate` tests, VUs that block on synchronous `client.invoke()` calls may exhaust the VU pool if gRPC latency spikes — the arrival rate drops below the configured rate because all VUs are blocked waiting for slow responses. Using `asyncInvoke()` with `Promise.all()` allows one VU to maintain N concurrent in-flight RPCs, significantly improving throughput per VU and reducing the `preAllocatedVUs` requirement.

```javascript
import grpc from "k6/net/grpc";
import { check } from "k6";

const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(["./proto"], "product.proto", "order.proto");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    grpc_load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 200, timeUnit: "1s", duration: "3m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 30,
      maxVUs: 50,
    },
  },
  thresholds: { grpc_req_duration: ["p(95)<200"] },
};

export function setup() {
  client.connect(`${__ENV.GRPC_HOST}:${__ENV.GRPC_PORT}`, { plaintext: true });
}

export default async function () {
  // Fan out two concurrent RPCs — reduces blocking time per VU
  const [productRes, inventoryRes] = await Promise.all([
    client.asyncInvoke("product.ProductService/GetProduct",  { id: "PROD-001" }),
    client.asyncInvoke("product.ProductService/GetInventory", { id: "PROD-001" }),
  ]);

  check(productRes, {
    "GetProduct OK":    (r) => r.status === grpc.StatusOK,
    "product id match": (r) => r.message?.id === "PROD-001",
  });
  check(inventoryRes, {
    "GetInventory OK":        (r) => r.status === grpc.StatusOK,
    "inventory non-negative": (r) => r.message?.quantity >= 0,
  });
}

export function teardown() {
  client.close();
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `asyncInvoke()` requires the test script to be authored with `async/await`. Mixing synchronous `invoke()` and asynchronous `asyncInvoke()` in the same VU iteration causes unexpected ordering — always pick one style per script. The gRPC client maintains a persistent HTTP/2 connection per VU; `Promise.all()` multiplexes concurrent RPCs over that single connection's stream pool. If the server enforces `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`, excess concurrent requests from a single VU will be queued at the server, not at k6. [official]

---

### 88. Per-Scenario Environment Variable Injection for Multi-Environment Regression Gates  [official]

Each scenario in `options.scenarios` accepts an `env` property that merges additional environment variables into the VU's `__ENV` object for that scenario only. This pattern eliminates the need for separate k6 script files for different environments: a single script runs production smoke tests and staging soak tests simultaneously by injecting different `BASE_URL` and `SLA_THRESHOLD` values per scenario. Combined with `options.scenarios[name].tags`, scenario-specific tags propagate to all metrics emitted by VUs in that scenario, enabling per-environment threshold expressions without code duplication.

```javascript
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    staging_soak: {
      executor: "constant-vus", vus: 20, duration: "10m",
      env: {
        BASE_URL:      "https://staging.example.com",
        ENV_NAME:      "staging",
        TRACE_ENABLED: "true",
      },
      tags: { environment: "staging" },
    },
    prod_smoke: {
      executor: "constant-vus", vus: 2, duration: "2m",
      env: {
        BASE_URL:      "https://prod.example.com",
        ENV_NAME:      "production",
        TRACE_ENABLED: "false",
      },
      tags: { environment: "production" },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_duration{environment:staging}":    ["p(95)<500"],
    "http_req_duration{environment:production}": ["p(95)<200"],
    "http_req_failed{environment:production}":   ["rate<0.001"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const traceEnabled = __ENV.TRACE_ENABLED === "true";
  const headers = traceEnabled
    ? { "X-Trace-Enabled": "true", "X-Env": __ENV.ENV_NAME }
    : { "X-Env": __ENV.ENV_NAME };

  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/health`, { headers });
  check(res, { [`[${__ENV.ENV_NAME}] health 200`]: (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** Scenario-level `env` values override but do not replace the global `__ENV` — variables not declared in the scenario `env` block retain their global values (from CLI `--env` flags or the OS environment). Test code that reads `__ENV.BASE_URL` unconditionally works correctly, but code that checks `Object.keys(__ENV)` for presence of a key may see different results per scenario if the key is only in the global env. Document which env variables are scenario-overridden and which come from the global environment to prevent confusion in code reviews. [official]

---

### 89. `dns` Option with Short TTL for Testing Service Discovery and DNS Failover  [official]

k6's `options.dns` controls DNS resolution caching behavior within the VU pool. Setting `ttl: "0s"` disables DNS caching and forces every TCP connection to re-resolve the hostname — the correct pattern for testing DNS-based failover, round-robin load balancing, and service discovery endpoints. Setting `ttl: "60s"` (default) means all VUs that resolved the hostname within the same 60-second window use the same IP, which masks DNS rotation behavior. The `policy` field controls which IP is selected when a hostname resolves to multiple addresses: `"roundRobin"` cycles through returned IPs, `"random"` picks one randomly per connection, and `"first"` always uses the first returned IP.

```javascript
export const options = {
  // Force per-connection DNS re-resolution for failover testing
  dns: {
    ttl:    "0s",          // no caching — each connection resolves fresh
    policy: "roundRobin",  // cycle across all A/AAAA records
    select: "first",       // after policy selects the pool, use the first
  },
  scenarios: {
    failover_test: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 30, timeUnit: "1s", duration: "5m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 40,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.05"],  // allow up to 5% error during failover
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Each request resolves the hostname independently — exercises all A records
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/health`, {
    tags: { test_type: "failover" },
  });
  check(res, { "health endpoint reachable": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `ttl: "0s"` with high VU counts produces a DNS query storm against the resolver — each new connection causes a DNS lookup, and at 500 RPS that is 500 DNS queries/s. Point `options.dns` at a local resolver (e.g., `127.0.0.1:1053`) to prevent DNS resolver overload from becoming a test bottleneck. For `policy: "roundRobin"`, the round-robin counter is per-VU, not global — VUs do not coordinate their IP selection, so the distribution across A records is statistical rather than perfectly even. [official]

---

### 90. `--summary-export` + Cross-Run Regression Gate via `handleSummary()` JSON Output  [official]

k6 v1.5.0 introduced `--new-machine-readable-summary` and enhanced the `handleSummary()` return format; the schema for this versioned JSON is published in the `grafana/k6-summary` GitHub repository. Integrating a CI step that reads `metrics.http_req_duration.values['p(95)']` and `metrics.http_req_failed.values.rate` from the summary JSON decouples the pass/fail decision from k6's threshold engine. This is the correct pattern when teams need multi-run trend comparison (fail if p95 regresses more than 10% vs. the 7-day rolling average) — a condition k6's native absolute threshold engine cannot express.

```javascript
import { textSummary } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.1.0/index.js";
import http from "k6/http";

export const options = {
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"], http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"] },
};

export default function () { /* ... */ }

export function handleSummary(data) {
  const p95   = data.metrics["http_req_duration"]?.values?.["p(95)"] ?? -1;
  const errRate = data.metrics["http_req_failed"]?.values?.rate ?? -1;

  // Post metrics to analytics service for cross-run trend analysis
  const analyticsPayload = JSON.stringify({
    runId:    __ENV.RUN_ID || "unknown",
    gitSha:   __ENV.GIT_SHA || "unknown",
    branch:   __ENV.BRANCH_NAME || "main",
    p95Ms:    p95,
    errRate:  errRate,
    passed:   Object.values(data.metrics)
                .every((m) => !m.thresholds || Object.values(m.thresholds).every((t) => t.ok)),
  });

  // Fire-and-forget to analytics — errors do not affect exit code
  http.post(`${__ENV.ANALYTICS_URL}/api/k6-results`, analyticsPayload, {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json",
               "Authorization": `Bearer ${__ENV.ANALYTICS_TOKEN}` },
    timeout: "5s",
  });

  return {
    stdout:              textSummary(data, { indent: " ", enableColors: true }),
    "/tmp/summary.json": JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
  };
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** The `handleSummary()` return map writes files using absolute or relative paths on the load generator's filesystem — not the cloud runner's filesystem when using `k6 cloud run --local-execution`. For cloud-managed runs, the only reliable output path is `stdout`/`stderr` (captured by the CI log) plus the remote POST shown above. The `data` schema changed between k6 versions; always pin the `k6-summary` import to a specific version tag (`/0.1.0/`) rather than `latest` to prevent breakage on library updates. [official]

## Cycle 36 — Community Gotchas

### Gotcha 129. `options.scenarios[name].env` overrides are not visible in `setup()` or `teardown()` — cross-phase env reads use global values only  [community]

**WHY:** The `setup()` and `teardown()` lifecycle functions run outside any scenario context — they execute in a special goroutine where scenario-specific `env` blocks are not applied. If a team defines per-scenario `BASE_URL` overrides and then reads `__ENV.BASE_URL` inside `setup()` to seed fixture data, they read the global value (from `--env BASE_URL=...` CLI flags or OS environment), not the scenario value. The mismatch is invisible during development on single-environment setups where global and scenario URLs are identical, and only surfaces in multi-environment CI pipelines where `setup()` pre-warms production data while the scenarios are supposed to target staging.

**Fix:** Pass the setup/teardown target URL as a separate explicitly-named env variable that is not overridden by any scenario: `export K6_SETUP_URL=https://staging.example.com k6 run script.js`. Inside `setup()`, read `__ENV.K6_SETUP_URL` exclusively. Add a startup assertion: `if (__ENV.K6_SETUP_URL === __ENV.BASE_URL) console.warn("[setup] K6_SETUP_URL equals BASE_URL — verify multi-env config is correct")`.

---

### Gotcha 130. Duplicate metric name keys in `options.thresholds` are silently discarded — only the first definition survives  [community]

**WHY:** JavaScript object literal syntax allows duplicate property keys without a syntax error — in most runtimes the last value wins, but k6 processes threshold keys in the order they appear and silently discards duplicates after the first. Teams that add a second threshold expression for the same metric (e.g., adding `"p(99)<1000"` to a key already containing `"p(95)<500"`) see only the first threshold enforced and receive no warning. The resulting test will pass even when the p99 threshold is violated, causing SLO breaches in production that the test was supposed to catch. The silent discard is especially dangerous because the threshold appears visually correct in code review.

**Fix:** Use an array of threshold expressions for a single metric key: `"http_req_duration": ["p(95)<500", "p(99)<1000"]`. k6 evaluates all expressions in the array and fails the test if any one is violated. Lint scripts for duplicate threshold keys using a small Node.js one-liner that parses the script's `options.thresholds` object and checks for repeated property names before committing.

---

### Gotcha 131. `client.connect()` in `setup()` does not persist the gRPC connection to VU goroutines — each VU must call `connect()` independently  [community]

**WHY:** The k6 `k6/net/grpc` `Client` object is not serializable across the `setup()`-to-VU boundary. When `client.connect()` is called in `setup()`, the underlying HTTP/2 connection is owned by the setup goroutine and is not transferred to VU goroutines. VUs that call `client.invoke()` without first calling `client.connect()` receive a "connection not established" runtime error. Since `setup()` runs without errors and the connection appears valid to the setup goroutine, teams assume the connection is shared and spend hours debugging gRPC errors that only appear when VUs start.

**Fix:** Call `client.connect()` inside the VU `default` function (or use a module-level `let connected = false` guard: `if (!connected) { client.connect(...); connected = true; }`). For scripts that need fresh connections per iteration rather than per-VU persistence, call `client.connect()` at the top of `default()` and `client.close()` at the bottom — the connection overhead is amortized over the test duration only if reuse is important, so benchmark both approaches for your target gRPC server.

---

### Gotcha 132. `abortOnFail` thresholds in fully-managed cloud runs are delayed by up to 60 seconds — early abort is not instantaneous  [community]

**WHY:** When running with `k6 cloud run` (fully managed, not `--local-execution`), threshold evaluation is performed server-side on Grafana Cloud k6 infrastructure on a 60-second polling cycle. A threshold with `abortOnFail: true` that is breached at T+5s will not trigger an abort until T+60s at the earliest. During those 55 seconds, VUs continue generating load against a system that has already failed. Teams that set tight `abortOnFail` thresholds to protect production systems during canary tests discover that "immediate abort" in cloud mode means "abort within ~60 seconds", which may be unacceptably slow for high-stakes production testing.

**Fix:** For production canary tests that require sub-second abort capability, use `k6 cloud run --local-execution` (k6 v2.0+) so threshold evaluation runs locally on the load generator and aborts are near-instantaneous. If fully-managed cloud execution is required, add a companion monitoring step (e.g., a Grafana alert rule or a webhook) that calls the k6 Cloud API to abort the run independently of the threshold polling cycle. Document the expected ~60s abort delay in test plan runbooks so oncall engineers do not interpret the delay as a k6 bug.

---

### Gotcha 133. `__ITER` is per-VU and not globally unique — using it as a `SharedArray` fixture index causes collisions across VUs  [community]

**WHY:** `__ITER` is the iteration counter for the current VU, resetting to 0 for each VU independently. In a test with 10 VUs, VU 1 and VU 2 both have `__ITER === 0` on their first iterations simultaneously — they pick the same fixture row if `__ITER` is used as a `SharedArray` index. The collision means two VUs log in with the same username, causing "user already active" session errors, duplicate purchase records in the test database, or test data corruption that invalidates load test results. The bug is invisible when running with a single VU (where `__ITER` is effectively globally unique) and only appears when VU count is increased above 1.

**Fix:** Use `exec.scenario.iterationInTest` as the primary fixture index — it is globally unique and monotonically increasing across all VUs within the scenario. Use modulo to wrap around the fixture array: `const user = users[exec.scenario.iterationInTest % users.length]`. For cross-scenario uniqueness, combine `exec.scenario.iterationInTest` with a scenario-name hash to produce a per-scenario offset. Never use `__ITER` alone for fixture indexing in multi-VU tests.

---

### Gotcha 134. Module-level `import` side effects run once per VU — code that mutates shared state in an `import` callback causes race conditions  [community]

**WHY:** k6 executes the module init scope (top-level code outside functions) once per VU during the initialization phase, not once globally. If a module exports a function that pushes to an array defined at module scope — and that array is shared via `SharedArray` or a global variable captured in a closure — each VU's init execution appends to the array independently. A test with 20 VUs that imports a module containing `registry.push(new Handler())` at module scope ends up with 20 duplicate handlers in `registry`, one per VU. Functions that iterate `registry` during the test run process each event 20 times, inflating metrics and creating spurious side effects in the system under test.

**Fix:** Treat all module-level code as "runs N times for N VUs" — never mutate global state in module init scope. Use `SharedArray` only for read-only data initialized in its constructor callback (which runs once). For singletons (connection pools, registries), use the `setup()` return value to pass immutable configuration to VUs, or use `exec.vu.idInTest === 1` guards to limit one-time initialization to the first VU and verify the guard with an explicit log line.

## Cycle 37 — 2026-05-14

### 91. `k6/secrets` Async Multi-Source Pattern for Per-Environment Credentials  [official]

The `k6/secrets` module (stable since v1.6.0) provides async secret retrieval with automatic redaction in logs. Scripts declare `import secrets from "k6/secrets"` and call `await secrets.get("key")` inside async VU functions. When multiple `--secret-source` flags are passed (e.g., a `file` source for dev and a `cloud` source for CI), call `secrets.source("sourceName").get("key")` to target a specific store — `secrets.get()` without arguments always reads the default source and throws if no default is configured. k6 v1.7.0 added the `K6_SECRET_SOURCE` environment variable as an alternative to the `--secret-source` flag, enabling source configuration in `.env` files without modifying the run command. Secrets rendered to `console.log` are replaced with `***SECRET_REDACTED***` before the string leaves the k6 process boundary, so they never appear in CI logs, test reports, or OpenTelemetry traces.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/secrets-multi-source.js
import { check } from "k6";
import http from "k6/http";
import secrets from "k6/secrets";

export const options = {
  vus: 5,
  duration: "30s",
  thresholds: { http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"] },
};

// K6_SECRET_SOURCE=file=path=./dev-secrets.env (set in CI environment)
// In production CI: K6_SECRET_SOURCE=cloud (auto-injected by k6 cloud run --local-execution)
export default async function () {
  // Retrieve from default source (resolved at runtime)
  const apiKey = await secrets.get("API_KEY");

  // Retrieve from a named secondary source (e.g., --secret-source=mock=name=mock2,API_KEY=staging-key)
  const stagingKey = await secrets.source("mock2").get("API_KEY");

  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/protected`, {
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
      "X-Staging-Key": stagingKey, // both values are redacted in all log output
    },
  });
  check(res, { "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `await` inside VU code requires the exported function to be `async`, which adds a microtask boundary per iteration. For extremely high-throughput tests (>10,000 RPS per VU), retrieve secrets once in `setup()` and pass them via the data parameter rather than awaiting per-iteration. Do **not** cache the resolved secret string in a module-level variable across iterations if secret rotation is required — each `await secrets.get()` call re-fetches from the source for live rotation support. [official]

---

### 92. `K6_SECRET_SOURCE` Environment Variable for CI-Agnostic Secret Configuration  [official]

k6 v1.7.0 introduced `K6_SECRET_SOURCE` as a first-class environment variable equivalent to the `--secret-source` CLI flag. This allows teams to configure secret sources in `.env` files, Docker environment blocks, or Kubernetes `ConfigMap` / `Secret` references without modifying the `k6 run` command itself — critical for GitOps workflows where the run command is templated and must not carry sensitive configuration. The variable accepts the same syntax as `--secret-source`: `file=path=./secrets.env`, `mock=default,KEY=value`, or `cloud` for Grafana Cloud auto-injection. Multiple sources can be specified by repeating the env variable with different names (the CLI `--secret-source` flag may be combined with `K6_SECRET_SOURCE` — they merge). The separation of secret source configuration from test scripts means the same `.js` test file runs unchanged across dev (file source), staging (URL source), and production (cloud source) environments.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/ci-secret-source.js
// Run: K6_SECRET_SOURCE=file=path=./secrets.env k6 run ci-secret-source.js
// Prod: K6_SECRET_SOURCE=cloud k6 cloud run --local-execution ci-secret-source.js
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import http from "k6/http";
import secrets from "k6/secrets";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 2,
      duration: "10s",
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const dbPassword = await secrets.get("DB_PASSWORD");
  const adminToken = await secrets.get("ADMIN_TOKEN");

  // Use secrets inline — both replaced with ***SECRET_REDACTED*** in all output
  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/admin/verify`, null, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${adminToken}` },
  });
  check(res, { "admin verify 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  console.log(`DB_PASSWORD received: ${dbPassword}`); // prints ***SECRET_REDACTED***
  sleep(1);
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `K6_SECRET_SOURCE=mock=default,KEY=value` exposes the secret value as a shell environment variable, which may appear in process listing (`ps aux`) and shell history. For production CI, prefer `file` or `cloud` sources over `mock`. Validate that `K6_SECRET_SOURCE` is not logged by your CI platform's "echo all env vars" debug mode — mask the variable in CI configuration (GitHub Actions: `env:` block secrets, GitLab: masked variables). [official]

### 93. `k6/experimental/csv` Streaming Parser for Memory-Efficient Fixture Loading  [official]

The `k6/experimental/csv` module offers two modes: `csv.parse()` (bulk, Go-native, fast but loads entire file into memory) and `csv.Parser` (streaming, line-by-line, slower but constant memory). For fixture files under ~50 MB, `csv.parse()` with `SharedArray` is the preferred pattern because Go-side parsing bypasses the JS runtime and shared memory means the dataset is read once regardless of VU count. For files over 100 MB or in memory-constrained environments, `csv.Parser` combined with `k6/experimental/fs` allows streaming without resident-set spikes. Both modes require `open()` in init context — `csv.parse()` returns a `Promise<string[][]>` that must be awaited inside `SharedArray`'s async-capable constructor variant. The `options.quotes` parameter controls whether RFC 4180 quoting is respected; setting `quotes: false` gives a 15-20% parsing speedup when data is known to contain no quoted commas.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/csv-streaming-fixture.js
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";
import csv from "k6/experimental/csv";
import { open } from "k6/experimental/fs";
import { check } from "k6";
import http from "k6/http";

// BULK MODE — preferred for files < 50 MB
const users = new SharedArray("users", async function () {
  const file = await open("./data/users.csv");
  const rows = await csv.parse(file, { skipFirstLine: true, asObject: true });
  return rows; // array of { username, password, role } objects
});

// STREAMING MODE — for large files (shown in default fn for illustration)
export const options = { vus: 10, duration: "20s" };

export default async function () {
  const user = users[__VU % users.length];
  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/login`, JSON.stringify({
    username: user.username,
    password: user.password,
  }), { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } });
  check(res, {
    "login 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "token present": (r) => r.json("token") !== undefined,
  });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `csv.parse()` with `asObject: true` maps header names to object keys, but adds a 10-15% memory overhead vs raw array mode — use `asObject: false` and index columns numerically for the most memory-efficient bulk approach. The streaming `csv.Parser` approach requires async VU functions, which adds a microtask overhead of ~0.05 ms per iteration. Avoid mixing `csv.Parser` reads across VUs sharing the same `File` handle — each VU needs its own `open()` call because `File` maintains per-reader cursor state. [official]

### 94. `k6/experimental/fs` Incremental Binary File Reading with `SeekMode`  [official]

The `k6/experimental/fs` module enables memory-efficient file I/O in init context by loading files into a single shared memory region accessible to all VUs without duplication. `open()` returns a `File` object with `read(buffer)`, `seek(offset, SeekMode)`, and `stat()` methods. `read(buffer)` fills a `Uint8Array` and returns bytes read (or `null` at EOF), enabling chunked processing without loading entire files into JS heap memory. `SeekMode.Start`, `SeekMode.Current`, and `SeekMode.End` provide positioning for random-access patterns — e.g., seeking to a known record offset in a binary fixture file. The module is particularly valuable for testing file upload endpoints: each VU seeks to its assigned byte range and reads only its chunk, simulating concurrent multipart uploads without 50 VUs each holding a 100 MB buffer.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/chunked-upload.js
import { open, SeekMode } from "k6/experimental/fs";
import { check } from "k6";
import http from "k6/http";
import exec from "k6/execution";

const CHUNK_SIZE = 1024 * 256; // 256 KB per VU chunk

// Init context — opened once, shared across all VUs
const filePromise = open("./data/upload-fixture.bin");

export const options = { vus: 4, duration: "15s" };

export default async function () {
  const file = await filePromise;
  const info = await file.stat();
  const vuIndex = exec.vu.idInTest - 1;
  const offset = (vuIndex * CHUNK_SIZE) % info.size;

  await file.seek(offset, SeekMode.Start);
  const buffer = new Uint8Array(CHUNK_SIZE);
  const bytesRead = await file.read(buffer);
  const chunk = buffer.slice(0, bytesRead ?? 0);

  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/upload`, chunk.buffer, {
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream",
      "X-Chunk-Offset": String(offset),
    },
  });
  check(res, { "upload 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** The `File` object's cursor is per-handle — all VUs share the same memory region but each `open()` call returns an independent cursor. If only one `open()` call is made at module scope (as in the example above), all VUs share the same cursor, causing race conditions when `seek()` and `read()` are interleaved across goroutines. The fix: call `open()` inside each VU's iteration or use `exec.vu.idInTest` to pre-compute offsets deterministically before seeking. For read-only constant data, `SharedArray` with `open()` + `JSON.parse()` is simpler — use `k6/experimental/fs` only when file size or format makes full-load impractical. [official]

### 95. Automatic Extension Resolution for Subcommand Extensions (k6 v1.7.0)  [official]

k6 v1.7.0 introduced automatic binary provisioning for subcommand extensions — custom `xk6` builds are no longer required for extensions that register CLI subcommands. When k6 encounters an unknown subcommand (e.g., `k6 disrupt pods`), it queries the extension registry, downloads a prebuilt binary containing the required extension, caches it locally, and re-executes the command transparently. This matches the existing experience for JavaScript-only extensions (e.g., `xk6-kafka`, `xk6-mqtt`) which had always auto-resolved at script import time. The practical impact: CI pipelines that previously needed a custom `xk6 build` step before using `xk6-disruptor` CLI commands can now use the stock `grafana/k6` Docker image without modification. The provisioning respects the same `--no-color`, `--quiet`, and output redirection options as normal k6 output so it integrates cleanly into CI log parsers.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/disruptor-auto-resolve.js
// No custom xk6 build needed — k6 v1.7.0+ auto-provisions xk6-disruptor
import { PodDisruptor } from "k6/x/disruptor";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    baseline: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 50,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
    },
    inject_fault: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      iterations: 1,
      vus: 1,
      startTime: "30s", // fault starts 30s into baseline load
      exec: "injectFault",
    },
  },
};

export function injectFault() {
  const disruptor = new PodDisruptor({
    namespace: "default",
    labelSelector: "app=my-api",
  });
  disruptor.injectHTTPFaults({
    errorRate: 0.1,       // 10% of requests return 500
    errorCode: 500,
    delay: "200ms",       // add 200 ms to all responses
    duration: "60s",
  });
}

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/health`);
  check(res, { "resilient under fault": (r) => r.status < 500 });
  sleep(0.1);
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** Auto-provisioning requires outbound internet access from the machine running k6 — air-gapped CI environments must still pre-build custom binaries with `xk6`. The downloaded binary is cached under `~/.config/k6/extensions/` and reused across runs; the cache is not versioned by default, so pinning extension versions with `--with k6/x/disruptor@v0.5.0` in a `k6 build` invocation remains the most reproducible approach for regulated environments. [official]
