### 96. `xk6-disruptor` `ServiceDisruptor` for Multi-Pod Fault Injection Without Pod Labels  [community]

While `PodDisruptor` targets pods directly by label selector, `ServiceDisruptor` targets all pods backing a Kubernetes Service — useful when pod labels are managed by the service mesh and not predictable. `ServiceDisruptor` intercepts traffic at the Service's virtual IP level by injecting a sidecar into each backing pod's network namespace, so it captures all traffic regardless of pod identity. The typical pattern uses a two-scenario script: one `constant-arrival-rate` scenario for baseline HTTP load and one `shared-iterations: 1` fault injector that begins partway through the test run. Fault parameters include `errorRate` (fraction of requests to fail), `errorCode` (HTTP status to inject), `delay` (ms to add to each request), and `duration`. Critically, `ServiceDisruptor` must be constructed during the VU iteration — it cannot be created in `setup()` because it establishes a live connection to the Kubernetes API server that does not serialize across the lifecycle boundary.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/service-disruptor-pattern.js
import { ServiceDisruptor } from "k6/x/disruptor";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Trend } from "k6/metrics";

const faultImpact = new Trend("fault_impact_latency_ms", true);

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.15"],          // allow up to 15% errors during fault
    "http_req_duration{scenario:load}": ["p(95)<800"],
  },
  scenarios: {
    load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 30, timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "90s", preAllocatedVUs: 15,
    },
    disrupt: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      vus: 1, iterations: 1, startTime: "20s",
      exec: "runDisruptor",
    },
  },
};

export function runDisruptor() {
  const svc = new ServiceDisruptor("my-service", "production");
  svc.injectHTTPFaults({ errorRate: 0.2, errorCode: 503, delay: "300ms", duration: "45s" });
}

export default function () {
  const start = Date.now();
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/products`);
  faultImpact.add(Date.now() - start);
  check(res, { "not 503": (r) => r.status !== 503 });
  sleep(0.2);
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `ServiceDisruptor` requires the k6 runner to have `cluster-admin` or a tightly-scoped RBAC role with `pods/exec`, `pods/ephemeralcontainers`, and `services/get` permissions in the target namespace. Always set `duration` on the fault to guarantee cleanup even if the k6 process is killed; the disruptor agent runs independently inside the pod network namespace. [community]

---

### 97. Tag-Filtered Threshold with `abortOnFail` and `delayAbortEval` for Early-Exit SLO Gates  [official]

k6 thresholds support per-tag filtering using `{tagName:tagValue}` syntax appended to the metric name, enabling distinct SLOs per endpoint group without separate metrics. Combined with `abortOnFail: true` and `delayAbortEval: "30s"`, this creates an early-exit gate that fires only after 30 seconds of metric collection — preventing premature abort from cold-start noise. The long-form threshold object syntax (`{ threshold: "...", abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: "30s" }`) must be used; the short-form string array does not support `abortOnFail`. For `k6 cloud run` (non-`--local-execution`), threshold evaluation runs server-side on a ~60-second polling cycle, so `delayAbortEval` values under 60s are effectively ignored — the abort will fire at the next evaluation tick. For immediate abort capability in cloud mode, use `k6 cloud run --local-execution` (k6 v2.0+) which evaluates thresholds on the load generator where the polling delay is eliminated.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/tag-threshold-abort.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: "5m",
  thresholds: {
    // Global error rate gate with early abort
    "http_req_failed": [{ threshold: "rate<0.05", abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: "30s" }],
    // Per-endpoint latency SLOs (tag-filtered, array of expressions)
    "http_req_duration{endpoint:catalog}": ["p(95)<200"],
    // Abort fast if checkout latency explodes
    "http_req_duration{endpoint:checkout}": [
      "p(95)<500",
      { threshold: "p(99)<2000", abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: "30s" },
    ],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/products`, {
    tags: { endpoint: "catalog" },
  });
  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/checkout`,
    JSON.stringify({ cartId: `cart-${__VU}` }),
    {
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      tags: { endpoint: "checkout" },
    },
  );
  check(res, { "checkout success": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** Tag-filtered thresholds only evaluate against requests that carry the matching tag at call time — requests missing the tag contribute to the global (unfiltered) metric but are invisible to tag-filtered thresholds. A common mistake is tagging requests inconsistently (e.g., `endpoint: "Checkout"` vs `endpoint: "checkout"`) resulting in the threshold never receiving matching data-points and silently passing with zero samples. Use a shared constant object for tag values or a helper wrapper function that enforces consistent tag shapes. [official]

---

### 98. `exec.vu.metrics.tags` Dynamic Tag Injection for Per-Iteration Context  [official]

`exec.vu.metrics.tags` provides a mutable tag bag that is automatically attached to all metrics emitted during the current VU iteration. Unlike per-request `tags` options (which must be repeated on every `http.get()` call), `exec.vu.metrics.tags` is set once at the start of an iteration and applies globally — enabling runtime-computed tags such as `user_tier`, `ab_group`, or `region` without modifying every request call site. Tags set via `exec.vu.metrics.tags` persist across the iteration unless explicitly overwritten; they are reset to the VU-level defaults between iterations. High-cardinality tags (user IDs, UUIDs, trace IDs) should be placed in `exec.vu.metrics.metadata` instead — metadata is forwarded to Grafana Cloud k6 as high-cardinality attributes but is excluded from Prometheus/time-series aggregation, preventing label explosion. Only strings, numbers, and booleans are accepted as tag/metadata values.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/dynamic-tag-injection.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import exec from "k6/execution";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

const users = new SharedArray("users", function () {
  return JSON.parse(open("./data/users.json"));
});

export const options = {
  vus: 10, duration: "30s",
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_duration{tier:premium}": ["p(95)<200"],
    "http_req_duration{tier:free}": ["p(95)<800"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const user = users[exec.scenario.iterationInTest % users.length];

  // Inject tier tag — applies to ALL requests in this iteration automatically
  exec.vu.metrics.tags["tier"] = user.tier;          // "premium" | "free"
  exec.vu.metrics.tags["ab_group"] = user.abGroup;   // "control" | "variant"

  // High-cardinality data → metadata (excluded from Prometheus label space)
  exec.vu.metrics.metadata["user_id"] = user.id;

  http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/dashboard`);
  http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/notifications`);
  check(http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/recommendations`), {
    "recommendations 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
  });
  sleep(1);
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `exec.vu.metrics.tags` mutations affect **all** metrics emitted after the assignment, including custom `Trend.add()` calls and check counters — verify that tag semantics are consistent across the iteration. In `ramping-arrival-rate` tests with high VU preallocation, VUs that have not yet been activated still emit lifecycle metrics that will not carry the dynamically-set tag; use `preAllocatedVUs` conservatively to minimize untagged lifecycle noise. [official]

---

### 99. `startTime` Scenario Offset for Sequential Phase Composition Without Separate Scripts  [official]

The `startTime` scenario option delays a scenario's start by a fixed offset from `t=0`, enabling sequential load phases — warmup → soak → spike → cooldown — in a single script file without chaining separate `k6 run` invocations or complex `stages` arrays. Each scenario independently controls its executor, VU count, and duration, so phases can use different executors: a `ramping-vus` warmup followed by a `constant-arrival-rate` soak followed by a `ramping-arrival-rate` spike. Thresholds are evaluated across the full test duration and can be scoped per-scenario using `{ scenario: "scenarioName" }` tag filters. The `gracefulStop` option on each scenario controls how long k6 waits for in-flight iterations to complete before forcefully terminating VUs at phase end — set `gracefulStop: "30s"` for APIs with slow P99 responses to avoid inflating the error rate with forceful termination artifacts.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/phased-load.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_duration{scenario:soak}": ["p(95)<400"],
    "http_req_failed": ["rate<0.01"],
  },
  scenarios: {
    warmup: {
      executor: "ramping-vus",
      startTime: "0s",
      startVUs: 1,
      stages: [{ duration: "30s", target: 10 }],
      gracefulRampDown: "10s",
      gracefulStop: "15s",
    },
    soak: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      startTime: "30s",         // starts after warmup phase ends
      rate: 50, timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 15,
      gracefulStop: "30s",
    },
    spike: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startTime: "150s",        // starts 30s before soak ends (overlap intentional)
      startRate: 50,
      stages: [
        { duration: "15s", target: 200 },
        { duration: "30s", target: 200 },
        { duration: "15s", target: 50 },
      ],
      preAllocatedVUs: 50, maxVUs: 100,
      gracefulStop: "10s",
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/home`);
  check(res, { "home 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `startTime` offsets are relative to the overall test start (`t=0`), not relative to the end of the previous scenario — use `exec.test.abort()` in a sentinel scenario if strict sequential ordering is required. Overlapping scenarios share the VU pool; ensure `preAllocatedVUs` across all scenarios doesn't exceed the machine's available memory. [official]

---

### 100. `gracefulStop` and `gracefulRampDown` Tuning to Prevent False Positive Errors  [official]

`gracefulStop` controls how long k6 waits for running iterations to finish naturally after a scenario's duration expires before forcefully aborting them. `gracefulRampDown` (specific to `ramping-vus`) controls the grace period during the ramp-down phase when VU count is decreasing. Both default to `30s` — insufficient for APIs whose P99 latency exceeds 30s (e.g., async jobs, file processing). When k6 forcefully terminates an iteration mid-flight, the in-flight HTTP request is aborted and counted as a failed request, inflating `http_req_failed` and causing threshold failures that are artifacts of test teardown rather than system behavior. Setting `gracefulStop` to at least `3×P99` of the slowest expected request ensures that all iterations complete naturally. For `ramping-arrival-rate` scenarios, `gracefulStop` also controls the time allowed for the final burst of VUs spawned at the peak arrival rate to complete — set it independently of `gracefulRampDown` since both fire at different lifecycle points.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/graceful-stop-tuning.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

// Scenario processes async job submissions — P99 latency = 8s, so gracefulStop = 30s
export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.02"],
    http_req_duration: ["p(99)<10000"],
  },
  scenarios: {
    job_submit: {
      executor: "ramping-vus",
      startVUs: 5,
      stages: [
        { duration: "1m", target: 20 },
        { duration: "2m", target: 20 },
        { duration: "30s", target: 0 },
      ],
      gracefulRampDown: "30s",  // allow in-flight during ramp-down to complete
      gracefulStop: "30s",      // allow up to 30s after scenario end for stragglers
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Simulate async job submission + poll for completion
  const submit = http.post(
    `${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/jobs`,
    JSON.stringify({ type: "report" }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } },
  );
  check(submit, { "job accepted": (r) => r.status === 202 });

  const jobId = submit.json("jobId");
  let done = false;
  for (let i = 0; i < 10 && !done; i++) {
    const poll = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/jobs/${jobId}`);
    done = poll.json("status") === "complete";
    if (!done) http.get("https://httpbin.test.k6.io/delay/1"); // 1s pacing
  }
  check(http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/jobs/${jobId}`), {
    "job complete": (r) => r.json("status") === "complete",
  });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** Excessively large `gracefulStop` values (e.g., `300s`) cause the test to appear "hung" in CI dashboards because the process does not exit until all iterations complete or the grace period expires. Set `gracefulStop` based on observed P99+buffer, not a blanket large value. For jobs that genuinely can take minutes, use a dedicated `per-vu-iterations` executor where job completion is the natural iteration end condition. [official]

---

### 101. `exec.scenario.iterationInTest` as Globally Unique Fixture Index with Modulo Wrap  [official]

`exec.scenario.iterationInTest` is the only built-in k6 counter guaranteed to be unique across all VUs within a scenario in all execution modes — local, distributed (`--execution-segment`), and Grafana Cloud k6 managed. Unlike `__ITER` (per-VU, not unique across VUs) or `exec.vu.idInTest` (VU identity, not iteration count), `iterationInTest` increments globally and monotonically, though with possible gaps in distributed mode. The standard pattern is modulo indexing into a `SharedArray`: `users[exec.scenario.iterationInTest % users.length]`. For multi-scenario tests requiring cross-scenario uniqueness, combine with a per-scenario seed: `(exec.scenario.iterationInTest + SCENARIO_OFFSET) % users.length` where `SCENARIO_OFFSET` is a constant unique per scenario. In `per-vu-iterations` executor tests, each VU iterates up to `iterations` times — `iterationInTest` still increments globally, so a 10-VU test with 5 iterations each produces `iterationInTest` values from 0 to 49 (with possible interleaving).

```javascript
// k6/scripts/global-unique-index.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import exec from "k6/execution";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

const SCENARIO_OFFSETS = { signup: 0, checkout: 10000, search: 20000 };

const users = new SharedArray("users", function () {
  return JSON.parse(open("./data/30000-users.json"));
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    signup: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 10, timeUnit: "1s", duration: "2m", preAllocatedVUs: 15,
    },
    checkout: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 10, timeUnit: "1s", duration: "2m", preAllocatedVUs: 15,
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const scenarioOffset = SCENARIO_OFFSETS[exec.scenario.name] ?? 0;
  // Globally unique, no collisions between scenarios
  const idx = (exec.scenario.iterationInTest + scenarioOffset) % users.length;
  const user = users[idx];

  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/login`, JSON.stringify({
    email: user.email, password: user.password,
  }), { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } });
  check(res, { "login 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `iterationInTest` may have gaps in distributed mode (`--execution-segment`) because each segment starts its own counter and coordination is not guaranteed. Use modulo indexing (not direct array access) to avoid out-of-bounds errors. For strict sequential unique assignment without any gaps or reuse, use a `SharedArray` with pre-sorted unique IDs and accept that some IDs near the end of the array may be unreachable if fewer iterations complete than planned. [official]

---

### 102. Kubernetes Operator Pattern for Distributed k6 Runs Without Manual Segment Coordination  [community]

The Grafana k6 Kubernetes Operator (`grafana/k6-operator`) eliminates manual `--execution-segment` coordination by managing a fleet of k6 `TestRun` custom resources. Defining a `TestRun` manifest with `parallelism: N` splits the test across N pods automatically, each receiving the correct `--execution-segment` and `--execution-segment-sequence` flags. Metrics from all pods are collected into a single InfluxDB/Prometheus endpoint configured in the `TestRun` spec. The operator handles pod scheduling, waits for all pods to reach `ready` state before starting the test, and tears down all pods on completion or failure — solving the three biggest pain points of manual distributed k6: pod synchronization, metric aggregation, and cleanup on failure. The `TestRun` spec also supports `arguments` for arbitrary `k6 run` flags and `configMap` for injecting test scripts without baking them into the Docker image.

```yaml
# k8s/testrun-distributed.yaml
apiVersion: k6.io/v1alpha1
kind: TestRun
metadata:
  name: api-load-test
spec:
  parallelism: 3                    # spawn 3 k6 pods, each gets 1/3 of the load
  script:
    configMap:
      name: k6-scripts
      file: load-test.js
  arguments: >
    --out influxdb=http://influxdb:8086/k6
    --env BASE_URL=https://staging.example.com
    --tag run_id=ci-${CI_PIPELINE_ID}
  runner:
    image: grafana/k6:latest
    resources:
      requests: { memory: "256Mi", cpu: "250m" }
      limits:   { memory: "512Mi", cpu: "500m" }
    env:
      - name: K6_SECRET_SOURCE
        valueFrom:
          secretKeyRef: { name: k6-secrets, key: source-config }
```

```javascript
// k6/scripts/load-test.js (referenced by ConfigMap above)
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
export const options = {
  vus: 30, duration: "5m",  // 30 VUs × 3 pods = 90 effective VUs
  thresholds: { http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"] },
};
export default function () {
  check(http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/health`), { "up": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** The k6 Kubernetes Operator aggregates metrics at the InfluxDB/Prometheus level but does NOT merge threshold evaluation — each pod evaluates thresholds independently against its own partial metric view, so a threshold like `p(95)<500` will be evaluated on 1/N of the traffic. For accurate threshold evaluation across the full distributed run, use Grafana Cloud k6 managed execution (which aggregates server-side) or post-process the merged metrics dataset after the run. Also note the operator requires CRD installation and RBAC setup in the target cluster. [community]

---

### 103. `k6 cloud project list` as CI Pre-Flight Gate for Multi-Project Account Validation  [official]

`k6 cloud project list --output json` (introduced in k6 v2.0.0) returns a machine-readable list of all Grafana Cloud k6 projects accessible to the configured API token. In CI pipelines managing tests across multiple teams or environments, this command serves as a pre-flight validation gate: run it before `k6 cloud run` to assert that the target `projectID` configured in `options.cloud` actually exists and the token has permission to write to it. A missing project ID causes `k6 cloud run` to fail mid-execution (after VU allocation and billing has started), whereas a pre-flight gate fails fast before any resources are consumed. Pipe the JSON output to `jq -e ".[] | select(.id == $TARGET_PROJECT_ID) | .id"` to assert existence; a non-zero exit code from `jq -e` means the project is missing or inaccessible.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/validate-k6-project.sh
set -euo pipefail

TARGET_PROJECT_ID="${K6_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID:?K6_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID must be set}"
K6_CLOUD_TOKEN="${K6_CLOUD_TOKEN:?K6_CLOUD_TOKEN must be set}"

echo "[pre-flight] Validating k6 Cloud project ${TARGET_PROJECT_ID}..."
PROJECTS=$(K6_CLOUD_TOKEN="${K6_CLOUD_TOKEN}" k6 cloud project list --output json 2>/dev/null)

if ! echo "${PROJECTS}" | jq -e ".[] | select(.id == ${TARGET_PROJECT_ID}) | .id" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "[ERROR] Project ${TARGET_PROJECT_ID} not found or token lacks access."
  echo "Available projects:"
  echo "${PROJECTS}" | jq -r ".[] | \"  \(.id): \(.name)\""
  exit 1
fi
echo "[pre-flight] Project ${TARGET_PROJECT_ID} validated."
```

```javascript
// k6/scripts/cloud-run-validated.js
export const options = {
  cloud: {
    projectID: 3653012,  // validated by ci/validate-k6-project.sh before run
    stackId: __ENV.K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID,  // mandatory in v2.0+
    name: "API Regression Gate",
  },
  vus: 50, duration: "5m",
};
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
export default function () {
  check(http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/status`), { "up": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `k6 cloud project list` makes an authenticated API call to Grafana Cloud on every CI run — at high pipeline frequency this adds ~1-2s latency and contributes to API rate limit consumption. Cache the project list output in CI with a short TTL (e.g., 15 minutes) when the same project ID is used across multiple parallel pipeline jobs. Also note that `options.cloud.stackId` is mandatory in k6 v2.0.0+ — if `stackId` is absent, `k6 cloud run` will fail even with a valid `projectID`. [official]

---

### 104. `--summary-mode=disabled` Migration from Removed `--no-summary` Flag (k6 v2.0.0)  [official]

k6 v2.0.0 removed the `--no-summary` CLI flag and the `--summary-mode=legacy` option as part of the breaking-change cleanup. Scripts or CI commands using `--no-summary` to suppress the end-of-test summary for machine-only pipelines must migrate to `--summary-mode=disabled`. The `--summary-mode` flag accepts three values: `compact` (new default, abbreviated table), `full` (previous default, detailed per-check breakdown), and `disabled` (suppresses all summary output). CI pipelines that parse the end-of-test summary via `handleSummary()` are unaffected — `handleSummary()` receives the full summary data object regardless of `--summary-mode`. The migration is a one-line find-and-replace in CI config files; however, `--no-summary` in older k6 scripts will cause a "flag provided but not defined" error at startup in v2.0.0+, so the migration is blocking for any CI pipeline that hasn't been updated.

```bash
# Before (k6 v1.x): suppress summary output in CI
# k6 run --no-summary --out influxdb=http://influxdb:8086/k6 script.js

# After (k6 v2.0+): equivalent command
# k6 run --summary-mode=disabled --out influxdb=http://influxdb:8086/k6 script.js

# Audit all usages in repo before v2.0 migration:
# grep -rn '\-\-no-summary' .ci/ scripts/ Makefile Dockerfile
```

```javascript
// k6/scripts/summary-migration-demo.js
// handleSummary fires regardless of --summary-mode value
import { textSummary } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.1.0/index.js";

export function handleSummary(data) {
  // Always called — use for machine-readable output (CI analytics, Slack, etc.)
  return {
    stdout: textSummary(data, { indent: " ", enableColors: false }),
    "/tmp/k6-summary.json": JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
  };
}

import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
export const options = { vus: 5, duration: "15s" };
export default function () {
  check(http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/ping`), { "pong": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

> **Tradeoff:** `--summary-mode=compact` (the new default in v2.0.0) displays fewer rows than the old default — teams relying on the full per-check breakdown in their CI logs must explicitly add `--summary-mode=full` to restore the previous verbosity. If your CI pipeline grepped the summary output for specific strings (e.g., checking for `✓` pass/fail indicators), the compact format may have changed those strings — prefer `handleSummary()` JSON output for machine-readable CI parsing rather than screen-scraping the summary table. [official]

---

### 105. Go Module Path Migration for xk6 Extension Authors (k6 v2.0.0)  [official]

k6 v2.0.0 updated its Go module path from `go.k6.io/k6` to `go.k6.io/k6/v2`. Any xk6 extension that imports k6 core packages (`go.k6.io/k6/js/modules`, `go.k6.io/k6/lib`, `go.k6.io/k6/metrics`) must update its `go.mod` and all import statements before it can be built against k6 v2.0.0. The migration is mechanical: update `go.mod` and find-replace all import paths. Extension authors must also remove usage of deleted APIs: the `externally-controlled` executor, HTTP server APIs, and `options.ext.loadimpact` config shim. Extensions that have not been updated will fail to compile against k6 v2.0.0 with import resolution errors — `xk6 build` will report the exact incompatible import paths. The k6 extension registry at `registry.k6.io` tracks which extensions have been updated; the automatic extension resolution feature (v1.7.0+) will refuse to provision an extension whose latest release is incompatible with the running k6 version.

```go
// xk6-my-extension/module.go — updated for k6 v2.0.0
package myextension

import (
    // Before: "go.k6.io/k6/js/modules"
    // After:
    "go.k6.io/k6/v2/js/modules"
)

type MyExtension struct{}

func (m *MyExtension) Exports() modules.Exports {
    return modules.Exports{
        Named: map[string]interface{}{
            "doSomething": m.DoSomething,
        },
    }
}

func (m *MyExtension) DoSomething() string {
    return "hello from v2 extension"
}

func init() {
    modules.Register("k6/x/my-extension", new(MyExtension))
}

// go.mod — before: require go.k6.io/k6 v1.7.0
// go.mod — after:  require go.k6.io/k6/v2 v2.0.0
```

> **Tradeoff:** The module path change is a one-time migration but requires a coordinated release — extension consumers that pin to a specific extension version in `xk6 build --with k6/x/my-extension@v0.3.0` will continue to use the v1-compatible release indefinitely until they explicitly upgrade. Publish a v2-compatible release with a minor or major version bump and clearly document the k6 version requirements in the extension's README. Extensions that wrap C libraries via cgo are additionally impacted if they use k6's VU runtime for cgo allocation — test against k6 v2.0.0 specifically as the runtime internals also changed. [official]

## Cycle 37 — Community Gotchas

### Gotcha 135. `csv.parse()` inside `SharedArray` requires the async constructor form — the sync form silently stores a Promise object instead of row data  [community]

**WHY:** `csv.parse()` returns a `Promise<string[][]>`, not a synchronous array. The `SharedArray` constructor's callback is called synchronously by default, and returning a Promise from a sync callback causes `SharedArray` to store the Promise object rather than its resolved value. When VU code indexes into the resulting `SharedArray`, it receives `Promise {}` objects instead of row arrays — causing silent `undefined` property accesses that produce NaN values in metric calculations or `null` bodies in HTTP requests. The bug is invisible during `k6 run --vus 1` if any value is truthy (a Promise object is truthy), and only reveals itself when rows are actually used in string interpolation or JSON serialization, often hours into a long soak test.

**Fix:** Use the async-capable `SharedArray` constructor form by wrapping the initialization in an async function: `new SharedArray("name", async function() { const file = await open("data.csv"); return await csv.parse(file, { skipFirstLine: true }); })`. As of k6 v2.0.0, async `SharedArray` initialization is fully supported. Verify initialization with a post-construction assertion: `if (typeof users[0] !== "object" || users[0] === null) throw new Error("SharedArray init failed — check csv.parse() async usage")`.

---

### Gotcha 136. `k6/experimental/fs` `open()` called inside `default()` exhausts OS file descriptors at scale  [community]

**WHY:** `open()` is designed for the init context and creates a kernel file descriptor per call. Calling it inside `default()` creates a new descriptor every iteration — with 50 VUs running 100 iterations each, 5,000 descriptors are opened. Most Linux systems default to a `ulimit -n` of 1,024 per process; k6 will throw "too many open files" errors at iteration ~1,000. The error surfaces as a generic JS runtime exception rather than an OS error, and the stack trace points to the `open()` call without explaining the file descriptor exhaustion. A common misreading of the module docs leads developers to place `open()` inside `default()` because the function is async and they believe init context does not support `async/await`.

**Fix:** Call `await open(path)` once at module scope (init context) and store the resulting `File` in a module-level variable: `const filePromise = open("./data.bin")`. Inside `default()`, use `const file = await filePromise` — awaiting an already-resolved Promise is near-instantaneous and returns the same handle. Each VU shares the underlying memory-mapped file but maintains its own cursor, so concurrent reads are safe as long as each VU seeks to its intended offset before reading.

---

### Gotcha 137. `abortOnFail` with a `gracefulStop` longer than in-flight request time inflates post-abort error counts  [community]

**WHY:** When `abortOnFail` fires, k6 sends a stop signal to all VUs. VUs that are mid-iteration are given `gracefulStop` seconds to finish. If `gracefulStop` is 30s but a VU is awaiting a 45s async job poll, the VU is forcefully terminated at T+30s, and the in-flight request is counted as an error. This creates a paradox: the threshold that triggered `abortOnFail` was designed to stop load on a broken system, but the forced termination itself generates additional error metrics that appear in the final summary. Teams debugging failures see a higher error count than the threshold's trigger count, leading to confusion about whether there were two distinct failure modes or one.

**Fix:** Set `gracefulStop` to a value shorter than the expected safe retry budget — not longer than the longest in-flight request. For async job tests, add an explicit timeout inside `default()` that cancels the polling loop and exits the iteration cleanly before `gracefulStop` fires: use a `startTime` local variable and break from the poll loop when `(Date.now() - startTime) > gracefulStopMs - buffer`. Log "iteration aborted by local timeout" to distinguish self-terminated iterations from forced terminations in post-mortem analysis.

---

### Gotcha 138. Setting `exec.vu.metrics.tags` to a non-string/non-number/non-boolean value silently no-ops — no error, no tag, no warning  [community]

**WHY:** k6's metrics system only accepts strings, numbers, and booleans as tag values. Assigning an object (`exec.vu.metrics.tags["meta"] = { env: "prod" }`) or `undefined` (`exec.vu.metrics.tags["region"] = __ENV.REGION`) when `REGION` is not set silently discards the assignment. The tag is not emitted with the metrics, threshold expressions that filter by that tag receive zero samples, and the threshold silently passes with no data — the same silent-pass failure mode as duplicate threshold keys. The absence of any console warning makes this especially dangerous: developers believe tagging is working because no error is thrown.

**Fix:** Validate tag values before assignment with a helper: `function safeTag(key, value) { const v = String(value ?? ""); if (v === "" || v === "undefined") { console.warn("[tagging] empty tag dropped: " + key); return; } exec.vu.metrics.tags[key] = v; }`. For environment variables used as tags, add a startup assertion in `setup()`: `["REGION","TIER","ENV"].forEach(k => { if (!__ENV[k]) throw new Error("Required env var " + k + " missing") })`.

---

### Gotcha 139. `k6 cloud project list` exits with code 0 and an empty JSON array when the token is expired — not a non-zero exit code  [community]

**WHY:** The Grafana Cloud k6 API returns HTTP 200 with an empty JSON array `[]` when the token is valid but has no project access, and also when the token is expired on some legacy account configurations. A CI pre-flight script that checks only the exit code (`if k6 cloud project list; then ...`) incorrectly infers success from exit code 0 even when the empty array indicates an access problem. The test then proceeds to `k6 cloud run` which fails with a 401 or "no projects found" error after VU allocation and cloud infrastructure spin-up, wasting billing minutes and CI time. The inconsistency between `k6 cloud project list` (silent empty) and `k6 cloud run` (hard fail) is a known UX gap documented in community issue trackers.

**Fix:** Always validate both the exit code AND the array length: `PROJECTS=$(k6 cloud project list --output json); if [ -z "$PROJECTS" ] || [ "$(echo "$PROJECTS" | jq length)" -eq 0 ]; then echo "ERROR: no projects accessible — verify K6_CLOUD_TOKEN"; exit 1; fi`. Separately validate that `jq` successfully parsed the output (non-empty, valid JSON) before the length check to distinguish a real empty-projects response from a network error returning non-JSON.

---

### Gotcha 140. `options.cloud.stackId` is mandatory in k6 v2.0.0 but silently accepted in v1.x — omitting it causes a hard fail that looks like a network error  [community]

**WHY:** k6 v2.0.0 enforces `options.cloud.stackId` (the Grafana Cloud organization stack identifier) as a required field for all cloud runs, removing the v1.x behavior of falling back to the first available stack. When `stackId` is absent, `k6 cloud run` fails with an error message that references "stack selection" which developers unfamiliar with Grafana Cloud terminology interpret as a network connectivity or authentication issue. CI pipelines migrating from v1.x to v2.0.0 hit this breakage even when no other options changed, because v1.x scripts never needed `stackId`. The error is particularly confusing in environments that run k6 v1.x and v2.0.0 side-by-side — the same script works on v1.x runners and fails on v2.0.0 runners with a message that doesn't clearly indicate the missing field.

**Fix:** Add `stackId` to `options.cloud` in all scripts, sourced from an environment variable for portability: `cloud: { stackId: __ENV.K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID, projectID: parseInt(__ENV.K6_CLOUD_PROJECT_ID), name: "My Test" }`. Add a startup validation in `setup()`: `if (!__ENV.K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID) console.warn("[cloud] K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID not set — cloud runs will fail in v2.0+")`. Run `grep -rn "options.cloud" . | grep -v stackId` in your test repository to find scripts that need updating before the v2.0.0 migration.

### 106. TypeScript-Native Test Modules (k6 v1.0+)  [official]

k6 v1.0 introduced first-class TypeScript support: `.ts` files are executed directly without a build step. The runtime uses esbuild to strip type annotations before execution — it does not perform type checking, but it does enable type-annotated test code, IDE autocompletion via `@types/k6`, and refactor-safe imports. Pass a `.ts` file directly to `k6 run` with no transpilation pipeline required. The `tsconfig.json` bundled by esbuild uses `"target": "ES2022"` and `"module": "ESNext"` — override with a project-level `tsconfig.json` in the same directory as the test file.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/typed-api-test.ts — TypeScript-native k6 test (no build step)
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Options } from "k6/options";
import { Counter, Trend } from "k6/metrics";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

// Type-safe options object — IDE catches typos at author time
export const options: Options = {
  scenarios: {
    typed_load: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate: 5,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 100,
      stages: [
        { target: 20, duration: "30s" },
        { target: 50, duration: "1m" },
        { target: 50, duration: "2m" },
        { target: 0,  duration: "15s" },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

interface User {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  password: string;
}

interface AuthPayload {
  token: string;
}

const users = new SharedArray<User>("users", function () {
  return JSON.parse(open("./data/users.json")) as User[];
});

const loginErrors = new Counter("login_errors");
const loginLatency = new Trend("login_latency_ms", true);

export function setup(): AuthPayload {
  const res = http.post(
    `${__ENV.API_URL}/api/auth/login`,
    JSON.stringify({ email: users[0].email, password: users[0].password }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } }
  );
  if (res.status !== 200) throw new Error(`Setup auth failed: ${res.status}`);
  return { token: res.json("token") as string };
}

export default function (data: AuthPayload): void {
  const user = users[__VU % users.length];
  const start = Date.now();
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/profile/${user.id}`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${data.token}` },
  });
  loginLatency.add(Date.now() - start);
  const ok = check(res, {
    "profile 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "has email":   (r) => (r.json("email") as string) === user.email,
  });
  if (!ok) loginErrors.add(1);
  sleep(0.5);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** esbuild strips types but does NOT type-check — TypeScript errors (wrong argument types, missing fields) are invisible at runtime unless you run `tsc --noEmit` as a separate CI step. The development workflow is: author with IDE type errors visible, CI runs `tsc --noEmit` as a lint gate, then `k6 run` executes the `.ts` file directly. Do not rely on k6's runtime to catch type errors. [official]

### 107. `k6/experimental/csv` Bulk Parse with `asObject` for Named-Column Access  [official]

`csv.parse()` with `{ asObject: true }` returns an array of plain objects keyed by the first-row header names instead of raw arrays of strings. This eliminates positional index fragility — adding a column to the CSV no longer shifts indices and breaks the test. The full file is parsed in Go before VU init, shared in a `SharedArray` for memory efficiency, and each VU receives a reference (not a copy). Use `{ skipFirstLine: true }` without `asObject` only when the CSV has no header row and you want maximum parse speed with positional access.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/csv-named-columns.js — CSV with named columns via asObject
import csv from "k6/experimental/csv";
import { open } from "k6/experimental/fs";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

// Init context: parse CSV once, share across all VUs
// CSV format:  username,password,role,tenant_id
const credFile = await open("./data/credentials.csv");
const credentials = new SharedArray("creds", async function () {
  return await csv.parse(credFile, { asObject: true });
  // Each row: { username: "alice", password: "s3cr3t", role: "admin", tenant_id: "t001" }
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    multi_tenant: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 50,
      duration: "3m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<400"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.005"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.API_URL || "http://localhost:3001";

export default function () {
  const cred = credentials[__VU % credentials.length];
  // Named access — resilient to column reordering
  const res = http.post(`${BASE}/api/login`, JSON.stringify({
    username:  cred.username,
    password:  cred.password,
    tenant_id: cred.tenant_id,
  }), { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } });

  check(res, {
    "login ok":     (r) => r.status === 200,
    "role matches": (r) => r.json("role") === cred.role,
  });
  sleep(0.3);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `asObject: true` incurs a ~15% higher memory cost versus raw array mode because each row becomes a JS object with string keys. For CSVs with millions of rows this matters; for typical fixture files (< 100K rows) the memory overhead is negligible and the maintainability gain is worth it. Large CSVs with `asObject: true` should be profiled with `k6 run --log-level debug` to observe `SharedArray` init time. [official]

### 108. `page.route()` Network Mocking in Browser Tests  [official]

`page.route(urlPattern, handler)` intercepts browser requests matching a URL pattern or regex. Use it to stub third-party APIs (analytics, payments, auth) that cannot be controlled in a load test environment, block costly resource loads (images, fonts) to isolate rendering performance metrics, and inject synthetic slow responses to test loading-state UI. The handler receives a `Route` object with three verbs: `route.abort()` (block), `route.fulfill({ status, body, headers })` (return a synthetic response), and `route.continue({ headers, postData })` (forward, optionally mutated).

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-mocked-api.js — block images, stub third-party, intercept auth
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mocked_browser: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 3,
      duration: "2m",
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "browser_web_vital_lcp": ["p(75)<2500"],
    checks:                  ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.APP_URL || "http://localhost:3000";

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    // 1. Block all image requests to reduce network noise
    await page.route(/\.(png|jpg|jpeg|gif|webp|ico)$/i, async (route) => {
      await route.abort();
    });

    // 2. Stub third-party analytics beacon
    await page.route(/analytics\.example\.com/, async (route) => {
      await route.fulfill({ status: 200, body: "{}" });
    });

    // 3. Intercept and add correlation header to all API calls
    await page.route(/\/api\//, async (route) => {
      await route.continue({
        headers: { ...route.request().headers(), "X-Load-Test": "true" },
      });
    });

    await page.goto(`${BASE}/dashboard`);
    await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");

    const heading = page.getByRole("heading", { level: 1 });
    await heading.waitFor({ state: "visible" });
    check(await heading.textContent(), {
      "dashboard heading visible": (t) => t != null && t.length > 0,
    });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Route handlers execute in the browser scenario's async context. If a handler `await`s a slow external resource, it can block other route handlers for the same page. Keep handlers synchronous when possible or use `route.fulfill()` with static responses. Also: only the **last** registered route handler matching a URL runs — register specific patterns before broad catch-all patterns to avoid shadowing. [official]

---

### 109. `page.waitForEvent()` Event-Gate Synchronization  [official]

`page.waitForEvent(event, opts?)` pauses execution until a specific browser event fires — `"download"`, `"filechooser"`, `"popup"`, `"console"`, `"request"`, `"response"`. This is the preferred pattern for testing file downloads, popup window flows, and multi-page user journeys that would otherwise require fragile `sleep()` calls or `waitForLoadState()` with incorrect states. Supply a `predicate` function to filter events by attribute (e.g., only match a specific popup URL) and a `timeout` in milliseconds to fail the test if the event never arrives.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-download-test.js — file download via waitForEvent
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    download_flow: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 2,
      duration: "1m",
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: { checks: ["rate>0.99"] },
};

const BASE = __ENV.APP_URL || "http://localhost:3000";

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${BASE}/reports`);
    await page.waitForLoadState("domcontentloaded");

    // waitForEvent and the click must race — start the event listener first
    const [download] = await Promise.all([
      page.waitForEvent("download", { timeout: 15000 }),
      page.getByRole("button", { name: "Export CSV" }).click(),
    ]);

    // download.suggestedFilename() is available after the event resolves
    check(download.suggestedFilename(), {
      "download filename is CSV": (fn) => fn.endsWith(".csv"),
    });

    // Cancel the download (we only want to verify the event fired)
    await download.cancel();
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `waitForEvent()` requires the browser to support the underlying CDP event. Some events (`"console"`, `"pageerror"`) fire frequently and may generate noise in long sessions. For popup tests, ensure the action that triggers the popup is executed inside the same `Promise.all()` block as `waitForEvent("popup")` — racing them sequentially causes the event to be missed if the popup opens before the listener is registered. [official]

---

### 110. `locator.pressSequentially()` for Realistic Keyboard-Input Simulation  [official]

`locator.pressSequentially(text, { delay: ms })` types each character of `text` with individual `keydown`, `keypress`, `input`, and `keyup` events, with an optional inter-character delay. This triggers JavaScript input validators, auto-complete dropdowns, and debounce-based search handlers that would be bypassed by `locator.fill()` (which sets the value property directly without individual keystroke events). Use `delay: 50` to simulate ~120 WPM typing; omit `delay` for maximum speed in throughput tests where realistic pacing is not required.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-search-autocomplete.js — test autocomplete widget under load
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    autocomplete_load: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 3,
      duration: "2m",
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "browser_web_vital_fcp": ["p(75)<1500"],
    checks:                  ["rate>0.98"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.APP_URL || "http://localhost:3000";

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${BASE}/search`);
    await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");

    const searchBox = page.getByRole("searchbox", { name: "Search products" });
    await searchBox.click();

    // Type character by character — triggers input events and debounced autocomplete
    await searchBox.pressSequentially("laptop pro", { delay: 60 });

    // Wait for autocomplete dropdown to appear
    const dropdown = page.getByRole("listbox");
    await dropdown.waitFor({ state: "visible", timeout: 5000 });

    const firstOption = dropdown.getByRole("option").first();
    check(await firstOption.textContent(), {
      "autocomplete result visible": (t) => t != null && t.length > 0,
    });

    // Select the first result and verify navigation
    await firstOption.click();
    await page.waitForURL(/\/products\//, { timeout: 5000 });
    check(page.url(), {
      "navigated to product page": (url) => url.includes("/products/"),
    });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `pressSequentially()` with `delay` is significantly slower than `fill()` — typing "laptop pro" at 60ms/char takes ~600ms per iteration. For autofill-form perf tests where typing realism matters for correctness but not for pacing, use `delay: 0` (fastest). For soak tests of debounced-search backend handlers, use `delay: 100-200` to prevent every VU from firing simultaneous searches at the exact same millisecond. [official]

### 111. `locator.filter()` for Scoped Element Selection in Complex UIs  [official]

`locator.filter({ hasText, hasNotText, has, hasNot })` narrows a multi-element locator match to items meeting a predicate — without changing the selector. This is cleaner than chaining multiple `.getBy*()` calls when the target element's identity depends on sibling or child content. `hasText` accepts a string (substring match, case-insensitive) or a `RegExp`. `has` accepts a child locator, enabling "find the card that contains a button labelled Submit." The method was introduced in k6 v1.3.0 alongside the full `getBy*` methods for frames and nested locators.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-table-row-filter.js — filter table rows by status badge
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    table_interaction: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 2,
      duration: "1m",
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: { checks: ["rate>0.99"] },
};

const BASE = __ENV.APP_URL || "http://localhost:3000";

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${BASE}/orders`);
    await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");

    const rows = page.getByRole("row");

    // Filter: only rows whose status badge says "Pending"
    const pendingRows = rows.filter({
      has: page.getByRole("status").filter({ hasText: "Pending" }),
    });

    const pendingCount = await pendingRows.count();
    check(pendingCount, {
      "pending orders visible": (n) => n >= 0,
    });

    if (pendingCount > 0) {
      // Interact only with the first Pending row's action button
      const firstPendingApprove = pendingRows.first().getByRole("button", { name: "Approve" });
      await firstPendingApprove.waitFor({ state: "visible" });
      check(await firstPendingApprove.isEnabled(), {
        "approve button enabled": (ok) => ok === true,
      });
    }
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `locator.filter()` with `has` creates a nested locator query evaluated inside the browser. For tables with thousands of rows, this can be slow — prefer a more specific initial selector to reduce the initial match set before filtering. `hasText` with a RegExp is faster than `has` with a child locator because it evaluates as a CSS `:has-text` pseudo-class rather than a full sub-tree locator walk. [official]

---

### 112. `k6/experimental/streams` ReadableStream for Incremental Large-File Processing  [official]

The Streams API (`k6/experimental/streams`) implements the WHATWG ReadableStream specification. Use it to process large fixture files or response streams line-by-line without loading the full content into memory. The `ReadableStream` constructor accepts a `start(controller)` method that enqueues chunks and a `pull(controller)` method called when the consumer is ready for more data. Pair with `k6/experimental/fs` for chunked file reads, or with `http.asyncRequest()` for streaming HTTP response bodies.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/streaming-fixture-loader.js — stream large JSON-Lines fixture file
import { ReadableStream } from "k6/experimental/streams";
import { open } from "k6/experimental/fs";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

// Stream-process a large JSONL file at init, storing only the first 1000 rows
const fixtureFile = await open("./data/events-large.jsonl");

const events = new SharedArray("events", async function () {
  const rows = [];
  const decoder = new TextDecoder();
  let remainder = "";

  const stream = new ReadableStream({
    async pull(controller) {
      const buf = new Uint8Array(64 * 1024); // 64 KB chunks
      const result = await fixtureFile.read(buf);
      if (result === null) { controller.close(); return; }
      const text = remainder + decoder.decode(buf.subarray(0, result));
      const lines = text.split("\n");
      remainder = lines.pop() ?? "";          // keep incomplete trailing line
      for (const line of lines) {
        if (line.trim()) rows.push(JSON.parse(line));
        if (rows.length >= 1000) { controller.close(); return; }
      }
      controller.enqueue(null); // signal: ready for more
    },
  });

  const reader = stream.getReader();
  while (true) {
    const { done } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;
  }
  return rows;
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    event_ingest: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 100,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 50,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<200"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.API_URL || "http://localhost:3001";

export default function () {
  const event = events[__VU % events.length];
  const res = http.post(`${BASE}/api/events`, JSON.stringify(event), {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  });
  check(res, { "event accepted": (r) => r.status === 202 });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** The `pull()` model gives fine-grained memory control but requires careful handling of the `remainder` buffer for line-delimited formats — a common bug is forgetting to prepend the partial last line. For files under 50MB, `csv.parse()` or `open()` + `JSON.parse()` are simpler. Use streams only when the file size exceeds available VU memory or when you need to start test execution before the fixture is fully loaded. [official]

---

### 113. `k6 deps` Command for CI Extension Dependency Analysis  [official]

`k6 deps [script]` inspects all `import` statements in a script (and transitive imports) and outputs the list of k6 extension modules required to build a custom k6 binary. Use `--json` for machine-readable output suitable for CI gates. Integrate into CI pipelines as a pre-run step that validates extension pinning and surfaces extension drift before the `xk6 build` step. As of k6 v1.6.0, `k6 deps` only recognizes ES module `import` statements — CommonJS `require()` calls are invisible to it.

```bash
# ci/check-extensions.sh — verify all script extensions are pinned and buildable
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT="${1:-k6/scripts/load.js}"
DEPS_JSON=$(k6 deps --json "$SCRIPT")

echo "Extensions required for $SCRIPT:"
echo "$DEPS_JSON" | jq -r '.[] | "  \(.name) @ \(.version // "latest")"'

# Gate: fail if any extension has no version pin (version is null)
UNPINNED=$(echo "$DEPS_JSON" | jq '[.[] | select(.version == null)] | length')
if [ "$UNPINNED" -gt 0 ]; then
  echo "ERROR: $UNPINNED unpinned extension(s) found."
  echo "$DEPS_JSON" | jq '[.[] | select(.version == null)]'
  exit 1
fi

echo "All extensions pinned. Building..."
BUILD_ARGS=$(echo "$DEPS_JSON" | jq -r '.[] | "--with \(.name)@\(.version)"' | tr '\n' ' ')
eval "xk6 build $BUILD_ARGS --output ./k6-custom"
echo "Build successful: ./k6-custom"
```

```javascript
// k6/scripts/load-with-extensions.js — pinned extension imports visible to k6 deps
import { Producer } from "k6/x/kafka";   // xk6-kafka v2.0.0 — k6 deps detects this
import { Client }   from "k6/x/redis";   // xk6-redis v0.4.0 — k6 deps detects this
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: { mixed: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 10, duration: "1m" } },
  thresholds: { http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"] },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(__ENV.API_URL + "/health");
  check(res, { "healthy": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `k6 deps` does static import analysis — dynamic imports (`import(expr)`) and runtime `require()` calls are invisible. Scripts that conditionally load extensions at runtime will appear extension-free to `k6 deps`. For full accuracy, annotate conditional extension usage with a top-level dummy import wrapped in a dead-code block that static analysis can still see. [official]

---

### 114. `k6-totp` TOTP Code Generation for 2FA-Protected APIs  [official]

The `k6-totp` jslib library generates RFC 6238 TOTP codes. Use it to load-test APIs or UIs that require a second-factor code in the authentication flow. The secret is a base32-encoded seed stored per test user in a fixture file. Rotate fixture users rather than sharing a single TOTP secret across VUs to avoid rate-limit collisions when multiple VUs generate the same code in the same 30-second window.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/totp-auth-flow.js — authenticate with TOTP 2FA per VU
import http from "k6/http";
import { totp } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-contrib/0.1.0/totp.js";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

// Each user has their own TOTP secret — prevents code collisions between VUs
const users = new SharedArray("mfa-users", function () {
  return JSON.parse(open("./data/mfa-users.json"));
  // Format: [{ email, password, totpSecret: "JBSWY3DP..." }, ...]
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mfa_login: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 10,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 15,
      maxVUs: 30,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<600"],  // MFA adds latency — widen SLO
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.API_URL || "http://localhost:3001";

export default function () {
  const user = users[__VU % users.length];

  // Step 1: Password auth
  const loginRes = http.post(`${BASE}/api/auth/password`, JSON.stringify({
    email: user.email, password: user.password,
  }), { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } });

  check(loginRes, { "password auth ok": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  if (loginRes.status !== 200) { sleep(1); return; }
  const sessionToken = loginRes.json("sessionToken");

  // Step 2: Generate current TOTP code from per-user secret
  // Guard window boundary: sleep if < 2s remain in current 30s window
  const remaining = 30 - (Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) % 30);
  if (remaining < 2) sleep(remaining + 0.1);
  const code = totp(user.totpSecret);

  // Step 3: Submit TOTP code to complete 2FA
  const mfaRes = http.post(`${BASE}/api/auth/totp`, JSON.stringify({ code }), {
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Authorization": `Bearer ${sessionToken}`,
    },
  });
  check(mfaRes, { "totp verified": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.5);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** TOTP codes are valid for a 30-second window. Without the window-boundary guard, a code generated at second 29 may expire before the HTTP request arrives, causing spurious 401s. The guard adds up to 2 seconds of sleep per iteration — account for this in your VU count and arrival-rate calculations when designing throughput targets for 2FA-protected flows. [official]

---

### 115. `browser_web_vital_inp` INP Metric Migration from Deprecated FID  [official]

k6 v1.6.0 deprecated `browser_web_vital_fid` (First Input Delay) in favour of `browser_web_vital_inp` (Interaction to Next Paint), aligning with Google's Core Web Vitals update (FID retired March 2024). INP measures total interaction latency including processing and rendering time, making it a more representative metric for interactive performance. INP is emitted per interaction event; k6 records the worst-case INP value across all interactions in the page session. Set thresholds on INP; FID thresholds pass trivially with zero samples once the metric is no longer emitted.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-inp-threshold.js — INP-based interactive performance gate
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    interactive_perf: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 3,
      duration: "3m",
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // Good INP < 200ms, Needs Improvement < 500ms, Poor >= 500ms (Core Web Vitals 2024)
    "browser_web_vital_inp": ["p(75)<200"],
    "browser_web_vital_lcp": ["p(75)<2500"],
    "browser_web_vital_cls": ["p(75)<0.1"],
    // browser_web_vital_fid REMOVED — use inp
    checks: ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.APP_URL || "http://localhost:3000";

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${BASE}/products`);
    await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");

    // Trigger interactions that INP will measure
    const filterBtn = page.getByRole("button", { name: "Filter" });
    await filterBtn.click();  // INP measures click → paint latency

    const priceSlider = page.getByRole("slider", { name: "Max Price" });
    if (await priceSlider.count() > 0) {
      await priceSlider.click();
    }

    await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");
    const productCards = page.getByRole("article");
    check(await productCards.count(), {
      "products rendered after filter": (n) => n > 0,
    });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** INP requires at least one interaction event to be emitted — `browser_web_vital_inp` will be absent from metrics output for navigation-only tests (no click/keyboard events). Teams migrating from FID-based dashboards should add `browser_web_vital_inp` panels before removing FID panels to avoid a monitoring gap. Run with `--log-level debug` to confirm INP samples are appearing. [official]

---

### 116. `locator.evaluate()` for In-Browser DOM Property Assertions  [official]

`locator.evaluate(fn, arg?)` executes a JavaScript function in the browser's page context, passing the matched DOM element as the first argument. Unlike `locator.textContent()` or `locator.getAttribute()`, `evaluate()` gives direct access to the full DOM API — computed styles, bounding rects, custom element properties, and any JavaScript state set by the application. Use it for assertions that the k6 browser API does not expose natively, such as checking CSS custom property values or reading a web component's internal state.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-dom-assertions.js — evaluate computed style and custom properties
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    dom_check: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 2,
      duration: "1m",
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: { checks: ["rate>0.99"] },
};

const BASE = __ENV.APP_URL || "http://localhost:3000";

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${BASE}/dashboard`);
    await page.waitForLoadState("networkidle");

    const alertBanner = page.getByRole("alert");

    // evaluate() passes the DOM element — run full JS in the page context
    const isHidden = await alertBanner.evaluate((el) => {
      const style = window.getComputedStyle(el);
      return style.display === "none" || style.visibility === "hidden";
    });
    check(isHidden, {
      "alert banner not visible on load": (hidden) => hidden === true,
    });

    // Read a CSS custom property from an element
    const themeColor = await page.getByTestId("theme-preview").evaluate((el) => {
      return window.getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue("--theme-color").trim();
    });
    check(themeColor, {
      "theme color is set": (color) => color.startsWith("#") || color.startsWith("rgb"),
    });

    // Read a web component's internal value property
    const sliderValue = await page.getByRole("slider").evaluate((el) => el.value);
    check(sliderValue, {
      "slider has default value": (v) => v !== "" && v !== undefined,
    });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `evaluate()` serializes the return value via structured clone — DOM nodes, functions, and closures cannot be returned. If the function throws inside the browser, the error propagates as a k6 runtime error (not a `check()` failure), potentially aborting the VU iteration. Wrap `evaluate()` calls in try/catch when the element may not be present, or use `locator.count()` before `evaluate()` to guard against empty locators. [official]

---

### 117. `page.waitForURL()` SPA Navigation Gate  [official]

`page.waitForURL(urlOrPattern, opts?)` blocks until the page URL matches a string, glob, or RegExp — the idiomatic way to assert that a Single Page Application has completed a client-side route transition. Unlike `waitForLoadState("networkidle")` which can resolve prematurely, `waitForURL()` directly observes the history API and fires as soon as `window.history.pushState()` or a hash change sets the expected URL. Supply `{ timeout: ms }` to fail fast on navigation hangs. Added in k6 v1.2.0 alongside `page.route()` and the full `getBy*` locator family.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-spa-navigation.js — assert SPA route transitions
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    spa_flow: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 3,
      duration: "2m",
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "browser_web_vital_lcp": ["p(75)<2500"],
    checks:                  ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.APP_URL || "http://localhost:3000";

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    // Step 1: Landing → Login
    await page.goto(`${BASE}/`);
    await page.getByRole("link", { name: "Sign In" }).click();
    await page.waitForURL(`${BASE}/login`, { timeout: 5000 });
    check(page.url(), { "navigated to /login": (u) => u.endsWith("/login") });

    // Step 2: Login → Dashboard (SPA client-side route change)
    await page.getByLabel("Email").fill(__ENV.TEST_USER_EMAIL || "test@example.com");
    await page.getByLabel("Password").fill(__ENV.TEST_USER_PASS || "password");
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Sign In" }).click();

    // waitForURL fires precisely when /dashboard appears in window.location
    await page.waitForURL(/\/dashboard(\/.*)?$/, { timeout: 10000 });
    check(page.url(), { "navigated to /dashboard": (u) => u.includes("/dashboard") });

    // Step 3: Sub-route via breadcrumb link
    await page.getByRole("link", { name: "Analytics" }).click();
    await page.waitForURL(`${BASE}/dashboard/analytics`, { timeout: 5000 });
    check(page.url(), { "analytics sub-route": (u) => u.endsWith("/analytics") });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `waitForURL()` is a navigation gate, not a content-ready gate — the URL may match before API data has loaded. Combine it with a subsequent `waitForLoadState("networkidle")` or a `locator.waitFor({ state: "visible" })` on a key element when you need both navigation and content readiness. For hash-routed SPAs (`#/dashboard`), pass the full URL including the hash fragment — `waitForURL()` supports hash changes. [official]

---

### 118. `--summary-mode=json` Machine-Readable CI Summary  [official]

`--summary-mode=json` (stable since k6 v2.0.0, previewed as `--new-machine-readable-summary` in v1.5.0) outputs the end-of-test summary as a JSON document to stdout, replacing the human-readable text table. Use it in CI pipelines to parse threshold results, extract p95 latency values, and post structured test reports to PR comments, Slack, or dashboards without screen-scraping ANSI text. The JSON contains: `metrics` (all metric values with stats), `thresholds` (per-threshold pass/fail + value), and `root_group` (check tree).

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# ci/k6-summary-gate.sh — run k6 and post structured results to GitHub PR
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT="${1:-k6/scripts/load.js}"
SUMMARY_FILE="results/summary.json"
mkdir -p results

# --summary-mode=json writes JSON to stdout; progress to stderr
k6 run \
  --summary-mode=json \
  --out "json=results/k6-raw.json.gz" \
  --no-color \
  "$SCRIPT" > "$SUMMARY_FILE"
EXIT_CODE=$?

# Parse JSON summary
P95=$(jq -r '.metrics.http_req_duration.values["p(95)"] | . * 100 | round / 100' "$SUMMARY_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo "N/A")
FAIL_RATE=$(jq -r '.metrics.http_req_failed.values.rate | . * 100 | round / 100' "$SUMMARY_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo "N/A")
THRESHOLDS_PASS=$(jq '[.thresholds | to_entries[] | .value.ok] | all' "$SUMMARY_FILE" 2>/dev/null || echo "false")

echo "p95 duration: ${P95}ms | error rate: ${FAIL_RATE}% | thresholds: $([ "$THRESHOLDS_PASS" = "true" ] && echo PASS || echo FAIL)"

# Post to GitHub PR if CI env vars present
if [ -n "${GITHUB_TOKEN:-}" ] && [ -n "${GITHUB_PR_NUMBER:-}" ]; then
  STATUS_EMOJI=$([ "$THRESHOLDS_PASS" = "true" ] && echo ":white_check_mark:" || echo ":x:")
  gh pr comment "$GITHUB_PR_NUMBER" --body "### k6 Load Test
- **p95:** ${P95}ms
- **error rate:** ${FAIL_RATE}%
- **thresholds:** ${STATUS_EMOJI} $([ "$THRESHOLDS_PASS" = "true" ] && echo PASS || echo FAIL)"
fi

exit $EXIT_CODE
```

**Tradeoff:** `--summary-mode=json` writes summary JSON to `stdout` and human progress output to `stderr`. CI systems that redirect both streams to the same log will interleave them — redirect stderr separately (`2>k6-progress.log`) if you need clean JSON parsing from stdout. The JSON schema changed between the preview (`--new-machine-readable-summary`, v1.5.0) and stable formats (v2.0.0) — pin the k6 version in CI and re-validate JSON parsing when upgrading. [official]

---

### 119. Automatic Extension Resolution for Subcommand Extensions (k6 v1.7.0+)  [official]

k6 v1.7.0 extended automatic extension resolution to cover `k6 subcommands` — CLI commands registered by extensions under the `k6 x` namespace. Before v1.7.0, running `k6 x mqtt connect ...` required a pre-built custom binary containing the extension; k6 would fail with "unknown command" on a stock binary. In v1.7.0+, k6 detects the `k6/x/` import in the script and automatically provisions the correct binary. Combine with `k6 deps` to audit which extensions will be auto-resolved. Enable community extensions with `K6_ENABLE_COMMUNITY_EXTENSIONS=true`.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/mqtt-pub.js — extension auto-resolved from import at k6 v1.7.0+
// No manual xk6 build required: K6_ENABLE_COMMUNITY_EXTENSIONS=true k6 run mqtt-pub.js
import { Client, MQTT_VERSION_5 } from "k6/x/mqtt";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Counter } from "k6/metrics";

const msgPublished = new Counter("mqtt_messages_published");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mqtt_load: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 10,
      duration: "2m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    mqtt_messages_published: ["count>100"],
    http_req_failed:         ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const client = new Client({
    addr:     __ENV.MQTT_BROKER || "mqtt://localhost:1883",
    clientId: `k6-vu-${__VU}`,
    version:  MQTT_VERSION_5,
  });

  client.connect();
  client.publish("test/load", JSON.stringify({ vu: __VU, iter: __ITER }), 1);
  msgPublished.add(1);
  client.disconnect();
  sleep(0.5);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** Auto-resolution downloads and caches a custom k6 binary on first use — this adds 10–60 seconds to the first run in a cold CI environment. For fully reproducible builds, disable auto-resolution with `K6_ENABLE_COMMUNITY_EXTENSIONS=false` and use an `xk6 build` step with pinned extension versions. Document required extensions in `k6 deps --json` output committed to the repository for reproducibility. [official]

---

### 120. `mcp-k6` AI-Assisted Test Script Scaffolding (k6 v1.6.0 Experimental)  [community]

`mcp-k6` is an experimental Model Context Protocol (MCP) server introduced in k6 v1.6.0 that exposes k6-specific tools to AI assistants (Claude, Copilot, Cursor). It scaffolds k6 test scripts from natural-language descriptions, validates existing scripts against current API patterns, and suggests threshold values based on test type. As of v1.6.0, `mcp-k6` is marked experimental — its tool interface may change across patch releases. Use it to bootstrap complex multi-scenario scripts or to audit large legacy test suites for deprecated APIs.

```bash
# Start mcp-k6 MCP server (k6 v1.6.0+)
export K6_ENABLE_COMMUNITY_EXTENSIONS=true
k6 x mcp --port 3333 &   # server on localhost:3333/sse

# Configure Cursor IDE
mkdir -p .cursor
cat > .cursor/mcp.json << 'MCPEOF'
{
  "servers": {
    "k6": { "url": "http://localhost:3333/sse", "type": "sse" }
  }
}
MCPEOF
```

```javascript
// k6/scripts/mcp-scaffolded-checkout.js — AI-scaffolded from:
// "50 VUs, 2 min, /api/checkout, fail if p95 > 500ms or error rate > 1%"
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout_load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 50,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 60,
      maxVUs: 120,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
    checks:            ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

const BASE = __ENV.API_URL || "http://localhost:3001";

export default function () {
  const res = http.post(
    `${BASE}/api/checkout`,
    JSON.stringify({ cartId: `cart-${__VU}`, currency: "USD" }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } }
  );
  check(res, {
    "checkout 200":  (r) => r.status === 200,
    "has order id":  (r) => r.json("orderId") != null,
  });
  sleep(0.1);
}
```

**Tradeoff:** AI-scaffolded scripts require human review before production use — the model may generate `sleep()` inside `constant-arrival-rate` (a documented anti-pattern), wrong executor for the described load shape, or missing `preAllocatedVUs`. The MCP server is stateless and has no memory of your system's SLOs or historical baseline latencies, so always override scaffolded threshold values with your actual observed p95 values. Treat `mcp-k6` output as a starting draft. [community]
