## Community Gotchas (Cycle 45)

### Gotcha 186. `secrets.get()` without `await` silently returns a `Promise` object instead of the secret string  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** The `k6/secrets` module's `get()` function is asynchronous and returns a Promise. Developers familiar with synchronous `__ENV.MY_SECRET` patterns write `const apiKey = secrets.get('api-key')` without `await`, then use `apiKey` as a header value. The header receives the string `[object Promise]`, causing every request to return `401 Unauthorized`. Because the HTTP status code is non-2xx but non-5xx, the test may not fail any threshold (depending on threshold configuration), and the `[object Promise]` header value is visible only in verbose `--http-debug` output. The failure rate is 100% but may appear as an authentication issue rather than a code bug.

**Fix:** Always declare the function containing `secrets.get()` as `async` and prefix every call with `await`: `const apiKey = await secrets.get('api-key')`. The safest pattern is to fetch all secrets in `setup()` with `await Promise.all([...])` and pass resolved string values to the synchronous `default()` function via the setup data object, eliminating the need for `async/await` in VU iteration code entirely.

---

### Gotcha 187. `k6 cloud run` without `--stack` fails with an opaque authentication error in k6 v2.0.0  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** k6 v1.x automatically selected the first available stack when `--stack` was omitted and the token had access to exactly one stack. k6 v2.0.0 removed this fallback — `--stack` is now mandatory for all `k6 cloud` commands. Teams upgrading from v1.x to v2.0.0 see a fatal error message that reads as an authentication failure ("could not authenticate with Grafana Cloud") rather than a missing-parameter error, because the stack-selection step happens before token validation is surfaced in the error path. Engineers waste time rotating tokens and rechecking permissions instead of examining the command flags.

**Fix:** Set `K6_CLOUD_STACK=your-org.grafana.net` as a CI environment variable and verify it is injected into every `k6 cloud` command invocation. Add `--stack "$K6_CLOUD_STACK"` explicitly rather than relying on the env var being read automatically, since some CI runners strip custom env vars from subprocess environments. After upgrading, run `k6 cloud project list --stack your-org.grafana.net` as a connectivity smoke test before the first cloud run.

---

### Gotcha 188. `options.ext.loadimpact` in k6 v2.0.0 causes a fatal parse-time error, not a silent ignore  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** Teams with large shared test libraries that set `options.ext.loadimpact` in a base configuration object and spread-merge it into individual scripts expect the deprecated key to be silently ignored in k6 v2.0.0 (following the pattern of most backwards-compatibility shims). Instead, k6 v2.0.0 throws a fatal validation error at script parse time: `"options.ext.loadimpact is not supported, use options.cloud instead"`. This kills the test immediately, before any VUs are started, producing a non-zero exit with no performance data. In a large test suite, every script that imports the shared base config fails simultaneously, making the v1→v2 upgrade appear to break the entire test suite.

**Fix:** Do a global search for `ext.loadimpact` (not just `loadimpact` or `ext`) across the entire test codebase, including shared library files. Rename every occurrence to `cloud`. If the base config file is maintained separately from scripts, update it first and verify all consumer scripts inherit the correct key before upgrading the binary. Run `grep -r 'ext\.loadimpact' k6/` as a pre-upgrade CI step to catch any remaining instances.

---

### Gotcha 189. `browser_web_vital_fid` metric disappears silently after upgrading to k6 v2.0.0  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** The FID (First Input Delay) metric was removed from the web-vitals library in v5.1.0, which k6 v2.0.0 bundles. Scripts and Grafana dashboards that define thresholds against `browser_web_vital_fid` do not fail — the metric simply produces no data, so `p(X)<Y` thresholds vacuously pass (no data = no violation). Teams interpret unchanged green dashboards as confirmation that the upgrade had no effect, unaware that the FID panel is now flat-zero and all FID-based SLO tracking has silently stopped. This is especially dangerous for compliance-driven performance programs where FID thresholds are part of a formal SLO contract.

**Fix:** Before upgrading to k6 v2.0.0, audit all threshold configurations and Grafana dashboards for `browser_web_vital_fid`. Replace each FID threshold with `browser_web_vital_inp` and adjust the threshold value (good INP ≤200 ms vs. good FID ≤100 ms). Add an end-of-cycle check that verifies `browser_web_vital_inp` is present in results — if it is absent (no user interactions occurred), the INP threshold is providing no SLO coverage. Update browser test scripts to include at least one `click()` or `fill()` interaction to generate INP signal.

---

### Gotcha 190. `k6 pause` / `k6 resume` commands are removed in v2.0.0; pipelines that call them receive "unknown command"  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** Sophisticated CI pipelines sometimes use `k6 pause` to freeze a running test at a specific stage while a canary deployment completes, then `k6 resume` to continue the remaining stages with the new build. In k6 v2.0.0 both commands are removed along with the REST API auto-start. CI scripts calling `k6 pause` after `k6 run &` now receive `"unknown command: pause"` and exit non-zero, which — depending on pipeline configuration — either kills the test process or silently no-ops. Either outcome invalidates the canary stage gates the pipeline was designed to enforce.

**Fix:** Replace `k6 pause`/`k6 resume` patterns with scenario-based stage gating: split the test into two separate k6 scripts (`pre-canary.js` and `post-canary.js`) and run them sequentially in the CI job, inserting the deployment step between them. Alternatively, use `sleep()` stages and a conditional `exec.test.abort()` based on an external signal file written by the deployment step — the VUs check the signal file each iteration and abort cleanly when the file is present.

---

### Gotcha 191. `externally-controlled` executor scripts fail silently with no data in k6 v2.0.0  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** Teams that used `executor: 'externally-controlled'` to dynamically resize VU counts via the REST API (e.g., ramp up VUs based on real-time queue depth read from Prometheus) find that their scripts produce zero data in k6 v2.0.0 without a clear error. The executor was removed, and k6 v2.0.0 rejects scripts that specify `executor: 'externally-controlled'` at parse time with a validation error. However, if the executor name is stored in a shared config file loaded via `__ENV` and string-interpolated into the scenario, k6 may not detect it at parse time — the error surfaces mid-run when the scenario attempts to initialize, producing an empty test result rather than an upfront failure.

**Fix:** Migrate `externally-controlled` scenarios to `ramping-vus` with stage arrays that cover the expected VU ramp profile, accepting that dynamic resizing is no longer possible mid-test. For use cases that genuinely require dynamic load injection (e.g., shadow traffic replication), switch to `k6 cloud run` with `constant-arrival-rate` and modulate target RPS between test runs via `K6_*` environment variables rather than mid-test REST API calls. Run `grep -r 'externally-controlled' k6/` as a pre-upgrade check.

## Cycle 46 — 2026-05-14

### 226. `k6/experimental/csv` `Parser` Streaming for Memory-Constrained Parameterization  [official]

The `k6/experimental/csv` module ships two distinct strategies for consuming CSV data: `csv.parse()` which bulk-loads the entire file into a `SharedArray` at init time, and `Parser` which iterates rows on demand inside VU code. The `Parser` approach is preferable when the dataset exceeds available memory per VU or when only a subset of rows needs to be consumed per iteration. Each call to `parser.next()` returns an iterator result `{ done, value }` matching the WHATWG Streams iterator protocol, making the API composable with other stream-based patterns. Because the underlying reader is backed by Go I/O rather than JavaScript, parsing throughput is significantly faster than a hand-rolled `Papa.parse()` shim imported from jslib.

```javascript
import { open } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import { Parser } from 'k6/experimental/csv';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

const file = await open('./users.csv');

export default async function () {
  const parser = new Parser(file, { delimiter: ',', skipFirstLine: true });
  let result = await parser.next();
  while (!result.done) {
    const [username, password] = result.value;
    const res = await http.asyncRequest('POST', 'https://api.example.com/login', {
      username,
      password,
    });
    check(res, { 'login 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
    result = await parser.next();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `Parser` re-reads from the file cursor position, which is shared within a VU across iterations but not across VUs. If you want each VU to work through the full dataset independently, you must construct a new `Parser` instance (and call `file.seek(0)`) at the start of each iteration. Sharing a single cursor at the VU level without reset means later iterations receive an empty `done: true` result immediately, silently skipping all requests.

---

### 227. `http.batch()` Named-Object Form for Parallel Asset Loading  [official]

`http.batch()` accepts an object whose keys are arbitrary names and whose values are request descriptors (URL string or `[method, url, body, params]` array). The return value is an object with the same keys mapping to `Response` objects, making result extraction more readable than positional array indexing. This form naturally models the multi-asset waterfall that browsers trigger on page load — CSS, fonts, hero images, and analytics beacons can all be batched in a single call, reflecting real concurrency on the test target. The `K6_BATCH` option (default 20) and `K6_BATCH_PER_HOST` (default 6) caps govern how many connections are opened simultaneously, mirroring browser connection-pool limits.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 50, duration: '1m' };

export default function () {
  const responses = http.batch({
    html:      'https://example.com/',
    css:       'https://example.com/assets/main.css',
    logo:      'https://example.com/assets/logo.svg',
    analytics: ['GET', 'https://analytics.example.com/collect', null,
                { tags: { type: 'analytics' } }],
  });

  check(responses.html,      { 'HTML 200':      (r) => r.status === 200 });
  check(responses.css,       { 'CSS 200':       (r) => r.status === 200 });
  check(responses.logo,      { 'Logo 200':      (r) => r.status === 200 });
  check(responses.analytics, { 'Analytics 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `http.batch()` blocks the VU until the slowest request in the batch completes, so a single slow CDN asset will delay the iteration timing for every asset in the batch. If you need independent timing for each asset (e.g., separate `http_req_duration` thresholds per asset class), tag each request individually and use `Promise.all([ http.asyncRequest(...), ... ])` instead, which lets each request emit its own metric independently without mutual blocking.

---

### 228. `exec.vu.metrics.tags` for Dynamic Per-VU Request Tagging  [official]

The `k6/execution` module's `exec.vu.metrics.tags` object is a mutable map that applies additional tags to every metric emitted by the current VU for the remainder of the iteration. Unlike per-request `tags` params (which must be repeated on every call), setting `exec.vu.metrics.tags` once at the top of the iteration automatically annotates all subsequent `http_req_*` metrics, check results, and custom metrics with the specified key-value pairs. This is especially powerful in scenarios that route different VU cohorts through different user roles, tenants, or geographic regions — the tag is set once based on scenario or VU index, then silently applies across dozens of downstream calls.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import exec from 'k6/execution';
import { check } from 'k6';

const TENANTS = ['acme', 'globex', 'initech'];

export default function () {
  // Pin this VU to a deterministic tenant for the whole iteration
  const tenant = TENANTS[exec.vu.idInTest % TENANTS.length];
  exec.vu.metrics.tags['tenant'] = tenant;
  exec.vu.metrics.tags['region'] = __ENV.K6_REGION || 'us-east-1';

  const base = `https://api.example.com/tenants/${tenant}`;
  const list = http.get(`${base}/items`);
  check(list, { 'items 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  const item = http.get(`${base}/items/1`);
  check(item, { 'item 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Tags set via `exec.vu.metrics.tags` persist for the lifetime of the VU iteration and do not reset between iterations automatically — you must explicitly remove or overwrite keys if different iterations should carry different tag values. If your scenario runs many short iterations per VU (e.g., `constant-arrival-rate`), stale tags from the previous iteration may silently bleed into the next one and produce misleading metric segmentations.

---

### 229. `tagWithCurrentStageProfile()` for Ramp-Phase Metric Segmentation  [official]

The `k6/execution` helper `tagWithCurrentStageProfile()` (exported from `https://jslib.k6.io/k6-utils/1.4.0/index.js`) automatically tags every metric emitted during the current VU iteration with `stage_profile: ramp-up | steady | ramp-down` based on whether the VU count is increasing, stable, or decreasing relative to the previous stage. This allows Grafana dashboards and threshold expressions to isolate steady-state performance from warm-up and wind-down noise without manually computing stage boundaries from `exec.scenario.startTime` and options. It complements `tagWithCurrentStageIndex()` (which tags with a numeric stage index) and can be applied together for maximum granularity.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { tagWithCurrentStageProfile, tagWithCurrentStageIndex } from
  'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-utils/1.4.0/index.js';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: '2m', target: 100 },
    { duration: '5m', target: 100 },
    { duration: '1m', target: 0 },
  ],
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{stage_profile:steady}': ['p(95)<400'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  tagWithCurrentStageProfile();
  tagWithCurrentStageIndex();

  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/healthz');
  check(res, { 'health 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `tagWithCurrentStageProfile()` depends on the `ramping-vus` executor's stage definition to determine profile; it has no meaning for `constant-vus`, `constant-arrival-rate`, or `per-vu-iterations` executors and will tag everything as `steady` in those contexts. If you mix executor types in a multi-scenario test, apply this helper only to the `ramping-vus` scenario function to avoid misleading steady-state labels on non-ramping scenarios.

---

### 230. `k6/websockets` Multiple Concurrent Connections per VU with Global Event Loop  [official]

The `k6/websockets` module (stable, not to be confused with deprecated `k6/ws`) uses k6's global event loop, which allows a single VU to maintain multiple simultaneous WebSocket connections without spawning additional goroutines. Each connection is an independent `WebSocket` instance; event handlers are registered via `addEventListener` following the browser WebSocket API spec. This architecture is more efficient than the legacy `k6/ws` callback-in-`connect()` pattern when simulating chat rooms, trading feeds, or notification hubs where one user session maintains several live subscriptions.

```javascript
import { WebSocket } from 'k6/websockets';
import { sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 20, duration: '2m' };

export default function () {
  const notifications = new WebSocket('wss://api.example.com/notifications');
  const presence      = new WebSocket('wss://api.example.com/presence');

  notifications.addEventListener('open', () => {
    notifications.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'subscribe', channel: 'alerts' }));
  });
  notifications.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(e.data);
    if (msg.type !== 'ping') console.log('alert:', msg.payload);
  });

  presence.addEventListener('open', () => {
    presence.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'heartbeat' }));
  });

  sleep(30);

  notifications.close();
  presence.close();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Because all connections on a VU share the same goroutine via the global event loop, a long-running synchronous operation inside an event handler (e.g., a slow `JSON.parse` on a 2 MB message) will block message dispatch for every other open socket on that VU for the duration of that handler. Keep event handlers short; if heavy processing is needed, queue the raw message string and process it after `sleep()` returns.

---

### 231. `k6/net/grpc` `asyncInvoke()` for Non-Blocking gRPC Calls  [official]

The `k6/net/grpc` module offers both `client.invoke()` (synchronous, blocks until the server responds) and `client.asyncInvoke()` (returns a `Promise`). Using `asyncInvoke()` with `Promise.all()` allows a VU to dispatch multiple RPC calls simultaneously and collect all responses in one await, accurately modeling microservice clients that fan out gRPC calls in parallel. The `asyncInvoke()` pattern also enables per-call timeout control by wrapping each promise with a `Promise.race()` against a timer, which is not possible with the synchronous form. gRPC-specific metrics (`grpc_req_duration`) are emitted for each call regardless of whether `invoke()` or `asyncInvoke()` is used.

```javascript
import grpc from 'k6/net/grpc';
import { check } from 'k6';

const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(['./proto'], 'inventory.proto', 'pricing.proto');

export default async function () {
  client.connect('grpc.example.com:443', { tls: true });

  const [inventory, pricing] = await Promise.all([
    client.asyncInvoke('inventory.InventoryService/GetStock',
      { sku: 'ABC-123' }),
    client.asyncInvoke('pricing.PricingService/GetPrice',
      { sku: 'ABC-123', currency: 'USD' }),
  ]);

  check(inventory, { 'stock OK':  (r) => r.status === grpc.StatusOK });
  check(pricing,   { 'price OK':  (r) => r.status === grpc.StatusOK });

  client.close();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `client.connect()` and `client.close()` are synchronous and should ideally be called in `setup()` / `teardown()` to avoid re-establishing the HTTP/2 connection every iteration (which is expensive and produces spurious `grpc_req_duration` spikes for the first call of each iteration). However, sharing a single client connection across all VUs (via setup data) is not supported — each VU must own its own `grpc.Client` instance. The correct pattern is to connect in the init stage (module scope) and close in a `teardown()` equivalent registered via a scenario `gracefulStop` hook.

---

### 232. Prometheus Remote Write with Native Histograms for High-Fidelity Trend Analysis  [official]

By default, k6's Prometheus remote-write output converts trend metrics (like `http_req_duration`) into multiple gauge metrics representing pre-computed percentiles (`p(99)` etc.) controlled by `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_STATS`. This is lossy — once summarised into fixed percentiles, you cannot retroactively query `p(75)` if you only exported `p(99)`. Enabling `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true` instead emits each trend as a Prometheus native histogram, preserving the full bucket distribution so that any percentile can be computed post-hoc using `histogram_quantile()`. Native histograms are supported by Prometheus 2.40+ and Grafana Mimir.

```bash
# docker-compose excerpt for a local Prometheus + k6 stack
# prometheus.yml: enable native histograms
#   feature_flags: [native-histograms]

K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:9090/api/v1/write \
K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true \
K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_PUSH_INTERVAL=2s \
k6 run -o experimental-prometheus-rw script.js
```

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    steady: { executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: 200, timeUnit: '1s',
              duration: '5m', preAllocatedVUs: 50 },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(99)<500'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v1/products');
  check(res, { 'products 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Native histograms are marked experimental in Prometheus and are not yet compatible with all alerting rules that reference classic histogram metrics. If your Grafana dashboards use `histogram_quantile()` on classic bucket metrics (e.g., `k6_http_req_duration_bucket`), they will break when you switch to native histograms because native histograms use a different internal bucket schema. Maintain parallel outputs during transition: keep the default `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_STATS=p(99),p(95)` for dashboards and enable native histograms on a separate scrape endpoint until all dashboards are migrated.

---

### 233. `exec.test.abort()` vs `exec.test.fail()` for Controlled Test Termination  [official]

The `k6/execution` module exposes two distinct exit paths: `exec.test.abort(message)` immediately halts all VUs and exits with code 108, while `exec.test.fail(message)` marks the test as failed (exit code 110) but allows currently running VU iterations to complete their `gracefulStop` window. Use `abort()` when a precondition failure makes all remaining data invalid (e.g., the auth service is down and no VU can obtain a token), and use `fail()` when you want to flag a policy violation but still let in-flight requests finish so they contribute to the final summary. Both functions accept a string message that appears in the test end-of-summary output.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import exec from 'k6/execution';
import { check } from 'k6';

let healthCheckPassed = false;

export function setup() {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/healthz');
  if (res.status !== 200) {
    // Abort immediately — no point running the test if the service is down
    exec.test.abort(`Health check failed: HTTP ${res.status}`);
  }
  healthCheckPassed = true;
  return { token: res.json('token') };
}

export default function (data) {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v1/orders', {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${data.token}` },
  });
  if (res.status === 503) {
    // Mark as failed but keep running to collect error-rate data
    exec.test.fail('Service returning 503 — SLO breach detected');
  }
  check(res, { 'orders ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `exec.test.abort()` does not wait for teardown to complete — any cleanup logic in `teardown()` (deleting test data, revoking tokens, clearing queues) will not run if `abort()` is called from within a VU. Move critical cleanup into a dedicated `pre-teardown` HTTP call inside `setup()` or use a separate CI job step that runs cleanup unconditionally after the k6 process exits.

---

### 234. CSV Output `timeFormat` and `saveInterval` Tuning for High-Frequency Analysis  [official]

k6's built-in CSV output writes one row per metric sample per `saveInterval` (default `1s`). For latency-sensitive root-cause analysis, setting `timeFormat=rfc3339_nano` and `saveInterval=100ms` provides sub-second timestamps that allow you to correlate k6 sample windows with application log entries and distributed traces. The compressed output form (`--out csv=results.gz`) writes a gzip stream in real-time, which reduces disk I/O without losing any sample resolution — useful on CI runners with slow disk I/O. The `metric_name`, `metric_value`, `tags`, and timestamp columns in each row enable offline aggregation via `pandas`, `DuckDB`, or simple `awk` pipelines.

```bash
K6_CSV_SAVE_INTERVAL=100ms \
K6_CSV_TIME_FORMAT=rfc3339_nano \
k6 run --out csv=results.gz script.js
```

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  vus: 100,
  duration: '5m',
  systemTags: ['status', 'method', 'url', 'scenario', 'name'],
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v1/search?q=test',
    { tags: { endpoint: 'search' } });
  check(res, { 'search 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Reducing `saveInterval` to `100ms` multiplies the number of CSV rows by 10x compared to the default `1s` interval, which can produce very large files (gigabytes per hour at high VU counts). Always combine sub-second intervals with compressed output (`results.gz`) and set `systemTags` explicitly to only include the tags you intend to query in post-processing — unused high-cardinality tags (e.g., `url` with query-string variation) can bloat CSV size dramatically and make post-processing impractical.

---

### 235. `abortOnFail` + `delayAbortEval` Threshold Pattern for Early Soak-Test Termination  [official]

Setting `abortOnFail: true` on a threshold tells k6 to stop the test immediately when the threshold first fails. However, for percentile thresholds evaluated over a short duration, early in the test a single slow response can cause a spurious `p(95) < 400ms` breach before enough samples have accumulated to produce a statistically meaningful value. `delayAbortEval: '30s'` defers threshold evaluation until at least 30 seconds of data has been collected, suppressing early noise while still aborting soak tests that have clearly regressed. This pattern is most valuable in overnight soak tests where you want to fail fast if the system degrades but not on the very first spike.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    soak: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 200,
      duration: '8h',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: [
      {
        threshold: 'p(95)<500',
        abortOnFail: true,
        delayAbortEval: '60s',   // wait 60 s before evaluating p(95)
      },
    ],
    http_req_failed: [
      {
        threshold: 'rate<0.01',
        abortOnFail: true,
        delayAbortEval: '30s',
      },
    ],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v1/status');
  check(res, { 'status 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `abortOnFail` triggers an exit code 99, which CI pipelines should handle as a distinct failure class (not just a non-zero exit). If your CI pipeline treats all non-zero exits identically, you lose the signal that the test was aborted early on a threshold versus failing cleanly at the end. Add a `|| test $? -eq 99` guard in your shell step to capture the abort code and emit a dedicated "SLO breach — soak aborted early" CI annotation.

---

### 236. `page.evaluate()` for DOM Assertion and JavaScript State Inspection in Browser Tests  [official]

`page.evaluate(fn, ...args)` executes an arbitrary JavaScript function inside the browser's V8 context and serializes the return value back to k6 via CDP. This bridges the gap between what k6 selectors can observe (DOM structure, Locator state) and what application JavaScript state holds at a given moment (Redux store, localStorage tokens, computed CSS values). The `args` parameter enables passing k6-side values into the browser function, avoiding the need to embed dynamic data as string-interpolated JavaScript. For complex object return values, the data must be JSON-serializable; functions, class instances, and DOM nodes cannot cross the boundary.

```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = { scenarios: {
  ui: { executor: 'shared-iterations', options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } } },
}};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

  // Inject auth token from k6 env into browser localStorage
  await page.evaluate((token) => {
    window.localStorage.setItem('auth_token', token);
  }, __ENV.AUTH_TOKEN);

  await page.reload();

  // Assert Redux-managed cart count without relying on a visible selector
  const cartCount = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return window.__STORE__?.getState()?.cart?.items?.length ?? -1;
  });

  check(null, { 'cart initialized': () => cartCount >= 0 });

  await page.close();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.evaluate()` executes synchronously in the browser context but is asynchronous from k6's perspective — you must always `await` it. If the evaluated function throws an uncaught exception inside the browser, k6 receives a rejected Promise that must be caught explicitly, otherwise it surfaces as a cryptic CDP protocol error rather than a meaningful assertion failure. Wrap `page.evaluate()` calls in `try/catch` blocks when evaluating third-party or minified application code that may throw unexpectedly.

---

### 237. `k6/experimental/streams` `ReadableStream` for Chunked Request Body Generation  [official]

The `k6/experimental/streams` module provides a WHATWG-compatible `ReadableStream` API that allows VUs to produce large request bodies incrementally without buffering the entire payload in memory first. This is particularly useful for load testing file-upload endpoints or streaming ingestion APIs where realistic test conditions require multi-megabyte payloads per request. A `ReadableStreamController` is used to enqueue typed array chunks, which are then consumed by `http.asyncRequest()` accepting a `ReadableStream` as the body. Because chunks are produced lazily, peak memory per VU is bounded by chunk size rather than total payload size.

```javascript
import { ReadableStream } from 'k6/experimental/streams';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

// Generate a ~1 MB streaming request body in 64 KB chunks
function createPayloadStream(totalBytes) {
  const chunkSize = 65536;
  let bytesProduced = 0;
  return new ReadableStream({
    pull(controller) {
      if (bytesProduced >= totalBytes) {
        controller.close();
        return;
      }
      const remaining = Math.min(chunkSize, totalBytes - bytesProduced);
      const chunk = new Uint8Array(remaining).fill(0x41); // 'A'
      controller.enqueue(chunk);
      bytesProduced += remaining;
    },
  });
}

export default async function () {
  const stream = createPayloadStream(1_048_576); // 1 MB
  const res = await http.asyncRequest('POST',
    'https://upload.example.com/v1/ingest',
    stream,
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/octet-stream' } });
  check(res, { 'upload accepted': (r) => r.status === 202 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `ReadableStream` bodies are consumed exactly once — once `http.asyncRequest()` has read the stream, attempting to re-use the same stream object in a retry or a second request will result in a "stream is locked" error. Construct a fresh `ReadableStream` instance for each request attempt; do not cache stream objects across retries or iterations.

---

### 238. Multi-Scenario Parallel Execution with Scenario-Scoped `exec` Functions  [official]

k6 scenarios support an `exec` property that names the exported function to run for that scenario, decoupling scenario configuration from function implementation. This allows a single script file to define distinct workload shapes — e.g., a read-heavy scenario and a write-heavy scenario — each routed to its own function, with independent VU counts, executors, env vars, and tags. All scenarios run in parallel by default, producing interleaved metric streams that can be split in Grafana using the `scenario` system tag. This is preferable to running multiple separate k6 processes when you need the scenarios to share setup data (via the `setup()` return value).

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    readers: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 500, timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 100,
      exec: 'readWorkload',
      tags: { workload: 'read' },
    },
    writers: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      stages: [
        { duration: '1m', target: 20 },
        { duration: '3m', target: 20 },
        { duration: '1m', target: 0 },
      ],
      exec: 'writeWorkload',
      tags: { workload: 'write' },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{workload:read}':  ['p(95)<200'],
    'http_req_duration{workload:write}': ['p(95)<600'],
  },
};

export function readWorkload() {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v1/items');
  check(res, { 'read 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

export function writeWorkload() {
  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/v1/items',
    JSON.stringify({ name: 'test', value: Math.random() }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  check(res, { 'write 201': (r) => r.status === 201 });
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** When scenarios run in parallel, the total VU count across all scenarios must not exceed the `maxVUs` option (default: the sum of `preAllocatedVUs` across all scenarios). If you add a third scenario without increasing `maxVUs`, k6 will silently reduce the VU count for the new scenario to fit within the cap rather than emitting a fatal error, causing unexpected throughput shortfalls that are not obviously attributed to VU starvation.

---

### 239. `group()` + Tagged Sub-Metrics for User-Journey SLO Decomposition  [official]

`group(name, fn)` wraps a set of requests in a named logical unit, causing all `http_req_*` metrics emitted inside the callback to also populate the `group_duration` summary metric with `group` tag set to `::name`. By nesting groups (e.g., `group('checkout', () => group('payment', () => ...))`) you build a path-based hierarchy that mirrors the user journey tree in dashboards. Threshold expressions can then target `group_duration{group:::checkout::payment}` to set independent SLOs on each journey step. Combining groups with per-request `tags` lets you slice by both the logical step and the raw HTTP endpoint.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { group, check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: '3m',
  thresholds: {
    'group_duration{group:::browse}':            ['p(95)<300'],
    'group_duration{group:::browse::search}':    ['p(95)<250'],
    'group_duration{group:::checkout}':          ['p(95)<600'],
    'group_duration{group:::checkout::payment}': ['p(95)<800'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  group('browse', () => {
    http.get('https://shop.example.com/');
    group('search', () => {
      http.get('https://shop.example.com/search?q=laptop');
    });
    sleep(1);
  });

  group('checkout', () => {
    http.post('https://shop.example.com/cart/add',
      JSON.stringify({ sku: 'LAPTOP-001', qty: 1 }),
      { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
    group('payment', () => {
      http.post('https://shop.example.com/checkout/pay',
        JSON.stringify({ card: '4111111111111111' }),
        { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
    });
    sleep(2);
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `group_duration` measures wall-clock time for the entire callback including `sleep()` calls, not just HTTP request time. If you have long `sleep()` delays inside a group to simulate user think time, `group_duration` thresholds will include that sleep and will never appear to breach a latency SLO even if the underlying requests are slow. Place `sleep()` calls outside the group boundaries, or subtract expected think time from your `group_duration` thresholds when the two cannot be separated.

---

### 240. `k6/experimental/csv` + `SharedArray` Hybrid for Fast Random-Access Parameterization  [official]

For test data sets that need to be accessed randomly (not sequentially), `csv.parse()` paired with `SharedArray` provides O(1) lookup by row index. `csv.parse()` bulk-loads the entire CSV into a `SharedArray` during init, meaning the underlying Go array is allocated once and shared across all VUs via a reference, not copied. VUs then use modular arithmetic on their unique iteration index (`exec.vu.iterationInScenario`) to select rows deterministically, ensuring each VU works through a non-overlapping slice of the data set when spread across a large VU count. This avoids the race conditions inherent in cursor-sharing when multiple VUs attempt to advance the same `Parser` instance.

```javascript
import { open } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import { parse } from 'k6/experimental/csv';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';
import http from 'k6/http';
import exec from 'k6/execution';
import { check } from 'k6';

// Parse once at init, share across all VUs — no per-VU copy
const file = await open('./test-users.csv');
const users = new SharedArray('users', async () => {
  const rows = await parse(file, { skipFirstLine: true });
  return rows; // array of [username, password, role] arrays
});

export const options = { vus: 200, duration: '10m' };

export default function () {
  // Each VU iteration deterministically maps to one user row
  const idx = exec.vu.iterationInScenario % users.length;
  const [username, password] = users[idx];

  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/auth/login',
    JSON.stringify({ username, password }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  check(res, { 'login 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `csv.parse()` in a `SharedArray` initializer loads the entire file into memory at startup, which can cause visible delays in the k6 init phase for files larger than ~100 MB. k6 will report "initializing VUs" for an extended period, which CI pipeline health checks may interpret as a hung process. For very large datasets (millions of rows), prefer the streaming `Parser` approach (Pattern 226) or pre-shard the CSV into multiple smaller files and assign each file to a VU cohort using scenario `env` variables.

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 46)

### Gotcha 192. `http.batch()` silent throughput cap when `K6_BATCH_PER_HOST` is lower than batch size  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** Developers using `http.batch()` to fire 20 requests to the same host expect all 20 to execute simultaneously. However, `K6_BATCH_PER_HOST` defaults to 6, which means only 6 of the 20 requests are sent concurrently; the remaining 14 queue internally and are dispatched in successive rounds of 6. The VU does not log a warning or expose this queuing — the batch call simply takes longer than expected. Engineers profiling the test see `http_req_waiting` spikes and blame the server, when in fact the delay is k6-side connection pooling. This inflates the measured latency of pages that load many same-host assets and produces incorrect recommendations to scale up the origin server.

**Fix:** Set `K6_BATCH_PER_HOST` to match the maximum batch size you intend to use, or use `Promise.all([ http.asyncRequest(...) ])` which bypasses the per-host connection pool limit entirely. When comparing load test latency results against RUM data, always document the `K6_BATCH` and `K6_BATCH_PER_HOST` values alongside the results so that reviewers can account for the artificial queuing overhead.

---

### Gotcha 193. `exec.vu.metrics.tags` changes persist across iterations and corrupt subsequent metric segmentation  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A test script sets `exec.vu.metrics.tags['user_type'] = 'admin'` during an admin-workflow iteration, then the same VU is reused for a regular-user iteration. The `user_type` tag is never cleared, so all metrics in the subsequent iteration are incorrectly tagged as `admin`. In Grafana, the `admin` segment appears to have double the request rate because both iteration types are attributed to it, while the `regular` segment appears empty. The bug is especially hard to find when the mismatch is in a low-cardinality tag like `region` or `tenant` rather than `user_type`, because the absolute numbers look plausible and only careful cross-referencing reveals the duplication.

**Fix:** At the beginning of every iteration, explicitly set all VU-level tags to their correct value for that iteration rather than assuming they carry the right value from the previous run. Alternatively, clear the tag map by setting each key to an empty string (k6 does not support deleting keys from `exec.vu.metrics.tags` in v2.0.0) before reassigning. Treat tag mutation as having iteration scope and enforce it architecturally by placing all tag-setting code at the top of the `default()` function before any HTTP calls.

---

### Gotcha 194. `group_duration` threshold breaches when `sleep()` is inside the group callback  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer writes a user-journey test that wraps an entire checkout flow — including `sleep(2)` think-time calls — inside a `group('checkout', ...)` block, then sets `'group_duration{group:::checkout}': ['p(95)<1000']`. The group consistently reports `p(95)` around 2400ms, vastly exceeding the 1000ms threshold, even though all HTTP requests inside the group complete within 300ms. The developer spends hours profiling backend APIs before realising that `group_duration` measures wall time of the callback, not the sum of request times, and that the 2-second `sleep()` is included in the measurement. The threshold is structurally impossible to pass with the current code layout.

**Fix:** Move `sleep()` calls outside the `group()` callback. Recalculate `group_duration` thresholds as `max_request_time_sum` (not `max_request_time_sum + think_time`). If think time must reside inside the group for business-logic readability, document the threshold value as `request_budget + sleep_budget` and add a code comment explaining why the threshold appears generous.

---

### Gotcha 195. `page.evaluate()` throwing in the browser context surfaces as an opaque CDP error in k6  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A k6 browser test calls `page.evaluate(() => window.nonExistentFunction())`. Inside the browser, the call throws `TypeError: window.nonExistentFunction is not a function`. k6 receives this as a rejected CDP `Runtime.callFunctionOn` promise, which surfaces in the k6 console as `GoError: cdp.Runtime.callFunctionOn: undefined is not a function` rather than the JavaScript exception message. Engineers searching for `nonExistentFunction` in logs find nothing, because the browser's JavaScript exception is stringified into a generic CDP error envelope. Debugging requires enabling `--http-debug` or attaching Chrome DevTools to the browser spawned by k6, neither of which is available in headless CI.

**Fix:** Wrap all `page.evaluate()` calls in a try/catch and re-throw with the error message formatted for k6 logging: `try { await page.evaluate(fn); } catch (e) { console.error('evaluate failed:', e.message); throw e; }`. For complex evaluations, add a browser-side try/catch inside the evaluated function that returns a structured `{ ok, error }` object instead of throwing, so k6 receives a usable error string rather than a CDP protocol exception.

---

### Gotcha 196. `ramping-arrival-rate` `startRate: 0` causes division-by-zero panic in k6 < v1.5.0  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** Teams writing `ramping-arrival-rate` scenarios that should start from zero RPS (to model a cold-start ramp) set `startRate: 0` thinking this is equivalent to starting from `0` iterations per time unit. In k6 versions before v1.5.0, setting `startRate: 0` triggers a division-by-zero panic during executor initialization, crashing the k6 process with a Go stack trace that mentions `goroutine` and `division by zero` but gives no indication of which script option caused the error. Teams running older k6 versions in locked CI containers waste significant time bisecting the script.

**Fix:** If you are on k6 < v1.5.0, avoid `startRate: 0`; instead set `startRate: 1` and use a very short first stage that ramps from 1 to your target rate within 5–10 seconds. In k6 >= v1.5.0 the issue is fixed and `startRate: 0` works as expected. Add a minimum-version check at the top of shared library files that define `ramping-arrival-rate` scenarios using `exec.test.abort()` when `k6 version` output is below the required minimum.

---

### Gotcha 197. `SharedArray` initializer receiving an `async` function silently returns `undefined` in k6 < v0.52.0  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** The `SharedArray` constructor accepts a callback whose return value is used as the backing data. In k6 versions prior to v0.52.0, the callback must be synchronous — passing an `async` function causes the constructor to receive a `Promise` (which is truthy but not array-like), and `SharedArray` silently wraps the Promise object as a single-element array. Every VU then logs `[object Promise]` or `undefined` when accessing array elements. The test runs to completion with no errors because `http.get(undefined)` is treated as a GET to the string `"undefined"`, which typically returns 404. Thresholds on `http_req_failed` will breach, but the root cause is non-obvious without examining the data values.

**Fix:** In k6 >= v0.52.0, `SharedArray` fully supports `async` initializers. For older versions, use a synchronous initializer: load file content with `open()` (which is synchronous in init context) and parse CSV/JSON using synchronous methods, then return the plain array. Pin k6 versions in CI using a `.tool-versions` or `Dockerfile` lock to prevent accidental downgrade to a version that does not support async `SharedArray` initializers.

## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### 241. `k6/experimental/fs` `open()` + `File.read()` for Memory-Efficient Binary Parameterization  [official]

The `k6/experimental/fs` module exposes a Promise-based `open()` function that returns a `File` handle instead of loading the entire file content into a JavaScript string. Unlike the legacy `open()` built-in (which allocates one string copy per VU), the `fs` module maps the file into a single shared OS memory region and provides `read()`, `seek()`, and `stat()` methods that operate on a typed-array buffer, keeping per-VU allocations proportional to the read-chunk size rather than the file size. This makes it practical to parameterize tests with multi-gigabyte binary payloads — for example, multi-part upload tests that stream a large PDF — without triggering out-of-memory kills in k6's Go runtime. The module is imported from `k6/experimental/fs` and all methods are async, requiring `await` and a top-level `async` init block.

```javascript
import { open, SeekMode } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

// init context: open once, shared across all VUs
const file = await open('./fixtures/sample-10mb.pdf');

export const options = { vus: 50, duration: '2m' };

export default async function () {
  // Rewind file pointer to start for each iteration
  await file.seek(0, SeekMode.Start);

  // Retrieve file size from metadata
  const info = await file.stat();
  const buf = new Uint8Array(info.size);

  // Read entire file content into buffer
  await file.read(buf);

  // Upload binary payload with correct content type
  const res = http.post(
    'https://api.example.com/documents/upload',
    buf.buffer,
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/pdf' } }
  );
  check(res, { 'upload accepted': (r) => r.status === 202 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Because `file.seek(0, SeekMode.Start)` is required at the start of every iteration to reset the read cursor, forgetting it causes every iteration after the first to read zero bytes (EOF condition), producing empty request bodies that fail with unexpected 400 errors. The module also does not reflect modifications to the underlying file once `open()` has been called, so updating fixture files mid-test requires a full k6 restart; this is by design to guarantee consistency across the distributed init phase.

---

### 242. `k6/secrets` for Credential Injection Without Environment Variable Exposure  [official]

The `k6/secrets` module provides a structured API for retrieving sensitive values — API keys, passwords, tokens — from a configured secret source at test startup without embedding them in script files or leaking them into k6's verbose HTTP debug output. `secrets.get(name)` returns a Promise resolving to the secret string; k6 automatically redacts the resolved value as `***SECRET_REDACTED***` in all console output and metric tags, preventing accidental credential exposure in CI logs. When multiple providers are configured (for example, both an environment-variable source and a HashiCorp Vault source), `secrets.source('vault').get('db_password')` lets you target a specific provider by its configured identifier. The module is most valuable in shared test suites where different team members run tests against different environments and must not hardcode credentials in version-controlled scripts.

```javascript
import secrets from 'k6/secrets';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

// Retrieve secrets once in init context — async init block required
const apiKey = await secrets.get('SERVICE_API_KEY');
const dbPassword = await secrets.source('vault').get('reporting_db_password');

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '30s' };

export default function () {
  // apiKey value is redacted in logs; safe to use in headers
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/reports', {
    headers: {
      'X-API-Key': apiKey,
      'Authorization': `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
    },
  });
  check(res, { 'authenticated': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  // Avoid logging `apiKey` directly — k6 redacts it automatically
  // but string interpolation into custom messages bypasses redaction
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `secrets.get()` is async and must be called in an `async` init context or inside `setup()`. Calling it inside the `default()` VU function works but reissues the secret lookup on every iteration, which adds latency overhead and may exhaust rate limits on remote secret backends. The preferred pattern is to resolve all secrets once in init context (or `setup()`) and pass the resolved values to VU functions via the `setup()` return value or a module-level variable. Note that module-level variables holding secret values are still redacted in k6 output.

---

### 243. `crypto.subtle` (WebCrypto API) for HMAC-SHA256 Request Signing in Load Tests  [official]

k6 exposes the standard Web Cryptography API through the global `crypto` object, giving load tests access to `crypto.subtle.importKey()`, `crypto.subtle.sign()`, and `crypto.subtle.digest()` for authentication schemes that require per-request HMAC signatures — such as AWS Signature V4, Shopify webhook validation, or custom API gateways. Unlike the legacy `k6/crypto` module, the WebCrypto API uses a `CryptoKey` object that encapsulates the raw key bytes and algorithm metadata, which prevents accidental key reuse across incompatible algorithms. The `crypto.getRandomValues()` and `crypto.randomUUID()` helpers are also available globally without any import statement, making nonce and idempotency-key generation straightforward.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import encoding from 'k6/encoding';

// Import the HMAC key once in init context — importKey is async
const signingKey = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
  'raw',
  new TextEncoder().encode('my-secret-signing-key'),
  { name: 'HMAC', hash: 'SHA-256' },
  false,         // not extractable
  ['sign']       // only permit signing operations
);

export const options = { vus: 20, duration: '1m' };

export default async function () {
  const requestId = crypto.randomUUID();
  const timestamp = Date.now().toString();
  const payload = `${requestId}:${timestamp}`;

  // Sign the canonical string with the pre-imported CryptoKey
  const signatureBytes = await crypto.subtle.sign(
    'HMAC',
    signingKey,
    new TextEncoder().encode(payload)
  );

  // Encode signature as base64 for the Authorization header
  const signature = encoding.b64encode(signatureBytes);

  const res = http.post(
    'https://api.example.com/events',
    JSON.stringify({ id: requestId, ts: timestamp }),
    {
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-Request-Id': requestId,
        'X-Timestamp': timestamp,
        'X-Signature': signature,
      },
    }
  );
  check(res, { 'event accepted': (r) => r.status === 201 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `crypto.subtle.importKey()` and `crypto.subtle.sign()` are async and must be awaited, which requires the entire default function to be declared `async`. This means k6 manages the VU iteration as a Promise chain rather than a synchronous call, which adds a small scheduling overhead per iteration. For extremely high-throughput tests (>1000 iterations/second per VU), consider caching the signing key at module scope (as shown above) rather than importing it each iteration, and profile whether the async overhead warrants switching to the lower-level `k6/crypto` `hmac()` synchronous API instead.

---

### 244. OpenTelemetry Output for End-to-End Trace Correlation Between k6 and Application Services  [official]

k6's built-in OpenTelemetry output (`--out opentelemetry`) converts k6 metric types to their OTEL equivalents and ships them to any OTEL-compatible collector endpoint over gRPC or HTTP/protobuf. This lets platform teams correlate k6-measured latency with distributed traces from the application under test: when the k6 test also injects W3C `traceparent` headers (via the `instrumentHTTP()` helper from `@grafana/k6-http-instrumentation-tempo` jslib), every backend span links back to the k6-originating synthetic trace, making it possible to identify which component in a microservice call chain caused the `p(99)` regression. Key configuration environment variables are `K6_OTEL_GRPC_EXPORTER_ENDPOINT` (default `localhost:4317`), `K6_OTEL_METRIC_PREFIX` (recommend `k6_` to avoid namespace collisions), and `K6_OTEL_EXPORT_INTERVAL` (default `10s`; lower for near-real-time dashboards during smoke tests).

```javascript
// Run with: K6_OTEL_GRPC_EXPORTER_INSECURE=true \
//           K6_OTEL_METRIC_PREFIX=k6_ \
//           K6_OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=checkout-load-test \
//           k6 run --out opentelemetry script.js

import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { instrumentHTTP } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/http-instrumentation-tempo/1.0.0/index.js';

// Attach W3C traceparent to every HTTP request automatically
instrumentHTTP({ propagator: 'w3c' });

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout: { executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: '1s', stages: [
        { target: 100, duration: '2m' },
        { target: 100, duration: '5m' },
        { target: 0,   duration: '1m' },
      ], preAllocatedVUs: 50 },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{scenario:checkout}': ['p(95)<500'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/checkout/start',
    JSON.stringify({ cartId: 'c-001' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  check(res, { 'checkout started': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The OTEL output serializes and ships metrics on a fixed `K6_OTEL_EXPORT_INTERVAL` cadence (default 10 s). If the k6 test is shorter than 10 seconds, the final flush may not complete before the process exits, causing partial or missing metrics in the OTEL backend. For sub-10-second smoke tests, set `K6_OTEL_EXPORT_INTERVAL=1s` and `K6_OTEL_FLUSH_INTERVAL=500ms`. Also note that OTEL `Rate` metrics are converted to two `Int64Counter` values (passes and total), which requires a `rate()` PromQL expression in Grafana rather than a direct gauge query.

### 245. `handleSummary()` for Multi-Format Test Reports (Console + JUnit XML + Custom HTML)  [official]

The `handleSummary(data)` lifecycle function receives the full aggregated metric snapshot at test end and returns a map of output destinations to their content, enabling a single k6 run to simultaneously print the default console summary, write a JUnit XML file for CI test result ingestion, and POST a JSON payload to a metrics aggregation service. The `data` object contains `metrics` (all metric types with their aggregated values), `thresholds` (pass/fail status per expression), and `root_group` (the nested group hierarchy). The `textSummary()` helper from `https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.3/index.js` reproduces the default terminal table from the function, allowing hybrid output without rewriting the console format from scratch.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { textSummary } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.3/index.js';

export const options = {
  vus: 10, duration: '30s',
  thresholds: { 'http_req_duration': ['p(95)<500'] },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/health');
}

export function handleSummary(data) {
  // Build a minimal JUnit XML string from threshold results
  const failures = Object.entries(data.thresholds)
    .filter(([, t]) => !t.ok)
    .map(([name, t]) => `  <testcase name="${name}"><failure message="${
      JSON.stringify(t)}" /></testcase>`)
    .join('\n');
  const junit = `<?xml version="1.0"?>\n<testsuite tests="${
    Object.keys(data.thresholds).length}" failures="${
    failures.split('<failure').length - 1}">\n${failures}\n</testsuite>`;

  return {
    stdout:                   textSummary(data, { indent: ' ', enableColors: true }),
    'reports/results.xml':    junit,
    'reports/summary.json':   JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `handleSummary()` runs after all VUs finish, so it cannot influence test flow or thresholds. File paths in the return map are relative to the working directory from which k6 was invoked, not the script file's location; this causes silent write failures when k6 is run from a different directory in CI pipelines. Always use absolute paths obtained via `__ENV` injection (`K6_REPORT_DIR=/tmp/reports`) or document the required working directory in the CI job configuration. Cloud-based k6 runs do not support custom file outputs from `handleSummary()` in all tiers.

---

### 246. `k6/timers` `setInterval` + `clearInterval` for Periodic Heartbeat Requests During Long VU Iterations  [official]

The `k6/timers` module (available globally without an import) provides `setTimeout` and `setInterval` that integrate with k6's VU-level event loop rather than a Node.js timer queue. This allows a VU to issue periodic "heartbeat" keep-alive requests to session-sensitive APIs while simultaneously processing long-running operations such as file uploads or SSE stream consumption — without spawning additional VUs. The pattern is especially useful when testing APIs that expire sessions after 30 seconds of inactivity: the main iteration logic processes data while `setInterval` fires a lightweight ping every 20 seconds to reset the server-side idle timer.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 5, duration: '3m' };

export default async function () {
  // Establish a session
  const loginRes = http.post('https://api.example.com/session',
    JSON.stringify({ user: 'load-test' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  const { sessionId } = loginRes.json();

  // Heartbeat: ping every 20s to prevent session expiry
  const heartbeatInterval = setInterval(() => {
    const r = http.get(`https://api.example.com/session/${sessionId}/ping`);
    if (r.status !== 200) {
      console.warn(`Heartbeat failed for session ${sessionId}: ${r.status}`);
    }
  }, 20_000);

  // Simulate a long-running multi-step operation (e.g. report generation)
  for (let step = 1; step <= 5; step++) {
    const stepRes = http.post(
      `https://api.example.com/report/step/${step}`,
      JSON.stringify({ sessionId }),
      { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } }
    );
    check(stepRes, { [`step ${step} ok`]: (r) => r.status === 200 });
    sleep(15); // simulate processing time between steps
  }

  // Cancel heartbeat before ending iteration
  clearInterval(heartbeatInterval);
  http.delete(`https://api.example.com/session/${sessionId}`);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Timer callbacks execute between Promise microtask checkpoints, not with preemptive concurrency. If the main VU code blocks synchronously for longer than the interval period (for example, a synchronous `http.get` that takes 25 seconds), the heartbeat fires immediately after the blocking call completes rather than at wall-clock intervals. For truly concurrent execution, separate the heartbeat into its own k6 scenario with a distinct VU pool rather than relying on `setInterval` inside a VU that performs long-duration synchronous operations.

---

### 247. `k6/html` `parseHTML()` + jQuery-Style Selection for CSRF Token Extraction  [official]

The `k6/html` module exposes a `parseHTML()` function that returns a jQuery-compatible `Selection` object, enabling k6 scripts to extract dynamic values — CSRF tokens, nonces, form action URLs, pagination cursors — from HTML response bodies without resorting to fragile regex patterns. `sel.find('meta[name="csrf-token"]').attr('content')` reads the CSRF token value exactly as a browser would, respecting nested DOM structure. This is the canonical k6 approach for multi-step form submission flows where the token changes on every page load and cannot be hardcoded as a test parameter.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { parseHTML } from 'k6/html';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '2m' };

export default function () {
  // Step 1: GET the login page to extract the CSRF token
  const loginPage = http.get('https://example.com/login');
  check(loginPage, { 'login page loaded': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  const doc = parseHTML(loginPage.body);

  // Extract CSRF token from <meta name="csrf-token" content="...">
  const csrfToken = doc.find('meta[name="csrf-token"]').attr('content');

  // Also extract the hidden form field as a fallback
  const hiddenToken = doc.find('input[name="_token"]').attr('value');
  const token = csrfToken || hiddenToken;

  if (!token) {
    console.error('CSRF token not found — page structure may have changed');
    return;
  }

  // Step 2: POST the login form with the extracted CSRF token
  const loginRes = http.post('https://example.com/login', {
    _token: token,
    email: 'user@example.com',
    password: 'secret',
  });
  check(loginRes, {
    'login succeeded': (r) => r.status === 200,
    'redirected to dashboard': (r) => r.url.includes('/dashboard'),
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `parseHTML()` builds a full DOM tree in memory for each call, which is appropriate for small-to-medium HTML responses but becomes a measurable performance overhead when applied to very large server-rendered pages (>500 KB). If only a single token value is needed and the token always appears in a predictable position (e.g., first `<meta>` tag), a `response.body.match(/<meta name="csrf-token" content="([^"]+)"/)?.[1]` regex is faster at the cost of brittle coupling to markup structure. Prefer `parseHTML()` for correctness and maintainability unless profiling shows it is a bottleneck.
