### 248. `exec.scenario` Context for Branching Logic Across Multi-Scenario Load Profiles  [official]

`k6/execution`'s `scenario` sub-object exposes the running scenario's name, executor, iteration counters, and start time inside the VU function, allowing a single shared `default` function to branch its behavior based on which load scenario is currently active. This eliminates the need to maintain separate script files for smoke, load, and stress test profiles: one file with multiple named scenarios and a single execution function that reads `exec.scenario.name` to choose the appropriate data set, think-time, or endpoint variant. It also enables precise iteration-scoped timing by computing elapsed time as `(new Date() - exec.scenario.startTime) / 1000`.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import exec from 'k6/execution';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke:   { executor: 'constant-vus',         vus: 2,  duration: '30s',
               exec: 'runTest', env: { PROFILE: 'smoke' } },
    load:    { executor: 'ramping-vus',
               stages: [{ target: 100, duration: '2m' }, { target: 100, duration: '5m' }],
               exec: 'runTest', env: { PROFILE: 'load' } },
    stress:  { executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startRate: 10,
               timeUnit: '1s', stages: [{ target: 500, duration: '3m' }],
               preAllocatedVUs: 200, exec: 'runTest', env: { PROFILE: 'stress' } },
  },
};

export function runTest() {
  const profile = __ENV.PROFILE || exec.scenario.name;
  const baseUrl = 'https://api.example.com';

  // Smoke: only critical path; Load/Stress: full user journey
  const res = http.get(`${baseUrl}/products`);
  check(res, { 'products listed': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  if (profile !== 'smoke') {
    const itemRes = http.get(`${baseUrl}/products/1`);
    check(itemRes, { 'product detail ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
    sleep(profile === 'stress' ? 0.5 : 2); // less think-time under stress
  }

  // Emit scenario name as a custom tag for metric segmentation
  exec.vu.metrics.tags['profile'] = profile;
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Using `exec.scenario.name` for branching tightly couples the shared function to the scenario naming convention. If a scenario is renamed in `options`, the branch condition silently falls through to default behavior instead of erroring, making the bug difficult to detect. Prefer the `env` property approach (`__ENV.PROFILE`) over raw `exec.scenario.name` comparisons: it makes the binding explicit, is overridable from the CLI (`-e PROFILE=stress`), and survives scenario renames without behavior changes.

---

### 249. `k6/encoding` `b64encode` / `b64decode` for Basic Auth and Binary Payload Handling  [official]

The `k6/encoding` module implements RFC 4648 Base64 encoding and decoding, providing the two functions `b64encode(input, encoding)` and `b64decode(input, encoding, format)`. The optional second argument accepts `'rawstd'`, `'rawurl'`, or `'url'` encoding variants, enabling URL-safe base64 without padding — required by JWT header/payload encoding, OAuth2 PKCE code challenges, and certain S3 pre-signed URL schemes. When combined with `k6/crypto` HMAC generation, `b64encode` produces complete Authorization headers for AWS Signature V4 without any external dependencies.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import encoding from 'k6/encoding';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 5, duration: '1m' };

export default function () {
  // Basic Authentication: base64-encode "username:password"
  const credentials = 'load-test-user:s3cr3t-p4ss';
  const basicAuth = encoding.b64encode(credentials);

  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/secure/resource', {
    headers: { Authorization: `Basic ${basicAuth}` },
  });
  check(res, { 'authenticated 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  // URL-safe base64 for a JWT payload segment (no padding)
  const payload = JSON.stringify({ sub: '1234', exp: Math.floor(Date.now()/1000) + 300 });
  const jwtPayload = encoding.b64encode(payload, 'rawurl');

  // Decode a base64-encoded response body field (e.g. embedded binary data)
  const body = res.json();
  if (body.thumbnail_b64) {
    const imageBytes = encoding.b64decode(body.thumbnail_b64, 'std', 'b');
    check(imageBytes, { 'thumbnail decoded': (b) => b.byteLength > 0 });
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `b64encode()` accepts a `string`, `ArrayBuffer`, or `Uint8Array` as input, but `b64decode()` returns either a `string` or an `ArrayBuffer` depending on the third `format` argument (`'s'` for string, `'b'` for `ArrayBuffer`). Mismatching the format argument — for example, expecting an `ArrayBuffer` to get binary bytes but omitting the `'b'` argument — returns a UTF-8 string that may silently corrupt binary data containing non-printable characters. Always pass `'b'` when decoding binary payloads and `'s'` when decoding text content.

---

### 250. `k6/browser` Locator API with `getByRole` / `getByLabel` for Resilient Browser Test Selectors  [official]

k6's browser module implements the Playwright-compatible Locator API, which locates elements using accessibility semantics (`getByRole`, `getByLabel`, `getByTestId`) rather than brittle CSS selectors or XPath expressions. Locators are evaluated lazily at interaction time rather than at query time, so they automatically re-query the DOM after navigations and dynamic re-renders, eliminating stale-element reference errors that plague `page.$()` and `page.$$()` patterns. Strict mode (enabled by default) causes locators that match more than one element to throw an error, forcing test authors to write unambiguous selectors rather than silently acting on the first match.

```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ui_checkout: {
      executor: 'shared-iterations', iterations: 10,
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://example.com/shop');

    // Resilient selectors using accessibility roles and labels
    const searchInput = page.getByLabel('Search products');
    await searchInput.fill('running shoes');
    await searchInput.press('Enter');

    // Wait for results list to appear by role
    const firstResult = page.getByRole('listitem').first();
    await firstResult.waitFor({ state: 'visible' });

    // Click the first product's "Add to Cart" button
    const addToCart = firstResult.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i });
    await addToCart.click();

    // Verify cart badge updates
    const cartBadge = page.getByTestId('cart-item-count');
    const count = await cartBadge.textContent();
    check(count, { 'cart updated': (c) => parseInt(c) > 0 });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `getByRole()` and `getByLabel()` depend on correct ARIA attributes and semantic HTML in the application under test. Applications that use non-semantic `<div>` soup without `aria-*` annotations will not expose queryable roles, causing locator queries to return empty sets and tests to fail with "locator not found" errors that mislead engineers into thinking the test code is wrong when the application accessibility is the root cause. In these cases, `getByTestId()` with a dedicated `data-testid` attribute is the preferred fallback; coordinate with the front-end team to add stable test IDs rather than coupling k6 tests to implementation-specific CSS class names.

---

### 251. `k6/browser` Device Emulation for Mobile Performance Benchmarking  [official]

The `browser.devices` dictionary in the k6 browser module contains predefined viewport, user-agent, and device-pixel-ratio settings for popular mobile and tablet devices. Passing a device descriptor to `browser.newContext({ ...browser.devices['iPhone 15'] })` creates a browser context that accurately simulates mobile rendering conditions, enabling load tests to measure Core Web Vitals under mobile network throttling and viewport constraints. This is critical for products with mobile-first traffic patterns, where desktop k6 browser tests may show acceptable LCP values that hide severely degraded mobile experiences caused by unoptimized image delivery or layout thrashing at small viewport widths.

```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mobile_home: {
      executor: 'constant-vus', vus: 3, duration: '1m',
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'browser_web_vital_lcp{scenario:mobile_home}': ['p(75)<2500'],
    'browser_web_vital_cls{scenario:mobile_home}': ['max<0.1'],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  // Emulate iPhone 15: 390×844 viewport, 3x DPR, mobile UA
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    ...browser.devices['iPhone 15'],
    // Optionally layer on network throttling via offline/slowmo
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://example.com/', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

    // Collect mobile-specific Core Web Vitals via JS evaluation
    const lcp = await page.evaluate(() =>
      new Promise(resolve =>
        new PerformanceObserver(list => {
          const entries = list.getEntries();
          resolve(entries[entries.length - 1].startTime);
        }).observe({ entryTypes: ['largest-contentful-paint'] })
      )
    );
    check(lcp, { 'mobile LCP < 2500ms': (v) => v < 2500 });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
    await context.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** k6's browser module does not implement true network throttling — it only sets the user-agent and viewport dimensions from the device descriptor. To measure performance under 4G or 3G conditions, you must either run the test against a staging environment behind a WAN emulator (e.g., `tc netem` on the server side), use `K6_BROWSER_ARGS=--enable-features=NetworkService` with Chrome's `--throttling-method` flag, or instrument the test with `page.emulateNetworkConditions()` (available via CDP). Simply applying a device descriptor without network throttling may produce optimistic mobile performance numbers.

---

### 252. `k6/net/grpc` Bidirectional Streaming for Testing Streaming RPC Endpoints  [official]

The `k6/net/grpc` module supports bidirectional streaming RPCs through `client.connect()` followed by `client.stream()`, allowing load tests to simulate long-lived gRPC streams where both the client and server send multiple messages over a single persistent connection. Bidirectional streams are common in real-time collaboration tools, telemetry pipelines, and chat services, but are frequently under-tested because most HTTP-centric load tools do not support them. k6's `Stream` object exposes `on('data', handler)`, `write(message)`, and `end()` methods that mirror the gRPC client streaming model, and the stream's lifecycle integrates with the VU event loop so that message handlers execute cooperatively between other async operations.

```javascript
import grpc from 'k6/net/grpc';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(['./proto'], 'chat.proto');

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '2m' };

export default async function () {
  client.connect('grpc.example.com:50051', { plaintext: false });

  const stream = client.stream('chat.ChatService/Chat', {
    metadata: { authorization: 'Bearer test-token' },
  });

  let messagesReceived = 0;
  stream.on('data', (msg) => {
    messagesReceived++;
    check(msg, { 'reply has content': (m) => m.text && m.text.length > 0 });
  });
  stream.on('error', (err) => {
    console.error(`Stream error: ${err.code} — ${err.message}`);
  });

  // Send 5 messages over the bidirectional stream
  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    stream.write({ text: `Hello from VU ${__VU}, message ${i}`, userId: __VU });
    sleep(0.5);
  }
  stream.end();

  // Wait for all replies to arrive before closing the connection
  sleep(2);
  check(messagesReceived, { 'received all replies': (n) => n === 5 });
  client.close();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** gRPC stream `on('data')` callbacks execute asynchronously and their timing is not deterministic relative to the main VU iteration flow. Placing `check()` calls inside `on('data')` handlers and relying on them for threshold evaluation is safe — k6 buffers all check results for the iteration — but the `client.close()` call at the end of `default()` will terminate any in-flight stream callbacks that have not yet been scheduled. Add a `sleep()` before `client.close()` sized to the maximum expected server response latency to prevent spurious `messagesReceived < 5` check failures caused by connection teardown racing against the final message delivery.

---

### 253. `options.gracefulStop` + `options.gracefulRampDown` for Zero-Interrupted-Iteration Test Conclusions  [official]

The `gracefulStop` scenario option (default `30s`) gives VUs that are still executing their current iteration a window to complete before k6 forcibly terminates them at test end. Without a sufficient `gracefulStop`, long-running iterations — multi-step checkout flows, file uploads, or SSE stream consumers — are interrupted mid-flight, inflating `http_req_failed` counts and producing misleading error rates in the final summary. The related `gracefulRampDown` option (available on `ramping-vus` executor) extends the same guarantee to VUs that are being reduced during a ramp-down stage: VUs whose current iteration would outlast the ramp-down window are given `gracefulRampDown` seconds to finish before being killed.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout_flow: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      stages: [
        { target: 100, duration: '2m' },   // ramp up
        { target: 100, duration: '5m' },   // steady state
        { target: 0,   duration: '2m' },   // ramp down
      ],
      // Allow up to 60s for current iterations to complete at ramp-down boundaries
      gracefulRampDown: '60s',
      // Allow up to 60s for iterations in progress at test end to finish
      gracefulStop: '60s',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // Do not count interrupted iterations as failures
    'http_req_failed': ['rate<0.01'],
    'iterations':      ['count>1000'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Simulate a 30-40s user journey across multiple steps
  const res1 = http.get('https://api.example.com/cart');
  check(res1, { 'cart loaded': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(5);

  const res2 = http.post('https://api.example.com/cart/checkout',
    JSON.stringify({ paymentMethod: 'card' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  check(res2, { 'checkout complete': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(3);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Setting `gracefulStop` or `gracefulRampDown` to values larger than the actual 99th-percentile iteration duration extends the total wall-clock test time by the unused portion of the grace window. In a 10-minute test with a 5-minute `gracefulStop`, the test may run for up to 15 minutes even if all VUs complete within 30 seconds. Set both values to `max_expected_iteration_duration * 1.5` rather than a fixed 30-second default, and document the expected maximum iteration duration in the script as a comment so future maintainers can adjust the grace window when new steps are added.

---

### 254. Custom `Trend` Metric for Business-Level SLO Tracking Alongside HTTP Metrics  [official]

k6's built-in `http_req_duration` metric measures raw HTTP round-trip time, but many SLOs are defined over business operations that span multiple HTTP calls — for example, "end-to-end checkout latency" covering login + cart load + order submission. Creating a custom `Trend` metric with `new Trend('checkout_duration')` and recording it with `checkoutTrend.add(elapsedMs)` decouples the business SLO from the individual HTTP step timings, enabling threshold expressions like `'checkout_duration': ['p(95)<3000']` that fail the test when the full multi-step flow exceeds the SLA even if no individual request breaches its own threshold. Custom `Trend` metrics also accept tags, so a single metric can be segmented by region, user tier, or product category in the Grafana output.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { Trend, Rate, Counter } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check } from 'k6';

// Declare custom metrics in init context
const checkoutDuration = new Trend('checkout_duration', true); // true = display in ms
const checkoutSuccessRate = new Rate('checkout_success_rate');
const abandonedCarts = new Counter('abandoned_carts');

export const options = {
  vus: 50, duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    'checkout_duration':     ['p(95)<3000', 'p(99)<5000'],
    'checkout_success_rate': ['rate>0.99'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const start = Date.now();
  let success = false;

  // Step 1: Add item to cart
  const cartRes = http.post('https://api.example.com/cart/items',
    JSON.stringify({ productId: 42, qty: 1 }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });

  if (!check(cartRes, { 'item added': (r) => r.status === 200 })) {
    abandonedCarts.add(1, { step: 'add_item' });
    return;
  }

  // Step 2: Submit order
  const orderRes = http.post('https://api.example.com/orders',
    JSON.stringify({ cartId: cartRes.json('cartId'), confirm: true }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });

  if (check(orderRes, { 'order placed': (r) => r.status === 201 })) {
    success = true;
  } else {
    abandonedCarts.add(1, { step: 'place_order' });
  }

  // Record end-to-end business metric regardless of outcome
  const elapsed = Date.now() - start;
  checkoutDuration.add(elapsed, { success: success ? 'true' : 'false' });
  checkoutSuccessRate.add(success);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom `Trend` metrics created with `new Trend('name', true)` emit values in milliseconds in the end-of-test summary. If you record non-duration values (e.g., byte counts, item counts) using a `Trend`, the second argument should be `false` (or omitted) to prevent the summary from appending `ms` to the aggregated values, which confuses downstream tooling that parses the text summary. Also note that `Trend` thresholds only evaluate `avg`, `min`, `max`, `med`, and `p(N)` — there is no `count` aggregation on `Trend`; use a `Counter` in parallel if you need both a distribution and a total invocation count.

---

### 255. `per-vu-iterations` Executor for Exhaustive Data-Set Coverage Without Overlap  [official]

The `per-vu-iterations` executor assigns each VU a fixed number of iterations (`iterations` option), guaranteeing that every VU executes exactly that many iterations before stopping. Unlike `shared-iterations` — where fast VUs may consume many more iterations than slow ones — `per-vu-iterations` produces balanced per-VU workloads that are ideal for exhaustive data-set walks: if you have 1 000 unique test users in a `SharedArray` and want every user tested exactly once, set `vus: 1000` and `iterations: 1`. Because iteration assignment is deterministic (`exec.vu.iterationInScenario` starts at 0 for every VU), combining `per-vu-iterations` with `SharedArray` index modulo guarantees that each data row is exercised at least once without duplication.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';
import exec from 'k6/execution';
import { check } from 'k6';

const users = new SharedArray('test-users', () =>
  JSON.parse(open('./fixtures/users.json'))
);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    full_coverage: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 100,
      iterations: 10,          // each VU processes 10 unique users
      maxDuration: '5m',       // safety cap; terminates if VUs hang
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_failed': ['rate<0.001'],  // allow 0.1% tolerance for flaky infra
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Deterministic mapping: VU 0 takes rows 0-9, VU 1 takes rows 10-19, etc.
  const userIndex =
    (exec.vu.idInTest - 1) * exec.scenario.iterationsPerVU +
    exec.vu.iterationInScenario;

  if (userIndex >= users.length) {
    // Guard: more VU×iterations than data rows; skip gracefully
    return;
  }

  const user = users[userIndex];
  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/auth/login',
    JSON.stringify({ email: user.email, password: user.password }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  check(res, {
    'login 200': (r) => r.status === 200,
    'token present': (r) => !!r.json('access_token'),
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `per-vu-iterations` waits for all VUs to complete their full `iterations` count before the scenario ends. If one VU encounters a slow or hung server response that outlasts `maxDuration`, k6 interrupts the hung VU but marks the scenario as having unfinished iterations, which inflates the `dropped_iterations` counter. This counter appears in the end-of-test summary and can trigger false-positive threshold violations on `iterations` count thresholds. Always set `maxDuration` to at least `expected_single_iteration_time * iterations * 2` to give legitimately slow VUs enough runway to finish while still protecting against true hangs.

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 47)

### Gotcha 198. `k6/experimental/fs` `File.read()` returns `null` on EOF, not `0`, breaking `while (bytesRead > 0)` loops  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** Engineers familiar with Node.js `fs.read()` expect a read-at-EOF to return `0` bytes read. The k6 `File.read()` API instead resolves its Promise with `null` when the end of file is reached, following the WHATWG Streams convention rather than POSIX. A `while ((bytesRead = await file.read(buf)) > 0)` loop treats `null > 0` as `false` (because `null` is coerced to `0` in JavaScript numeric comparison), which accidentally exits the loop without signalling an error — but the loop body never executes the final partial-buffer read that contains the last chunk of the file. The truncation is silent: `check(totalBytesRead === fileSize)` fails with a value short by exactly the final chunk size, and the uploaded binary payload is corrupted with a missing tail segment that downstream decompressors reject with an opaque "unexpected end of archive" error.

**Fix:** Use `null` as the EOF sentinel explicitly: `while ((bytesRead = await file.read(buf)) !== null)`. This matches the documented API contract and handles both full-buffer and partial final-read cases correctly. Add a post-loop assertion `check(totalBytesRead, { 'read full file': (n) => n === fileSize })` using `file.stat().size` to detect truncation in CI.

---

### Gotcha 199. `handleSummary()` file paths are resolved relative to the k6 invocation directory, not the script file  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A team stores k6 scripts under `tests/load/` and their `handleSummary()` returns `{ 'reports/results.xml': junitXml }`, expecting the XML file to appear at `tests/load/reports/results.xml`. When CI runs `k6 run tests/load/checkout.js` from the repository root, the file is written to `./reports/results.xml` relative to the repository root — outside the `tests/load/` directory — but the CI artifact upload step looks for `tests/load/reports/results.xml` and finds nothing. The test "succeeds" from k6's perspective (exit 0) but the CI pipeline reports "no artifacts found" and the JUnit results are silently lost. The discrepancy only surfaces when a developer investigates missing test history in their CI dashboard.

**Fix:** Always construct the output path from `__ENV` injection — pass `K6_REPORT_DIR` from the CI environment and use it as the base: `{ [`${__ENV.K6_REPORT_DIR || '.'}/results.xml`]: junitXml }`. Alternatively, document that `k6 run` must be invoked from a specific directory and enforce this with a `Makefile` target or CI step that `cd`s into the correct directory before running k6.

---

### Gotcha 200. `crypto.subtle.importKey()` called inside `default()` per-iteration exhausts memory under high concurrency because `CryptoKey` objects are not garbage-collected between iterations  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer writes an HMAC-signing helper function that calls `crypto.subtle.importKey()` at the start of the `default()` function to keep the signing logic self-contained. Under light load (5 VUs) the test passes without issue. When the VU count is raised to 200, the k6 process RSS climbs steadily throughout the test and eventually triggers an OOM kill after ~20 minutes of a 30-minute soak test. The root cause is that each `importKey()` call allocates a `CryptoKey` object in the Go runtime's WebCrypto layer, and Go's garbage collector does not reclaim these objects as aggressively as the JavaScript GC would reclaim ordinary objects. With 200 VUs each calling `importKey()` hundreds of times, the cumulative allocation rate exceeds the GC collection rate and memory grows unboundedly.

**Fix:** Call `crypto.subtle.importKey()` exactly once in the init context (module scope) or in `setup()`, and store the resulting `CryptoKey` object in a module-level variable. Pass it to the `default()` function via module scope — `CryptoKey` objects are read-only after creation and are safe to share across VU iterations. This reduces the total number of `CryptoKey` allocations from `(VU_count × iterations)` to `1` (or `VU_count` if init code runs per-VU).

---

### Gotcha 201. `browser.devices` dictionary key names are case-sensitive and must match exactly — `'iphone 15'` (lowercase) throws "device not found"  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer copies a device name from an online article that uses lowercase formatting (`browser.devices['iphone 15']`) and receives an unhelpful `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'userAgent')` error when k6 tries to spread the device descriptor into `browser.newContext()`. The k6 browser module uses Playwright's device descriptor dictionary, which uses title-case names like `'iPhone 15'`, `'Pixel 7'`, and `'Galaxy S9+'`. The error message does not say "device not found" — it propagates from the attempted property access on `undefined`, which makes the root cause opaque to engineers unfamiliar with the Playwright device naming convention. Fuzzy-matching or case-insensitive lookups are not performed.

**Fix:** Use the exact device names from the Playwright devices reference (`https://playwright.dev/docs/emulation#devices`). Print the available keys at script startup for debugging: `console.log(Object.keys(browser.devices).filter(k => k.toLowerCase().includes('iphone')).join(', '))`. Add a guard check in shared browser helpers: `if (!browser.devices[deviceName]) { throw new Error(\`Unknown device: ${deviceName}. Available: ${Object.keys(browser.devices).join(', ')}\`) }`.

---

### Gotcha 202. `exec.scenario.iterationsPerVU` is `undefined` for non-`per-vu-iterations` executors, causing `NaN` index calculations that silently access `users[NaN]`  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A team maintains a single k6 test file that is run under multiple executor configurations depending on the environment. The data-set index calculation `(exec.vu.idInTest - 1) * exec.scenario.iterationsPerVU + exec.vu.iterationInScenario` works correctly under `per-vu-iterations`. When the same file is run under `ramping-vus` for a performance regression test, `exec.scenario.iterationsPerVU` returns `undefined` because the property is only defined for the `per-vu-iterations` executor. The multiplication produces `NaN`, the array index becomes `users[NaN]`, which JavaScript evaluates as `undefined`, and every HTTP request is made with `undefined` credentials — which the API rejects with 401. The test logs hundreds of `check: login 200` failures but no JavaScript error, because `users[NaN]` does not throw; it silently returns `undefined`.

**Fix:** Guard the index calculation with an executor-type check: `const iterPerVU = exec.scenario.executor === 'per-vu-iterations' ? exec.scenario.iterationsPerVU : 1`. For non-`per-vu-iterations` executors, fall back to the modulo pattern: `const userIndex = exec.vu.iterationInScenario % users.length`. Add a startup assertion in `setup()` that validates `users.length > 0` and logs the executor name so that data-mapping logic mismatches are visible in the k6 init output.

---

### Gotcha 203. `setInterval` callbacks continue firing after `client.close()` on gRPC streams, sending requests on a closed connection and logging confusing "transport is closing" errors  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer uses `setInterval` to send periodic gRPC stream write messages while awaiting a long-duration server-side streaming response. When the main iteration finishes and calls `client.close()`, the `setInterval` timer is not automatically cleared, so the next scheduled callback fires and calls `stream.write()` on a connection that has already been closed by `client.close()`. k6 logs `GoError: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = transport is closing` from the timer callback. Because this error occurs inside a timer callback rather than the main iteration flow, it does not increment `http_req_failed` (gRPC errors use `grpc_req_duration` and `grpc_req_failed`) and does not trigger any threshold. Engineers monitoring only the summary metrics see a clean test, while the k6 console is flooded with error messages that obscure legitimate failures.

**Fix:** Always call `clearInterval(intervalHandle)` before `client.close()`. Structure the VU function so that the timer handle is captured in a variable scoped to the iteration, and add a `try...finally` block to guarantee `clearInterval` is called even when the iteration throws. If the gRPC stream lifecycle is complex, move the interval management into a helper class with explicit `start()` and `stop()` methods that wrap the `setInterval`/`clearInterval` calls, making it easier to audit cleanup paths.

### 256. `http.asyncRequest()` with `Promise.all()` for Parallel Independent API Calls Within a Single VU  [official]

When a single page load triggers several independent API calls, using `http.asyncRequest()` with `Promise.all()` lets one VU fire all requests concurrently and wait for the last one to complete, closely mirroring real browser behaviour. This pattern avoids the artificial serialisation introduced by chaining synchronous `http.get()` calls and produces more accurate iteration-level latency measurements for pages that depend on fan-out API patterns.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    fanout: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 20,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '2m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 30,
      maxVUs: 60,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{name:user_profile}': ['p(95)<400'],
    'http_req_duration{name:feed}': ['p(95)<600'],
    'http_req_duration{name:notifications}': ['p(95)<300'],
    'http_req_failed': ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const base = 'https://api.example.com';
  const token = `Bearer ${__ENV.API_TOKEN}`;
  const headers = { Authorization: token, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' };

  // Fire three requests concurrently; each is independently named for per-metric thresholds
  const [profileRes, feedRes, notifRes] = await Promise.all([
    http.asyncRequest('GET', `${base}/user/profile`, null,
      { headers, tags: { name: 'user_profile' } }),
    http.asyncRequest('GET', `${base}/feed?limit=20`, null,
      { headers, tags: { name: 'feed' } }),
    http.asyncRequest('GET', `${base}/notifications?unread=true`, null,
      { headers, tags: { name: 'notifications' } }),
  ]);

  check(profileRes, { 'profile 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  check(feedRes,    { 'feed 200':    (r) => r.status === 200 });
  check(notifRes,   { 'notif 200':   (r) => r.status === 200 });

  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `http.asyncRequest()` has no built-in abort mechanism: if `Promise.all()` rejects because one request throws, the other in-flight requests continue consuming VU goroutines until they complete or time out. This means `maxDuration` remains the only safeguard against hung VUs when one of the parallel legs stalls. Additionally, k6's `http_req_duration` metric records the wall-clock time of each individual request starting from when it was dispatched — not the total elapsed time of the `Promise.all()` block — so the per-metric p95 values will be lower than the actual page-load time experienced by a user. To measure the full fan-out duration, wrap the `Promise.all()` call with a manual `Trend` metric recorded before and after the await.

---

### 257. `ramping-arrival-rate` Executor with `startRate` and `timeUnit` for Realistic Traffic Curves  [official]

The `ramping-arrival-rate` executor implements an open model where iterations begin independently of system response time. Pairing a non-zero `startRate` with multi-phase `stages` and a `timeUnit` of `'1m'` (rather than the default `'1s'`) produces smooth, human-readable rate configurations that match capacity-planning documents expressed in requests-per-minute. The `preAllocatedVUs` pool is reserved at test start; k6 auto-scales up to `maxVUs` as each stage ramp increases demand.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { getCurrentStageIndex } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-utils/1.4.0/index.js';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    realistic_ramp: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate',
      startRate: 60,         // 60 req/min at t=0 (warm-up floor)
      timeUnit: '1m',        // rates expressed per minute
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,   // reserved from the start
      maxVUs: 150,           // ceiling; k6 auto-scales up to this
      stages: [
        { target: 60,  duration: '2m' },  // hold warm-up rate
        { target: 300, duration: '5m' },  // ramp to peak
        { target: 300, duration: '5m' },  // sustain peak
        { target: 60,  duration: '3m' },  // ramp down
      ],
      gracefulStop: '30s',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(99)<1000'],
    dropped_iterations: ['count<50'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const stageIndex = getCurrentStageIndex();
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/search?q=k6',
    { tags: { stage: String(stageIndex) } });
  check(res, { 'search 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** When the target rate exceeds the capacity of the current `preAllocatedVUs` pool and k6 cannot allocate additional VUs fast enough to meet the `maxVUs` ceiling, iterations are dropped and counted in `dropped_iterations`. This counter does NOT trigger a non-zero exit code on its own — you must add a threshold on `dropped_iterations` (e.g., `count<50`) to surface capacity shortfalls as test failures. A high `dropped_iterations` rate indicates that `maxVUs` or iteration throughput is the bottleneck rather than the SUT, invalidating load measurements for that stage.

---

### 258. Tag-Scoped Thresholds for Granular Per-Endpoint SLA Enforcement  [official]

k6 threshold expressions can be scoped to a subset of metric samples using tag filters. By attaching a `name` tag to every request (either via `http.url` template literals or the `params.tags` object), you can define separate p95 thresholds per endpoint in the same test, receiving a distinct pass/fail signal per SLA without running separate scripts. This approach is the idiomatic replacement for maintaining multiple single-endpoint scripts.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    // Global error-rate gate
    'http_req_failed': ['rate<0.005'],
    // Per-endpoint latency SLAs scoped by the 'name' tag
    'http_req_duration{name:auth_login}':     ['p(95)<500', 'p(99)<1000'],
    'http_req_duration{name:product_search}': ['p(95)<800'],
    'http_req_duration{name:checkout}':       ['p(95)<1200', { threshold: 'p(99)<3000', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '30s' }],
  },
  scenarios: {
    mixed_flow: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 50,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '3m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 40,
      maxVUs: 80,
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Use the url`` template tag to set the canonical name for grouping
  const loginRes = http.post(
    http.url`https://api.example.com/auth/login`,
    JSON.stringify({ user: 'test', pass: 'test' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, tags: { name: 'auth_login' } }
  );
  check(loginRes, { 'login ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  const searchRes = http.get(
    http.url`https://api.example.com/products?q=widget`,
    { tags: { name: 'product_search' } }
  );
  check(searchRes, { 'search ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  const checkoutRes = http.post(
    http.url`https://api.example.com/checkout`,
    JSON.stringify({ cartId: 'abc123' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, tags: { name: 'checkout' } }
  );
  check(checkoutRes, { 'checkout ok': (r) => r.status === 201 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Tag-scoped thresholds are evaluated against the full sample set collected during the test run; they do not provide time-window granularity. If the checkout endpoint is fast during warm-up and slow during peak, the p95 will still pass as long as the overall distribution is below the limit. To surface per-phase regressions, combine tag-scoped thresholds with the `stage` tag (from `getCurrentStageIndex()`) and export to Prometheus or Grafana Cloud, where time-series PromQL queries can identify the degradation window.

---

### 259. `abortOnFail` + `delayAbortEval` for Early Test Termination Under Runaway Errors  [official]

Setting `abortOnFail: true` on a threshold causes k6 to terminate the test run as soon as that threshold is violated, preventing prolonged soak runs from burning VUH budget on a clearly broken deployment. The companion `delayAbortEval` property postpones the first evaluation until the specified duration has elapsed, giving the metric enough samples for a statistically meaningful p-value before abort logic fires.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    soak: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 50,
      duration: '30m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // Abort early if more than 5% of requests fail — but wait 60s for sample warm-up
    http_req_failed: [{
      threshold: 'rate>0.05',
      abortOnFail: true,
      delayAbortEval: '60s',
    }],
    // Abort if p99 exceeds 5s — give 2 minutes for JVM warm-up before enforcing
    http_req_duration: [{
      threshold: 'p(99)>5000',
      abortOnFail: true,
      delayAbortEval: '2m',
    }],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/health');
  check(res, {
    'healthy': (r) => r.status === 200,
    'fast':    (r) => r.timings.duration < 2000,
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** When `abortOnFail` triggers, k6 exits with code `99` (threshold failure). CI pipelines that only check for non-zero exit codes will treat this the same as a passed-threshold failure. If your pipeline needs to distinguish between "test ran to completion and failed thresholds" versus "test was aborted early", check for exit code `99` explicitly. Also note that `teardown()` still runs after an abort, allowing resource cleanup — but `handleSummary()` is called with partial data reflecting only the metrics collected before the abort, so any summary assertions that rely on iteration count will produce misleading results.

---

### 260. `k6/experimental/streams` `ReadableStream` for Incremental Large-File Processing Without Full In-Memory Load  [official]

The `k6/experimental/streams` module brings the WHATWG Streams API to k6 init context, enabling line-by-line processing of large CSV fixtures without loading the entire file into memory. Combining `ReadableStream` with the `k6/experimental/fs` module produces a composable pipeline: the fs layer provides raw bytes; the stream layer buffers incomplete lines and emits complete records. This pattern is essential when fixture files exceed 100 MB and would otherwise cause OOM kills under high VU counts.

```javascript
import { open } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import { ReadableStream } from 'k6/experimental/streams';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

// Build a SharedArray from a large CSV by streaming it line-by-line in init context
const users = new SharedArray('csv-users', async () => {
  const file = await open('./fixtures/large-users.csv');
  const records = [];
  let remainder = '';

  const stream = new ReadableStream({
    async pull(controller) {
      const buf = new Uint8Array(65536); // 64 KB chunks
      const bytesRead = await file.read(buf);
      if (bytesRead === null) {
        // Flush any unterminated final line
        if (remainder.length > 0) {
          controller.enqueue(remainder);
        }
        controller.close();
        return;
      }
      const chunk = new TextDecoder().decode(buf.subarray(0, bytesRead));
      const lines = (remainder + chunk).split('\n');
      remainder = lines.pop(); // hold incomplete final line
      for (const line of lines) {
        if (line.trim()) controller.enqueue(line.trim());
      }
    },
  });

  const reader = stream.getReader();
  let first = true;
  while (true) {
    const { done, value } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;
    if (first) { first = false; continue; } // skip CSV header
    const [email, password, role] = value.split(',');
    records.push({ email, password, role });
  }
  return records;
});

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: '5m',
};

export default function () {
  const user = users[Math.floor(Math.random() * users.length)];
  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/login',
    JSON.stringify({ email: user.email, password: user.password }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  check(res, { 'login ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `ReadableStream` and `k6/experimental/fs` are both experimental modules and may introduce breaking changes before promotion to stable. The stream is constructed once during the `SharedArray` initialiser (init context), which runs in a single goroutine — not per-VU — so the memory saving is fully realised. However, if the `pull()` callback throws (e.g., a malformed UTF-8 byte sequence in the CSV), the stream silently enters an errored state and `reader.read()` will reject on the next call. Wrap the `while` loop body in a `try/catch` and log the line number to aid debugging of encoding issues in fixture files sourced from third-party systems.

---

### 261. `k6/secrets` Multi-Source Secret Injection with Auto-Redaction for Secure CI Pipelines  [official]

The `k6/secrets` module retrieves sensitive values at runtime from configurable sources (env-var mock, file, URL, or Grafana Cloud) and automatically redacts them from all k6 log output as `***SECRET_REDACTED***`. This lets you safely pipe k6 logs to a SIEM or CI log aggregator without pre-filtering. Defining multiple secret sources with different precedence levels enables a "local override" pattern: the file source is used in developer workstations, while the cloud source takes precedence in CI.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import secrets from 'k6/secrets';
import { check } from 'k6';

// Secret sources are configured via --secret-source CLI flag:
//   k6 run --secret-source=mock=apiKey=s3cr3t,dbPass=hunter2 script.js
// Or in CI: --secret-source=file=secrets.env

export const options = {
  vus: 10,
  duration: '1m',
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  // Async retrieval — value is live-fetched, not cached between iterations
  const apiKey = await secrets.get('apiKey');
  const dbPass = await secrets.get('dbPass');

  // apiKey and dbPass are automatically redacted in any console.log() or error trace
  const res = await http.asyncRequest('POST',
    'https://api.example.com/admin/provision',
    JSON.stringify({ password: dbPass }),
    {
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-API-Key': apiKey,           // never appears in k6 logs
      },
    }
  );

  check(res, { 'provision 201': (r) => r.status === 201 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Each `secrets.get()` call is asynchronous and incurs a small round-trip cost to the secret source backend on every invocation. For the `file` and `mock` sources this is a local memory lookup and is negligible; for the `url` source it involves an HTTP request to an external vault endpoint per-VU per-iteration, which will appear in k6's `http_req_duration` metrics and inflate reported latency if not tagged separately. Retrieve secrets once in `setup()` and pass them to VUs via the return value to eliminate per-iteration overhead, keeping `secrets.get()` in `default()` only when credential rotation during a test run is an explicit requirement.

---

### 262. `k6/websockets` Stable Module with Multiple Concurrent Connections Per VU via the Global Event Loop  [official]

The stable `k6/websockets` module (promoted from `k6/experimental/websockets`) uses a global event loop that allows a single VU to maintain multiple simultaneous WebSocket connections. Each connection runs asynchronously; the VU does not block on a single socket's event stream. This is the canonical pattern for testing WebSocket fan-out scenarios — e.g., an IoT gateway or a pub/sub broker — where each "user" has subscriptions across multiple channels.

```javascript
import { WebSocket } from 'k6/websockets';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ws_fanout: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 20,
      duration: '3m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    ws_msgs_received: ['count>0'],
    ws_connecting:    ['p(95)<500'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const received = { channelA: 0, channelB: 0 };

  // VU holds two concurrent connections to different channels
  const wsA = new WebSocket('wss://broker.example.com/topics/channel-A');
  const wsB = new WebSocket('wss://broker.example.com/topics/channel-B');

  wsA.onmessage = (evt) => {
    received.channelA++;
    check(evt, { 'channelA msg non-empty': (e) => e.data.length > 0 });
  };
  wsA.onerror = (evt) => console.error(`WS-A error: ${evt.error}`);

  wsB.onmessage = (evt) => {
    received.channelB++;
    check(evt, { 'channelB msg non-empty': (e) => e.data.length > 0 });
  };
  wsB.onerror = (evt) => console.error(`WS-B error: ${evt.error}`);

  // Hold connections open for 10 seconds, then close both
  sleep(10);

  wsA.close();
  wsB.close();

  check(received, {
    'got channelA msgs': (r) => r.channelA > 0,
    'got channelB msgs': (r) => r.channelB > 0,
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** With multiple concurrent WebSocket connections per VU, the `ws_session` built-in metric counts each `new WebSocket()` call as a separate session, so `ws_session` counts will be a multiple of the actual number of VUs. Grafana dashboards that display "active VU count" derived from `ws_session` will overstate user concurrency by the number of connections per VU. Explicitly tag each `new WebSocket()` with a `channel` tag (`{ tags: { channel: 'A' } }` via the `params` argument) and filter dashboards by VU ID or scenario rather than raw session count for accurate concurrency reporting.

---

### 263. `xk6-disruptor` `PodDisruptor` HTTP Fault Injection Alongside k6 Load Scenarios  [community]

The `xk6-disruptor` extension adds a `PodDisruptor` class that targets Kubernetes pods by label selector and injects configurable HTTP faults (error rates, latency) while k6 simultaneously drives load. Running fault injection in `setup()` or a dedicated scenario function (via `exec`) allows precise control over the fault window — enabling SLO validation tests: "does the system meet its p99 SLA when 10% of pod responses return 503?"

```javascript
// Run with: k6 run --out cloud script.js
// Requires: k6 built with xk6-disruptor extension
import http from 'k6/http';
import { PodDisruptor } from 'k6/x/disruptor';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    // Phase 1: baseline load
    baseline: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 100,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '1m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 40,
      tags: { phase: 'baseline' },
    },
    // Phase 2: load under fault injection (starts after 1m baseline)
    fault_window: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 100,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      startTime: '1m',
      duration: '1m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 40,
      tags: { phase: 'fault_window' },
      exec: 'loadWithFaults',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{phase:baseline}':     ['p(99)<500'],
    'http_req_duration{phase:fault_window}': ['p(99)<2000'], // relaxed SLA during faults
  },
};

export function setup() {
  return {}; // baseline data if needed
}

export function loadWithFaults() {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/products');
}

// Fault injection wired to a dedicated scenario exec function
export async function injectFaults() {
  const disruptor = new PodDisruptor({
    namespace: 'default',
    selectPods: { app: 'api-service' },
    injectTimeout: '70s',  // longer than fault duration to avoid race
  });

  await disruptor.injectHTTPFaults(
    { averageDelay: '200ms', errorRate: 0.10, errorCode: 503 },
    '60s'
  );
}

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/products');
  check(res, { 'products ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.5);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `xk6-disruptor` requires a Kubernetes cluster with the `xk6-disruptor-agent` DaemonSet pre-deployed — it does not work on bare-metal or Docker-Compose-based test environments. The custom k6 binary built with the extension cannot be used with `k6 cloud run` (Grafana-managed runners) unless you also provide a custom runner image. For teams on Grafana Cloud k6, the standard workflow is `k6 cloud run --local-execution`, which runs the binary on the engineer's machine (with cluster access) while streaming results to the cloud. Keep the `injectTimeout` at least 10s longer than the fault `duration` argument to prevent a race where the timeout fires before the fault window expires, leaving the disruptor agent in an inconsistent state.

### 264. Prometheus Native Histograms for Accurate `histogram_quantile()` Without Pre-Committed Bucket Widths  [official]

Enabling `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true` sends each k6 `Trend` metric as a Prometheus native histogram, avoiding the static bucket problem of conventional histograms. `histogram_quantile()` queries then use Prometheus's DDSketch merge for accurate quantile estimation across scraped intervals. This is the recommended approach for SLO dashboards that need sub-1% quantile accuracy without pre-committing to `le` bucket boundaries that may miss production latency distributions.

```javascript
// k6 script: nothing special required — use standard Trend metrics
// Run with:
//   K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_SERVER_URL=http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/write \
//   K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true \
//   K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_PUSH_INTERVAL=5s \
//   K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_STALE_MARKERS=true \
//   k6 run -o experimental-prometheus-rw script.js

import http from 'k6/http';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check } from 'k6';

const checkoutDuration = new Trend('checkout_duration', true);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    soak: { executor: 'constant-vus', vus: 50, duration: '30m' },
  },
  // Thresholds still evaluated locally by k6 using its own aggregator
  thresholds: {
    checkout_duration: ['p(95)<2000'],
    http_req_failed:   ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const start = Date.now();

  const cartRes = http.post('https://api.example.com/cart/add',
    JSON.stringify({ sku: 'WIDGET-42', qty: 1 }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });

  if (check(cartRes, { 'cart ok': (r) => r.status === 200 })) {
    const orderRes = http.post('https://api.example.com/checkout',
      JSON.stringify({ cartId: cartRes.json('cartId') }),
      { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
    check(orderRes, { 'checkout ok': (r) => r.status === 201 });
    checkoutDuration.add(Date.now() - start, { flow: 'full' });
  } else {
    checkoutDuration.add(Date.now() - start, { flow: 'cart_fail' });
  }
}
```

*Prometheus query for p99 across any scrape interval:*
```promql
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(k6_checkout_duration_bucket[5m])))
```

**Tradeoff.** Native histograms require Prometheus v2.40.0+ with `--enable-feature=native-histograms` AND the remote write endpoint must support the native histogram protobuf encoding. Older Prometheus versions, Thanos, and some cloud Prometheus-compatible APIs (e.g., Amazon Managed Prometheus at the time of writing) silently drop native histogram samples, resulting in empty metric series. Always verify native histogram support in the target TSDB before switching from `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_STATS` to native histograms; a missing series in a Grafana panel fails silently with "No data" rather than an error, making the misconfiguration difficult to spot in a fresh CI pipeline.

### 265. Scenario-Level `env` and `tags` for Zero-Code Environment-Parameterised Multi-Tenant Tests  [official]

Each scenario in `options.scenarios` accepts its own `env` object (injected into `__ENV` for that scenario's VUs) and `tags` object (applied to all metrics emitted during that scenario). Combined, they allow a single script to exercise multiple tenants or environments simultaneously without any conditional branching in the VU function itself — the scenario configuration drives the parameterisation entirely.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    tenant_a: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 30, timeUnit: '1s', duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 10, maxVUs: 20,
      env:  { BASE_URL: 'https://tenant-a.example.com', PLAN: 'enterprise' },
      tags: { tenant: 'a', plan: 'enterprise' },
    },
    tenant_b: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 15, timeUnit: '1s', duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 5, maxVUs: 10,
      env:  { BASE_URL: 'https://tenant-b.example.com', PLAN: 'starter' },
      tags: { tenant: 'b', plan: 'starter' },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{tenant:a}': ['p(95)<400'],
    'http_req_duration{tenant:b}': ['p(95)<800'],  // looser SLA for starter tier
  },
};

export default function () {
  // __ENV.BASE_URL is scenario-specific; no if/else needed
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/dashboard`,
    { tags: { plan: __ENV.PLAN } });
  check(res, { 'dashboard ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Scenario-level `env` values override top-level `--env` CLI flags only for VUs running within that scenario. If a VU needs to access a secret that is global (e.g., an admin token passed via `--env ADMIN_TOKEN=...`), and the scenario also defines `env: { ... }`, the top-level `__ENV.ADMIN_TOKEN` is still accessible because scenario `env` merges with — not replaces — the global env. However, if you define the same key in both the scenario `env` and the global CLI env, the scenario `env` value wins, which can create subtle credential mismatches when the same key is accidentally reused across context boundaries.

---

### 266. Page Object Model (POM) Pattern for Reusable k6 Browser Test Abstractions  [official]

Structuring k6 browser tests around Page Object classes encapsulates locator queries and interaction sequences behind stable method names. When the application's HTML structure changes, only the Page Object needs updating rather than every test script. This mirrors the POM pattern from Playwright/Selenium but adapted for k6's async browser API, which requires `async/await` on all page interactions.

```javascript
// pages/LoginPage.js
export class LoginPage {
  constructor(page) {
    this.page = page;
    this.emailInput    = page.locator('[data-testid="email"]');
    this.passwordInput = page.locator('[data-testid="password"]');
    this.submitButton  = page.locator('[data-testid="login-submit"]');
    this.errorBanner   = page.locator('[role="alert"]');
  }

  async navigate() {
    await this.page.goto('https://app.example.com/login');
    await this.page.waitForSelector('[data-testid="email"]');
  }

  async login(email, password) {
    await this.emailInput.fill(email);
    await this.passwordInput.fill(password);
    await this.submitButton.click();
  }

  async isLoginError() {
    return this.errorBanner.isVisible();
  }
}

// test-login.js
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { LoginPage } from './pages/LoginPage.js';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browser_login: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 3,
      duration: '2m',
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();

  try {
    const loginPage = new LoginPage(page);
    await loginPage.navigate();
    await loginPage.login('user@example.com', 'password123');
    await page.waitForNavigation();

    check(page, { 'redirected to dashboard': (p) => p.url().includes('/dashboard') });
    const hasError = await loginPage.isLoginError();
    check(null, { 'no error banner': () => !hasError });
  } finally {
    await page.close(); // always close to avoid VU goroutine leaks
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** k6 does not provide a built-in module system for loading Page Object files from relative paths the way Node.js does. You must use k6's local import syntax (`import { LoginPage } from './pages/LoginPage.js'`) and ensure the pages directory is present wherever the script is archived (e.g., with `k6 archive` or `k6 cloud run`). If the Page Object is imported by multiple test scripts and the import path differs (e.g., `'./pages/LoginPage.js'` vs `'../pages/LoginPage.js'`), k6 will bundle two separate copies of the module into the test archive — this is not a runtime error but doubles the bundle size and can produce confusing stack traces on failure.

---

### 267. `http.url` Template Tag for Automatic URL Grouping Without Manual `tags.name` Annotation  [official]

The `http.url` template literal tag replaces variable path segments with their template placeholder text for the `http_req_duration` metric `name` tag. This prevents the default behaviour where unique resource IDs in URLs create unbounded cardinality in metric labels (e.g., `/users/1`, `/users/2`, …), which overloads time-series databases and makes aggregate threshold evaluation impossible.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';
import { check } from 'k6';

const users = new SharedArray('users', () =>
  JSON.parse(open('./fixtures/users.json'))
);

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: '2m',
  thresholds: {
    // Threshold targets the grouped name, not individual IDs
    'http_req_duration{name:GET /users/${id}}': ['p(95)<300'],
    'http_req_duration{name:GET /orders/${id}/items}': ['p(95)<500'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const user = users[Math.floor(Math.random() * users.length)];

  // http.url`` sets name tag to the template string (with ${id} as literal text)
  const profileRes = http.get(
    http.url`https://api.example.com/users/${user.id}`,
    { tags: { flow: 'profile' } }
  );
  check(profileRes, { 'profile 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  const ordersRes = http.get(
    http.url`https://api.example.com/orders/${user.orderId}/items`,
    { tags: { flow: 'orders' } }
  );
  check(ordersRes, { 'orders 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The `name` tag set by `http.url` takes precedence over any `tags.name` specified in the `params` object for the same request. If you mix `http.url` for some requests and `params.tags.name` for others in the same script, the inconsistency is invisible at runtime — both produce a `name` tag, but maintaining the convention becomes a cognitive burden across large teams. Choose one strategy per codebase: either always use `http.url` for URL grouping, or always use `params.tags.name`, and document the choice in your k6 style guide.

---

### 268. `k6/net/grpc` Connection Reuse Across Iterations by Moving `client.connect()` to Init Context  [official]

By default, each iteration calls `client.connect()` and `client.close()` within the `default()` function, creating a new TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 connection per iteration. For gRPC services where connection establishment is expensive (mutual TLS, long-lived streaming, connection reuse with multiplexing), moving `client.connect()` to the init context eliminates per-iteration handshake overhead and produces latency measurements that reflect actual RPC processing time rather than connection setup time.

```javascript
import grpc from 'k6/net/grpc';
import { check } from 'k6';
import exec from 'k6/execution';

const client = new grpc.Client();

// connect() called in init context: connection is reused across all iterations
client.connect('grpc.example.com:443', {
  tls: true,
  // Uncomment for mTLS:
  // tlsClientCertPem: open('./certs/client.crt'),
  // tlsClientKeyPem:  open('./certs/client.key'),
  // tlsCACertPem:     open('./certs/ca.crt'),
});

// Load the protobuf descriptor once in init context
client.load(['./proto'], 'product.proto');

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    grpc_load: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 200,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 30,
      maxVUs: 60,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    grpc_req_duration: ['p(95)<200', 'p(99)<500'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  // No connect() here — reuse the init-context connection
  const res = client.invoke('example.ProductService/GetProduct',
    { productId: `product-${exec.vu.iterationInScenario % 1000}` }
  );

  check(res, {
    'grpc ok':   () => res.status === grpc.StatusOK,
    'has price': () => res.message && res.message.price > 0,
  });
}

export function teardown() {
  client.close();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Moving `client.connect()` to the init context means all VUs share the same underlying connection object. In k6's gRPC implementation, each VU holds its own goroutine but the `Client` object's connection pool is shared. If the gRPC server applies per-connection concurrency limits (e.g., `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`), sharing a single `Client` across all VUs means all VUs are multiplexed over the same HTTP/2 connection and can collectively hit the stream limit. In this case, instantiate one `Client` per VU by moving `new grpc.Client()` and `client.connect()` into the `default()` function (at the cost of per-iteration TLS handshake overhead), or confirm that the server's `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` setting is at least equal to the target VU count.

---

### 269. `exec.scenario.startTime` and `Date.now()` for Elapsed-Time-Aware Load Logic  [official]

`exec.scenario.startTime` returns the Unix timestamp (in milliseconds) at which the current scenario began. Subtracting it from `Date.now()` gives the elapsed scenario time, enabling VU-level logic that adapts to the current phase of the test — for example, suppressing think-time during the ramp-up phase or switching to a heavier endpoint mix only after the warm-up period.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';
import exec from 'k6/execution';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    adaptive_load: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      stages: [
        { target: 50,  duration: '2m' },  // ramp-up
        { target: 50,  duration: '8m' },  // steady-state
        { target: 0,   duration: '2m' },  // ramp-down
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{phase:warmup}':       ['p(95)<600'],
    'http_req_duration{phase:steady_state}': ['p(95)<400'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const elapsedMs = Date.now() - exec.scenario.startTime;
  const WARMUP_MS = 2 * 60 * 1000; // 2 minutes
  const phase = elapsedMs < WARMUP_MS ? 'warmup' : 'steady_state';

  // Use lighter endpoint during warm-up to avoid skewing SUT cache
  const url = phase === 'warmup'
    ? 'https://api.example.com/health'
    : 'https://api.example.com/feed?limit=50';

  const res = http.get(url, { tags: { phase } });
  check(res, { 'ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  // Reduce think time during warm-up to reach steady state faster
  sleep(phase === 'warmup' ? 0.5 : 1.5);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `exec.scenario.startTime` is a JavaScript number (Unix ms), not a Date object, so arithmetic is straightforward. However, the value is set at scenario initialisation time — if the k6 controller process takes several seconds to allocate VUs after the scenario conceptually starts, the elapsed time seen by early iterations will slightly undercount the true scenario age. For fine-grained phase control where the switch must occur at a precise wall-clock offset (e.g., triggering fault injection exactly 5 minutes into the test), prefer comparing against `exec.scenario.startTime + OFFSET_MS` using `Date.now()` rather than relying on VU iteration count, which varies with request latency.

---

### 270. `handleSummary()` JUnit XML Output for Native CI Integration Without External Converters  [official]

Returning a JUnit XML string from `handleSummary()` allows CI systems (Jenkins, GitLab, GitHub Actions) to parse k6 threshold results as native test cases without a post-processing conversion step. Each threshold becomes a `<testcase>` element; threshold failures become `<failure>` elements with the threshold expression and actual measured value in the message. This approach surfaces k6 SLA violations directly in the CI test results panel alongside unit test failures.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: '1m',
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration:          ['p(95)<500', 'p(99)<1000'],
    http_req_failed:            ['rate<0.01'],
    'checks{check:login_200}':  ['rate>0.99'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/login',
    JSON.stringify({ email: 'user@test.com', password: 'pass' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  check(res, { 'login_200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

export function handleSummary(data) {
  const suiteAttrs = `name="k6" tests="${Object.keys(data.metrics).length}" timestamp="${new Date().toISOString()}"`;
  const cases = Object.entries(data.metrics).flatMap(([metricName, metric]) => {
    return (metric.thresholds || []).map((t) => {
      const failed = t.ok === false;
      const failureXml = failed
        ? `<failure message="Threshold failed: ${t.source}">${metricName}: ${JSON.stringify(metric.values)}</failure>`
        : '';
      return `  <testcase classname="k6.thresholds" name="${metricName}: ${t.source}" time="0">${failureXml}</testcase>`;
    });
  });

  const xml = `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<testsuite ${suiteAttrs}>
${cases.join('\n')}
</testsuite>`;

  return {
    // stdout for human-readable summary
    stdout: JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
    // JUnit XML for CI test-results parsing — path resolved from k6 invocation directory
    [`${__ENV.REPORT_DIR || '.'}/k6-results.xml`]: xml,
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The `data` object passed to `handleSummary()` contains only aggregate metrics as summarised by k6 — it does not contain individual raw samples. The `metric.thresholds` array structure changed between k6 v0.x and v1.x; the `t.source` field (the threshold expression string) and `t.ok` boolean were not always present in older summary data shapes. If you are sharing a `handleSummary` implementation across k6 versions in a polyglot CI fleet, add a guard: `if (!metric.thresholds) return []` before iterating thresholds to prevent errors on metrics that had no threshold configured.

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 48)

### Gotcha 204. `Promise.all()` with `http.asyncRequest()` does not cancel in-flight requests when one rejects — VU goroutines hang until each request individually times out  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A team uses `Promise.all([http.asyncRequest(...), http.asyncRequest(...)])` for concurrent API calls. When the first request returns a network error (the server closed the connection), the `Promise.all()` rejects immediately in JavaScript — but the second request's TCP connection remains open and is being processed by k6's underlying Go HTTP client. The VU goroutine does not terminate until that second request either completes or times out via the `timeout` param (or the global default timeout). During a 3-minute soak test, hundreds of these "half-rejected" iterations accumulate, each holding a Go goroutine, causing k6 process memory and goroutine count to grow without bound. The k6 summary reports the correct error rate (the rejected iterations are counted) but the goroutine leak only shows up as growing RSS memory and eventual OOM after ~45 minutes.

**Fix:** Set an explicit `timeout` in the params object of every `asyncRequest()` call: `{ timeout: '10s' }`. This caps the maximum goroutine lifetime per request regardless of JavaScript Promise resolution. Also add a `maxDuration` to the scenario as a safety ceiling. For critical flows, wrap `Promise.all()` in a `Promise.race()` with a timeout sentinel using `new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('timeout')), 8000))` to enforce a JavaScript-level deadline independently of Go-level TCP timeouts.

---

### Gotcha 205. Scenario `env` values are strings only — numeric comparisons silently pass because `__ENV.NUM > 5` coerces `"10"` correctly but `__ENV.NUM === 10` always returns `false`  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** An engineer sets `env: { CONCURRENCY: 10 }` in a scenario block, expecting `if (__ENV.CONCURRENCY > 5)` to work for conditional logic. It does, because JavaScript coerces the string `"10"` to a number in `>` comparisons. The bug appears when the same engineer uses strict equality: `if (__ENV.CONCURRENCY === 10)` — this always evaluates to `false` because `"10" === 10` is `false` in JavaScript. The test appears to run but the conditional code path that scales up VU iterations is never activated, producing a test that always runs at the minimum load without any error or warning. The engineer spends two hours convinced the executor is ignoring the `env` setting.

**Fix:** Always coerce `__ENV` values before use: `const concurrency = parseInt(__ENV.CONCURRENCY, 10)` or `Number(__ENV.CONCURRENCY)`. Document this in your shared k6 utility module with a typed `getEnvInt(name, defaultValue)` helper that throws if the value cannot be parsed, catching misconfiguration at iteration start rather than silently taking the wrong code path.

---

### Gotcha 206. `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true` silently produces empty metric series in Prometheus when the remote write endpoint does not support the native histogram protobuf encoding  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A team enables native histograms for a k6 soak test streaming to Amazon Managed Prometheus (AMP). k6 sends the samples in the native histogram protobuf format; AMP's remote write endpoint silently accepts the request with HTTP 204 but drops all native histogram series because AMP (at the time of writing) does not support the native histogram encoding. The Grafana dashboard for the test shows "No data" for every `histogram_quantile()` panel. Because the remote write requests returned 204 (success), k6 does not log any errors, and there is no k6-side indicator that the samples were dropped. The team spends an hour verifying network connectivity before discovering the silent drop by querying AMP's metric labels directly and finding no k6 series present.

**Fix:** Verify native histogram support in the target TSDB before switching. Run `curl -s http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/metadata?metric=k6_http_req_duration` after a short test run and confirm the metric type is `histogram` (not `gauge`). If the series is absent, fall back to `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_STATS=p(50),p(95),p(99),min,max`. Add a CI validation step that queries the Prometheus metadata API after every k6 run and fails if the expected k6 metric series are missing.

---

### Gotcha 207. `client.connect()` called in the init context for gRPC tests causes `grpc_req_duration` to measure only RPC round-trip time, not connection establishment — "improvements" reported after init-context optimisation are often measurement artefacts  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** After optimising a gRPC test to call `client.connect()` in the init context (Pattern 268), a performance engineer notices that `grpc_req_duration` values drop dramatically — from ~250ms to ~20ms. The engineer reports a "10x performance improvement" to leadership. The actual latency experienced by end-users (who establish a fresh TLS+HTTP/2 connection per session) is still ~250ms; the ~230ms reduction is entirely connection-setup time that k6 is no longer measuring. The `grpc_req_duration` metric in k6 starts when the RPC is dispatched on an already-connected client and ends when the response is received — it does not include TLS handshake or HTTP/2 SETTINGS frame exchange when connection reuse is in play.

**Fix:** Use init-context connection reuse intentionally and document the measurement boundary clearly: `grpc_req_duration` with connection reuse = "RPC processing + serialisation latency only". If the goal is to measure total connection lifecycle latency (as seen by a new client), use a separate `Trend` metric that wraps `Date.now()` around `client.connect()` + the first `client.invoke()` call, run in a `per-vu-iterations` scenario where each VU connects fresh. Include both "cold-start latency" and "warm RPC latency" metrics in SLO dashboards for a complete picture.

---

### Gotcha 208. `handleSummary()` is called with an empty `data` object when `--summary-mode=disabled` is set — JUnit XML output files are created but contain zero test cases, producing a silent false-green CI signal  [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A team migrated from k6 v1.x (which used `--no-summary` to suppress the end-of-test summary) to k6 v2.0.0 (where the flag was renamed to `--summary-mode=disabled`). During migration, they added `--summary-mode=disabled` to their CI baseline script to suppress console output while relying on a custom `handleSummary()` to write JUnit XML. This combination is contradictory: `--summary-mode=disabled` also suppresses the data passed to `handleSummary()`, which is called with an empty `data` object containing no metric values. The JUnit XML output file is created (non-empty path is returned from `handleSummary`) but contains zero `<testcase>` elements. CI reports "0 tests, 0 failures" — a green signal — even when all thresholds are violated. The bug only surfaces during a post-mortem when an engineer notices the JUnit file contents.

**Fix:** Remove `--summary-mode=disabled` from any CI invocation that relies on `handleSummary()` for output — they are mutually exclusive. To suppress the built-in console summary while still getting `handleSummary()` data, return `{ stdout: '' }` from `handleSummary()` (overriding stdout with an empty string) and do not use `--summary-mode`. Alternatively, use `--summary-mode=json` which writes the summary as JSON to a file without suppressing the `handleSummary()` invocation.

---

| 263 | `xk6-disruptor` `PodDisruptor` fault injection | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/testing-guides/injecting-faults-with-xk6-disruptor/first-steps/ | Kubernetes-only; `injectHTTPFaults(fault, duration)`; `averageDelay`, `errorRate`, `errorCode`; custom binary required; `injectTimeout` guard |
| 264 | Prometheus native histograms | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/results-output/real-time/prometheus-remote-write/ | `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true`; requires Prometheus v2.40.0+; `--enable-feature=native-histograms`; `histogram_quantile()` DDSketch merge |
| 265 | Scenario-level `env` + `tags` | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/scenarios/ | Per-scenario `__ENV` override; merges with global CLI env (scenario wins on collision); tags auto-applied to all metrics in scenario |
| 266 | Browser Page Object Model | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6-browser/recommended-practices/ | Encapsulates locators + interactions; `async/await` required; `page.close()` in `finally`; import path consistency for archive |
| 267 | `http.url` template tag for URL grouping | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/javascript-api/k6-http/ | Sets `name` tag to template literal text; prevents unbounded label cardinality; overrides `params.tags.name` if both are set |
| 268 | gRPC connection reuse via init context | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/javascript-api/k6-net-grpc/ | Eliminates per-iteration TLS handshake; `grpc_req_duration` measures RPC only (not connect); `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` limit applies to shared connection |
| 269 | `exec.scenario.startTime` for phase-aware logic | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/javascript-api/k6-execution/ | Unix ms timestamp; `Date.now() - exec.scenario.startTime` = elapsed; VU-level conditional branching without `--env` flag |
