## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 301. Multi-threshold percentile ladder on a single metric [official]

Define three percentile thresholds (`p(90)`, `p(95)`, `p(99.9)`) in a single array on `http_req_duration` to encode your full SLO ladder in one place. k6 evaluates each expression independently and fails the run if any breach occurs, giving you per-tier visibility in CI logs.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/threshold-ladder.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: "2m",
  thresholds: {
    // SLO ladder: p90 < 400 ms, p95 < 800 ms, p99.9 < 2000 ms
    http_req_duration: [
      "p(90)<400",
      "p(95)<800",
      "p(99.9)<2000",
    ],
    // Error budget: fewer than 1% of requests may fail
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/items`);
  // check() records granular pass/fail; threshold provides the CI gate
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** A single p(99.9) threshold catches tail latency but may be noisy in short tests with few samples. Use `delayAbortEval` when combined with `abortOnFail` so the percentile stabilises over at least 100 data points before the gate fires. For very short smoke tests, prefer `avg` over high percentiles to avoid single-outlier false positives. [official]

---

### Pattern 302. Tag-scoped thresholds to enforce separate SLOs per endpoint [official]

Apply per-tag thresholds with `'http_req_duration{name:login}'` to enforce distinct latency budgets for different API tiers without splitting the script into multiple scenarios. Tags propagate to Grafana dashboards, allowing per-endpoint SLO heatmaps alongside the test run.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/tag-threshold.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  vus: 30,
  duration: "3m",
  thresholds: {
    // Tighter SLO for the auth endpoint (sync operations)
    "http_req_duration{name:login}": ["p(95)<300"],
    // Looser SLO for the search endpoint (DB-heavy)
    "http_req_duration{name:search}": ["p(95)<1200"],
    // Static assets should be very fast
    "http_req_duration{name:static}": ["p(95)<100"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/auth/login`,   { tags: { name: "login" } });
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/search`,   { tags: { name: "search" } });
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/static/app.js`,{ tags: { name: "static" } });
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Tag-scoped thresholds create high-cardinality metric streams in Prometheus / Grafana if the tag value set is unbounded (e.g., per-user-id tags). Always use low-cardinality tag values (endpoint name, tier, HTTP method) rather than dynamic values extracted from responses. Avoid more than 20 distinct tag values per metric to prevent Prometheus label explosion. [official]

---

### Pattern 303. `constant-arrival-rate` executor for RPS-anchored load [official]

Use `constant-arrival-rate` when you need to deliver a fixed number of iterations per time unit regardless of response time, modelling an open system where new requests arrive whether or not previous ones have completed. Set `preAllocatedVUs` generously and specify `maxVUs` as a hard ceiling to prevent runaway VU allocation.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/arrival-rate.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    constant_rps: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 100,           // 100 iterations/second
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "5m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 150, // = rate × p99_latency_s × 1.5
      maxVUs: 300,          // hard ceiling; test fails gracefully if hit
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500"],
    dropped_iterations: ["count<10"],  // alert if VU pool exhausted
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/data`);
  check(res, { "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  // No sleep() — arrival-rate executor paces iteration starts
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `constant-arrival-rate` is an open-loop model: the SUT receives load even when it is already overloaded, producing realistic queue buildup that VU-based models cannot replicate. The downside is that the VU pool must be pre-sized correctly — if `maxVUs` is too low, k6 drops iterations silently (visible only via the `dropped_iterations` counter). Monitor `dropped_iterations` as a threshold to detect under-provisioned VU pools. [official]

---

### Pattern 304. `ramping-arrival-rate` for realistic traffic ramp with open-model semantics [official]

`ramping-arrival-rate` is the open-model counterpart of `ramping-vus`. It models organic traffic growth where request arrival rate follows a schedule, independent of server response time. This mirrors production environments where users arrive at a rate driven by marketing or time-of-day patterns.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/ramping-arrival.js
import http from "k6/http";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp_traffic: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate: 0,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 200,
      maxVUs: 500,
      stages: [
        { target: 50,  duration: "2m" }, // ramp 0 → 50 rps
        { target: 50,  duration: "5m" }, // hold 50 rps
        { target: 200, duration: "3m" }, // spike to 200 rps
        { target: 0,   duration: "1m" }, // ramp down
      ],
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/feed`);
  // No sleep() — executor controls pacing
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Like `constant-arrival-rate`, `ramping-arrival-rate` requires careful `preAllocatedVUs` sizing. The spike stage (200 rps × p99 latency) determines peak VU demand. Under-sizing `maxVUs` for the spike stage produces load shedding, making the test underestimate failure rates during bursts. Multiply peak rate by your p99 response time (in seconds) and add 25% headroom for the pre-allocated pool. [official]

---

### Pattern 305. WebSocket connection lifecycle with `k6/websockets` stable module [official]

The stable `k6/websockets` module (promoted from experimental in k6 v0.55) implements the W3C WebSocket API, making test scripts portable across environments and easier to review against browser-side WebSocket code. Each VU runs an asynchronous event loop; the default function returns only after `ws.close()` or the connection drops.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/websocket-stable.js
import { WebSocket } from "k6/websockets";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: "2m",
};

export default function () {
  const ws = new WebSocket(`${__ENV.WS_URL}/ws/chat`);

  ws.onopen = () => {
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "join", room: "test" }));
  };

  ws.onmessage = (event) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(event.data);
    check(msg, { "received welcome": (m) => m.type === "welcome" });
    // Close after receiving the welcome message
    ws.close();
  };

  ws.onerror = (err) => {
    console.error("WebSocket error:", err.error());
  };

  // The function blocks here until ws.close() is called or connection drops
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The `k6/websockets` module uses a per-VU event loop, so each VU holds one persistent connection. For high-concurrency WebSocket tests, VU count directly maps to concurrent connections — ensure the SUT's connection table and the OS's ephemeral port range can accommodate the VU count. The legacy `k6/ws` module is still available for compatibility but new tests should use `k6/websockets`. [official]

---

### Pattern 306. gRPC unary request with reflection-based schema loading [official]

Use `client.connect()` with `reflect: true` to load the protobuf schema dynamically from the gRPC reflection endpoint, eliminating the need to bundle `.proto` files alongside the test script. This is particularly useful in CI pipelines where schema changes are frequent.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/grpc-reflect.js
import grpc from "k6/net/grpc";
import { check } from "k6";

const client = new grpc.Client();

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: "1m",
};

export default function () {
  // connect() with reflect: true fetches the schema from the server
  client.connect(`${__ENV.GRPC_HOST}:50051`, {
    reflect: true,
    timeout: "5s",
  });

  const response = client.invoke("users.UserService/GetUser", {
    user_id: `user-${__VU}`,
  });

  check(response, {
    "gRPC status OK":     (r) => r && r.status === grpc.StatusOK,
    "has user name":      (r) => r && r.message && r.message.name.length > 0,
  });

  client.close();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Reflection adds one round-trip per VU startup to fetch the schema; in short tests this is negligible but in long soak tests you should move `client.connect()` to the init context (without `reflect`) and bundle `.proto` files for performance. `reflect: true` also requires the server to enable the gRPC reflection service — not all gRPC servers expose it in production. [official]

---

### Pattern 307. gRPC bidirectional streaming with half-close and clean teardown [official]

Bidirectional gRPC streaming requires explicit half-close (`stream.end()`) and a coordinated teardown pattern to drain pending server messages before the VU exits. Failing to half-close leaves server goroutines dangling, inflating the server's connection count in metrics.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/grpc-bidi-stream.js
import grpc from "k6/net/grpc";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(["./proto"], "chat.proto");

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: "2m" };

export default function () {
  client.connect(`${__ENV.GRPC_HOST}:50051`, { plaintext: true });

  const stream = new grpc.Stream(client, "chat.ChatService/Chat");
  let serverDone = false;

  stream.on("data",  (msg)  => { check(msg, { "has text": (m) => !!m.text }); });
  stream.on("end",   ()     => { serverDone = true; });
  stream.on("error", (err)  => { console.error("stream error:", JSON.stringify(err)); });

  // Send a burst of messages then half-close the client stream
  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    stream.write({ text: `hello ${i}`, sender: `vu-${__VU}` });
    sleep(0.2);
  }
  stream.end(); // half-close: tells server no more client messages

  // Wait for server to finish draining (max 5 s)
  const deadline = Date.now() + 5000;
  while (!serverDone && Date.now() < deadline) {
    sleep(0.1);
  }
  client.close();
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The busy-wait loop polling `serverDone` is a pragmatic workaround; k6 does not expose `await` on stream end in the VU function body. Adjust the drain timeout based on your server's response latency. For high-throughput streams, increase the deadline or move the drain logic to a `setInterval` callback. [official]

---

### Pattern 308. Browser module try-finally resource cleanup [official]

The k6 browser module's `newPage()` allocates a Chromium page instance that must be explicitly closed to release memory and ensure accurate Web Vitals measurement. Wrap all page interactions in a `try-finally` block so `page.close()` executes even when an assertion throws.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-vitals.js
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browser_smoke: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      vus: 2,
      iterations: 5,
      options: {
        browser: { type: "chromium" },
      },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    browser_web_vital_lcp: ["p(75)<2500"],
    browser_web_vital_cls: ["p(75)<0.1"],
    browser_web_vital_inp: ["p(75)<200"], // INP replaces FID in k6 v2.0+
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${__ENV.APP_URL}/`);
    await page.locator("h1").waitFor({ state: "visible" });

    const title = await page.locator("h1").textContent();
    check(title, { "headline visible": (t) => t.length > 0 });

    await page.screenshot({ path: `screenshots/home-vu${__VU}.png` });
  } finally {
    await page.close(); // always release resources
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Browser VUs are significantly heavier than protocol-level VUs (~50–200 MB RAM per VU depending on page complexity). Limit `vus` for browser scenarios to the minimum needed for coverage, and combine them with protocol-level scenarios via multi-scenario scripts so heavy browser VUs cover critical user journeys while lighter HTTP VUs generate bulk load. [official]

---

### Pattern 309. `k6/browser` `locator.getByRole()` for resilient element selection [official]

Prefer ARIA role selectors over CSS/XPath to make browser tests resilient to DOM restructuring. `getByRole()` targets elements by their semantic role and accessible name, matching how assistive technologies see the page, which is more stable than implementation-specific class names.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-aria.js
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout_flow: {
      executor: "per-vu-iterations",
      vus: 1,
      iterations: 3,
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${__ENV.APP_URL}/shop`);

    // Prefer role-based selectors over CSS classes
    const addBtn = page.locator("button[role='button']");
    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Add to Cart" }).click();
    await page.getByRole("link",   { name: "View Cart" }).click();

    const header = await page.getByRole("heading", { level: 1 }).textContent();
    check(header, { "cart page loaded": (h) => h.includes("Cart") });

    await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Checkout" }).click();
    await page.waitForURL("**/checkout");
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Role-based selectors require the SUT to use correct ARIA semantics; missing `role` attributes or incorrect `aria-label` values cause locator failures that look like test bugs but are actually accessibility defects. Treat `getByRole()` failures as both test failures and accessibility findings — they are a free a11y audit baked into your performance tests. [official]

---

### Pattern 310. OpenTelemetry output with `k6_` metric prefix and `test-id` tag [official]

Export k6 metrics as OTLP via `--out opentelemetry` for integration with OpenTelemetry Collector pipelines. Set `K6_OTEL_METRIC_PREFIX=k6_` to namespace metrics in shared Prometheus/Grafana stacks and always tag the run with a unique `test-id` to correlate k6 metrics with application traces captured by the same collector.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/otel-tagged-run.js
// Run: K6_OTEL_GRPC_EXPORTER_INSECURE=true \
//      K6_OTEL_METRIC_PREFIX=k6_ \
//      k6 run --tag test-id=$(date +%s) -o opentelemetry script.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: "5m",
  // test-id tag injected via --tag CLI flag; no changes needed in script
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/catalog`);
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `K6_OTEL_EXPORT_INTERVAL` defaults to 10 seconds, meaning the collector receives batched metrics every 10 s; real-time dashboards have a lag window of up to `flush_interval + export_interval` (11 s by default). For near-real-time alerting during tests, use `--out influxdb` or `--out prometheus-remote-write` which have 1-second flush cadences. The OTLP output is ideal for post-hoc correlation with distributed traces but is not a drop-in replacement for time-series outputs in latency-sensitive monitoring setups. [official]

### Pattern 311. Modular test library with local module extraction [official]

Extract shared helper functions (auth, request wrappers, assertion sets) into local modules to prevent copy-paste drift across test scripts. k6 resolves local modules using browser-like resolution, requiring explicit `.js` extensions and relative paths.

```javascript
// k6/lib/auth.js  — shared auth module
import http from "k6/http";

export function login(baseUrl, email, password) {
  const res = http.post(`${baseUrl}/auth/login`,
    JSON.stringify({ email, password }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } }
  );
  if (res.status !== 200) throw new Error(`Login failed: ${res.status}`);
  return res.json("token");
}

// k6/scripts/products-test.js  — consumes shared module
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { login } from "../lib/auth.js"; // explicit .js extension required

export function setup() {
  const token = login(__ENV.API_URL, __ENV.TEST_EMAIL, __ENV.TEST_PASSWORD);
  return { token };
}

export default function ({ token }) {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/products`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
  check(res, { "products listed": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Local modules are resolved relative to the script file's directory at load time. If the test is run from a different working directory (common in CI), relative paths break. Use `__ENV.K6_ROOT` or a project-level `package.json` `exports` map combined with a bundler (Webpack / esbuild) to produce single-file bundles that are path-independent. For remote teams, host bundled libraries on a trusted HTTPS endpoint rather than importing raw GitHub URLs — raw imports execute remotely downloaded code without a lockfile. [community]

---

### Pattern 312. Webpack bundle for npm dependency consumption in k6 [community]

k6 does not resolve Node.js `node_modules` natively. To use npm packages (e.g., `faker-js`, `jsonwebtoken`), bundle the script with Webpack or esbuild, producing a single `bundle.js` that k6 executes. This unlocks the full npm ecosystem while maintaining k6's performance characteristics.

```javascript
// webpack.config.js
const path = require("path");
module.exports = {
  mode: "production",
  entry: { bundle: "./src/test.js" },
  output: {
    path:     path.resolve(__dirname, "dist"),
    filename: "[name].js",
    libraryTarget: "commonjs",
  },
  target: "web", // k6 is browser-like, not Node.js
  externals: /^(k6|https?:\/\/)(\/.*)?/, // keep k6 built-ins as externals
  module: {
    rules: [{ test: /\.js$/, use: "babel-loader", exclude: /node_modules/ }],
  },
};

// src/test.js — uses npm packages
import http from "k6/http";
import { faker } from "@faker-js/faker";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: "30s" };

export default function () {
  const payload = {
    name:  faker.person.fullName(),
    email: faker.internet.email(),
  };
  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/users`,
    JSON.stringify(payload),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } }
  );
  check(res, { "created": (r) => r.status === 201 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Bundling adds a build step to the CI pipeline and produces opaque single-file output that is harder to debug. Pin all npm dependencies with `package-lock.json` and include the lockfile in version control to prevent supply-chain drift. Set `target: "web"` in Webpack (not `"node"`) because k6's JavaScript runtime is not Node.js and lacks `process`, `fs`, and other Node globals. [community]

---

### Pattern 313. Distributed load with `--execution-segment` and segment sequence [official]

Split a single k6 test across multiple machines using `--execution-segment` and `--execution-segment-sequence` to shard the VU and iteration space without a centralised coordinator. Each node receives an independent slice of the workload; aggregate metrics in Grafana Cloud or Prometheus federation after the run.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/distributed.js
// Node 0: k6 run --execution-segment "0:1/3" --execution-segment-sequence "0,1/3,2/3,1" script.js
// Node 1: k6 run --execution-segment "1/3:2/3" --execution-segment-sequence "0,1/3,2/3,1" script.js
// Node 2: k6 run --execution-segment "2/3:1" --execution-segment-sequence "0,1/3,2/3,1" script.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";
import { check } from "k6";

// SharedArray loads the correct shard for this segment
const users = new SharedArray("users", () => JSON.parse(open("./data/users.json")));

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    distributed_load: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      vus: 100,       // per-segment; 3 nodes = 300 total VUs
      iterations: 1000, // per-segment; 3 nodes = 3000 total iterations
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const user = users[__VU % users.length];
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/user/${user.id}`);
  check(res, { "OK": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `--execution-segment` distributes the workload but does NOT aggregate thresholds across nodes — each node evaluates its own thresholds independently. A threshold breach on node 1 alone marks that node's run as failed but other nodes may succeed. For CI gates, add an external aggregation step (e.g., Grafana Cloud or a Prometheus recording rule over a `test_id` label) that evaluates thresholds over the combined metric stream. Also note: `setup()` runs once on each node, which can cause duplicated side effects (e.g., creating test resources). [official]

---

### Pattern 314. OS tuning for high-concurrency single-machine runs [official]

Before scaling to distributed testing, maximise single-machine capacity through OS-level tuning. A properly tuned Linux host can drive 30,000–40,000 VUs and up to 300,000 HTTP RPS from a single k6 process, deferring the complexity of distributed orchestration.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# k6/scripts/tune-os.sh — run before high-concurrency tests

# 1. Expand ephemeral port range (default 32768-60999 → 1024-65535)
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="1024 65535"

# 2. Enable fast socket reuse (avoid TIME_WAIT exhaustion)
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1

# 3. Raise file-descriptor limit for the k6 process
ulimit -n 250000

# 4. Confirm settings
echo "Port range: $(cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range)"
echo "FD limit:   $(ulimit -n)"
```

```javascript
// k6/scripts/high-concurrency.js
import http from "k6/http";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    max_load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 5000,       // 5000 rps — requires OS tuning above
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "10m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 8000,
      maxVUs: 12000,
    },
  },
  // discardResponseBodies reduces memory ~60% at high VU counts
  discardResponseBodies: true,
};

export default function () {
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/ping`);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `discardResponseBodies: true` globally reduces memory consumption but prevents `check()` assertions on response bodies. Use selective per-request override (`responseType: "text"` or `"binary"`) for endpoints that require body validation, and `discardResponseBodies: true` as the global default for bulk load generation. Monitor k6's CPU via `htop` — exceeding 80% CPU saturation on the load generator distorts timing metrics; scale down VUs or add a second node before hitting that ceiling. [official]

---

### Pattern 315. Custom `handleSummary()` with multi-destination output [official]

Override `handleSummary()` to produce both a machine-readable JSON summary (for CI artifact storage) and a human-readable text summary (for PR comments), emitting both simultaneously from the same function by returning multiple keys.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/custom-summary.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { textSummary } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js";

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: "1m",
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ["p(95)<400"] },
};

export default function () {
  http.get(`${__ENV.API_URL}/api/status`);
}

export function handleSummary(data) {
  const timestamp = new Date().toISOString().replace(/[:.]/g, "-");

  return {
    // Machine-readable for CI artifact upload
    [`./results/summary-${timestamp}.json`]: JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
    // Human-readable for PR comment / Slack notification
    stdout: textSummary(data, { indent: " ", enableColors: true }),
    // Optionally pipe to a webhook (use k6/http in handleSummary)
  };
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `handleSummary()` receives only end-of-test aggregated data — it cannot emit individual data points or time-series. For real-time streaming alongside custom summary output, combine `--out influxdb` (or `--out opentelemetry`) with `handleSummary()` in the same run. Note that `textSummary` from `jslib.k6.io` downloads at test start, adding latency in air-gapped environments; vendor the file locally or bundle it with your test package in constrained CI networks. [official]

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 51)

### Gotcha 219. `client.connect()` inside the `default` function establishes a new gRPC connection on every iteration, exhausting server connection slots within minutes [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer writes `export default function() { client.connect(...); client.invoke(...); client.close(); }` following an example that was intended for a one-shot smoke test, not a sustained load test. Each VU calls `connect()` on every iteration, creating and immediately tearing down a TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 connection per request. Under 50 VUs × 100 iterations = 5,000 connections, the server's accept queue and TLS session cache are saturated. Observed symptoms include: `connection reset by peer` errors after ~1 minute, gRPC `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` status codes, and server-side Prometheus showing the connection count growing monotonically without a matching close rate. The developer suspects a server bug rather than the test script.

**Fix:** Move `client.connect()` to the init context (module level) and call `client.close()` only in `teardown()`. gRPC connections are multiplexed over a single HTTP/2 stream; a single per-VU connection supports concurrent RPCs. This reduces connection count from `VUs × iterations` to `VUs` — a 100× reduction for a 100-iteration test.

---

### Gotcha 220. `--execution-segment` causes `setup()` to run once per node, creating duplicate test fixtures and triggering unique-constraint violations in the SUT database [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A distributed test spread across 3 k6 nodes uses `setup()` to seed the test database with 100 unique user records via `http.post()`. Each of the 3 nodes runs its own `setup()`, resulting in 3 × 100 = 300 insert attempts for the same 100 user IDs. The server returns HTTP 409 Conflict for the duplicate inserts on nodes 2 and 3; `setup()` returns `{ users: [] }` on those nodes because the response parsing logic was written to handle only HTTP 201. The default function on nodes 2 and 3 receives an empty users array and immediately throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')`, causing 100% error rate on 2 of 3 nodes. The team investigates the SUT database as the source of the 409s rather than the test harness.

**Fix:** In distributed runs, designate one node as the "setup node" and handle idempotent upserts (HTTP PUT or `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`) in `setup()`. Alternatively, pre-seed the database before the test run via a separate migration script and use `setup()` only for authentication (fetching tokens), which is naturally idempotent.

---

### Gotcha 221. `page.close()` called outside a `try-finally` block leaves orphaned Chromium renderer processes when an `await` expression throws, inflating memory usage and skewing Web Vitals for subsequent VU iterations [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A browser test written as `const page = await browser.newPage(); await page.goto(url); await page.locator('#submit').click(); await page.close();` works correctly during development but fails in production when `page.goto()` times out (e.g., the staging server is overloaded). The `await page.goto()` throws a timeout error, the function exits early, and `page.close()` is never reached. The Chromium renderer process remains alive, consuming ~80 MB of RAM per orphaned instance. After 20 VU iterations with a 30-second timeout, 20 orphaned renderers accumulate, consuming 1.6 GB of RAM, which triggers OOM-kill of the k6 process. The test appears to "crash" with no clear error message pointing to resource leaks.

**Fix:** Always wrap browser page interactions in `try-finally`: `const page = await browser.newPage(); try { ... } finally { await page.close(); }`. This is the canonical k6 browser pattern documented in every official example. Add a linting rule or a code review checklist item that flags `browser.newPage()` without a matching `page.close()` in a finally block.

---

### Gotcha 222. `textSummary` from `jslib.k6.io` is fetched over the network at test start in every CI run, causing intermittent `ECONNREFUSED` failures in air-gapped or rate-limited environments [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A team uses `import { textSummary } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js"` for custom `handleSummary()` output. The import works in local development but fails intermittently in CI environments with strict egress firewall rules (common in enterprise/regulated industries). The failure manifests as a cryptic `GoError: could not load module: not found` at the top of the run, before any VUs start, causing the entire test to fail even though the SUT and k6 binary are both healthy. The team spends an hour debugging k6 version mismatches before discovering the network block.

**Fix:** Download the library once and vendor it into the repository: `curl -o k6/lib/k6-summary.js https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js && git add k6/lib/k6-summary.js`. Update the import to the local path: `import { textSummary } from "../lib/k6-summary.js"`. Add a `pre-commit` hook that flags `import.*https://jslib.k6.io` to prevent future re-introduction of remote imports.

---

### Gotcha 223. `faker.person.fullName()` and similar stateful npm imports produce identical output across VUs when the Webpack bundle is executed in k6's init context, bypassing per-VU RNG seeding [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer bundles `@faker-js/faker` with Webpack and calls `faker.person.fullName()` inside the `default` function expecting unique names per iteration. Because Webpack bundles the module as a singleton and k6 evaluates the init context once per VU (not per iteration), the RNG state in Faker is initialised once at VU start with the same default seed across all VUs. Under some Webpack configurations where the bundle's module-level code runs in the VU init context, all VUs share identical RNG output for the first iteration, producing duplicate payloads that trigger unique-constraint violations in the SUT database. The developer observes HTTP 409 responses and attributes them to a database bug.

**Fix:** Explicitly seed Faker per VU using `__VU` and a per-iteration counter: `faker.seed(__VU * 100000 + iterationCounter++)`. This guarantees different sequences per VU and per iteration. Alternatively, pre-generate the data corpus with a Node.js script and load it into a `SharedArray`, which avoids runtime RNG seeding entirely and is the preferred pattern for deterministic reproducible tests.

---

| 304 | `ramping-arrival-rate` executor | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/scenarios/executors/ramping-arrival-rate/ | Open-loop ramp; size `preAllocatedVUs` for spike stage; 25% headroom; no `sleep()` inside |

| 308 | Browser `try-finally` resource cleanup | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6-browser/running-browser-tests/ | `page.close()` in finally ensures Web Vital accuracy; ~50-200 MB RAM per browser VU; combine with protocol-level scenarios |

| 312 | Webpack bundle for npm packages | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/modules/ | `target: "web"` not "node"; externals pattern for k6 built-ins; `package-lock.json` for supply-chain pinning |

| 314 | OS tuning for high-concurrency | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/testing-guides/running-large-tests/ | Port range 1024-65535; `tcp_tw_reuse=1`; `ulimit -n 250000`; `discardResponseBodies` saves ~60% RAM |

## Cycle 52 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 315. Multi-scenario mixed executor composition with `startTime` and `exec` overrides

Different traffic shapes often represent different user populations (authenticated vs anonymous, read vs write). Composing multiple scenarios with different executors, staggered `startTime` values, and dedicated `exec` functions lets a single k6 run faithfully model a heterogeneous production mix without requiring separate test files. Each scenario emits its own tagged metrics, making per-population SLO analysis straightforward in Grafana.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    anonymous_browse: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 100,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 50,
      exec: 'browsePublic',
      tags: { population: 'anon' },
    },
    authenticated_checkout: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      startTime: '1m',   // let browse traffic stabilise first
      stages: [
        { duration: '2m', target: 30 },
        { duration: '2m', target: 30 },
        { duration: '1m', target: 0 },
      ],
      exec: 'checkout',
      tags: { population: 'auth' },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{population:anon}': ['p(95)<300'],
    'http_req_duration{population:auth}': ['p(95)<800'],
  },
};

export function browsePublic() {
  http.get('https://example.com/products');
  sleep(1);
}

export function checkout() {
  http.post('https://example.com/cart', JSON.stringify({ sku: 'ABC' }), {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
  sleep(2);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `startTime` offsets help avoid a thundering-herd at t=0, but also mean the total test wall-clock duration equals `max(startTime + scenario_duration)` — budget accordingly. Per-scenario `maxVUs` caps prevent one population from consuming all available system threads under unexpected latency spikes. [official]

---

### Pattern 316. `SharedArray` with inline CSV parsing to avoid per-VU file-open overhead

Loading a large user CSV into a `SharedArray` using `papaparse` (or a lightweight hand-rolled CSV parser) eliminates the O(VU) memory cost of opening and parsing the file independently in each VU's init context. Memory footprint at 100,000 rows drops from ~9 GB (individual arrays) to ~275 MB (shared backing store). The array is read-only after construction, so concurrent VU access is safe without locks.

```javascript
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';

// CSV: username,password,region
const users = new SharedArray('users', function () {
  const raw = open('./data/users.csv');
  const lines = raw.trim().split('\n');
  const header = lines[0].split(',');
  return lines.slice(1).map((line) => {
    const cols = line.split(',');
    return Object.fromEntries(header.map((h, i) => [h.trim(), cols[i].trim()]));
  });
});

export default function () {
  // Spread users evenly across VUs; wrap with modulo for safety
  const user = users[(__VU - 1 + __ITER) % users.length];
  const res = http.post('https://example.com/login', JSON.stringify({
    username: user.username,
    password: user.password,
  }), { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  check(res, { 'logged in': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `SharedArray` is read-only — you cannot push correlation IDs or session tokens back into it during the run. For stateful per-VU tokens, use a module-level `Map` keyed by `__VU`, accepting the O(VU) memory cost for that small stateful slice. Also avoid calling `.filter()` on a `SharedArray` outside the constructor; this materialises a regular array per call and negates all memory savings. [official]

---

### Pattern 317. Graceful ramp-down with `gracefulRampDown` to drain in-flight requests before VU removal

When a `ramping-vus` stage reduces VU count, k6 by default interrupts VUs that are mid-iteration, producing artificially high error counts in dashboards. Setting `gracefulRampDown` (default `30s`) gives VUs a window to finish their current iteration naturally before the executor terminates them. This is especially important for checkout or payment flows where an interrupted VU leaves dangling database state.

```javascript
export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp_and_hold: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      stages: [
        { duration: '2m', target: 50 },
        { duration: '5m', target: 50 },
        { duration: '2m', target: 0 },   // ramp-down phase
      ],
      gracefulRampDown: '60s',  // give long-running iterations time to complete
      gracefulStop: '30s',       // additional grace after test end
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.005'],   // < 0.5% errors validates graceful shutdown
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Simulate a multi-step checkout that takes up to 45 seconds end-to-end
  const cart = http.post('https://example.com/cart/add', '{"sku":"X1"}');
  check(cart, { 'item added': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(5);
  const order = http.post('https://example.com/order/confirm', '{}');
  check(order, { 'order confirmed': (r) => r.status === 201 });
  sleep(2);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `gracefulRampDown` extends the effective test duration beyond what the `stages` array specifies — a 2-minute ramp-down with `gracefulRampDown: '60s'` may hold VUs alive for up to 3 minutes. Set the value to your 99th-percentile iteration duration plus a 20% buffer. For extremely long iterations (soak tests with 5-minute think times), consider setting `gracefulRampDown: '0s'` intentionally and instead structuring the test so VUs naturally complete iterations at the ramp boundary. [official]

---

### Pattern 318. Per-scenario environment variables for parallel staging-vs-production runs

Using the scenario-level `env` map, a single test script can target different base URLs or feature flags without any conditional logic in the test body. Combined with `--env` CLI injection for secrets (auth tokens, API keys), this enables running identical load patterns simultaneously against staging and production environments within one k6 invocation, with metrics tagged by environment for direct comparison.

```javascript
export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    staging: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 10,
      duration: '3m',
      env: { BASE_URL: 'https://staging.example.com', ENV_NAME: 'staging' },
      exec: 'runTest',
      tags: { env: 'staging' },
    },
    production: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 10,
      duration: '3m',
      env: { BASE_URL: 'https://api.example.com', ENV_NAME: 'production' },
      exec: 'runTest',
      tags: { env: 'production' },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{env:staging}': ['p(95)<600'],
    'http_req_duration{env:production}': ['p(95)<400'],
  },
};

export function runTest() {
  // __ENV.BASE_URL resolves to the scenario-specific value
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/health`);
  check(res, {
    'status 200': (r) => r.status === 200,
    'env label present': (r) => r.json('env') === __ENV.ENV_NAME,
  });
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Scenario-level `env` values are plaintext in the script and committed to source control — never place secrets there. Inject secrets via CLI `--env SECRET_TOKEN=...` or environment variable injection in CI. Also note that both scenarios share the same VU pool from the OS perspective; if production latency spikes and production VUs block, the staging scenario is unaffected, but both draw from the same `ulimit -n` file-descriptor budget. [official]

---

### Pattern 319. `abortOnFail` threshold with `delayAbortEval` to skip transient startup noise

Aborting a test immediately when a threshold is breached prevents wasting cloud budget on a run that has already failed. However, evaluating thresholds at t=0 (before the system under test has warmed up) causes false aborts due to JVM/connection-pool cold-start latency. `delayAbortEval` defers the first evaluation to let the system reach steady state before applying the abort criterion.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    load: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 50,
      duration: '10m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: [
      { threshold: 'p(99)<1000', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '30s' },
    ],
    http_req_failed: [
      { threshold: 'rate<0.01', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '60s' },
    ],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://example.com/api/data');
  check(res, {
    'status ok':     (r) => r.status === 200,
    'body non-empty': (r) => r.body.length > 0,
  });
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `delayAbortEval` applies to all phases including the ramp-up stage, so if your ramp-up takes 5 minutes and `delayAbortEval` is 30 seconds, the threshold activates well before steady state. Align `delayAbortEval` with the ramp-up duration. Also, `abortOnFail: true` sets exit code 99 — ensure your CI pipeline treats exit 99 as a test failure rather than an infrastructure error (some pipelines only check for exit 0 vs non-zero). [official]

---

### Pattern 320. Custom Trend metric for measuring business-logic latency separate from HTTP transport

k6's built-in `http_req_duration` measures total HTTP round-trip time including DNS, TLS, and transfer. For business-level SLOs — such as "time from order submission to payment confirmation" — a custom `Trend` metric lets you record only the meaningful application-layer duration, unaffected by network variance, and set independent thresholds on it.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { Trend, Counter } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

const checkoutDuration = new Trend('checkout_duration_ms', true); // true = display as ms
const checkoutErrors   = new Counter('checkout_errors_total');

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    checkout_duration_ms: ['p(95)<2000', 'p(99)<5000'],
    checkout_errors_total: ['count<10'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  // Step 1: add to cart
  http.post('https://example.com/cart', '{"sku":"P99"}');
  sleep(0.5);

  // Step 2: measure only the checkout confirmation RTT
  const startMs = Date.now();
  const res = http.post('https://example.com/order/confirm', '{}', {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
  checkoutDuration.add(Date.now() - startMs);

  const ok = check(res, { 'order created': (r) => r.status === 201 });
  if (!ok) checkoutErrors.add(1);
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom metrics increase cardinality in time-series databases. For Prometheus or InfluxDB outputs, each unique tag combination creates a new series. Keep tag cardinality low (avoid per-request unique IDs as tag values) and document custom metric names in a metrics registry file alongside the test. Custom `Trend` metrics are not automatically included in k6's end-of-test text summary — add them explicitly in `handleSummary()` if CI engineers rely on stdout output. [official]

---

### Pattern 321. Browser module mixed scenario — protocol VUs do the heavy load, one browser VU validates real-user experience

Running 500 protocol-level HTTP VUs alongside a single browser VU in the same test provides two complementary signals: raw throughput and error rate from the protocol side, and realistic Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, FID) from the browser side under genuine load. The browser VU is intentionally kept to a low count (1-5) because each browser VU consumes ~100-200 MB RAM and a Chromium process.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    protocol_load: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 200,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 40,
      exec: 'apiLoad',
    },
    browser_sample: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 1,
      duration: '5m',
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
      exec: 'browserSample',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{scenario:protocol_load}': ['p(95)<500'],
    'browser_web_vital_lcp': ['p(75)<2500'],
  },
};

export function apiLoad() {
  http.get('https://example.com/api/products');
  sleep(Math.random() * 2);
}

export async function browserSample() {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://example.com/products');
    await page.waitForSelector('.product-card');
    const title = await page.locator('h1').textContent();
    check(title, { 'headline visible': (t) => t && t.length > 0 });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Browser scenarios require `K6_BROWSER_ENABLED=true` and a Chromium binary on the test runner. In containerised CI, add `--cap-add=SYS_ADMIN` (or `--no-sandbox` for the Chromium process) to the Docker `run` command. Browser VUs increase test runner RAM requirements significantly; do not collocate high browser VU counts with large arrival-rate protocol scenarios on the same machine. [official]

---

### Pattern 322. `handleSummary()` with conditional Slack webhook notification on threshold breach

Integrating test results directly into team communication channels closes the feedback loop between a nightly load test and the on-call engineer. By inspecting `data.metrics` inside `handleSummary()`, the function can conditionally POST a compact summary to Slack only when thresholds are breached, avoiding notification fatigue on green runs.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { textSummary } from '../lib/k6-summary.js'; // vendored local copy

export function handleSummary(data) {
  const p95 = data.metrics['http_req_duration']?.values?.['p(95)'] ?? 0;
  const errRate = data.metrics['http_req_failed']?.values?.rate ?? 0;
  const passed = data.state.testRunDuration > 0 &&
                 p95 < 500 && errRate < 0.01;

  const slackBody = {
    text: passed
      ? `:white_check_mark: Load test PASSED — p95=${p95.toFixed(0)}ms err=${(errRate*100).toFixed(2)}%`
      : `:rotating_light: Load test FAILED — p95=${p95.toFixed(0)}ms err=${(errRate*100).toFixed(2)}%`,
    username: 'k6-bot',
    icon_emoji: ':chart_with_upwards_trend:',
  };

  const outputs = {
    stdout: textSummary(data, { indent: ' ', enableColors: true }),
    './results/summary.json': JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
  };

  if (!passed && __ENV.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL) {
    http.post(
      __ENV.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL,
      JSON.stringify(slackBody),
      { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } }
    );
  }

  return outputs;
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `handleSummary()` runs after all VUs finish and receives only aggregated end-of-test data — it cannot be used to send real-time alerts during the test. For in-flight alerting, use Grafana alerting rules against the Prometheus remote-write stream instead. Also note that making HTTP calls inside `handleSummary()` with a failing webhook URL will silently swallow the error unless you add explicit `check()` assertions on the POST response. [official]

---

### Pattern 323. `k6/experimental/csv` module for streaming large CSV files without full in-memory load

The experimental CSV module (introduced in k6 v0.55) provides a streaming `parse()` API that processes rows one at a time without loading the entire file into memory. For CSV files exceeding 1 GB (e.g., production traffic replays), this eliminates the OOM failures that occur when the entire file is buffered into a `SharedArray` during init.

```javascript
import { open } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import csv from 'k6/experimental/csv';
import { scenario } from 'k6/execution';

let file;
let parser;

export async function setup() {
  file = await open('./data/traffic-replay.csv');
  parser = csv.parse(file, { skipFirstLine: true });
}

export default async function () {
  // Each VU reads its own sequence of rows via the async iterator
  const { done, value } = await parser.next();
  if (done) {
    // File exhausted — reset or stop depending on test design
    return;
  }
  const [userId, endpoint, method] = value;
  const res = await http.asyncRequest(method, `https://example.com${endpoint}`, null, {
    headers: { 'X-User-Id': userId },
  });
  check(res, { 'status ok': (r) => r.status < 400 });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** The `k6/experimental/csv` module is subject to breaking API changes before it graduates to a stable module. Pin your k6 version in CI (`k6 version: v0.55.0` in your GitHub Actions workflow) to avoid unexpected breakage. Streaming CSV means rows are consumed in order; if multiple VUs race on the same parser, row distribution is non-deterministic. For reproducible VU-to-row mapping, use `SharedArray` for files small enough to fit in memory and reserve streaming CSV for truly large datasets. [official]

---

### Pattern 324. `k6/experimental/fs` for reading files at runtime instead of init context to reduce VU startup time

The experimental `fs` module provides async file I/O that runs during the VU execution phase rather than the init context. This matters when test fixtures change between iterations (e.g., rotating token files written by a sidecar process) or when init-context file loading creates unacceptably long VU startup pauses for large binary payloads.

```javascript
import { open } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

// File handle is opened once at VU init — reads happen at runtime
let imageFile;

export async function setup() {
  // Pre-warm: ensure the file is accessible before VUs start
  const f = await open('./assets/test-image.jpg');
  await f.close();
}

export default async function () {
  const f = await open('./assets/test-image.jpg');
  try {
    const stat = await f.stat();
    const buf  = new Uint8Array(stat.size);
    await f.read(buf);

    const res = http.post('https://example.com/upload', buf.buffer, {
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'image/jpeg' },
    });
    check(res, { 'upload accepted': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  } finally {
    await f.close();
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `k6/experimental/fs` uses async/await, which requires the VU default function to also be `async`. Mixing async and sync k6 APIs in the same function is safe, but watch for implicit promise returns — an unhandled rejected promise from an async default function surfaces as a cryptic `GoError` rather than a clean JavaScript stack trace. Always `await` all async calls within `async function` bodies. [official]

---

### Pattern 325. `per-vu-iterations` executor for deterministic smoke and canary tests

For smoke tests and canary deployments, the goal is to validate that a known finite set of scenarios complete successfully, not to sustain a given throughput. `per-vu-iterations` assigns a fixed iteration count per VU and exits cleanly when all iterations finish, making the test duration self-limiting and the assertion semantics ("all 10 iterations must pass") naturally aligned with a quality gate.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 5,
      iterations: 10,       // 5 VUs × 10 iterations = 50 total requests
      maxDuration: '2m',    // safety cap; test should finish in ~30s
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate==0'],        // zero tolerance for errors in smoke
    http_req_duration: ['p(99)<1000'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://example.com/api/health');
  check(res, {
    'status 200':   (r) => r.status === 200,
    'body valid':   (r) => r.json('status') === 'ok',
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `per-vu-iterations` is a closed-loop model — it does not model open-system arrival rates. If your SUT is an API gateway with rate limiting, a 5-VU × 10-iteration smoke test may complete so quickly (sub-second) that it does not exercise connection-pool warm-up at all. Add a minimal `sleep(0.5)` between iterations to spread requests over time and give the server realistic response-time data. For arrival-rate smoke tests, prefer `constant-arrival-rate` with a low `rate` and a short `duration`. [official]

---

### Pattern 326. Prometheus remote-write output with custom metric prefix for multi-team dashboard isolation

When multiple teams run k6 tests against shared Prometheus and Grafana infrastructure, metric name collisions corrupt dashboards. The `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_STATS` and `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_METRIC_NAME_LABEL` env vars let each team namespace their k6 metrics, and the `K6_OTEL_METRIC_PREFIX` variable serves the same purpose for OpenTelemetry output. Isolating by prefix also enables team-specific alerting rules without cross-team noise.

```javascript
// k6 run --out experimental-prometheus-rw script.js
// Set these environment variables in CI:
//   K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_SERVER_URL=http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/write
//   K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_STATS=p(50),p(95),p(99),max
//   K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_METRIC_NAME_LABEL=team_checkout
//   K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_PUSH_INTERVAL=5s

import http from 'k6/http';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

// Custom metric will be exported as: team_checkout_cart_add_ms
const cartAddDuration = new Trend('cart_add_ms', true);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout_load: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      stages: [
        { duration: '1m', target: 20 },
        { duration: '3m', target: 20 },
        { duration: '1m', target: 0 },
      ],
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const start = Date.now();
  const res = http.post('https://example.com/cart/add', '{"sku":"X1"}', {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    tags: { team: 'checkout' },
  });
  cartAddDuration.add(Date.now() - start);
  check(res, { 'cart updated': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Prometheus remote-write is listed as "experimental" in k6 and the env var names may change across minor versions. Pin k6 version in CI and review the release changelog before upgrades. The `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_STATS` variable defaults to `p(99)` only; explicitly adding `p(50),p(95)` catches median regressions that p(99) alone misses. High-cardinality tag combinations (scenario + team + endpoint) multiply the number of Prometheus series — monitor Prometheus memory usage when first deploying. [official]

---

### Pattern 327. `shared-iterations` executor for equitable user-journey distribution without VU starvation

When the number of VUs is not evenly divisible by the number of intended journeys, `per-vu-iterations` wastes capacity or leaves journeys incomplete. `shared-iterations` distributes a total iteration count across the VU pool on a first-available basis, so faster VUs pick up more iterations and the total completes sooner without any VU sitting idle.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    batch_validation: {
      executor: 'shared-iterations',
      vus: 20,
      iterations: 500,   // 500 / 20 = average 25 per VU, but faster VUs do more
      maxDuration: '5m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.02'],
    iterations:      ['count==500'],  // assert all iterations completed
  },
};

export default function () {
  const userId = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10000) + 1;
  const res = http.get(`https://example.com/api/user/${userId}/profile`);
  check(res, {
    'profile found': (r) => r.status === 200,
    'has email':     (r) => r.json('email') !== undefined,
  });
  sleep(0.2);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `shared-iterations` is still a closed-loop model — VUs wait for the previous iteration to finish before starting the next. If the SUT becomes slow and iterations take longer, total test duration grows beyond estimates. Combine with `maxDuration` as a safety cap. Also note that `iterations` thresholds check `count` not `rate`, so the assertion `iterations count==500` will fail if any iteration is dropped by `maxDuration` expiry — use `count>=490` to allow for a small late-finish buffer. [official]

---

### Pattern 328. Test lifecycle `setup()` / `teardown()` for authentication token injection across all VUs

Fetching authentication tokens once in `setup()` and distributing them to VUs via the return value avoids `VU × iteration` login requests that inflate auth-server load metrics and skew the test's focus metric. The token array is passed as the `data` argument to both `default()` and `teardown()`, giving all phases consistent access to pre-authenticated session state.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

const BASE = 'https://example.com';
const USERS = [
  { username: 'user1', password: 's3cr3t1' },
  { username: 'user2', password: 's3cr3t2' },
  { username: 'user3', password: 's3cr3t3' },
];

export function setup() {
  // Runs ONCE before VUs start; return value is serialised to JSON
  const tokens = USERS.map((u) => {
    const res = http.post(`${BASE}/auth/login`, JSON.stringify(u), {
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    });
    check(res, { 'login ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
    return res.json('token');
  });
  return { tokens }; // must be JSON-serialisable
}

export default function (data) {
  // Each VU picks a token by VU index, cycling if VUs > tokens
  const token = data.tokens[(__VU - 1) % data.tokens.length];
  const res = http.get(`${BASE}/api/orders`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
  check(res, { 'orders ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}

export function teardown(data) {
  // Revoke all tokens to keep auth-server session count clean
  data.tokens.forEach((token) => {
    http.del(`${BASE}/auth/session`, null, {
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
    });
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Tokens fetched in `setup()` have a finite expiry. For tests longer than the token TTL (typically 15-60 minutes), tokens will expire mid-test and cause authentication errors that are hard to distinguish from SUT bugs in dashboards. For long-duration soak tests, either extend the token TTL on the auth server for the test user accounts, or implement in-VU token refresh logic using a `Rate` metric to track refresh frequency. [official]

---

### Pattern 329. Tag-based threshold isolation for multi-endpoint SLO enforcement without separate test files

Rather than writing one test file per endpoint with duplicate scenario scaffolding, apply low-cardinality request-level `tags` to group requests and define per-group thresholds. This creates endpoint-specific SLO gates within a single test run, with each tag group appearing as a separate series in Grafana dashboards.

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  vus: 30,
  duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{endpoint:search}':   ['p(95)<200'],
    'http_req_duration{endpoint:checkout}': ['p(95)<800'],
    'http_req_duration{endpoint:health}':   ['p(99)<50'],
    'http_req_failed{endpoint:checkout}':   ['rate<0.001'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://example.com/api/health', {
    tags: { endpoint: 'health' },
  });

  http.get('https://example.com/api/search?q=shoes', {
    tags: { endpoint: 'search' },
  });
  sleep(0.5);

  http.post('https://example.com/api/checkout', '{"cart_id":"c99"}', {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    tags: { endpoint: 'checkout' },
  });
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** Tag-based thresholds only work with tags that exist at request time — scenario-level tags are automatically inherited, but custom tags must be passed explicitly in `params.tags` for every request. A missed tag means the request falls into the untagged `http_req_duration` aggregate and inflates the baseline without contributing to the specific threshold. Add a lint step that validates all `http.get/post/del/put` calls have the `endpoint` tag to catch omissions in code review. [community]

---

## Community Gotchas (Cycle 52)

### Gotcha 224. `sleep()` inside a `constant-arrival-rate` iteration causes the executor to spawn unbounded extra VUs trying to meet the target rate, exhausting all `maxVUs` within seconds [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer migrates a test from `constant-vus` (where `sleep()` is the correct pacing mechanism) to `constant-arrival-rate` to get open-system semantics. They keep the `sleep(1)` call in the iteration body. The `constant-arrival-rate` executor measures how long each iteration takes and allocates new VUs to hit the target rate. Because each iteration now takes ~1 second longer, the executor perceives a shortfall and spawns new VUs aggressively. Within 30 seconds, `maxVUs` is reached, the executor starts dropping iterations, and `dropped_iterations` climbs to 50% of target. The dashboard shows both high error rate and low throughput simultaneously, a combination the developer attributes to a SUT bug rather than a test misconfiguration.

**Fix:** Remove all `sleep()` calls from iteration bodies used with `constant-arrival-rate` or `ramping-arrival-rate` executors. Pacing is handled by the executor's rate parameter, not by in-iteration delays. If think time between logical requests within one iteration is required for realism (e.g., simulating page-read time), model it as a separate scenario with a `constant-vus` executor rather than embedding sleep inside an arrival-rate scenario.

---

### Gotcha 225. `check()` return value ignored — failed checks increment `checks` metric but do not halt iteration, masking cascading errors downstream [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer writes `check(loginRes, { 'auth ok': (r) => r.status === 200 }); const token = loginRes.json('token'); http.get(url, { headers: { Authorization: \`Bearer ${token}\` } });`. When the login endpoint returns HTTP 503 during a load spike, `check()` records the failure but the next line still executes, extracting `token` as `undefined`. The downstream `http.get` sends `Authorization: Bearer undefined`, receives HTTP 401, and that request also appears as an error in the dashboard. The team sees a 2× error rate amplification — one for the login failure and one for the cascading auth failure — and incorrectly sizes the incident as twice as severe as it is.

**Fix:** Capture the `check()` boolean return value and use it as a guard: `const ok = check(loginRes, { ... }); if (!ok) { return; }`. For workflows with multiple dependent steps, wrap the entire chain in a guard block that short-circuits on first failure, recording only the root-cause error. Add a custom `Counter` metric (`auth_failures_total`) to distinguish root-cause failures from cascading ones in dashboards.

---

### Gotcha 226. Using `JSON.stringify()` on a full `SharedArray` object destroys its memory efficiency, consuming the same RAM as a regular array [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer needs to log a sample of the test dataset for debugging and writes `console.log(JSON.stringify(usersSharedArray))`. This serialises the entire backing store of the `SharedArray` into a single JavaScript string in the calling VU's heap — allocating ~100 MB for a 100,000-row array. If this line runs in the default function (once per iteration), GC pressure spikes, p99 latency for all requests in that VU grows by 200-400 ms, and the test appears to show a periodic latency sawtooth pattern that developers attribute to SUT GC pauses rather than the test script.

**Fix:** Only serialise individual elements: `console.log(JSON.stringify(usersSharedArray[0]))`. For debugging samples, use `Array.from(usersSharedArray.slice(0, 5))` (which materialises only 5 rows) and log that. Remove all full-array debug logging before committing the test to CI. Add a `lint-k6` custom ESLint rule that flags `JSON.stringify` applied to variables named with common `SharedArray` naming conventions (`users`, `data`, `records`).

---

### Gotcha 227. Returning a `SharedArray` from `setup()` causes marshalling to a plain JSON array on every VU, negating all memory savings and inflating VU startup time [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer constructs a large `SharedArray` inside `setup()` and returns it as part of the data object: `return { users: usersSharedArray }`. k6 serialises the `setup()` return value to JSON and deserialises it into each VU's execution context. The `SharedArray` becomes a plain JavaScript array on every VU, consuming the full per-VU memory. For a 50,000-row array, this means 50 VUs × 15 MB per array = 750 MB of extra heap — roughly 6× the memory of the correct pattern. VU startup also slows noticeably as JSON deserialisation of 50,000 objects runs in each VU's init context.

**Fix:** Declare `SharedArray` in the **module-level init context** (outside all exported functions), not inside `setup()`. The `SharedArray` constructor runs once per k6 process, and VUs share the underlying memory automatically without any serialisation step. Only use `setup()` for operations that require a running network connection (e.g., fetching auth tokens, seeding database state).

---

### Gotcha 228. `__ENV` variables are strings — comparing to numbers or booleans with `===` always returns `false`, causing silent misconfiguration of thresholds and VU counts [community]

**WHY this bites you:** A developer parameterises VU count via `--env VU_COUNT=50` and writes `if (__ENV.VU_COUNT === 50) { ... }` expecting the condition to be true. Because `__ENV` values are always JavaScript strings, `__ENV.VU_COUNT === 50` evaluates to `false` (string vs. number strict equality), and the condition silently takes the else branch. The developer then sets `vus: __ENV.VU_COUNT` in `options` without parsing, resulting in `vus: "50"` (a string) which k6 coerces to `vus: 0` internally, running the test with zero VUs. The test completes in under 1 second with 0 iterations and no obvious error message — just an empty results summary.

**Fix:** Always parse `__ENV` values before use: `const vuCount = parseInt(__ENV.VU_COUNT, 10) || 10;`. For boolean flags, use explicit string comparison: `const debug = __ENV.DEBUG === 'true';`. Add a validation block at the top of the init context that asserts required env vars are present and numeric using `isNaN()` checks, failing fast with a descriptive message rather than running a misconfigured test silently.

---

| 325 | `per-vu-iterations` for smoke/canary gates | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/scenarios/executors/per-vu-iterations/ | `iterations count==N` threshold; closed-loop model; add `sleep(0.5)` for connection-pool warm-up |
| 326 | Prometheus remote-write with metric prefix | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/results-output/real-time/prometheus-remote-write/ | `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_STATS`; add p50+p95; high-cardinality tags inflate Prometheus series count |
| 327 | `shared-iterations` for equitable distribution | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/scenarios/executors/shared-iterations/ | `maxDuration` safety cap; `iterations count>=N` threshold with buffer; closed-loop model |
| 328 | `setup()`/`teardown()` token injection | https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/test-lifecycle/ | JSON-serialisable return only; token TTL < test duration needs in-VU refresh; `teardown()` for cleanup |

## Cycle 53 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 329. TypeScript-native k6 tests with esbuild transpilation (no Webpack required) [official]

Since k6 v0.57, TypeScript (`.ts` files) is transpiled automatically by the embedded esbuild compiler. Type information is stripped but not type-checked — use `tsc --noEmit` in CI as a separate step if you need type safety. This means teams can adopt TypeScript for editor autocomplete and interface documentation without adding a build step to their local workflow.

```typescript
// k6/scripts/typed-api-test.ts
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';
import { Options } from 'k6/options';

interface LoginResponse {
  token: string;
  userId: number;
}

export const options: Options = {
  vus: 10,
  duration: '30s',
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500'],
    checks: ['rate>0.99'],
  },
};

export default function (): void {
  const res = http.post<string>(
    'https://example.com/api/login',
    JSON.stringify({ username: 'user@test.com', password: 'secret' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } }
  );

  const ok = check(res, {
    'login 200': (r) => r.status === 200,
    'token present': (r) => {
      const body = r.json() as LoginResponse;
      return typeof body.token === 'string' && body.token.length > 0;
    },
  });

  if (!ok) return;
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** esbuild strips types but does not enforce them — a wrong type annotation silently passes at runtime. Always run `npx tsc --noEmit --strict` in CI. The `--compatibility-mode=base` flag removes the `global` shim that some legacy libraries depend on, so stick with `extended` (default) when mixing community jslib modules. [official]

### Pattern 330. `k6/execution` module — dynamic per-VU tagging and graceful `test.fail()` [official]

The `k6/execution` module exposes runtime context: `vu.idInTest`, `scenario.iterationInTest`, `instance.vusActive`, and `test.options`. Use `exec.vu.metrics.tags` to attach dynamic tags (e.g., the active region or user tier) at the VU level without passing them on every individual HTTP call. `test.fail()` marks the test as failed (exit code 110) without halting iteration execution, which is ideal for SLO-breach detection in long soak tests where you want to preserve the trace but flag CI.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/execution-context.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import exec from 'k6/execution';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    api_load: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 50,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '2m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(99)<800'],
  },
};

// Assign region tag once per VU at init time based on VU index
const REGIONS = ['us-east', 'eu-west', 'ap-south'];

export default function () {
  // Attach region tag to all metrics emitted by this VU
  const region = REGIONS[exec.vu.idInTest % REGIONS.length];
  exec.vu.metrics.tags['region'] = region;

  const res = http.get('https://example.com/api/data');

  const ok = check(res, { 'status 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  // Flag failure without aborting — preserves full soak trace for post-run analysis
  if (!ok && exec.scenario.progress > 0.1) {
    exec.test.fail(`SLO breach at iteration ${exec.scenario.iterationInTest}`);
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `exec.vu.metrics.tags` mutations are VU-local and persist for the lifetime of the VU, not just the current iteration. If a VU is reused across scenarios in a multi-scenario test, tags from the first scenario leak into the second unless explicitly cleared. Always reset VU-level tags at the start of each iteration in multi-scenario scripts. `test.fail()` sets exit code 110, which CI systems must be configured to treat as a test failure distinct from 99 (threshold breach) and 108 (abort). [official]

---

### Pattern 331. `ramping-arrival-rate` with `getCurrentStageIndex()` for stage-aware tagging [official]

The `ramping-arrival-rate` executor is the open-model counterpart to `ramping-vus`. Unlike `ramping-vus`, it starts iterations at a variable rate regardless of whether VUs have completed their previous iteration, modelling real traffic bursts. The `getCurrentStageIndex()` helper from `k6/execution` lets scripts detect which stage is active and attach a descriptive tag, enabling stage-level performance breakdowns in Grafana dashboards without requiring separate scenarios.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/ramping-rate-stages.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import exec from 'k6/execution';
import { getCurrentStageIndex } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-utils/1.4.0/index.js';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate',
      startRate: 0,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 200,
      stages: [
        { target: 100, duration: '2m' }, // ramp up
        { target: 100, duration: '5m' }, // sustain
        { target: 200, duration: '3m' }, // spike
        { target: 50,  duration: '2m' }, // ramp down
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{stage:sustain}': ['p(95)<300'],
    'http_req_duration{stage:spike}': ['p(95)<600'],
  },
};

const STAGE_NAMES = ['ramp-up', 'sustain', 'spike', 'ramp-down'];

export default function () {
  const stageIdx = getCurrentStageIndex();
  const stageName = STAGE_NAMES[stageIdx] || 'unknown';

  const res = http.get('https://example.com/api/products', {
    tags: { stage: stageName },
  });

  check(res, { 'status 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  // NO sleep — arrival-rate executor handles pacing via rate/timeUnit
}
```

**Tradeoff.** `preAllocatedVUs` are allocated before the test starts and consumed from a pool. If iterations take longer than `1 / rate` seconds, k6 draws from `maxVUs`. Always set `maxVUs` to at least 2× `preAllocatedVUs` for spiky workloads to absorb burst demand without dropping iterations. Monitor `dropped_iterations` in dashboards — consistent drops indicate `maxVUs` is undersized rather than a SUT failure. [official]

---

### Pattern 332. Per-request local cookie jar for isolated session simulation [official]

By default, k6 gives each VU a shared `CookieJar` that persists cookies across all requests in that VU's lifetime, mimicking a browser's persistent session. For tests that need to simulate distinct user sessions within a single VU iteration (e.g., a test that logs in as multiple users sequentially), create a local `CookieJar` instance and pass it via `params.jar` to scope cookies to specific request chains rather than the entire VU.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/per-request-cookie-jar.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';

const users = new SharedArray('users', () => JSON.parse(open('./data/users.json')));

export const options = {
  vus: 10,
  duration: '1m',
};

export default function () {
  // Create an isolated cookie jar per simulated user session
  const jar = new http.CookieJar();

  const userIdx = __VU % users.length;
  const { username, password } = users[userIdx];

  // Login — server sets session cookie into our isolated jar
  const loginRes = http.post(
    'https://example.com/login',
    { username, password },
    { jar }
  );

  check(loginRes, { 'login 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  // All subsequent requests using `jar` carry the session cookie automatically
  const dashboardRes = http.get('https://example.com/dashboard', { jar });
  check(dashboardRes, { 'dashboard loaded': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  // Retrieve cookies for debugging if needed
  const cookies = jar.cookiesForURL('https://example.com');
  if (!cookies['session']) {
    console.warn(`VU ${__VU}: no session cookie after login`);
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff.** A new `CookieJar` per iteration means cookies are never persisted between iterations — this matches real user sessions that start fresh. If your SUT uses cookie-based CSRF tokens that persist across sessions, the default VU-level jar is more appropriate. Creating `new http.CookieJar()` inside `default` has negligible overhead (Go allocation), so per-iteration isolation is safe at high VU counts. [official]

### Pattern 333. OpenTelemetry metrics export with metric prefix and attribute mapping [official]

k6 can stream live metrics directly to any OpenTelemetry Collector via `--out opentelemetry`, mapping k6 metric types to OTEL equivalents (Counter → `Float64Counter`, Trend → `Float64Histogram`, Rate → `Int64Counter` with `condition` attribute). This enables unified observability pipelines where k6 metrics land alongside APM traces in Grafana Tempo or Jaeger without a separate Prometheus scrape layer.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/otel-export-demo.js
// Run with: K6_OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=checkout-svc \
//           K6_OTEL_METRIC_PREFIX=k6_ \
//           K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_PROTOCOL=grpc \
//           K6_OTEL_GRPC_EXPORTER_ENDPOINT=otel-collector:4317 \
//           k6 run --out opentelemetry script.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { Trend, Counter } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check } from 'k6';

const checkoutDuration = new Trend('checkout_duration_ms', true);
const checkoutErrors   = new Counter('checkout_errors_total');

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    checkout_duration_ms: ['p(95)<1000'],
    checkout_errors_total: ['count<10'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const start = Date.now();

  const res = http.post(
    'https://example.com/api/checkout',
    JSON.stringify({ cart_id: `cart-${__VU}` }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } }
  );

  checkoutDuration.add(Date.now() - start);

  const ok = check(res, { 'checkout 201': (r) => r.status === 201 });
  if (!ok) checkoutErrors.add(1);
}
```

**Tradeoff.** OTEL export uses `K6_OTEL_FLUSH_INTERVAL` (default `1s`) and `K6_OTEL_EXPORT_INTERVAL` (default `10s`) — these are independent timers, so there can be up to 11 seconds of latency before a metric appears in your OTEL backend. For real-time alerting on test progress, prefer Prometheus remote-write (latency ~1s). OTEL export and Prometheus remote-write can run simultaneously with `--out opentelemetry --out experimental-prometheus-rw`. [official]
