## Cycle 57 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 391** — Scenario-scoped Tags for Granular Threshold Isolation
```javascript
// k6/scripts/scenario-tags-thresholds.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browse: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 50,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      tags: { flow: "browse" },
    },
    checkout: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 10,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 10,
      tags: { flow: "checkout" },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_duration{flow:browse}": ["p(95)<300"],
    "http_req_duration{flow:checkout}": ["p(95)<800"],
    "http_req_failed{flow:checkout}": ["rate<0.001"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const flow = __ENV.K6_SCENARIO_NAME || "browse";
  if (flow === "browse") {
    http.get("https://example.com/products");
    sleep(0.5);
  } else {
    http.post("https://example.com/checkout", JSON.stringify({ cartId: "abc" }), {
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    });
    sleep(1);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Scenario-scoped tags let you enforce separate SLOs per user journey, but each tag combination creates a distinct metric series — in long tests with many tag values this can increase Prometheus/InfluxDB cardinality noticeably.

**Pattern 392** — `ramping-arrival-rate` Breakpoint Finder with Early Abort
```javascript
// k6/scripts/breakpoint-finder.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    breakpoint: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 500,
      stages: [
        { target: 10,  duration: "1m" },
        { target: 50,  duration: "2m" },
        { target: 100, duration: "2m" },
        { target: 200, duration: "2m" },
        { target: 400, duration: "3m" },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed:   [{ threshold: "rate<0.05",  abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: "15s" }],
    http_req_duration: [{ threshold: "p(95)<2000", abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: "15s" }],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get("https://example.com/api/heavy");
  check(res, { "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `abortOnFail` with `delayAbortEval` stops runaway cost at saturation; the 15s delay window prevents premature abort on transient spikes. However, once aborted, post-saturation behaviour is lost — capture the abort point from exit code 109 in CI for the breakpoint RPS record.

**Pattern 393** — Per-VU CookieJar for Isolated Session Management
```javascript
// k6/scripts/per-vu-cookiejar.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, group } from "k6";
import { CookieJar } from "k6/http";

export const options = { vus: 20, duration: "2m" };

export default function () {
  // Each VU creates its own isolated jar — no cross-VU cookie bleed
  const jar = new CookieJar();
  const params = { jar };

  group("login-flow", () => {
    const loginRes = http.post(
      "https://example.com/login",
      JSON.stringify({ user: `vu-${__VU}`, pass: "secret" }),
      { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, ...params }
    );
    check(loginRes, { "login 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  });

  group("authenticated-request", () => {
    // Session cookie from login is in jar, not in global scope
    const profileRes = http.get("https://example.com/profile", params);
    check(profileRes, { "profile 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: Explicit per-VU jars eliminate accidental cross-VU cookie pollution (critical when auth cookies contain VU-specific JWT claims), but require passing `params` explicitly to every request — easy to forget on a single call, silently falling back to the global jar.

**Pattern 394** — `k6/execution` Scenario-Aware Dynamic Base URL
```javascript
// k6/scripts/dynamic-base-url.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import exec from "k6/execution";

const BASE_URLS = {
  staging:    "https://staging.example.com",
  production: "https://api.example.com",
  canary:     "https://canary.example.com",
};

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    staging:    { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 5,  duration: "1m" },
    production: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 20, duration: "1m" },
    canary:     { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 5,  duration: "1m" },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const scenarioName = exec.scenario.name;
  const base = BASE_URLS[scenarioName] || BASE_URLS.staging;

  const res = http.get(`${base}/health`);
  check(res, {
    "healthy": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "fast":    (r) => r.timings.duration < 500,
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: A single script drives multi-environment parallel traffic, enabling canary comparison in one run. The tradeoff is that scenario names must exactly match the `BASE_URLS` keys — a typo silently falls back to staging, sending production-intended load to the wrong target.

**Pattern 395** — `handleSummary()` with JSON + Markdown Dual Output
```javascript
// k6/scripts/dual-summary.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { textSummary } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js";

export const options = {
  vus: 10,
  duration: "30s",
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500"],
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get("https://example.com/api/data");
}

export function handleSummary(data) {
  const now = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10);

  // Build markdown table of key metrics
  const p95  = data.metrics.http_req_duration?.values?.["p(95)"]?.toFixed(1) ?? "N/A";
  const rps  = data.metrics.http_reqs?.values?.rate?.toFixed(1) ?? "N/A";
  const errs = ((data.metrics.http_req_failed?.values?.rate ?? 0) * 100).toFixed(2);

  const md = `# k6 Summary — ${now}\n\n| Metric | Value |\n|--------|-------|\n| p95 latency | ${p95} ms |\n| RPS | ${rps} |\n| Error rate | ${errs}% |\n`;

  return {
    "stdout":            textSummary(data, { indent: " ", enableColors: true }),
    [`summary-${now}.json`]: JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
    [`summary-${now}.md`]:   md,
  };
}
```
Tradeoff: Dual output gives CI-friendly machine-readable JSON and human-readable markdown in one pass; the jslib CDN import adds a network dependency at script startup — cache it locally with `--no-summary` and a pre-download step in air-gapped environments.

**Pattern 396** — Shared `Rate` Custom Metric for Business-Level Error Tracking
```javascript
// k6/scripts/business-error-rate.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { Rate } from "k6/metrics";

// Declared in init context — shared across all VUs
const paymentErrors    = new Rate("payment_errors");
const inventoryErrors  = new Rate("inventory_errors");
const checkoutComplete = new Rate("checkout_complete");

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: "3m",
  thresholds: {
    payment_errors:    ["rate<0.005"],
    inventory_errors:  ["rate<0.01"],
    checkout_complete: ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const cartRes = http.post("https://example.com/cart/add", JSON.stringify({ sku: "A1" }), {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  });
  const inventoryOk = check(cartRes, { "cart 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  inventoryErrors.add(!inventoryOk);

  const payRes = http.post("https://example.com/pay", JSON.stringify({ amount: 99 }), {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  });
  const payOk = check(payRes, { "pay 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  paymentErrors.add(!payOk);

  checkoutComplete.add(inventoryOk && payOk);
}
```
Tradeoff: Business-level `Rate` metrics map directly to SLOs and appear in dashboards alongside technical metrics; however, `Rate` records a boolean per call — it cannot express partial success or weighted failures, so multi-step transactions need one `Rate` per step.

**Pattern 397** — `http.batch()` for Parallel Asset Loading Simulation
```javascript
// k6/scripts/batch-assets.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: "1m" };

export default function () {
  // Simulate browser loading a page + its critical assets in parallel
  const responses = http.batch([
    ["GET", "https://example.com/",                        null, { tags: { asset: "page" } }],
    ["GET", "https://example.com/static/app.js",           null, { tags: { asset: "js" } }],
    ["GET", "https://example.com/static/style.css",        null, { tags: { asset: "css" } }],
    ["GET", "https://example.com/api/config",              null, { tags: { asset: "api" } }],
    ["GET", "https://example.com/static/logo.png",         null, { tags: { asset: "img" } }],
  ]);

  check(responses[0], { "page 200":  (r) => r.status === 200 });
  check(responses[3], { "config 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });

  // All batch requests share one VU iteration — total time is max(individual times)
  sleep(1);
}
```
Tradeoff: `http.batch()` issues all requests concurrently from the same VU, closely mirroring browser parallelism (6 connections). The tradeoff is that all batch members must complete before iteration advances — a single slow asset (e.g., a large image) blocks the VU, making per-asset `Trend` metrics essential for diagnosis.

**Pattern 398** — `k6/experimental/fs` Streaming Large CSV Without Memory Spike
```javascript
// k6/scripts/fs-streaming-csv.js
import { open, SeekMode } from "k6/experimental/fs";
import { check } from "k6";
import http from "k6/http";

let file;

export async function setup() {
  file = await open("./users.csv");
}

export default async function () {
  // Read next line without loading entire file into memory
  const buf = new Uint8Array(256);
  const bytesRead = await file.read(buf);
  if (bytesRead === null) {
    // EOF — rewind and re-read from start
    await file.seek(0, SeekMode.Start);
    return;
  }

  const line = String.fromCharCode(...buf.slice(0, bytesRead)).trim();
  const [username, password] = line.split(",");
  if (!username) return;

  const res = http.post(
    "https://example.com/login",
    JSON.stringify({ username, password }),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } }
  );
  check(res, { "login ok": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: File-handle streaming keeps memory flat even for multi-GB CSVs, unlike `SharedArray` which loads the entire file at init. The cost is async/await propagation through default — mixing async and sync k6 APIs in the same script requires care to avoid unhandled promise rejections.

**Pattern 399** — xk6-disruptor Pod Fault Injection During Load Test
```javascript
// k6/scripts/disruptor-pod-fault.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { PodDisruptor } from "k6/x/disruptor";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 30,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "4m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 30,
    },
    fault: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      iterations: 1,
      startTime: "60s",       // inject fault after 1-minute baseline
      exec: "injectFault",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.05"],
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<1000"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get("https://example.com/api/orders");
  check(res, { "orders 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.2);
}

export function injectFault() {
  const disruptor = new PodDisruptor({
    namespace: "default",
    labelSelector: { app: "orders-service" },
  });
  // 50% HTTP error rate for 90 seconds
  disruptor.injectHTTPFaults({ errorRate: 0.5, port: 8080 }, 90);
}
```
Tradeoff: Combining load generation with fault injection in one script captures the resilience profile (error rate, p95 latency under fault) as a first-class CI artefact. Requires the xk6-disruptor binary and in-cluster k6 execution — not usable in k6 Cloud or standard binary builds.

**Pattern 400** — WebSocket Multi-Connection Fan-Out with `k6/websockets`
```javascript
// k6/scripts/ws-fan-out.js
import { WebSocket } from "k6/websockets";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Counter } from "k6/metrics";

const messagesReceived = new Counter("ws_messages_received");

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: "2m" };

export default function () {
  // Open two connections per VU to simulate multi-tab behaviour
  const ws1 = new WebSocket("wss://example.com/feed?channel=prices");
  const ws2 = new WebSocket("wss://example.com/feed?channel=news");

  ws1.onmessage = (e) => { messagesReceived.add(1); };
  ws2.onmessage = (e) => { messagesReceived.add(1); };

  ws1.onerror = (e) => console.error(`ws1 error: ${e.error}`);
  ws2.onerror = (e) => console.error(`ws2 error: ${e.error}`);

  // Let both connections receive messages for 10s then close cleanly
  sleep(10);

  ws1.close();
  ws2.close();

  check(messagesReceived, { "received messages": () => messagesReceived.value > 0 });
}
```
Tradeoff: The stable `k6/websockets` module (not experimental) supports multiple independent connections per VU iteration. Closing with `ws.close()` sends a clean `1000 Normal Closure` frame; forgetting to close leaks server-side connection state and inflates the `ws_sessions` metric, making capacity graphs misleading.

**Pattern 401** — gRPC Bidirectional Streaming Load Test
```javascript
// k6/scripts/grpc-bidi-stream.js
import { Client, StatusOK } from "k6/net/grpc";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

const client = new Client();
client.load(["./protos"], "chat.proto");

export const options = { vus: 5, duration: "1m" };

export function setup() {
  // Connect once; shared connection is safe for read-only metadata
  client.connect("grpc.example.com:443", { plaintext: false });
}

export default function () {
  const stream = client.invokeClientStreaming("chat.ChatService/Chat", {}, {
    tags: { rpc: "chat-bidi" },
  });

  // Send 3 messages per iteration
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    stream.write({ message: `hello from VU ${__VU} msg ${i}` });
    sleep(0.1);
  }

  // Half-close to signal end of client stream
  stream.end();

  const response = stream.readAll();
  check(response, { "messages received": (r) => r && r.length > 0 });
}

export function teardown() {
  client.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: Client-streaming gRPC load testing validates server-side aggregation and back-pressure handling. Calling `client.close()` in `teardown()` (not `default`) avoids the common pitfall of closing the shared client mid-test; however, this means a crashed VU will not close the underlying connection until teardown runs.

**Pattern 402** — Prometheus Remote Write with Native Histograms
```javascript
// k6/scripts/prometheus-native-histograms.js
// Run with: k6 run --out experimental-prometheus-rw script.js
// Env: K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_SERVER_URL=http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/write
//      K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true
import http from "k6/http";
import { Trend } from "k6/metrics";

const checkoutLatency = new Trend("checkout_latency_seconds", true); // native histogram

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: "3m",
  thresholds: {
    checkout_latency_seconds: ["p(95)<1"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const start = Date.now();
  http.post("https://example.com/checkout", JSON.stringify({ cart: "xyz" }), {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  });
  // Record in seconds for Prometheus convention
  checkoutLatency.add((Date.now() - start) / 1000);
}
```
Tradeoff: Native histograms use 70–90% less storage than classic summary metrics in Prometheus and enable accurate quantile aggregation across replicas. Requires Prometheus 2.40+ with `--enable-feature=native-histograms`; older Prometheus instances silently drop native histogram samples.

**Pattern 403** — `shared-iterations` for Deterministic Smoke Batch
```javascript
// k6/scripts/smoke-batch.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

const endpoints = new SharedArray("endpoints", function () {
  return JSON.parse(open("./endpoints.json"));
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: {
      executor: "shared-iterations",
      iterations: endpoints.length,  // exactly one request per endpoint
      vus: Math.min(endpoints.length, 10),
      maxDuration: "2m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed:   ["rate<0.001"],
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<1000"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  // k6 distributes iterations; each endpoint hit exactly once total
  const ep = endpoints[Math.floor(Math.random() * endpoints.length)];
  const res = http.get(ep.url, { tags: { name: ep.name } });
  check(res, {
    "status 2xx": (r) => r.status >= 200 && r.status < 300,
    "no error body": (r) => !r.body?.includes("error"),
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `shared-iterations` guarantees a fixed total iteration count (not per-VU), so the entire endpoint list is exercised exactly once regardless of VU count — ideal for smoke gates. The tradeoff: VU count and iteration count are decoupled, so a slow VU can cause others to sit idle; set `maxDuration` conservatively and monitor `iteration_duration` spread.

**Pattern 404** — `k6/crypto` HMAC Request Signing for API Auth
```javascript
// k6/scripts/hmac-signing.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { hmac } from "k6/crypto";

const SECRET_KEY = __ENV.API_SECRET || "dev-secret-change-in-prod";

function signRequest(method, path, body, timestamp) {
  const payload = `${method}\n${path}\n${timestamp}\n${body}`;
  return hmac("sha256", SECRET_KEY, payload, "hex");
}

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: "1m" };

export default function () {
  const method    = "POST";
  const path      = "/api/v1/orders";
  const body      = JSON.stringify({ item: "widget", qty: 1 });
  const timestamp = Date.now().toString();
  const sig       = signRequest(method, path, body, timestamp);

  const res = http.post(`https://example.com${path}`, body, {
    headers: {
      "Content-Type":  "application/json",
      "X-Timestamp":   timestamp,
      "X-Signature":   sig,
    },
  });

  check(res, {
    "order accepted": (r) => r.status === 201,
    "sig not rejected": (r) => r.status !== 401,
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: Computing HMAC per request in `default` adds ~0.1ms CPU overhead per iteration, negligible at low VU counts but measurable at 500+ VUs on a single k6 machine. Pre-compute static portions of the signing string in the init context to minimise hot-path cost.

**Pattern 405** — `k6/experimental/webcrypto` AES-GCM Payload Encryption Test
```javascript
// k6/scripts/webcrypto-aes.js
import { crypto } from "k6/experimental/webcrypto";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

// Generate key once per VU in init-like pattern (called once per VU scenario start)
let aesKey;

export async function setup() {
  aesKey = await crypto.subtle.generateKey(
    { name: "AES-GCM", length: 256 },
    true,
    ["encrypt", "decrypt"]
  );
  const exported = await crypto.subtle.exportKey("raw", aesKey);
  return { keyBuffer: Array.from(new Uint8Array(exported)) };
}

export default async function (data) {
  const iv        = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12));
  const plaintext = new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify({ user: `vu-${__VU}` }));
  const keyBuffer = new Uint8Array(data.keyBuffer);

  const importedKey = await crypto.subtle.importKey("raw", keyBuffer, "AES-GCM", false, ["encrypt"]);
  const ciphertext  = await crypto.subtle.encrypt({ name: "AES-GCM", iv }, importedKey, plaintext);

  const res = http.post(
    "https://example.com/api/secure",
    new Uint8Array(ciphertext),
    { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream" } }
  );
  check(res, { "secure endpoint 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: WebCrypto AES-GCM testing validates end-to-end encrypted API endpoints and measures crypto overhead under load. Async `default` requires the k6 async event loop — do not mix with synchronous `sleep()` in the same iteration without explicit `await` ordering or Promise chaining.

### Community Gotchas

**G249** — `http.batch()` shares VU scope — per-request cookie isolation is lost
A team simulates 5 parallel asset fetches with `http.batch()`. One of the batch members hits a Set-Cookie endpoint. The new cookie is written to the VU's global jar and is immediately visible to all subsequent requests in the iteration, including unrelated API calls that were not meant to carry that cookie.

Why this matters: `http.batch()` is a convenience wrapper — all batch members share the same VU execution context and therefore the same default CookieJar. There is no per-request jar scoping within a batch. Developers expecting browser-style origin-isolated cookie storage get cross-request pollution instead.

Fix: Pass an explicit `jar` parameter per batch entry: `[['GET', url, null, { jar: myJar }]]`. Create one `CookieJar` per logical origin and pass it consistently. Alternatively, disable automatic cookie handling entirely with `cookieJar: null` and manage `Cookie` headers manually.

**G250** — `preAllocatedVUs` set lower than peak demand causes `dropped_iterations` without warning
A `constant-arrival-rate` scenario sets `rate: 100` (req/s) and `preAllocatedVUs: 5` without specifying `maxVUs`. k6 can only run as many iterations as there are available VUs. When 5 VUs cannot sustain 100 RPS (because each iteration takes >50ms), k6 silently drops the excess iterations. The `dropped_iterations` counter climbs but no log warning is emitted at `INFO` level.

Why this matters: The test appears to run successfully — exit code 0, thresholds pass — but the achieved RPS is far below the target. Without explicitly monitoring `dropped_iterations` in CI, teams believe they have validated 100 RPS when they have only validated ~20 RPS.

Fix: Always set `maxVUs` to at least `rate × p99_iteration_duration_seconds × 1.2`. Add a threshold: `dropped_iterations: ['count<1']` to hard-fail when any iterations are dropped. Use `k6 run --verbose` during script development to see VU allocation debug output.

**G251** — `group()` nesting depth affects metric label length and truncates in dashboards
A developer creates deeply nested groups: `group('API', () => group('v2', () => group('orders', () => group('POST', () => { ... }))))`. The resulting `group_duration` metric tag value becomes `::API::v2::orders::POST`, which exceeds Grafana label value display limits, truncates in Prometheus label storage at 256 characters, and causes InfluxDB tag index bloat.

Why this matters: k6 uses the full `::parent::child::grandchild` path as the metric tag value. There is no configured truncation — the full string is sent to all output destinations. Prometheus by default accepts labels up to 256 chars but truncation varies by version and remote write implementation, silently losing the deepest nesting levels.

Fix: Keep group nesting to 2–3 levels maximum. Use flat `tags` on individual requests rather than group nesting for fine-grained labelling: `http.get(url, { tags: { endpoint: 'POST /orders', version: 'v2' } })`. Use `group()` only for logical transaction boundaries that map to user-facing SLOs.

**G252** — `teardown()` receives a *copy* of `setup()` return value — mutations in `default` are invisible
A team passes a `{ sessions: [] }` object from `setup()`. VU iterations push session IDs into `data.sessions`. In `teardown()`, they iterate `data.sessions` to delete created sessions — but the array is always empty. The test finishes with orphaned sessions in the database.

Why this matters: k6 deep-copies the `setup()` return value before distributing it to each VU and to `teardown()`. In-place mutations (array pushes, property assignments) inside `default` are local to each VU's copy and are never propagated back. `teardown()` always sees the original unmodified value returned from `setup()`.

Fix: Do not rely on `default`-side mutations for teardown coordination. Instead, have `teardown()` query the system under test to discover created resources (e.g., `GET /api/test-sessions?tag=k6-run-${__ENV.K6_RUN_ID}`) and delete them. Tag all created resources with a unique run ID at creation time so teardown can find them without shared mutable state.

**G253** — `--execution-segment` runs `setup()` on every segment node, creating duplicate resources
A distributed 3-node run uses `--execution-segment 0:1/3`, `1/3:2/3`, `2/3:1`. Each node independently calls `setup()`, which creates a test user in the database, resulting in 3 test users instead of 1. The `teardown()` on each node only cleans up that node's user, but cross-node references cause foreign key errors.

Why this matters: k6's distributed execution model does not coordinate `setup()` across segment nodes. The `--execution-segment` flag splits only VU/iteration execution, not lifecycle hooks. `setup()` and `teardown()` run independently on every node that executes the script.

Fix: Use the `--execution-segment-sequence` flag with a coordination script: have node 0 run setup, export the result to a shared store (Redis, S3, or a file share), and have other nodes load from the store at init time using `open()` or an HTTP call in `setup()` with a readiness check. Alternatively, make `setup()` idempotent with upsert semantics so multiple invocations produce the same single resource.

## Cycle 58 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 406** — `ramping-arrival-rate` with `preAllocatedVUs` Auto-Tuning
```javascript
// k6/scripts/ramping-arrival-rate-autotuned.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp_to_peak: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 300,
      stages: [
        { duration: "2m", target: 50 },
        { duration: "5m", target: 100 },
        { duration: "3m", target: 200 },
        { duration: "2m", target: 0 },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    dropped_iterations: ["count<1"],
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/products`);
  check(res, {
    "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "body non-empty": (r) => r.body.length > 0,
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `ramping-arrival-rate` models open-system load where the arrival rate is fixed regardless of VU availability. Setting `maxVUs` generously avoids dropped iterations at peak, but over-provisioning wastes memory. The `dropped_iterations` threshold acts as a hard gate — if the system cannot keep up with the configured rate, the test fails explicitly rather than silently underdelivering load.

**Pattern 407** — Per-Scenario Thresholds with `scenarioTag` Isolation
```javascript
// k6/scripts/per-scenario-thresholds.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    read_api: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 50, timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "5m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 30,
      tags: { scenario: "read_api" },
      exec: "readFlow",
    },
    write_api: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 10, timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "5m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      tags: { scenario: "write_api" },
      exec: "writeFlow",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_duration{scenario:read_api}":  ["p(95)<200"],
    "http_req_duration{scenario:write_api}": ["p(95)<800"],
    "http_req_failed{scenario:read_api}":    ["rate<0.001"],
    "http_req_failed{scenario:write_api}":   ["rate<0.005"],
  },
};

export function readFlow() {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/items`);
  check(res, { "read 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

export function writeFlow() {
  const payload = JSON.stringify({ name: `item-${Date.now()}`, value: Math.random() });
  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/items`, payload, {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  });
  check(res, { "write 201": (r) => r.status === 201 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Tag-scoped thresholds give separate SLO enforcement per scenario, so a write-heavy slowdown does not mask read degradation. The tradeoff is increased threshold declaration verbosity — each combination of metric × scenario tag must be spelled out. Prometheus remote write preserves these tags, enabling per-scenario PromQL dashboards without additional labelling effort.

**Pattern 408** — `k6/execution` Dynamic Scenario Branching
```javascript
// k6/scripts/execution-api-branching.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import execution from "k6/execution";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mobile_users:  { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 20, duration: "5m", exec: "mainFlow" },
    desktop_users: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 30, duration: "5m", exec: "mainFlow" },
  },
};

export default function mainFlow() {
  const scenario = execution.scenario.name;
  const isMobile = scenario === "mobile_users";
  const headers  = isMobile
    ? { "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 17_0)" }
    : { "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)" };

  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/`, { headers });
  check(res, {
    "page loads": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "mobile served": (r) => !isMobile || r.body.includes("viewport"),
  });
  sleep(isMobile ? 2 : 1); // mobile users read slower
}
```
Tradeoff: Sharing a single `exec` function across scenarios reduces code duplication and keeps business logic in one place. The `k6/execution` API adds a runtime branch on `scenario.name`, which is cheap (string comparison) but means the function cannot be statically analysed for per-scenario configuration. Use this pattern when flows diverge only in headers, think times, or minor payload variations — not when the request sequence itself differs fundamentally.

**Pattern 409** — `SharedArray` with JSON-Lines for Streaming User Fixture Loading
```javascript
// k6/scripts/shared-array-jsonl.js
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

// Each line in users.jsonl is a JSON object: {"email":"...","token":"..."}
const users = new SharedArray("users", function () {
  return open("./data/users.jsonl")
    .split("\n")
    .filter((line) => line.trim().length > 0)
    .map((line) => JSON.parse(line));
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    load: { executor: "ramping-vus", stages: [
      { duration: "2m", target: 50 },
      { duration: "5m", target: 50 },
      { duration: "1m", target: 0 },
    ]},
  },
};

export default function () {
  const user = users[(__VU - 1) % users.length];
  const res  = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/me`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${user.token}` },
  });
  check(res, { "auth ok": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: JSON-Lines format allows one record per line — easy to append during fixture generation without re-encoding the entire file. `SharedArray` loads the parsed array once in memory and shares it across all VUs without duplication. The `(__VU - 1) % users.length` index distributes VUs round-robin. Ensure the fixture file has at least as many users as peak VU count to avoid credential collision during login-based tests.

**Pattern 410** — `handleSummary()` Posting Results to a Webhook
```javascript
// k6/scripts/summary-webhook.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { textSummary } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js";

export const options = {
  scenarios: { smoke: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 5, duration: "1m" } },
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ["p(95)<400"] },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/health`);
  check(res, { "healthy": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}

export function handleSummary(data) {
  const passed   = data.state.testRunDuration > 0;
  const p95      = data.metrics.http_req_duration?.values?.["p(95)"] ?? -1;
  const payload  = JSON.stringify({
    run_id:     __ENV.K6_RUN_ID || "local",
    p95_ms:     p95,
    passed,
    timestamp:  new Date().toISOString(),
  });

  http.post(__ENV.WEBHOOK_URL || "https://httpbin.org/post", payload, {
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  });

  return {
    stdout: textSummary(data, { indent: " ", enableColors: true }),
    "summary.json": JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
  };
}
```
Tradeoff: `handleSummary()` runs after all VU iterations complete and receives the full metrics tree. Posting to a webhook enables Slack/Teams notifications and CI dashboard integration without external tooling. The HTTP call inside `handleSummary()` counts against `http_req_*` metrics, so use a dedicated tag (`tags: { summary_hook: "true" }`) to exclude it from threshold evaluation, or make the call with `http.post(..., { responseType: "none" })` to minimise overhead.

**Pattern 411** — Circuit-Breaker Guard with Custom `Rate` Metric
```javascript
// k6/scripts/circuit-breaker-guard.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Rate } from "k6/metrics";

const errorRate = new Rate("custom_error_rate");
let circuitOpen = false;
let cooldownUntil = 0;

export const options = {
  scenarios: { load: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 40, duration: "10m" } },
  thresholds: { custom_error_rate: ["rate<0.05"] },
};

export default function () {
  const now = Date.now();

  if (circuitOpen && now < cooldownUntil) {
    sleep(1); // VU idles while circuit is open
    return;
  }
  circuitOpen = false;

  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/data`);
  const ok  = check(res, { "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  errorRate.add(!ok);

  if (!ok) {
    circuitOpen  = true;
    cooldownUntil = now + 5000; // 5-second cooldown per-VU
  }
  sleep(0.5);
}
```
Tradeoff: A per-VU circuit breaker prevents a failing endpoint from monopolising VU time and inflating error counts during a prolonged outage. The `custom_error_rate` threshold provides a cleaner signal than `http_req_failed` because it is scoped to application-level errors, not transport errors. Note that `circuitOpen` and `cooldownUntil` are module-level variables — they are per-VU in k6's execution model (each VU has its own JS runtime), so there is no shared state race condition. The downside is that circuit state is not globally coordinated across VUs.

**Pattern 412** — `k6/websockets` Stable API Fan-Out Pattern
```javascript
// k6/scripts/websockets-fan-out.js
import { WebSocket } from "k6/websockets";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Counter } from "k6/metrics";

const messagesReceived = new Counter("ws_messages_received");
const connectionsOpened = new Counter("ws_connections_opened");

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ws_load: { executor: "ramping-vus", stages: [
      { duration: "1m", target: 100 },
      { duration: "3m", target: 100 },
      { duration: "30s", target: 0 },
    ]},
  },
  thresholds: {
    ws_messages_received: ["count>500"],
    ws_session_duration:  ["p(95)<10000"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const ws = new WebSocket(`${__ENV.WS_URL}/feed`);
  connectionsOpened.add(1);

  ws.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
    messagesReceived.add(1);
    const msg = JSON.parse(event.data);
    check(msg, { "has timestamp": (m) => typeof m.timestamp === "number" });
  });

  ws.addEventListener("error", (event) => {
    console.error(`WS error on VU ${__VU}: ${event.message}`);
  });

  ws.addEventListener("open", () => {
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "subscribe", channel: "prices" }));
  });

  // Keep connection open for 8 seconds, then close
  sleep(8);
  ws.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: The stable `k6/websockets` module uses a global event loop per VU rather than the legacy `k6/ws` callback model, enabling cleaner async composition. `ws_session_duration` is automatically tracked by the module. The fan-out pattern — one VU per connection — accurately models server-sent event fanout load. For broadcast scenarios where the server pushes to all connected VUs simultaneously, ensure `maxVUs` matches the target concurrent connection count rather than the request rate.

**Pattern 413** — gRPC Unary Load Test with TLS and Metadata
```javascript
// k6/scripts/grpc-unary-tls.js
import grpc from "k6/net/grpc";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(["./proto"], "product.proto");

export const options = {
  scenarios: { grpc_load: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 20, duration: "5m" } },
  thresholds: { "grpc_req_duration": ["p(95)<300"] },
};

export function setup() {
  // Obtain a JWT for the test run
  return { token: __ENV.GRPC_TOKEN };
}

export default function (data) {
  client.connect(`${__ENV.GRPC_HOST}:443`, { tls: true });

  const response = client.invoke("product.ProductService/GetProduct", {
    product_id: `prod-${(__VU % 100) + 1}`,
  }, {
    metadata: { authorization: `Bearer ${data.token}` },
    timeout: "10s",
  });

  check(response, {
    "grpc status OK":  (r) => r && r.status === grpc.StatusOK,
    "product has id":  (r) => r && r.message && r.message.product_id !== undefined,
  });

  client.close();
  sleep(0.2);
}
```
Tradeoff: Calling `client.connect()` and `client.close()` on every iteration simulates realistic short-lived connections but adds TLS handshake overhead per iteration. For sustained-connection tests (streaming or long-lived gRPC channels), move `client.connect()` into the init context using a module-level connection managed with `setup()`. Per-iteration connect is appropriate for unary RPC benchmarks where connection setup cost is part of the SLO being measured.

**Pattern 414** — Browser Test with `page.waitForSelector()` and Core Web Vitals
```javascript
// k6/scripts/browser-cwv.js
import { browser } from "k6/browser";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browser_scenario: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 3,
      duration: "2m",
      options: { browser: { type: "chromium" } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    browser_web_vital_lcp: ["p(75)<2500"],
    browser_web_vital_cls: ["p(75)<0.1"],
    browser_web_vital_inp: ["p(75)<200"],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/`, { waitUntil: "networkidle" });

    const hero = page.locator("h1");
    await hero.waitFor({ state: "visible", timeout: 5000 });

    check(await hero.textContent(), { "hero visible": (t) => t.length > 0 });

    await page.screenshot({ path: `screenshots/vu-${__VU}.png` });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Browser scenarios consume significantly more CPU and memory than protocol-level tests — 3–5 VUs is typically the maximum per k6 instance without resource contention. Core Web Vitals (`LCP`, `CLS`, `INP`) thresholds map directly to Google's "Good" UX thresholds, enabling automated regression gating on perceived performance. Run browser scenarios separately from HTTP scenarios to avoid CPU starvation. The `finally` block ensures `page.close()` is called even on assertion failures, preventing Chrome process leaks.

**Pattern 415** — Streaming Response Processing with `k6/experimental/streams`
```javascript
// k6/scripts/streaming-response.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: { stream_test: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 10, duration: "3m" } },
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ["p(95)<2000"] },
};

export default async function () {
  const res = await http.asyncRequest("GET", `${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/events/stream`, null, {
    responseType: "stream",
  });

  check(res, { "stream connected": (r) => r.status === 200 });

  let eventCount = 0;
  const decoder  = new TextDecoder();
  const reader   = res.body.getReader();

  // Read up to 5 server-sent events then release the stream
  while (eventCount < 5) {
    const { done, value } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;
    const chunk = decoder.decode(value, { stream: true });
    if (chunk.startsWith("data:")) eventCount++;
  }
  reader.cancel();

  check(eventCount, { "received 5 events": (n) => n === 5 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `k6/experimental/streams` enables incremental processing of SSE (Server-Sent Events) and large response payloads without buffering the entire body in memory. `reader.cancel()` closes the underlying HTTP connection cleanly, ensuring the server-side stream handler terminates. Using `asyncRequest` with `responseType: "stream"` is required — regular `http.get()` buffers the full response. This pattern is marked experimental; the API may change in future k6 releases.

**Pattern 416** — Multi-Source Secret Injection with `k6/secrets`
```javascript
// k6/scripts/multi-source-secrets.js
// Run: k6 run --secret-source=file=./secrets.env script.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { secret } from "k6/secrets";

export const options = {
  scenarios: { auth_test: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 5, duration: "2m" } },
};

export async function setup() {
  // Secrets are resolved at runtime — never appear in logs or k6 output
  const apiKey    = await secret.get("API_KEY");
  const clientId  = await secret.get("CLIENT_ID");
  const clientSec = await secret.get("CLIENT_SECRET");

  const tokenRes = http.post(`${__ENV.AUTH_URL}/oauth/token`, {
    grant_type:    "client_credentials",
    client_id:     clientId,
    client_secret: clientSec,
  });
  return { token: tokenRes.json("access_token"), apiKey };
}

export default function (data) {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/secure-resource`, {
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${data.token}`,
      "X-API-Key":   data.apiKey,
    },
  });
  check(res, { "authorized": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `k6/secrets` prevents credentials from appearing in `k6 run` command history, process environment dumps, or k6 JSON output (secrets are redacted as `[secret]` in all output streams). The `--secret-source=file=` flag reads from a `.env`-format file at test startup. In k6 Cloud, secrets auto-inject from the configured secret store when running with `--local-execution`. The tradeoff is that `secret.get()` returns a Promise, requiring `async setup()` — this is straightforward but easy to forget, causing `[object Promise]` to be passed to VUs instead of the resolved string.

**Pattern 417** — `xk6-disruptor` Service Fault Injection During Load
```javascript
// k6/scripts/fault-injection.js
// Requires: xk6-disruptor extension built into the k6 binary
import { ServiceDisruptor } from "k6/x/disruptor";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    inject_fault: { executor: "shared-iterations", iterations: 1, vus: 1, exec: "injectFault" },
    load:         { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 30, duration: "3m", exec: "loadTest",
                    startTime: "15s" }, // give fault injection time to arm
  },
};

export function injectFault() {
  const disruptor = new ServiceDisruptor("product-service", "default");
  disruptor.injectHTTPFaults({ errorRate: 0.1, errorCode: 503 }, "2m");
}

export function loadTest() {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/products`);
  check(res, {
    "not 503": (r) => r.status !== 503,
    "or graceful": (r) => r.status === 503 || r.status === 200,
  });
  sleep(0.5);
}
```
Tradeoff: `xk6-disruptor` injects faults at the Kubernetes service level without modifying application code, making it suitable for testing resilience of downstream consumers. The `shared-iterations` executor with 1 iteration ensures fault injection runs exactly once. The 15-second `startTime` delay for the load scenario prevents load traffic from hitting the endpoint before the fault is armed. The primary tradeoff is that `xk6-disruptor` requires a Kubernetes cluster — it cannot fault-inject against non-Kubernetes services.

**Pattern 418** — Prometheus Remote Write Histogram Bucketing Override
```javascript
// k6/scripts/prometheus-histogram.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";
import { Trend } from "k6/metrics";

const checkoutLatency = new Trend("checkout_latency_ms", true); // native histogram

export const options = {
  scenarios: { checkout: { executor: "constant-arrival-rate", rate: 20, timeUnit: "1s",
                           duration: "5m", preAllocatedVUs: 40 } },
  thresholds: { checkout_latency_ms: ["p(99)<3000"] },
  ext: {
    // Prometheus remote write native histograms
    prometheus: {
      url:     __ENV.PROM_REMOTE_WRITE_URL,
      headers: { Authorization: `Basic ${__ENV.PROM_AUTH}` },
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const start = Date.now();
  const res   = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/checkout`, JSON.stringify({
    cart_id: `cart-${__VU}-${__ITER}`,
    payment: "card",
  }), { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" } });

  checkoutLatency.add(Date.now() - start);

  check(res, {
    "checkout success": (r) => r.status === 200 || r.status === 201,
    "order id present": (r) => r.json("order_id") !== undefined,
  });
  sleep(0.1);
}
```
Tradeoff: Declaring a `Trend` metric with `true` as the second argument emits it as a native histogram in Prometheus remote write output, enabling server-side quantile calculation with `histogram_quantile()` PromQL — far more accurate than client-side percentile approximation. The `checkout_latency_ms` metric is business-specific and separate from `http_req_duration`, giving a clean signal for checkout SLO dashboards. Native histograms require Prometheus 2.40+ with the `--enable-feature=native-histograms` flag.

**Pattern 419** — `per-vu-iterations` for Deterministic Data Migration Testing
```javascript
// k6/scripts/migration-test.js
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

const records = new SharedArray("records", function () {
  return JSON.parse(open("./data/migration-records.json"));
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    migrate: {
      executor: "per-vu-iterations",
      vus: 10,
      iterations: 50, // each VU processes 50 records = 500 total
      maxDuration: "10m",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.001"],
    http_req_duration: ["p(99)<1000"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  // VU-index + iteration index maps to a unique record
  const index  = ((__VU - 1) * 50) + __ITER;
  const record = records[index % records.length];

  const res = http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/migrate`, JSON.stringify(record), {
    headers: {
      "Content-Type":  "application/json",
      "X-Batch-Run":   __ENV.RUN_ID || "dev",
    },
  });
  check(res, {
    "migrated":     (r) => r.status === 200,
    "idempotent":   (r) => r.json("duplicate") !== true,
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `per-vu-iterations` guarantees each VU runs exactly N iterations — useful for data migration tests where you need to process exactly M records with no duplicates or gaps. The VU-index sharding formula `((__VU - 1) * iterations) + __ITER` gives each VU a contiguous, non-overlapping slice of the record set. The `idempotent` check validates that re-running the migration does not create duplicate records — critical for safe migration rollback scenarios. Ensure `vus × iterations` does not exceed the record count.

**Pattern 420** — `k6/experimental/fs` Chunked CSV Processing for Large Fixture Files
```javascript
// k6/scripts/fs-csv-chunked.js
import { open, SeekMode } from "k6/experimental/fs";
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

let fileHandle;

export async function setup() {
  fileHandle = await open("./data/large-users.csv");
  // Skip CSV header row
  const headerBuf = new Uint8Array(256);
  await fileHandle.read(headerBuf);
  return {};
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: { csv_load: { executor: "constant-vus", vus: 5, duration: "3m" } },
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ["p(95)<600"] },
};

export default async function () {
  const lineBuf = new Uint8Array(512);
  const bytesRead = await fileHandle.read(lineBuf);
  if (bytesRead === null) {
    // EOF — seek back to start for next VU cycle
    await fileHandle.seek(0, SeekMode.Start);
    return;
  }
  const line   = new TextDecoder().decode(lineBuf.subarray(0, bytesRead)).trim();
  const [email, token] = line.split(",");
  if (!email || !token) return;

  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/user/profile`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token.trim()}` },
  });
  check(res, { "profile loaded": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.2);
}
```
Tradeoff: `k6/experimental/fs` reads files incrementally from disk rather than loading the entire CSV into memory via `open()`, reducing memory usage from O(file size) to O(buffer size). This is essential for fixture files over 100 MB. The `SeekMode.Start` reset allows VUs to cycle through the file multiple times in long-duration tests. The tradeoff is that concurrent VU reads on the same `fileHandle` are serialized by the event loop — for high-VU scenarios, consider partitioning the file into per-VU slices and opening separate handles per VU.

### Community Gotchas

**G254** — `sleep()` in async `default` blocks the event loop for all pending Promises
A developer migrates a test to use `async default function()` for `k6/experimental/streams` compatibility, but leaves `sleep(1)` at the end of the function. The test runs correctly in isolation but shows unexpectedly high `ws_session_duration` values and WebSocket messages are received in bursts rather than continuously.

Why this matters: In k6's async model, `sleep()` is a synchronous blocking call that suspends the **entire VU event loop** for the specified duration — it does not yield to pending Promise microtasks. When `sleep()` is used after triggering async I/O (WebSocket listeners, stream readers), those callbacks are queued but not processed until `sleep()` completes. This produces artificial latency spikes and burst message patterns that do not reflect real server behaviour.

Fix: Replace `sleep(n)` with `await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, n * 1000))` inside async functions. This suspends only the current async context and allows the event loop to process other pending callbacks during the wait. For purely synchronous HTTP scripts, `sleep()` remains correct and preferred.

**G255** — `check()` second argument must be an object literal — dynamic keys are silently truncated
A test uses a loop to build check conditions: `check(res, checks)` where `checks` is built with `Object.assign({}, ...)` from an array. During the run, only the last check key appears in the summary output — all previous keys are overwritten because `check()` collapses the object to its last key-value pair when duplicate keys exist.

Why this matters: `check()` internally uses the check name (object key) as the metric label in the `checks` counter. If two check conditions share the same key string (e.g., both named `"status ok"` from a loop iteration), only the last one is recorded. The summary shows deceptively high pass rates because the total check count is lower than expected — the test appears to validate more than it actually does.

Fix: Ensure all check keys are unique within a single `check()` call. Use template literals to include dynamic context: `{ [\`status 200 for ${endpoint}\`]: (r) => r.status === 200 }`. Prefer flat `check()` calls over dynamically constructed objects. Run `k6 run --verbose` and inspect the `checks` metric names in the output to verify all expected checks are registered.

**G256** — `http.get()` with `responseType: "none"` still parses response headers — `Content-Length` mismatch causes false errors
A team sets `responseType: "none"` on large binary download tests to skip response body allocation. They observe `http_req_failed` spikes on endpoints that return correct `200` responses with a chunked `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header and no `Content-Length`.

Why this matters: `responseType: "none"` discards the response body but still processes response metadata. On chunked responses, k6's HTTP client expects either a `Content-Length` header or chunked encoding termination signal. A misconfigured reverse proxy that strips `Transfer-Encoding` headers while omitting `Content-Length` causes k6 to report the request as failed with a transport-level error, even though the server sent a valid response. This inflates `http_req_failed` rates and may cause threshold failures that obscure real application errors.

Fix: Use `responseType: "none"` only with servers that send proper `Content-Length` or well-formed chunked encoding. For binary endpoints without `Content-Length`, use `responseType: "binary"` and check `res.body instanceof ArrayBuffer` — k6 will correctly handle chunked streaming. Validate proxy configuration with `curl -v` before running k6 to confirm headers are preserved end-to-end.

**G257** — `scenarios[*].env` variables are not available during `setup()` — only `__ENV` is
A test defines per-scenario `env` overrides to point two scenarios at different base URLs (`env: { BASE_URL: "https://staging.example.com" }`). The `setup()` function uses `__ENV.BASE_URL` to pre-fetch an auth token, but always hits the default value set via `k6 run -e BASE_URL=...`, never the scenario-scoped override.

Why this matters: `scenarios[*].env` overrides are applied **only to the VU execution context** for that scenario — they are not available during `setup()` or `teardown()`. The `setup()` function always sees the global `__ENV` populated from CLI `-e` flags and OS environment. This causes `setup()` to authenticate against the wrong environment, leading to token mismatches or missing test data when scenarios target different environments.

Fix: Do not rely on scenario-scoped `env` in `setup()`. Either use a single global `BASE_URL` CLI variable and perform per-scenario URL construction inside `exec` functions using `execution.scenario.name`, or run separate k6 processes (one per environment) with different global `-e` flags. Document this lifecycle constraint prominently in test script comments to prevent future regressions.

**G258** — `Trend` metric `add()` with negative values produces misleading percentile output
A team tracks `latency_delta_ms` as the difference between two timestamps: `trend.add(endTime - startTime)`. A clock skew issue between the load generator and the SUT causes occasional negative values (e.g., `-12` ms). The k6 summary shows `p(50)` near 0 ms and `p(99)` at an unexpectedly low value, masking real tail latencies.

Why this matters: k6's `Trend` metric stores all recorded values and computes percentiles over the full distribution. Negative values are valid inputs — k6 does not reject or clamp them. When a significant fraction of values are negative (e.g., 5% of iterations), they pull percentile boundaries down, compressing the positive tail. The `p(95)` threshold may pass even when real latencies are far above the SLO target, because negative values shift the distribution leftward.

Fix: Guard `trend.add()` calls with a positivity check: `const delta = end - start; if (delta >= 0) latencyTrend.add(delta);`. Alternatively, track `abs(delta)` and emit a separate `Rate` metric for clock-skew occurrences: `clockSkewRate.add(delta < 0)`. Add a threshold `clock_skew_rate: ['rate<0.01']` to fail the test if clock skew exceeds 1% of samples. Investigate NTP configuration on load generator instances if clock skew is systematic.
