## Cycle 61 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 451** — `executionSegment` and `executionSegmentSequence` for distributed load generation without iteration overlap
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';

export const options = {
  // Each k6 instance runs only its slice of VUs and iterations
  // Instance 0 of 3: 0:1/3, Instance 1: 1/3:2/3, Instance 2: 2/3:1
  executionSegment: '0:1/3',
  executionSegmentSequence: '0,1/3,2/3,1',
  scenarios: {
    load: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      stages: [
        { duration: '2m', target: 300 },
        { duration: '5m', target: 300 },
        { duration: '1m', target: 0 },
      ],
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/resource');
}
```
Tradeoff: `executionSegment` cleanly partitions VU allocation and iteration counts across machines so results aggregate without double-counting, but each instance must receive the same full `options` block — if any instance uses a different `executionSegmentSequence`, iteration boundaries shift and the total VU count diverges from intent. A CI matrix strategy that injects segment values via `--env` and assembles them in a post-step is safer than hardcoding segments in the script.

**Pattern 452** — `minIterationDuration` to enforce minimum pacing and prevent VU starvation during fast-response phases
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout_flow: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 50,
      duration: '10m',
      // VUs that finish faster than 5s will wait before starting the next iteration
      options: { minIterationDuration: '5s' },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{scenario:checkout_flow}': ['p(95)<800'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/checkout', JSON.stringify({ cart: 'abc' }), {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
  // minIterationDuration backstop; explicit sleep models user think time
  sleep(Math.random() * 2 + 1);
}
```
Tradeoff: `minIterationDuration` prevents the constant-vus executor from spinning at maximum RPS when individual iterations complete much faster than expected (e.g., due to caching), which would artificially elevate throughput beyond the intended load model. The tradeoff is that the option is set per scenario inside the `options` key of the scenario object — not at the top-level `options` — and is silently ignored if placed at the wrong level, making it an easy misconfiguration to miss in code review.

**Pattern 453** — `noConnectionReuse: true` combined with `dns` TTL to isolate connection-establishment latency as a standalone metric
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';

export const options = {
  // Force a fresh TCP handshake per request to measure connection overhead
  noConnectionReuse: true,
  // Force fresh DNS lookups every 10 s to simulate DNS-based failover scenarios
  dns: { ttl: '10s', select: 'roundRobin', policy: 'preferIPv4' },
  scenarios: {
    cold_start: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 20,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '3m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 40,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_connecting': ['p(95)<50'],      // TCP handshake budget
    'http_req_tls_handshaking': ['p(95)<80'], // TLS budget
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/health');
}
```
Tradeoff: Disabling connection reuse makes `http_req_connecting` and `http_req_tls_handshaking` meaningful as isolated sub-metrics for CDN and origin latency audits. The cost is that throughput drops significantly — each VU spends 20–150ms per request on connection setup instead of reusing keep-alive connections, so the test cannot simultaneously model realistic concurrent user throughput and connection-overhead measurement. Run this as a dedicated connection-profiling scenario, not as part of a combined load test.

**Pattern 454** — `setup()` returning auth tokens distributed to all VUs via the data parameter
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: '5m',
  setupTimeout: '30s',
};

export function setup() {
  // Runs once; token is shared across all VUs (read-only copy per VU)
  const res = http.post('https://auth.example.com/token', {
    client_id: __ENV.CLIENT_ID,
    client_secret: __ENV.CLIENT_SECRET,
    grant_type: 'client_credentials',
  });
  check(res, { 'auth ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
  return { token: res.json('access_token'), expiresAt: Date.now() + 3500_000 };
}

export default function (data) {
  const headers = { Authorization: `Bearer ${data.token}` };
  http.get('https://api.example.com/protected', { headers });
}

export function teardown(data) {
  // Revoke token after all VUs finish
  http.post('https://auth.example.com/revoke', { token: data.token });
}
```
Tradeoff: Centralising token acquisition in `setup()` avoids N×VU authentication requests at test start, reducing noise in the auth server's metrics. The limitation is that the token is a static snapshot — if the test runs longer than the token TTL, all VUs will fail simultaneously with 401s mid-test. Add a TTL guard in `default()` using `data.expiresAt` and abort early with `exec.test.abort('token expired')` if the clock exceeds it, rather than silently accumulating auth failures.

**Pattern 455** — Scenario-scoped `env` variables to fan out a single script across multiple environments without conditional branching
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    staging: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 10,
      duration: '3m',
      env: { BASE_URL: 'https://staging.example.com', ENV_NAME: 'staging' },
      tags: { env: 'staging' },
    },
    production_canary: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 2,
      duration: '3m',
      startTime: '1m', // delayed start — let staging warm up first
      env: { BASE_URL: 'https://api.example.com', ENV_NAME: 'production' },
      tags: { env: 'production' },
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/health`);
  // Metrics are automatically tagged with env: staging | production
}
```
Tradeoff: Per-scenario `env` overrides allow a single test file to drive comparative load simultaneously across environments, with metrics automatically segregated by the scenario `tags`. The key constraint is that `__ENV` values set at the scenario level override top-level `--env` CLI flags only within that scenario's execution context — if two scenarios share a global variable set via `--env`, the scenario-level `env` wins, which can silently break scripts that expect the CLI flag to be authoritative.

**Pattern 456** — `k6/crypto` for HMAC request signing inside VU context without external dependencies
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { hmac } from 'k6/crypto';
import { check } from 'k6';

const API_KEY    = __ENV.API_KEY;
const API_SECRET = __ENV.API_SECRET;

export default function () {
  const timestamp = Date.now().toString();
  const payload   = `GET\n/api/orders\n${timestamp}`;
  const signature = hmac('sha256', API_SECRET, payload, 'hex');

  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/api/orders', {
    headers: {
      'X-Api-Key':   API_KEY,
      'X-Timestamp': timestamp,
      'X-Signature': signature,
    },
  });
  check(res, { 'signed request ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `k6/crypto` for in-process HMAC signing eliminates the need for an external signing proxy or pre-computed static signatures, making the test portable across environments. The limitation is that `k6/crypto` exposes a limited subset of Node.js crypto — ECDSA and RSA signing are not available; for asymmetric signing schemes, a setup-phase token fetch pattern (Pattern 454) is a better fit than attempting to polyfill via `TextEncoder` hacks.

**Pattern 457** — `k6/websockets` (new API) with event-driven message validation and per-session latency tracking
```javascript
import { WebSocket } from 'k6/websockets';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Counter, Trend } from 'k6/metrics';

const wsMessages = new Counter('ws_messages_received');
const wsLatency  = new Trend('ws_message_latency_ms');

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ws_load: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 30,
      duration: '5m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'ws_message_latency_ms': ['p(95)<200'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const ws     = new WebSocket('wss://ws.example.com/feed');
  const sentAt = {};

  ws.addEventListener('open', () => {
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'subscribe', channel: 'prices' }));
    sentAt['subscribe'] = Date.now();
  });

  ws.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(e.data);
    wsMessages.add(1);
    if (sentAt[msg.type]) {
      wsLatency.add(Date.now() - sentAt[msg.type]);
      delete sentAt[msg.type];
    }
    check(msg, { 'has channel field': (m) => !!m.channel });
    ws.close();
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: The `k6/websockets` EventTarget API mirrors the browser WebSocket standard, making the test code transferable and readable to frontend engineers. The tradeoff versus the legacy `k6/ws.connect()` callback style is that the new API is fully async and non-blocking — `ws.addEventListener` returns immediately, so any logic that must execute after the socket closes must be placed inside the `close` event listener, not after the `new WebSocket(...)` line, otherwise it runs before the handshake completes.

**Pattern 458** — `Trend` custom metric with tagged sub-dimensions for segmented p99 SLOs per API version
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check } from 'k6';

const apiLatency = new Trend('api_latency_ms', true); // true = expose as histogram

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: '10m',
  thresholds: {
    'api_latency_ms{version:v1}': ['p(99)<300'],
    'api_latency_ms{version:v2}': ['p(99)<150'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const v1 = http.get('https://api.example.com/v1/products');
  apiLatency.add(v1.timings.duration, { version: 'v1' });
  check(v1, { 'v1 ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  const v2 = http.get('https://api.example.com/v2/products');
  apiLatency.add(v2.timings.duration, { version: 'v2' });
  check(v2, { 'v2 ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Tagging a custom `Trend` with dimension keys like `version` allows per-tag threshold enforcement — k6 evaluates `api_latency_ms{version:v1}` as a completely independent threshold from `api_latency_ms{version:v2}`, enabling a single test to enforce different SLOs for different API versions simultaneously. The gotcha is that tag cardinality explodes if the tag values are dynamic (e.g., user IDs or UUIDs) — k6 creates an in-memory time series per unique tag combination, which can cause OOM on the load generator for high-cardinality tag sets.

**Pattern 459** — `handleSummary()` writing structured JSON for downstream CI assertion and multi-destination fan-out
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { textSummary } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js';

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: '3m',
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration': ['p(95)<500'],
    'http_req_failed':   ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/items');
}

export function handleSummary(data) {
  const passed  = !Object.values(data.metrics).some(
    (m) => m.thresholds && Object.values(m.thresholds).some((t) => !t.ok)
  );
  const summary = {
    passed,
    p95:       data.metrics.http_req_duration?.values?.['p(95)'],
    errorRate: data.metrics.http_req_failed?.values?.rate,
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
  };

  return {
    'stdout':           textSummary(data, { indent: '  ', enableColors: true }),
    'summary.json':     JSON.stringify(summary, null, 2),
    'raw-metrics.json': JSON.stringify(data),
  };
}
```
Tradeoff: Returning multiple keys from `handleSummary()` fans output to stdout, a structured JSON file, and a raw metrics dump simultaneously — CI pipelines can then `jq .passed summary.json` to gate deployments without parsing human-readable text. The limitation is that `handleSummary()` runs in the init context after test completion, meaning it cannot make HTTP requests to push results to Slack or PagerDuty directly; use a post-test shell script or GitHub Actions step that reads `summary.json` and calls the webhook instead.

**Pattern 460** — `per-vu-iterations` executor with `SharedArray`-indexed unique user credentials for zero-collision authentication testing
```javascript
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

// Loaded once in init context, shared across all VUs (read-only)
const users = new SharedArray('users', function () {
  return JSON.parse(open('./data/users.json'));
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    unique_users: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 100,
      iterations: 1,
      maxDuration: '2m',
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  // __VU is 1-indexed; each VU gets a guaranteed-unique user
  const user  = users[__VU - 1];
  const login = http.post('https://auth.example.com/login', JSON.stringify(user), {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
  check(login, { 'login ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  const token = login.json('token');
  http.get('https://api.example.com/profile', {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `per-vu-iterations` with `iterations: 1` guarantees exactly one execution per VU, so `__VU - 1` is a safe and static index into the `SharedArray` — each VU gets a unique credential with no scheduler-induced collision. The constraint is that `vus` must not exceed `users.length`; add a guard in the init context (`if (users.length < __ENV.VUS) { throw new Error(...) }`) to fail fast rather than silently wrap credentials with the modulo operator.

**Pattern 461** — `ramping-arrival-rate` with `preAllocatedVUs` auto-sizing formula based on expected p99 response time
```javascript
// Sizing formula: preAllocatedVUs >= ceil(peakRPS × p99_seconds × safetyFactor)
// Example: 500 RPS × 0.3s p99 × 1.5 safety = 225 VUs
import http from 'k6/http';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    spike: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate',
      startRate: 50,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 225,  // from formula above
      maxVUs: 350,           // 1.5x preAllocated as overflow buffer
      stages: [
        { duration: '2m', target: 50  },  // warm-up
        { duration: '1m', target: 500 },  // spike to peak
        { duration: '3m', target: 500 },  // sustain
        { duration: '2m', target: 50  },  // recovery
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration':  ['p(99)<300'],
    'dropped_iterations': ['count<10'],  // alert if VU pool is undersized
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/catalog');
}
```
Tradeoff: Deriving `preAllocatedVUs` from `ceil(peakRPS × p99_seconds × safetyFactor)` ensures the executor has enough VUs to sustain the target rate without dropping iterations when p99 latency is at its worst-case budget. The failure mode of underestimating is the `dropped_iterations` metric climbing silently — the executor cannot spawn new VUs fast enough and discards iteration slots, making the actual RPS lower than the configured `target` while reporting no errors, which produces falsely optimistic latency metrics.

**Pattern 462** — `k6/browser` multi-tab workflow using `browserContext.newPage()` for concurrent LCP measurement
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';

const lcp = new Trend('browser_lcp_ms', true);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browser_load: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 5,
      duration: '3m',
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page    = await context.newPage();

  try {
    const response = await page.goto('https://example.com/dashboard', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });
    check(response, { 'page loaded': (r) => r && r.status() === 200 });

    // Capture LCP from Performance API
    const lcpValue = await page.evaluate(() => {
      return new Promise((resolve) => {
        new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
          const entries = list.getEntries();
          resolve(entries[entries.length - 1].startTime);
        }).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });
      });
    });
    lcp.add(lcpValue);
    check(null, { 'LCP under 2.5s': () => lcpValue < 2500 });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
    await context.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Creating a fresh `browserContext` per VU iteration enforces strict session isolation (cookies, localStorage, service worker registrations are not shared between iterations), which is essential for accurate LCP measurement since cached resources would deflate the metric. The cost is that context creation adds 200–400ms of overhead per iteration; for high-frequency browser tests, this overhead is significant relative to short page loads — amortise it by reusing the context across multiple pages in one iteration rather than closing after a single navigation.

**Pattern 463** — `--include-system-env-vars false` (default) combined with explicit `--env` injection for secret-safe CI pipelines
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

// All secrets injected via CLI: k6 run --env DB_TOKEN=$SECRET script.js
const DB_TOKEN   = __ENV.DB_TOKEN   || (() => { throw new Error('DB_TOKEN required'); })();
const TARGET_ENV = __ENV.TARGET_ENV || 'staging';

export const options = {
  vus: 10,
  duration: '2m',
  tags: { env: TARGET_ENV },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`https://${TARGET_ENV}.example.com/api/data`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${DB_TOKEN}` },
  });
  check(res, { 'authorized': (r) => r.status !== 401 });
}
```
Tradeoff: k6 defaults to `--include-system-env-vars=false`, meaning process environment variables are NOT automatically available in `__ENV` — secrets must be explicitly passed via `--env` or `--env-file`. This is a security guardrail that prevents inadvertent leakage of `PATH`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, or SSH keys into k6 cloud runs. The tradeoff is that scripts which previously relied on ambient environment variables (e.g., from a `.env` sourced by a shell wrapper) will silently receive `undefined` instead of erroring; the defensive guard pattern `__ENV.KEY || (() => { throw ... })()` converts silent failures into immediate test-abort errors.

**Pattern 464** — `gracefulStop` and `gracefulRampDown` tuning to drain in-flight VUs cleanly during CI teardown
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    api_soak: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      stages: [
        { duration: '5m',  target: 100 },
        { duration: '20m', target: 100 },
        { duration: '2m',  target: 0   },
      ],
      // Allow in-flight iterations up to 30s to complete before hard-killing VUs
      gracefulStop: '30s',
      // Allow VUs to finish their current iteration before reducing VU count
      gracefulRampDown: '20s',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration': ['p(95)<400'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/orders');
  sleep(2);
}
```
Tradeoff: `gracefulStop` controls how long k6 waits after the scenario duration ends before forcibly interrupting VUs; `gracefulRampDown` controls how long VUs are given to finish their current iteration when the executor reduces the VU count during a ramp-down stage. Setting both too low causes `interrupted` errors to appear in the summary, inflating the `http_req_failed` rate in the final seconds of the test; setting them too high extends total CI wall-clock time. A safe heuristic is `gracefulStop = p99_iteration_duration + 5s` and `gracefulRampDown = p95_iteration_duration`.

**Pattern 465** — `Gauge` custom metric for tracking peak concurrent database connections as a test-time leading indicator
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { Gauge, Counter } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check } from 'k6';

const dbConns        = new Gauge('db_connections_gauge');
const dbPoolViolations = new Counter('db_pool_violations');

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    // Alert if pool violations (connections >= limit) occur at all
    'db_pool_violations': ['count<1'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/metrics/db-connections');
  check(res, { 'metrics ok': (r) => r.status === 200 });

  if (res.status === 200) {
    const connections = res.json('active_connections');
    // Gauge stores min/max/last — useful for observing peak connection headroom
    dbConns.add(connections);
    if (connections >= 80) {
      dbPoolViolations.add(1);
    }
    check(null, { 'db pool headroom ok': () => connections < 80 });
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: A `Gauge` metric stores min, max, and last-seen values — unlike `Trend`, it does not compute percentiles, making it appropriate for point-in-time readings like connection counts, queue depths, or JVM heap usage polled from a metrics endpoint. The threshold `value<80` on a `Gauge` evaluates against the last-reported value at test end, not the peak — if connections spike to 95 mid-test but drop to 30 before the test ends, the threshold passes silently. For peak-violation detection, pair the `Gauge` with a `Counter` that increments whenever the polled value exceeds the limit, and threshold on the counter instead.

### Community Gotchas

**G269** — `--rps` flag is a blunt global limiter that conflicts with arrival-rate executors — avoid in favour of `constant-arrival-rate`
A team uses `k6 run --rps 100 script.js` to cap test throughput at 100 requests per second while using a `ramping-vus` scenario. Unexpectedly, the RPS cap applies globally across all VUs and does not account for the ramping shape — as VUs increase, the cap is hit early and VUs queue up, making latency appear artificially high during the ramp-up phase and masking actual system degradation.

Why this matters: The `--rps` flag implements a token-bucket limiter across all virtual users as a post-hoc throttle, which interacts unpredictably with executor scheduling. It was designed as a quick smoke-test guardrail, not a precise load-shaping tool. Arrival-rate executors (`constant-arrival-rate`, `ramping-arrival-rate`) control RPS at the scheduler level before VUs are dispatched, producing clean rate shapes without artefacts.

Fix: Replace `--rps` with a `constant-arrival-rate` scenario: set `rate: 100`, `timeUnit: '1s'`, and `preAllocatedVUs: ceil(100 × p99_latency_seconds × 1.5)`. This gives deterministic iteration scheduling and exposes `dropped_iterations` when the VU pool is undersized, which `--rps` does not.

**G270** — `open()` is only available in the init context — calling it inside `default()` throws a runtime error
A developer refactors a test to load a per-iteration data file by moving `open('./payload.json')` inside the `default()` function to "load fresh data each time." k6 throws `GoError: open() can only be called in the init context` at runtime, aborting the test after the first VU reaches that line.

Why this matters: `open()` is a synchronous filesystem read that runs during the init phase — before any VU is started — because k6 needs to validate file paths, allocate memory, and distribute file contents to VUs before the test begins. Calling it in the VU context is intentionally blocked. This trips up developers migrating from Node.js where `fs.readFileSync()` can be called anywhere.

Fix: Move all `open()` calls to the init context (module-level code, outside any function). For large datasets that change per iteration, use `SharedArray` with a parsed JSON/CSV array and index by `exec.scenario.iterationInTest` or `__ITER`. For truly dynamic payloads, generate them procedurally inside `default()` using `k6/faker` or template strings rather than reading files.

**G271** — `scenario.tags` does not automatically propagate to custom metrics — you must add tags manually via `add()` calls
A team tags their scenario with `tags: { team: 'payments' }` and expects all custom `Trend` metric samples emitted within that scenario to be queryable by `team:payments` in Grafana. When filtering in the dashboard, custom metric samples show no `team` tag — only built-in HTTP metrics inherit the scenario tag automatically.

Why this matters: k6 automatically attaches scenario-level tags to built-in metrics (`http_req_duration`, `http_reqs`, etc.) but does NOT automatically propagate those tags to custom metrics created with `k6/metrics`. Each `metric.add(value, tags)` call must explicitly pass the desired tags as the second argument, otherwise the sample is recorded without the tag.

Fix: Create a shared tag object and pass it to every custom metric `add()` call:
```javascript
const scenarioTags = { team: 'payments', env: __ENV.TARGET_ENV };
myTrend.add(value, scenarioTags);
myCounter.add(1, scenarioTags);
```
Alternatively, use `vu.metrics.tags` from `k6/execution` to set persistent tags on the VU that auto-apply to all subsequent metric samples, including custom ones.

**G272** — `http.batch()` does not inherit global `http.params` defaults — each request in the batch needs explicit params
A developer sets a default `Authorization` header via a shared `params` object and calls `http.batch([url1, url2, url3])` expecting the header to apply to all three requests. The batch requests go out without the header and return 401s because `http.batch()` does not inherit any global params or per-VU tag context set on `http`.

Why this matters: `http.batch()` accepts an array of request tuples in the form `[method, url, body, params]` — if the fourth element is omitted, no params are applied. Unlike `http.get()` or `http.post()` which can read from a shared params variable in scope, `http.batch()` evaluates each request tuple independently with no implicit inheritance. This is a common trap when refactoring sequential requests into a parallel batch.

Fix: Build the params object once and spread it into each tuple explicitly:
```javascript
const authParams = { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } };
const responses  = http.batch([
  ['GET', 'https://api.example.com/a', null, authParams],
  ['GET', 'https://api.example.com/b', null, authParams],
  ['GET', 'https://api.example.com/c', null, authParams],
]);
```
This also enables per-request param overrides without mutating the shared object.

**G273** — `teardown()` data parameter is a copy of `setup()` return value — mutations in `default()` are not visible in `teardown()`
A developer uses `setup()` to create a test resource (e.g., a database seed record), stores its ID in the returned object, and attempts to track VU-level mutations to that object throughout `default()`. In `teardown()`, the object still reflects the original `setup()` snapshot — none of the per-VU updates are present because each VU receives a frozen copy of the setup data.

Why this matters: k6's execution model serialises the `setup()` return value to JSON and distributes an independent copy to each VU and to `teardown()`. There is no shared mutable state between the VU context and the teardown phase. Any runtime state accumulated in `default()` (counters, collected IDs, flags) is lost when the VU terminates — `teardown()` only has the original setup snapshot.

Fix: For cleanup tasks that depend on IDs created during the test (e.g., deleting records created by VUs), generate all IDs deterministically in `setup()` using a predictable naming scheme (`resource-vu{n}-iter{m}`) so `teardown()` can reconstruct the full list without needing runtime data. Alternatively, use a `handleSummary()` post-processing step to emit the IDs to a file and run cleanup in a separate post-test script.

## Cycle 62 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**P465** — `noCookiesReset: true` to maintain session state across iterations within a single VU

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    stateful_session: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 20,
      duration: '2m',
    },
  },
  // Cookies set in one iteration persist into the next for the same VU
  noCookiesReset: true,
};

export default function () {
  // First iteration: login sets a session cookie
  const loginRes = http.post('https://api.example.com/login', JSON.stringify({
    username: `user_${__VU}`,
    password: 'secret',
  }), { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });

  check(loginRes, { 'login ok': r => r.status === 200 });

  // Subsequent iterations reuse the session cookie automatically
  const profileRes = http.get('https://api.example.com/profile');
  check(profileRes, { 'profile accessible': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `noCookiesReset: true` enables realistic stateful session simulation where VUs accumulate cookies across iterations — exactly matching a browser that stays logged in — but it also means a cookie set in iteration 1 silently influences all later iterations, making test behaviour harder to reason about when debugging failures. If a test run is restarted mid-way through (e.g., after a crash), residual cookies from previous iterations do not persist because cookies live in VU memory, not on disk. Use this flag only when the target application relies on sticky sessions or shopping-cart-style state across page loads; for stateless API tests it adds invisible coupling with no benefit.

---

**P466** — `k6/experimental/fs` for memory-efficient large file streaming without loading the entire payload into VU memory

```javascript
import { open, SeekMode } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export default async function () {
  // Each VU opens and reads independently to avoid seek-position conflicts
  const fh = await open('./fixtures/large-payload-10mb.bin');

  // Read just the first 4 KB as a probe
  const buf = new Uint8Array(4096);
  await fh.read(buf);

  // Seek back to the beginning before sending
  await fh.seek(0, SeekMode.Start);

  // Read entire file for upload
  const fullBuf = new Uint8Array(10 * 1024 * 1024);
  await fh.read(fullBuf);

  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/upload', fullBuf.buffer, {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/octet-stream' },
  });
  check(res, { 'upload accepted': r => r.status === 202 });
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    upload_test: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 10,
      duration: '3m',
    },
  },
};
```
Tradeoff: `k6/experimental/fs` streams file data on demand rather than loading the full content into each VU's memory at init time, which dramatically reduces peak RAM when testing file-upload endpoints with payloads of tens of megabytes per VU. The cost is that file I/O is async and requires `await`, forcing the default function to be `async` — mixing async and sync `http.*` calls in the same function is valid but increases cognitive load. Additionally, each VU opens its own file descriptor, so very high VU counts can hit OS file descriptor limits; increase `ulimit -n` on the load generator if running 200+ VUs against large files.

---

**P467** — Multi-scenario `startTime` chaining for sequential load phases without overlap artefacts

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 2,
      duration: '1m',
      startTime: '0s',
      tags: { phase: 'smoke' },
    },
    load: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      startVUs: 0,
      stages: [
        { duration: '2m', target: 50 },
        { duration: '5m', target: 50 },
        { duration: '1m', target: 0 },
      ],
      startTime: '1m10s',  // 10 s gap after smoke ends
      tags: { phase: 'load' },
    },
    spike: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      startVUs: 0,
      stages: [
        { duration: '30s', target: 200 },
        { duration: '1m', target: 200 },
        { duration: '30s', target: 0 },
      ],
      startTime: '9m20s',  // 10 s gap after load ends
      tags: { phase: 'spike' },
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/health');
  sleep(1);
}
```
Tradeoff: Chaining scenarios via `startTime` with explicit gap offsets keeps phases cleanly separated in Grafana time-series views and prevents VU tear-down from one scenario overlapping the ramp-up of the next, which would distort p99 latency readings at phase boundaries. The gap (10 s here) must exceed `gracefulStop` (default 30 s) plus the ramp-down duration — if it is too short, lingering VUs from the prior phase still run concurrently and inflate VU counts in dashboards. A robust pattern is `gap = gracefulStop + rampDown + 5s` as a formula, computed outside the script and injected via environment variables.

**P468** — `k6/net/grpc` bidirectional streaming with `Stream.on('data')` handler and custom Trend metric

```javascript
import grpc from 'k6/net/grpc';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(['./proto'], 'chat.proto');

const streamLatency = new Trend('grpc_stream_message_latency', true);

export default function () {
  client.connect('grpc.example.com:50051', { plaintext: false });

  const stream = new grpc.Stream(client, 'chat.ChatService/BidiChat');
  let msgCount = 0;
  let sendTs;

  stream.on('data', (msg) => {
    const latencyMs = Date.now() - sendTs;
    streamLatency.add(latencyMs, { stream_type: 'bidi' });
    msgCount++;
    if (msgCount >= 5) {
      stream.end();
    }
  });

  stream.on('error', (err) => {
    console.error(`stream error: ${JSON.stringify(err)}`);
  });

  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    sendTs = Date.now();
    stream.write({ message: `ping-${i}` });
    sleep(0.2);
  }

  stream.end();
  client.close();
}

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    'grpc_stream_message_latency': ['p(95)<500'],
  },
};
```
Tradeoff: Measuring per-message latency in a bidirectional gRPC stream gives fine-grained observability that the built-in `grpc_req_duration` metric (which only covers the full stream lifecycle) cannot provide. The manual timestamp approach (`Date.now()` at send, captured in closure at receive) works reliably for ping-pong patterns but breaks for server-push streams where messages arrive without a corresponding client send — in those cases, instrument server-side emit timestamps in message payloads and compute latency from payload data instead.

**P469** — `page.throttleNetwork()` and `page.throttleCPU()` for browser-based Core Web Vitals under simulated mobile constraints

```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';

const lcpTrend = new Trend('browser_lcp_mobile', true);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mobile_cwv: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 3,
      duration: '2m',
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const ctx = await browser.newContext({
    viewport: { width: 390, height: 844 },  // iPhone 14 viewport
    userAgent: 'Mozilla/5.0 (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 17_0 like Mac OS X)',
  });
  const page = await ctx.newPage();

  // Simulate Slow 3G: 400 kbps down, 400 kbps up, 200 ms RTT
  await page.throttleNetwork({
    downloadThroughput: 400 * 1024 / 8,
    uploadThroughput: 400 * 1024 / 8,
    latency: 200,
  });

  // Simulate mid-range Android CPU (4x slowdown)
  await page.throttleCPU({ rate: 4 });

  await page.goto('https://www.example.com/', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });

  const lcp = await page.evaluate(() => {
    return new Promise(resolve => {
      new PerformanceObserver(list => {
        const entries = list.getEntries();
        resolve(entries[entries.length - 1].startTime);
      }).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });
    });
  });

  lcpTrend.add(lcp, { device: 'mobile' });
  check(lcp, { 'LCP under 4s on mobile': v => v < 4000 });

  await page.close();
  await ctx.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: Combining `throttleNetwork` and `throttleCPU` in the browser scenario produces Core Web Vitals measurements that accurately reflect the mobile percentile experience — Google's CrUX data shows that p75 LCP for mobile is typically 2-3x worse than desktop. The tradeoff is that Chromium-based k6 browser VUs are memory-heavy (300–600 MB each), so throttling at high concurrency amplifies resource consumption on the load generator; run browser scenarios with 3–5 VUs maximum and use protocol-level VUs for the bulk throughput test, reserving browser VUs for synthetic monitoring.

**P470** — `systemTags` filtering to reduce metric cardinality and InfluxDB/Prometheus storage costs

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  // Only keep tags that provide actionable grouping; drop noisy high-cardinality tags
  systemTags: ['status', 'method', 'name', 'group', 'scenario', 'error'],
  // 'url' is excluded to prevent per-URL cardinality explosion when hitting
  // parameterised endpoints like /users/{id}
  tags: {
    environment: __ENV.TARGET_ENV || 'staging',
    release: __ENV.BUILD_VERSION || 'unknown',
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{status:200}':  ['p(95)<300'],
    'http_req_duration{status:500}':  ['count<5'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const userId = Math.floor(Math.random() * 10000) + 1;
  // Use http_req_name tag to group parameterised URLs under one series
  const res = http.get(`https://api.example.com/users/${userId}`, {
    tags: { name: 'GET /users/{id}' },
  });
  check(res, { 'user found': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Excluding `url` from `systemTags` and grouping parameterised endpoints under a stable `name` tag prevents time-series cardinality from exploding in Prometheus or InfluxDB when user IDs, UUIDs, or timestamps appear in paths — a 10 000-user test hitting `/users/{id}` would otherwise generate 10 000 unique `url` label values, causing metric ingestion backends to OOM or time out on queries. The tradeoff is that raw per-URL breakdown is lost; if you later need URL-level debugging, re-enable the `url` tag for a short targeted run rather than permanently including it.

**P471** — `abortOnFail` with `delayAbortEval` for SLO-guarded load tests that terminate before full duration if error rate spikes

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    slo_guard: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate',
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 200,
      stages: [
        { duration: '2m', target: 50 },
        { duration: '5m', target: 50 },
        { duration: '2m', target: 100 },
        { duration: '5m', target: 100 },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // Abort immediately if p99 exceeds 2 s, but only after 90 s of data
    'http_req_duration': [
      { threshold: 'p(99)<2000', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '90s' },
    ],
    // Abort if error rate exceeds 5 % after 60 s of data collection
    'http_req_failed': [
      { threshold: 'rate<0.05', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '60s' },
    ],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/search?q=test');
  check(res, {
    'status 200': r => r.status === 200,
    'latency ok':  r => r.timings.duration < 1500,
  });
  sleep(0);
}
```
Tradeoff: `abortOnFail` combined with `delayAbortEval` creates a self-terminating test that protects the system under test from prolonged overload during capacity runs — if the service degrades beyond SLO bounds the test exits with a non-zero code and the CI pipeline fails fast without needing a human to cancel it. The `delayAbortEval` window must be long enough for the metric aggregator to accumulate statistically meaningful samples (typically 60–120 s at low rates); setting it too short causes false positives during ramp-up when a handful of slow requests can transiently push p99 above threshold before the distribution stabilises.

**P472** — `k6/execution` `vu.metrics.tags` for persistent per-VU tagging without passing tags to every `add()` call

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { Counter, Trend } from 'k6/metrics';
import { execution } from 'k6';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';

const users = new SharedArray('users', () =>
  JSON.parse(open('./fixtures/users.json'))
);

const apiErrors    = new Counter('api_errors');
const apiDuration  = new Trend('api_duration_ms', true);

export default function () {
  const user = users[(__VU - 1) % users.length];

  // Set persistent tags on the VU once per iteration start
  // All subsequent metric samples (including http_req_duration) inherit these tags
  execution.vu.metrics.tags['userId']   = user.id;
  execution.vu.metrics.tags['userTier'] = user.tier;
  execution.vu.metrics.tags['region']   = __ENV.REGION || 'eu-west-1';

  const start = Date.now();
  const res = http.get(`https://api.example.com/dashboard/${user.id}`);
  apiDuration.add(Date.now() - start);  // inherits userId + userTier automatically

  if (res.status !== 200) {
    apiErrors.add(1);  // also inherits VU tags without explicit second argument
  }
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: { main: { executor: 'per-vu-iterations', vus: 50, iterations: 20 } },
  thresholds: {
    'api_duration_ms{userTier:premium}': ['p(95)<200'],
    'api_duration_ms{userTier:free}':    ['p(95)<500'],
  },
};
```
Tradeoff: `execution.vu.metrics.tags` provides a clean mechanism for attaching per-VU context (user ID, tenant, region) to every metric emitted by that VU — including built-in `http_req_duration` — without threading a tags object through every `add()` call. The risk is that VU tags persist across the entire iteration and can bleed into metrics that should not carry them; reset the tags object at the start of each iteration or use scoped tags (second argument to `add()`) for metrics that should not carry VU identity.

**P473** — `hosts` option with wildcard glob patterns for DNS overriding in blue/green deployment canary tests

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Rate } from 'k6/metrics';

const greenErrors = new Rate('green_error_rate');
const blueErrors  = new Rate('blue_error_rate');

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    blue_traffic: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 20, timeUnit: '1s', duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 40, maxVUs: 80,
      tags: { cluster: 'blue' },
      env: { TARGET_IP: '10.0.1.20' },
    },
    green_traffic: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 20, timeUnit: '1s', duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 40, maxVUs: 80,
      tags: { cluster: 'green' },
      env: { TARGET_IP: '10.0.1.50' },
    },
  },
  // Wildcard glob overrides: all *.api.example.com subdomains resolve to the scenario-specific IP
  hosts: { '*.api.example.com': __ENV.TARGET_IP || '10.0.1.20' },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v2/items');
  const ok  = check(res, { 'items returned': r => r.status === 200 });

  if (__ENV.TARGET_IP === '10.0.1.50') {
    greenErrors.add(!ok ? 1 : 0);
  } else {
    blueErrors.add(!ok ? 1 : 0);
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `hosts` with wildcard glob patterns (`*.api.example.com`) routes all subdomains to specific backend IPs without modifying `/etc/hosts` or DNS — ideal for canary comparisons where both clusters serve the same hostname but on different IPs. The `hosts` option is evaluated at init time using the `__ENV` value resolved for that VU's scenario, so per-scenario IP routing works correctly. For canary tests at scale, prefer two separate named scenarios each with their own `env` variable pointing to different base URLs, which provides cleaner metric separation and avoids the `hosts` evaluation order subtlety.

**P474** — `k6/timers` `setTimeout` with recursive scheduling for adaptive polling without busy-waiting

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';
import { setTimeout } from 'k6/timers';
import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';

const pollLatency = new Trend('async_job_poll_latency_ms', true);

function pollUntilDone(jobId, deadline, pollCount, resolve) {
  const now = Date.now();
  if (now > deadline) {
    resolve({ timedOut: true, polls: pollCount });
    return;
  }

  const res = http.get(`https://api.example.com/jobs/${jobId}/status`);
  if (res.status === 200 && JSON.parse(res.body).state === 'completed') {
    resolve({ timedOut: false, polls: pollCount });
    return;
  }

  // Exponential back-off: 200 ms → 300 ms → 450 ms → ... capped at 5 s
  const backoff = Math.min(200 * Math.pow(1.5, pollCount), 5000);
  setTimeout(() => pollUntilDone(jobId, deadline, pollCount + 1, resolve), backoff);
}

export default function () {
  const submitRes = http.post('https://api.example.com/jobs', '{"type":"report"}', {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
  check(submitRes, { 'job submitted': r => r.status === 202 });

  const jobId    = JSON.parse(submitRes.body).jobId;
  const start    = Date.now();
  const deadline = start + 30000;  // 30 s timeout

  let result;
  pollUntilDone(jobId, deadline, 0, (r) => { result = r; });

  // Yield to k6 event loop while waiting for timer callbacks
  while (!result) {
    sleep(0.05);
  }

  pollLatency.add(Date.now() - start, { timedOut: String(result.timedOut) });
  check(result, { 'job completed in time': r => !r.timedOut });
}
```
Tradeoff: `k6/timers.setTimeout` enables realistic asynchronous polling patterns — exponential back-off included — that are not possible with `sleep()` alone, because `sleep()` always blocks for the full duration whereas `setTimeout` schedules work cooperatively via the k6 event loop. The back-off calculation uses a separate `pollCount` integer passed through recursion, keeping measurement instrumentation cleanly separated from control-flow logic. The `while (!result) { sleep(0.05) }` pattern yields the event loop so timer callbacks can fire; without the yield, the main function would spin at 100 % CPU waiting for a callback that can never execute.

**P475** — `localIPs` with CIDR range notation for multi-NIC load generator IP rotation to defeat per-IP rate limiting

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Rate } from 'k6/metrics';

const rateLimitHits = new Rate('rate_limit_hit');

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ip_rotation: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 500,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 100,
      maxVUs: 200,
    },
  },
  // Rotate source IPs across the entire /24 subnet (254 usable IPs)
  // Requires each IP to be bound to a NIC or alias on the load generator
  localIPs: '10.0.0.1-10.0.0.254',
  thresholds: {
    'rate_limit_hit': ['rate<0.01'],  // fewer than 1 % of requests rate-limited
    'http_req_duration': ['p(95)<400'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/data', {
    headers: { 'X-Request-ID': `${__VU}-${__ITER}` },
  });

  const limited = res.status === 429;
  rateLimitHits.add(limited ? 1 : 0);

  check(res, {
    'not rate-limited': r => r.status !== 429,
    'data returned':    r => r.status === 200,
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `localIPs` with a range transparently cycles source IP addresses round-robin across VUs, allowing a single load generator to present as hundreds of distinct client IPs — essential when testing per-IP rate limiters, WAF rules, or geographic routing logic. The requirement is that all IP addresses in the range must be assigned to network interfaces or aliases on the machine running k6; on Linux, bulk alias creation with `ip addr add` is scriptable, but cloud instances typically only assign a small number of IPs per NIC, so this pattern is most practical in bare-metal or dedicated VM environments with pre-configured IP pools.

**P476** — Web Crypto `subtle.importKey` + `subtle.sign` for in-VU JWT ES256 signing without an external token service

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { b64encode } from 'k6/encoding';

// Load PEM key once at init — held in VU memory for the test duration
const EC_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM = open('./fixtures/ec-private-key.pem');

function base64url(buffer) {
  return b64encode(buffer, 'rawurl');
}

function pemToArrayBuffer(pem) {
  const b64 = pem.replace(/-----[^-]+-----/g, '').replace(/\s+/g, '');
  const binary = atob(b64);
  const buf = new Uint8Array(binary.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < binary.length; i++) buf[i] = binary.charCodeAt(i);
  return buf.buffer;
}

async function signJwt(payload) {
  const header  = { alg: 'ES256', typ: 'JWT' };
  const encHeader  = base64url(new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(header)));
  const encPayload = base64url(new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(payload)));
  const signingInput = `${encHeader}.${encPayload}`;

  const keyData = pemToArrayBuffer(EC_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM);
  const cryptoKey = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
    'pkcs8', keyData,
    { name: 'ECDSA', namedCurve: 'P-256' },
    false,
    ['sign']
  );

  const signature = await crypto.subtle.sign(
    { name: 'ECDSA', hash: 'SHA-256' },
    cryptoKey,
    new TextEncoder().encode(signingInput)
  );

  return `${signingInput}.${base64url(signature)}`;
}

export default async function () {
  const now   = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  const token = await signJwt({ sub: `vu-${__VU}`, iat: now, exp: now + 300 });

  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/secure', {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
  check(res, { 'authorized': r => r.status === 200 });
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: { jwt_test: { executor: 'constant-vus', vus: 50, duration: '3m' } },
};
```
Tradeoff: Using the Web Crypto `subtle` API to sign JWTs inside VUs removes the dependency on a separate token-vending service, which would become a test bottleneck or single point of failure during high-concurrency runs. Each VU issues short-lived tokens (5 min here) autonomously without needing network round-trips. The cost is that the private key is loaded from a file at init time and held in VU memory — treat the key file as a test-only credential and rotate it after the test. The WebCrypto API is available globally in k6 without an import, so `crypto.subtle` works out of the box in extended compatibility mode (the default since k6 v0.33).

---

**P477** — Prometheus remote-write output with native histograms for full-fidelity percentile queries at query time

```javascript

// K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_SERVER_URL=http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/write \
// K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true \
// k6 run --out=experimental-prometheus-rw script.js

import { Trend } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

const checkoutDuration = new Trend('checkout_duration_ms', true);
const searchDuration   = new Trend('search_duration_ms', true);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 20, timeUnit: '1s', duration: '10m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50, maxVUs: 100,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'checkout_duration_ms': ['p(99)<1500'],
    'search_duration_ms':   ['p(99)<300'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const t0 = Date.now();
  const searchRes = http.get('https://shop.example.com/search?q=shoes');
  searchDuration.add(Date.now() - t0);
```

Tradeoff: Enabling `K6_PROMETHEUS_RW_TREND_AS_NATIVE_HISTOGRAM=true` sends `Trend` metrics as OpenMetrics native histograms rather than pre-aggregated statistics, which allows Prometheus to compute any percentile (`p(99.9)`, `p(50)`) at query time with full fidelity — contrast with the default aggregated export that fixes `p(90)` and `p(95)` at collection time and discards the raw distribution. The requirement is Prometheus 2.40+ with `--enable-feature=native-histograms` and Grafana 10+ for rendering; older stacks receive no data for the histogram series and display blank panels without error, which can be silently misleading in mixed-version environments.

**P478** — `summaryTrendStats` with extended percentiles and `summaryTimeUnit: 'ms'` for consistent CI output parsing

```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';
import { textSummary } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js';

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: '3m',
  // Report p(99.9) in addition to standard stats for tail-latency visibility
  summaryTrendStats: ['avg', 'min', 'med', 'max', 'p(90)', 'p(95)', 'p(99)', 'p(99.9)'],
  // Force all time values to milliseconds so CI log parsers need no unit inference
  summaryTimeUnit: 'ms',
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration': [
      'p(99)<1000',
      'p(99.9)<3000',
    ],
    'http_req_failed': ['rate<0.001'],
  },
};

export function handleSummary(data) {
  // Emit a machine-readable JSON for the CI parser alongside the human summary
  const p99   = data.metrics.http_req_duration.values['p(99)'];
  const p999  = data.metrics.http_req_duration.values['p(99.9)'];
  const passed = data.metrics.http_req_duration.thresholds['p(99)<1000'].ok;

  return {
    stdout: textSummary(data, { indent: ' ', enableColors: false }),
    'summary.json': JSON.stringify({ p99, p999, passed }, null, 2),
  };
}

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/orders');
  check(res, { 'orders ok': r => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}
```
Tradeoff: Adding `p(99.9)` to `summaryTrendStats` surfaces tail-latency outliers that `p(95)` or `p(99)` miss — in high-throughput services, the 0.1 % tail often represents timeout or retry storms that have disproportionate business impact. `summaryTimeUnit: 'ms'` eliminates the mixed-unit display (k6 auto-selects µs for sub-1 ms values and ms for larger ones) that breaks naive CI log parsers expecting a uniform format. The tradeoff is that `p(99.9)` requires at least 1 000 samples for statistical significance; at low request counts the value is meaningless noise — only enable high-order percentiles when the test produces 10 000+ requests.

**P479** — `k6/experimental/csv` streaming `Parser.next()` for million-row test datasets without full in-memory load

```javascript
import { open } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import csv from 'k6/experimental/csv';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

// Per-VU file handle and parser — initialised lazily on first iteration
let fileHandle;
let parser;

export default async function () {
  // Lazy init: open file and create parser once per VU
  if (!fileHandle) {
    fileHandle = await open('./fixtures/accounts.csv');
    parser = new csv.Parser(fileHandle, { skipFirstLine: true });
  }

  const { done, value } = await parser.next();
  if (done) {
    // csv.Parser has no rewind — re-open to cycle through the dataset again
    fileHandle = await open('./fixtures/accounts.csv');
    parser = new csv.Parser(fileHandle, { skipFirstLine: true });
    const next = await parser.next();
    if (next.done) return;
    const [accountId, apiKey] = next.value;
    return doRequest(accountId, apiKey);
  }

  const [accountId, apiKey] = value;
  return doRequest(accountId, apiKey);
}

function doRequest(accountId, apiKey) {
  const res = http.get(`https://api.example.com/accounts/${accountId}`, {
    headers: { 'X-API-Key': apiKey },
  });
  check(res, { 'account accessible': r => r.status === 200 });
}

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    stream_csv: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 10,
      duration: '5m',
    },
  },
};
```
Tradeoff: `k6/experimental/csv` with `Parser.next()` reads one CSV row per iteration without loading the entire file into memory, making it viable for test datasets of millions of rows (e.g., full account databases) that would OOM a load generator with `SharedArray`. The limitation is that `csv.Parser` has no built-in seek/rewind — when rows are exhausted, the file handle must be closed and re-opened, incurring a small I/O cost. Unlike `SharedArray` which distributes data index-based across VUs deterministically, the streaming parser approach means VUs race for rows in arrival order and row assignment is non-deterministic across runs, making it unsuitable for scenarios requiring stable per-VU user assignment.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G274** — `stages` shorthand and an explicit `ramping-vus` scenario produce different `dropped_iterations` counts when `gracefulRampDown` is non-zero
A team migrates from the top-level `stages` option to an explicit `ramping-vus` scenario for better per-phase tagging, keeping all duration and target values identical. After migration, the CI pipeline occasionally reports a non-zero `dropped_iterations` counter that was absent before, causing flaky test failures on the threshold `dropped_iterations == 0`.

Why this matters: The `stages` shorthand sets `gracefulRampDown` to the duration of the final ramp stage, automatically allowing in-flight iterations to complete. When you define the equivalent `ramping-vus` scenario explicitly, `gracefulRampDown` defaults to `30s` — independent of your stage durations. If iterations take longer than 30 s, or if the final ramp-down stage is shorter than 30 s, VUs are forcibly interrupted, producing `dropped_iterations`. The shorthand silently sets a different effective `gracefulRampDown` than the scenario default, making behaviour unexpectedly change on migration.

Fix: When converting `stages` to a `ramping-vus` scenario, explicitly set `gracefulRampDown` to match or exceed the maximum expected iteration duration. As a rule, set `gracefulRampDown` to `max_iteration_duration + 10s`. Add a threshold `'dropped_iterations': ['count==0']` to surface the issue immediately rather than relying on silent behaviour differences between the shorthand and explicit forms.

---

**G275** — `check()` does not stop execution or throw — a failed check does not skip subsequent requests in the same iteration
A developer writes a login flow where `check(loginRes, { 'login ok': r => r.status === 200 })` is followed by `http.get('/dashboard')` using the session cookie. When the login endpoint is down and returns 503, the check fails but execution continues — the dashboard request also fails, and both failures are double-counted. The developer expected the failed check to short-circuit the iteration.

Why this matters: `check()` in k6 is a passive assertion that records pass/fail counts in the `checks` metric — it has no effect on control flow. Unlike assertion libraries in test frameworks that throw on failure, `check()` always returns `true` or `false` and never throws. This means downstream requests that depend on a successful earlier step will still fire, potentially generating misleading error metrics and skewing response-time distributions with invalid requests sent against an already-failed session.

Fix: Use the return value of `check()` to guard subsequent steps:
```javascript
const loginOk = check(loginRes, { 'login ok': r => r.status === 200 });
if (!loginOk) return;  // skip the rest of the iteration on login failure

const dashRes = http.get('https://api.example.com/dashboard');
```
Alternatively, use `fail()` if you want to abort the iteration and record it as an error, but be aware that `fail()` increments the error counter in the summary and may trigger `abortOnFail` thresholds.

---

**G276** — `__ENV` variables are always strings — numeric comparisons without `parseInt` / `parseFloat` produce silent type coercion bugs
A developer passes `VUS=50` via `--env VUS=50` and writes `if (__ENV.VUS > 10)` expecting a numeric comparison. The condition always evaluates to `true` regardless of the value because JavaScript's `>` applies implicit left-operand coercion, which works correctly for most values but fails silently for edge cases like `'5' > 10` (false — accidentally correct) versus `'50' > 10` (true — correct) versus `'2.5' > 10` (false — correct), making the bug environment-dependent and hard to detect.

Why this matters: k6 passes all `--env` values to `__ENV` as strings, without any automatic type inference. JavaScript's comparison operators apply implicit coercion, which works "mostly right" for simple cases and causes the bug to hide in production until an unusual edge-case value is used (e.g., a leading zero `'05'` or a float `'1.5'`). The issue is especially dangerous in scenario configurations where `parseInt(__ENV.VUSERS)` is used to compute `preAllocatedVUs` — a `NaN` result silently defaults to `0` in some contexts, producing a test that schedules no VUs and passes all thresholds vacuously.

Fix: Always parse `__ENV` numeric values explicitly at the top of the init context:
```javascript
const TARGET_VUS = parseInt(__ENV.VUS || '10', 10);
const RAMP_RATE  = parseFloat(__ENV.RAMP_RATE || '1.5');
if (isNaN(TARGET_VUS)) throw new Error(`Invalid VUS value: "${__ENV.VUS}"`);
```
Validate with `isNaN()` guards and throw descriptive errors during init rather than silently defaulting, so misconfigured CI pipelines fail loudly at startup rather than silently at result time.

---

**G277** — `http.asyncRequest()` does not automatically follow redirects — you must handle 3xx responses manually
A team migrates from `http.get()` to `http.asyncRequest('GET', url)` for throughput improvements in async scenarios. Requests to an endpoint that returns `301 Moved Permanently` now expose the redirect response (status 301) instead of the final resource (status 200), breaking checks and inflating error counters.

Why this matters: `http.get()` and `http.post()` automatically follow redirects up to `maxRedirects` (default 10). The async counterpart `http.asyncRequest()` returns the raw response including redirects, giving callers full control over redirect handling at the cost of requiring explicit follow-through. This asymmetry is intentional — async callers may want to inspect `Location` headers or audit redirect chains — but it surprises teams who assume API parity with the synchronous methods. The issue is invisible during smoke tests against the final URL and only surfaces when infrastructure adds a redirect layer (e.g., HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade, CDN region routing).

Fix: Re-enable redirect following by setting `redirects: maxRedirects` in the async request params explicitly:
```javascript
const res = await http.asyncRequest('GET', url, null, { redirects: 10 });
```
Or handle redirects manually by inspecting `res.status >= 300 && res.status < 400` and following `res.headers['Location']` for controlled redirect auditing. Verify the correct value in the k6 changelog for your version — redirect behaviour in `asyncRequest` has evolved across minor releases.

---

**G278** — `teardown()` always runs even when `abortOnFail` exits the test early — do not assume teardown is skipped on threshold failure
A team designs their test teardown to delete seeded database records and preserve them for post-mortem investigation when the test fails. After a threshold failure causes `abortOnFail` to exit the test early, they notice the teardown still fires and deletes records that should have been preserved for debugging.

Why this matters: k6's test lifecycle guarantees that `teardown()` runs after `default()` completes — regardless of whether the test passed, failed thresholds, or was aborted via `abortOnFail`. This is intentional: teardown is responsible for cleaning up external resources (database seeds, test accounts, allocated capacity) that must be removed even when the test fails. The consequence is that any destructive cleanup logic in `teardown()` runs unconditionally, including operations you might want to skip for forensic purposes after a failure.

Fix: Pass test-outcome context through environment flags to conditionally skip destructive cleanup:
```javascript
export function teardown(data) {
  if (__ENV.SKIP_CLEANUP_ON_FAILURE === 'true' && data.setupFailed) return;
  deleteSeededRecords(data.createdIds);
}
```
Alternatively, move forensic-preservation logic to `handleSummary()` which receives final threshold results — emit a "preserve artifacts" marker to a file and run cleanup in a separate post-test script that checks the marker before deciding whether to delete records.
