## Cycle 63 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 480** — Ramping arrival-rate executor with pre-allocated VUs for sustained throughput ramps
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    sustained_ramp: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate',
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 200,
      stages: [
        { target: 50,  duration: '2m' },
        { target: 100, duration: '5m' },
        { target: 50,  duration: '2m' },
        { target: 0,   duration: '1m' },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration:  ['p(95)<400'],
    dropped_iterations: ['count<50'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/products');
  check(res, { 'status 200': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `preAllocatedVUs` pre-warms goroutines before the test starts, eliminating cold-start latency spikes at stage transitions, but over-allocating by 4x the peak rate wastes ~2 MB of baseline RAM per unused VU slot — size `maxVUs` no larger than 2x your expected peak to bound memory growth in cloud runs.

**Pattern 481** — Per-scenario environment variables and tags for multi-service fan-out tests
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout_service: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 20,
      duration: '5m',
      env:  { SERVICE_URL: 'https://checkout.example.com' },
      tags: { service: 'checkout', team: 'payments' },
    },
    catalog_service: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 40,
      duration: '5m',
      env:  { SERVICE_URL: 'https://catalog.example.com' },
      tags: { service: 'catalog', team: 'discovery' },
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(__ENV.SERVICE_URL + '/health');
  check(res, { 'healthy': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Per-scenario `tags` let you split threshold evaluations by service without writing separate scripts, but all scenarios share the same `default` function — if service-specific logic diverges significantly, use the `exec` property to point each scenario at its own exported function rather than growing a chain of `if (__ENV.SERVICE_URL.includes(...))` conditionals.

**Pattern 482** — `shared-iterations` executor for fixed-budget smoke tests with parallel VU drain
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: {
      executor:    'shared-iterations',
      vus:         5,
      iterations:  100,
      maxDuration: '2m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed:   ['rate<0.01'],
    http_req_duration: ['p(99)<300'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/status');
  check(res, {
    'status ok':      r => r.status === 200,
    'body not empty': r => r.body.length > 0,
  });
  sleep(0.1);
}
```
Tradeoff: `shared-iterations` guarantees exactly N total requests regardless of VU count or iteration speed, making it ideal for budget-constrained API cost tests, but fast VUs drain the pool faster than slow ones — latency outliers from slow VUs do not delay the end of the test, so you may miss tail-latency regressions that only appear after extended run durations.

**Pattern 483** — `abortOnFail` with `delayAbortEval` to guard SLOs without false-positive early exits
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';

export const options = {
  vus:      50,
  duration: '10m',
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: [
      {
        threshold:      'p(95)<500',
        abortOnFail:    true,
        delayAbortEval: '30s',
      },
    ],
    http_req_failed: [
      {
        threshold:      'rate<0.02',
        abortOnFail:    true,
        delayAbortEval: '15s',
      },
    ],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/orders');
}
```
Tradeoff: `delayAbortEval` prevents threshold evaluation during the warm-up window when sample variance is high, but it also means a catastrophic regression (e.g., 100% error rate from a bad deploy) will not abort the test until the delay expires — use `'10s'` for error-rate thresholds and `'30s'` for latency thresholds to balance false-positive suppression against blast-radius containment.

**Pattern 484** — Tagged sub-resource thresholds using `http_req_duration{name:...}` for endpoint-level SLOs
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  vus:      20,
  duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{name:search}':   ['p(95)<200', 'p(99)<400'],
    'http_req_duration{name:checkout}': ['p(95)<500', 'p(99)<800'],
    'http_req_duration{name:health}':   ['p(99)<50'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/search',
    { tags: { name: 'search' } });
  http.post('https://api.example.com/checkout',
    JSON.stringify({ item: 'abc' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, tags: { name: 'checkout' } });
  http.get('https://api.example.com/health',
    { tags: { name: 'health' } });
}
```
Tradeoff: Endpoint-level tagged thresholds produce granular CI pass/fail signals without requiring separate scripts per endpoint, but each `{name:...}` variant creates a distinct time series in Prometheus remote-write — avoid more than ~50 unique tag values per metric to prevent cardinality explosions in your TSDB.

**Pattern 485** — Browser module Web Vitals measurement alongside protocol load using mixed scenario types
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import http from 'k6/http';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    protocol_load: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus:      100,
      duration: '5m',
    },
    browser_vitals: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus:      2,
      duration: '5m',
      options:  { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    browser_web_vital_lcp: ['p(75)<2500'],
    browser_web_vital_cls: ['p(75)<0.1'],
    browser_web_vital_fid: ['p(75)<100'],
  },
};

export async function browser_vitals() {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://example.com/');
    await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/data');
}
```
Tradeoff: Running browser VUs alongside protocol VUs in a single test captures realistic Web Vitals under actual concurrent load, but each Chromium VU consumes ~150–300 MB of RAM and one CPU core — limit browser VUs to 2–5 even in large tests and never colocate browser scenarios on the same agent nodes handling protocol-level load generation.

**Pattern 486** — `page.locator()` with `waitFor()` for resilient browser element interaction under load
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ui_flow: {
      executor:   'per-vu-iterations',
      vus:        3,
      iterations: 5,
      options:    { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
};

export async function ui_flow() {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://example.com/login');
    const usernameField = page.locator('input[name="username"]');
    const passwordField = page.locator('input[name="password"]');
    await usernameField.waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 5000 });
    await usernameField.type('testuser');
    await passwordField.type('secret');
    await page.locator('button[type="submit"]').click();
    await page.waitForNavigation({ waitUntil: 'networkidle' });
    check(page, { 'dashboard loaded': p => p.url().includes('/dashboard') });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `locator().waitFor()` is far more resilient under load than raw `page.$(selector)` because it retries until the element appears or times out, but every additional `waitFor` call adds wall-clock time to the iteration — set `timeout` no higher than your p99 page-load SLO to avoid masking regressions where elements load but do so slowly.

**Pattern 487** — `k6/experimental/csv` streaming parser for million-row parameterised datasets
```javascript
import csv  from 'k6/experimental/csv';
import { open } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

let fileHandle;

export async function setup() {
  fileHandle = await open('test-data/users.csv');
  return {};
}

export const options = { vus: 50, duration: '5m' };

export default async function () {
  const parser = new csv.Parser(fileHandle);
  const { done, value } = await parser.next();
  if (done) return;
  const [userId, email] = value;
  const res = http.get(`https://api.example.com/users/${userId}`, {
    headers: { 'X-Email': email },
  });
  check(res, { 'user found': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `csv.Parser.next()` reads one row at a time from a file descriptor, keeping memory constant at ~4 KB regardless of CSV size — unlike `SharedArray` which loads the entire file into shared memory at init. The tradeoff is that async file reads add ~0.1–0.5 ms of I/O overhead per iteration; for datasets under 100k rows the `SharedArray` approach is simpler and measurably faster.

**Pattern 488** — `k6/experimental/fs` `SeekMode` for random-access binary fixture sampling
```javascript
import { open, SeekMode } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import http from 'k6/http';
import exec from 'k6/execution';

let fileHandle;
const RECORD_SIZE = 64; // fixed-width record bytes

export async function setup() {
  fileHandle = await open('fixtures/payloads.bin');
  const stat  = await fileHandle.stat();
  return { totalRecords: Math.floor(stat.size / RECORD_SIZE) };
}

export const options = { vus: 20, duration: '3m' };

export default async function (data) {
  const vuIdx  = exec.vu.idInTest - 1;
  const offset = (vuIdx % data.totalRecords) * RECORD_SIZE;
  await fileHandle.seek(offset, SeekMode.Start);
  const buf = new Uint8Array(RECORD_SIZE);
  await fileHandle.read(buf);
  http.post('https://api.example.com/ingest', buf.buffer,
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/octet-stream' } });
}
```
Tradeoff: `SeekMode` random-access lets each VU read a unique slice of a large binary fixture without loading it into memory, enabling ~1 GB+ payload diversity at constant ~8 MB RSS — but concurrent VU seeks on a shared file descriptor are serialized by the k6 runtime, capping throughput at ~10k seeks/sec; split into per-VU file shards above that rate.

**Pattern 489** — `execution.vu.metrics.tags` for persistent per-VU correlation ID propagation
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import exec from 'k6/execution';
import { uuidv4 } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-utils/1.4.0/index.js';

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '2m' };

export default function () {
  // Set once per VU at the start of every iteration
  exec.vu.metrics.tags.set('vu_session', uuidv4());
  exec.vu.metrics.tags.set('region', __ENV.REGION || 'us-east-1');

  // All subsequent metric emissions from this VU carry the tags above
  http.get('https://api.example.com/session', {
    tags: { step: 'init' },
  });
  http.get(`https://api.example.com/data?vu=${exec.vu.idInTest}`, {
    tags: { step: 'fetch' },
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `exec.vu.metrics.tags.set()` attaches a tag to every metric emitted by that VU — including all HTTP requests, checks, and custom metrics — enabling end-to-end session correlation in Grafana without per-request boilerplate. The tradeoff is that persistent VU tags survive across iterations unless explicitly overwritten; always re-set session tags at the start of each iteration when they encode per-iteration context.

**Pattern 490** — `ramping-vus` executor with `gracefulRampDown` for clean connection pool drain
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    load_test: {
      executor:         'ramping-vus',
      gracefulRampDown: '30s',
      gracefulStop:     '60s',
      startVUs:         0,
      stages: [
        { target: 200, duration: '5m'  },
        { target: 200, duration: '10m' },
        { target: 0,   duration: '3m'  },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<300'],
    http_req_failed:   ['rate<0.005'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/items');
  sleep(1);
}
```
Tradeoff: `gracefulRampDown` allows in-flight iterations to complete when VUs are scaled down during the ramp-down stage, preventing forced interruptions that would artificially inflate error rates — but setting it too high (e.g., `'5m'`) causes the ramp-down stage to take much longer than specified as k6 waits for long-running iterations; keep `gracefulRampDown` at 2–3x your p99 iteration duration.

**Pattern 491** — xk6 custom output extension for streaming metrics to a NATS subject
```javascript
// Built with: xk6 build --with github.com/yourorg/xk6-output-nats
// Run with:   k6 run --out nats=nats://broker:4222/k6.metrics script.js
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  vus:      25,
  duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<250'],
    http_req_failed:   ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v2/items', {
    tags: { endpoint: 'list-items', version: 'v2' },
  });
  check(res, {
    'status 200': r => r.status === 200,
    'has items':  r => JSON.parse(r.body).items.length > 0,
  });
  sleep(Math.random() * 0.5 + 0.1);
}
```
Tradeoff: xk6 output extensions enable real-time metric streaming to any message broker without polling Prometheus remote-write, ideal for event-driven alerting pipelines — but building a custom k6 binary via `xk6 build` pins you to a specific k6 version and breaks automatic upgrades; pin your binary with a checksum in CI and schedule quarterly upgrade reviews.

**Pattern 492** — `k6/net/grpc` bidirectional streaming with `Stream.on('data')` for real-time chat load testing
```javascript
import grpc from 'k6/net/grpc';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(['proto'], 'chat.proto');

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '3m' };

export default function () {
  client.connect('grpc.example.com:50051', { plaintext: false });
  const stream = new grpc.Stream(client, 'chat.ChatService/BidirectionalChat');
  let receivedCount = 0;

  stream.on('data',  _msg => { receivedCount++; });
  stream.on('error', err  => { console.error('stream error', JSON.stringify(err)); });
  stream.on('end',   ()   => {
    check(null, { 'received ≥3 messages': () => receivedCount >= 3 });
  });

  stream.write({ user: 'vu', text: 'hello' });
  sleep(0.5);
  stream.write({ user: 'vu', text: 'ping' });
  sleep(0.5);
  stream.write({ user: 'vu', text: 'bye' });
  stream.end();
  client.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: Bidirectional gRPC streaming with event handlers accurately models real-time telemetry clients, but each `grpc.Client` instance holds an HTTP/2 connection that is not pooled across iterations — calling `connect()` + `close()` every iteration creates TCP handshake overhead; move `connect` to module scope and reuse the client, or use `reconnect: true` to let k6 manage the connection lifecycle.

**Pattern 493** — `k6/timers` `setInterval` for periodic heartbeat requests within a single long iteration
```javascript
import { setInterval, clearInterval, setTimeout } from 'k6/timers';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 5, duration: '5m' };

export default async function () {
  let heartbeatCount = 0;

  const intervalId = setInterval(() => {
    const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/heartbeat');
    check(res, { 'heartbeat ok': r => r.status === 200 });
    heartbeatCount++;
  }, 5000); // fire every 5 seconds

  // Simulate a long-lived session for 30 seconds
  await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 30000));

  clearInterval(intervalId);
  check(null, { 'sent ≥6 heartbeats': () => heartbeatCount >= 6 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `setInterval` inside an async iteration accurately models clients that send periodic keep-alive signals over long-lived connections — something impossible with synchronous execution — but timers are tied to the VU's event loop and will be silently dropped if `gracefulStop` expires mid-interval; always `clearInterval` before returning and set `gracefulStop` ≥ your longest expected iteration duration.

**Pattern 494** — WebCrypto `subtle.sign` ES256 JWT minting for zero-dependency in-VU auth token generation
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { crypto } from 'k6/experimental/webcrypto';
import encoding from 'k6/encoding';

const PRIVATE_KEY_JWK = JSON.parse(open('keys/es256-private.jwk'));
let signingKey;

export async function setup() {
  signingKey = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
    'jwk',
    PRIVATE_KEY_JWK,
    { name: 'ECDSA', namedCurve: 'P-256' },
    false,
    ['sign']
  );
  return {};
}

async function mintJWT(payload) {
  const header   = { alg: 'ES256', typ: 'JWT' };
  const b64hdr   = encoding.b64encode(JSON.stringify(header),  'rawurl');
  const b64pay   = encoding.b64encode(JSON.stringify(payload), 'rawurl');
  const sigInput = new TextEncoder().encode(`${b64hdr}.${b64pay}`);
  const sigBuf   = await crypto.subtle.sign(
    { name: 'ECDSA', hash: 'SHA-256' }, signingKey, sigInput
  );
  const b64sig = encoding.b64encode(sigBuf, 'rawurl');
  return `${b64hdr}.${b64pay}.${b64sig}`;
}

export default async function () {
  const token = await mintJWT({
    sub: 'vu-test',
    exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 300,
  });
  http.get('https://api.example.com/secure', {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: In-VU JWT minting with WebCrypto eliminates the need for a pre-generated token list or an external auth service during load tests, enabling truly unique tokens per request — but ES256 ECDSA signing takes ~0.5–2 ms per call on typical test hardware; if signing latency becomes a bottleneck at >1k rps, pre-mint tokens in `setup()` into a `SharedArray` and rotate through them instead.

### Community Gotchas

**G279** — `per-vu-iterations` executor silently drops remaining iterations when a VU hits `maxDuration` mid-run
A team sets `executor: 'per-vu-iterations'` with `vus: 10` and `iterations: 100` expecting 1000 total requests. After the test, the summary shows 847 completed iterations. Three VUs hit `maxDuration` (the default `10m`) while still mid-iteration — their remaining iterations were cancelled silently, not counted as failures.

Why this matters: With `per-vu-iterations`, each VU independently runs its assigned iteration count. If any VU's iteration takes longer than `maxDuration` allows, that VU's remaining iterations are cancelled — not failed, just dropped — and do not appear in the summary. The total iteration count is only guaranteed when all VUs finish within `maxDuration`. The silent drop is especially dangerous in correctness tests (e.g., "run exactly 1000 DB writes") where a shortfall corrupts the test's intent without any visible signal.

Fix: Set `maxDuration` generously above your expected worst-case completion time and add a `dropped_iterations` threshold to detect silent drops:
```javascript
scenarios: {
  my_test: {
    executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
    vus: 10, iterations: 100,
    maxDuration: '30m',
  },
},
thresholds: {
  dropped_iterations: ['count==0'],
},
```

---

**G280** — Scenario `startTime` offsets are relative to test start (`t=0`), not the previous scenario's end
A team designs a two-phase test with a `warmup` scenario (2 minutes) and a `soak` scenario (10 minutes). They set `soak.startTime: '2m'` expecting soak to start after warmup finishes. When reviewing the Grafana timeline, they see soak begins at exactly `t=2m` — while warmup's `gracefulStop` window is still active — causing unexpected load overlap that invalidates the isolation assumption.

Why this matters: `startTime` in scenario configuration is always measured from test start (`t=0`), not from the end of any preceding scenario. If the preceding scenario's `duration + gracefulStop` extends beyond `startTime`, both scenarios run concurrently. Teams that design multi-phase tests assuming sequential execution get mixed-traffic results that are impossible to attribute to a single phase.

Fix: Calculate `startTime` as `duration + gracefulStop + desired_gap` of the preceding scenario:
```javascript
warmup: { executor: 'ramping-vus', duration: '2m', gracefulStop: '30s' },
soak:   { executor: 'constant-vus', startTime: '2m30s', duration: '10m' },
```

---

**G281** — Browser `page.close()` not called in a `finally` block causes Chromium process leaks on iteration failure
A developer writes a browser scenario where `page.goto()` throws a navigation timeout. The `page.close()` call at the end of the function is never reached, leaving a Chromium renderer process running. After 50 iterations, the test agent has 50 zombie Chromium processes consuming ~15 GB of RAM and triggering OOM kills.

Why this matters: The k6 browser module does not automatically close pages when an exception propagates out of the test function. Each leaked `Page` holds a Chromium renderer process (~300 MB), open WebSocket connections, and a JavaScript isolate. Unlike HTTP connections that time out naturally, Chromium renderers keep running until explicitly closed. This is the most common cause of k6-browser OOM crashes in CI pipelines.

Fix: Always wrap browser interactions in a `try/finally` block:
```javascript
export async function default_() {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://example.com');
    // ... test logic
  } finally {
    await page.close(); // guaranteed even on throw
  }
}
```

---

**G282** — `SharedArray` constructor callback runs in the init context — `http` calls inside it always throw
A developer attempts to fetch test fixture data from an internal API inside a `SharedArray` constructor to populate dynamic test data at startup. The `http.get()` call inside the callback throws `cannot make http requests in init context`.

Why this matters: k6 enforces a strict separation between the init context (module-level code and `SharedArray` constructors) and the VU execution context. Network I/O is only permitted inside `default()`, lifecycle hooks (`setup`/`teardown`), and async browser functions. The `SharedArray` callback runs synchronously in the init context to build shared memory before VUs start — making HTTP calls there violates the execution model and throws at startup. This surprises developers who expect `SharedArray` to behave like a lazy-loaded async initializer.

Fix: Fetch dynamic fixture data in `setup()` and return it as the setup data object; consume it in `default()`:
```javascript
export function setup() {
  return { users: http.get('https://api.example.com/seed-users').json('items') };
}
export default function (data) {
  const user = data.users[exec.vu.idInTest % data.users.length];
  // use user...
}
```
For very large datasets, write the fixture to a CSV file before the run and load it row-by-row with `k6/experimental/csv`.

---

**G283** — `constant-arrival-rate` silently drops iterations when `preAllocatedVUs` is exhausted — `dropped_iterations` is the only signal
A team runs a constant-arrival-rate test at 500 iterations/sec with `preAllocatedVUs: 50`. Under a regression that doubles response time, VUs become occupied and k6 begins dropping scheduled iterations. The test completes with exit code 0 and no obvious error — the team did not add a `dropped_iterations` threshold, so the regression is invisible.

Why this matters: `constant-arrival-rate` and `ramping-arrival-rate` executors drop scheduled iterations rather than queue them when all VUs are busy — intentionally, to maintain a constant open-loop arrival rate. Dropped iterations are tracked in the `dropped_iterations` counter metric but do not increment `http_req_failed`, do not appear in response-time distributions, and do not cause a non-zero exit code unless explicitly thresholded. A regression that causes 40% of iterations to be dropped can produce a test that reports green p95 latency because only the fastest 60% of requests are measured.

Fix: Always add a `dropped_iterations` threshold alongside latency thresholds:
```javascript
thresholds: {
  http_req_duration:  ['p(95)<400'],
  dropped_iterations: ['rate<0.01'],  // fail if >1% of iterations are dropped
},
```

## Cycle 64 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 495** — Per-scenario `exec` + `env` isolation for multi-service fan-out
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    api_gateway: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 200, duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 20, maxVUs: 50,
      exec: 'hitGateway',
      env: { BASE_URL: 'https://api.example.com', SERVICE: 'gateway' },
      tags: { service: 'gateway' },
    },
    auth_service: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 50, duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 10, maxVUs: 20,
      exec: 'hitAuth',
      env: { BASE_URL: 'https://auth.example.com', SERVICE: 'auth' },
      tags: { service: 'auth' },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{service:gateway}': ['p(95)<300'],
    'http_req_duration{service:auth}': ['p(95)<500'],
  },
};

export function hitGateway() {
  check(http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/health`), { 'gateway ok': r => r.status === 200 });
}

export function hitAuth() {
  check(http.post(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/token`, JSON.stringify({ grant_type: 'client_credentials' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } }),
    { 'auth ok': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Each scenario's `env` block is fully isolated — `__ENV.BASE_URL` inside `hitGateway` never bleeds into `hitAuth` — but all scenarios share the same VU pool budget, so `maxVUs` across all scenarios must fit within your infrastructure limit or the test will be over-allocated at start.

**Pattern 496** — `ramping-arrival-rate` soak ramp with `preAllocatedVUs` headroom staging
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    soak_ramp: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate',
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 200,
      stages: [
        { target: 50,  duration: '2m' },   // ramp up
        { target: 50,  duration: '10m' },  // soak plateau
        { target: 100, duration: '3m' },   // stress spike
        { target: 0,   duration: '1m' },   // ramp down
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration:  ['p(95)<600', 'p(99)<1200'],
    dropped_iterations: ['rate<0.005'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://test.example.com/api/v1/resource');
}
```
Tradeoff: Setting `preAllocatedVUs` too low forces k6 to spin up VUs dynamically mid-ramp (expensive OS-level goroutine allocation), spiking VU creation latency into your p95 measurement window; over-provisioning wastes memory at a rate of roughly 2–4 MB per idle VU.

---

**Pattern 497** — `shared-iterations` smoke test with deterministic fixed-budget termination
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: {
      executor: 'shared-iterations',
      vus: 5,
      iterations: 100,
      maxDuration: '2m',
      exec: 'smokeCheck',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed:   ['rate<0.01'],
    http_req_duration: ['p(99)<2000'],
    checks:            ['rate>0.99'],
  },
};

export function smokeCheck() {
  const res = http.get('https://test.example.com/');
  check(res, {
    'status 200':       r => r.status === 200,
    'body not empty':   r => r.body && r.body.length > 0,
    'latency < 1500ms': r => r.timings.duration < 1500,
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `shared-iterations` finishes as soon as the 100th iteration completes — whichever VU gets there first — so actual per-VU workload is uneven and VUs that start slow will run fewer iterations, giving faster VUs disproportionate weight in the latency distribution.

---

**Pattern 498** — Layered multi-percentile SLO thresholds with `abortOnFail` and `delayAbortEval`
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';

export const options = {
  vus: 50, duration: '10m',
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: [
      { threshold: 'p(90)<400',  abortOnFail: false },
      { threshold: 'p(95)<800',  abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '30s' },
      { threshold: 'p(99)<2000', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '60s' },
    ],
    http_req_failed: [
      { threshold: 'rate<0.02', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '15s' },
    ],
    checks: [
      { threshold: 'rate>0.98', abortOnFail: false },
    ],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://test.example.com/api/resource');
}
```
Tradeoff: `delayAbortEval` prevents false-positive aborts during the JIT warmup window but means a catastrophic regression (500% latency spike) will still burn `delayAbortEval` seconds of infrastructure cost before terminating — balance this against the savings from early exit.

---

**Pattern 499** — Tag-scoped threshold on named sub-resource for endpoint-level SLOs
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  vus: 30, duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{name:search}':   ['p(95)<250'],
    'http_req_duration{name:checkout}': ['p(95)<800'],
    'http_req_duration{name:homepage}': ['p(95)<150'],
    'http_req_failed{name:checkout}':   ['rate<0.005'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://example.com/',           { tags: { name: 'homepage' } });
  http.get('https://example.com/search?q=k', { tags: { name: 'search' } });
  http.post('https://example.com/checkout',
    JSON.stringify({ item_id: 42, qty: 1 }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, tags: { name: 'checkout' } });
}
```
Tradeoff: Tag-scoped thresholds create separate time-series per tag value in Grafana output, multiplying storage cardinality — in a test with 100 distinct `name` tag values, you generate 100x as many metric streams, which can overload Prometheus remote-write endpoints on high-throughput tests.

---

**Pattern 500** — Custom `Trend` metric for business-transaction timing alongside HTTP metrics
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { Trend, Counter, Rate } from 'k6/metrics';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

const checkoutDuration = new Trend('checkout_e2e_duration', true);
const checkoutErrors   = new Counter('checkout_errors');
const checkoutSuccess  = new Rate('checkout_success_rate');

export const options = {
  vus: 20, duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    checkout_e2e_duration: ['p(95)<3000', 'avg<1500'],
    checkout_errors:       ['count<10'],
    checkout_success_rate: ['rate>0.99'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const start  = Date.now();
  const addRes = http.post('https://example.com/cart', JSON.stringify({ item: 1 }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  const payRes = http.post('https://example.com/pay',  JSON.stringify({ token: 'tok_test' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  const elapsed = Date.now() - start;

  const ok = check(payRes, { 'payment accepted': r => r.status === 201 });
  checkoutDuration.add(elapsed);
  checkoutSuccess.add(ok);
  if (!ok) checkoutErrors.add(1);
  sleep(1);
}
```
Tradeoff: A `Trend` metric with `isTime: true` stores every sample in memory for percentile calculation — on a 10-minute test with 500 VUs at 1 req/s, this accumulates 300,000 data points per Trend metric; use batched flushing or switch to a Counter + histogram approach if memory pressure matters.

---

**Pattern 501** — `browser.newContext()` with device emulation for mobile Web Vitals baseline
```javascript
import { browser, devices } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mobile_vitals: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 2, iterations: 5,
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
};

export async function default_() {
  const ctx  = await browser.newContext({ ...devices['iPhone 12'] });
  const page = await ctx.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://test.example.com/', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });
    const lcp = await page.evaluate(() =>
      new Promise(resolve => new PerformanceObserver(list => {
        const entries = list.getEntries();
        resolve(entries[entries.length - 1].startTime);
      }).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true }))
    );
    check(null, { 'LCP < 2500ms': () => lcp < 2500 });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
    await ctx.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `devices['iPhone 12']` sets viewport, `userAgent`, and `deviceScaleFactor` but does NOT throttle the CPU or network — measured LCP will be far lower than real mobile users experience; combine with `page.emulateNetworkConditions` or a Grafana Cloud Browser agent for realistic mobile simulation.

**Pattern 502** — `page.locator()` with `waitFor` for robust SPA element interaction
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    spa_flow: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 3, duration: '3m',
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
};

export async function default_() {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://test.example.com/login');
    const userInput = page.locator('input[name="username"]');
    const passInput = page.locator('input[name="password"]');
    const submitBtn = page.locator('button[type="submit"]');

    await userInput.waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 5000 });
    await userInput.fill('testuser@example.com');
    await passInput.fill('s3cr3t');
    await submitBtn.click();

    const dashboard = page.locator('[data-testid="dashboard-header"]');
    await dashboard.waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 10000 });
    check(page, { 'dashboard loaded': () => page.url().includes('/dashboard') });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `locator()` lazily evaluates selectors on each action (no stale element handles), making it far more resilient to React re-renders than `page.$()` — but each `waitFor` adds a polling loop with a default 100ms interval, so chaining 10 `waitFor` calls on a slow CI runner can add 1–2 seconds of overhead to every iteration.

---

**Pattern 503** — Browser `page.screenshot()` on failure for CI failure triage
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    checkout_flow: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 1, iterations: 10,
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
};

export async function default_() {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  let passed = false;
  try {
    await page.goto('https://test.example.com/checkout');
    await page.locator('#pay-now').waitFor({ state: 'visible' });
    await page.locator('#pay-now').click();
    await page.locator('[data-testid="confirmation"]').waitFor({ timeout: 8000 });
    passed = check(page, { 'confirmation shown': () =>
      page.url().includes('/confirmation') });
  } catch (e) {
    console.error(`Iteration failed: ${e.message}`);
  } finally {
    if (!passed) {
      await page.screenshot({ path: `screenshots/fail-vu${__VU}-iter${__ITER}.png` });
    }
    await page.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Screenshots are written synchronously to disk inside the `finally` block, blocking the VU goroutine — on a 50-VU test with frequent failures, concurrent `screenshot()` calls can saturate I/O and double iteration duration; limit screenshot capture to the first N failures using a `Counter` metric guard.

**Pattern 504** — `k6/experimental/csv` streaming parser for large fixture datasets without memory overload
```javascript
import { open }  from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import csv       from 'k6/experimental/csv';
import http      from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 20, duration: '5m' };

let file;
let parser;

export async function setup() {
  file   = await open('./fixtures/users.csv');
  parser = new csv.Parser(file);
}

export default async function () {
  const { done, value } = await parser.next();
  if (done) return; // CSV exhausted before test ends — size fixture accordingly

  const [userId, email, token] = value;
  const res = http.get(`https://api.example.com/users/${userId}`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
  check(res, {
    'user found':    r => r.status === 200,
    'email matches': r => r.json('email') === email,
  });
}

export async function teardown() {
  await file.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: `csv.Parser.next()` reads one row per call from a buffered file handle — memory usage is O(row size) rather than O(file size), enabling 10M-row fixtures — but the async `await` per iteration adds ~0.2ms overhead compared to a pre-loaded `SharedArray`, which matters when targeting >5000 iterations/sec.

---

**Pattern 505** — `k6/experimental/fs` random-access `seek()` for stratified sampling across a binary fixture
```javascript
import { open, SeekMode } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '3m' };

let fileHandle;
const ROW_SIZE = 64; // fixed-width binary record: 8 bytes ID + 56 bytes payload

export async function setup() {
  fileHandle = await open('./fixtures/accounts.bin');
}

export default async function () {
  // Seek to a random record using VU ID + iteration for deterministic spread
  const offset = ((__VU - 1 + __ITER) % 10000) * ROW_SIZE;
  await fileHandle.seek(offset, SeekMode.Start);

  const buf = new Uint8Array(ROW_SIZE);
  await fileHandle.read(buf);

  const accountId = new DataView(buf.buffer).getBigInt64(0, false);
  const res = http.get(`https://api.example.com/accounts/${accountId}`);
  check(res, { 'account exists': r => r.status === 200 });
}

export async function teardown() {
  await fileHandle.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: Fixed-width binary records enable O(1) random seeks and eliminate CSV parsing overhead, but the fixture pipeline (generate, pack, validate) is significantly more complex than CSV; a mismatched `ROW_SIZE` constant causes silent data corruption where account IDs are read from mid-record offsets.

---

**Pattern 506** — `execution.vu.metrics.tags.set()` for persistent per-VU correlation ID propagation
```javascript
import http    from 'k6/http';
import exec    from 'k6/execution';
import { uuidv4 } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-utils/1.4.0/index.js';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '3m' };

export default function () {
  // Set a persistent correlation tag on the VU — propagates to ALL subsequent metrics
  exec.vu.metrics.tags.set('correlation_id', uuidv4());
  exec.vu.metrics.tags.set('vu_scenario',    exec.scenario.name);

  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/order/123');
  check(res, { 'order found': r => r.status === 200 });

  http.post('https://api.example.com/order/123/confirm',
    JSON.stringify({ confirmed: true }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
}
```
Tradeoff: Tags set via `exec.vu.metrics.tags.set()` persist for the lifetime of the VU — every metric emitted after the call carries the tag — so if you set a `correlation_id` at the start of a multi-step flow but forget to clear it, all subsequent iterations of that VU will emit metrics tagged with a stale ID, producing misleading trace correlations in Grafana Tempo.

---

**Pattern 507** — xk6 JavaScript extension for native HMAC-SHA256 request signing without crypto overhead
```javascript
// Build command: xk6 build --with github.com/szkiba/xk6-crypto
// The extension exposes crypto.hmac() natively without the WebCrypto async overhead
import http   from 'k6/http';
import crypto from 'k6/x/crypto';
import { check } from 'k6';

const AWS_KEY    = __ENV.AWS_ACCESS_KEY;
const AWS_SECRET = __ENV.AWS_SECRET_KEY;
const REGION     = 'us-east-1';
const SERVICE    = 'execute-api';

function sign(secret, message) {
  return crypto.hmac('sha256', secret, message, 'hex');
}

function awsV4Headers(method, path, body) {
  const ts        = new Date().toISOString().replace(/[:-]/g, '').replace(/\.\d{3}/, '');
  const date      = ts.slice(0, 8);
  const bodyHash  = crypto.sha256(body, 'hex');
  const credScope = `${date}/${REGION}/${SERVICE}/aws4_request`;
  const signedHeaders  = 'content-type;host;x-amz-date';
  const canonicalReq   = `${method}\n${path}\n\ncontent-type:application/json\nhost:api.example.com\nx-amz-date:${ts}\n\n${signedHeaders}\n${bodyHash}`;
  const strToSign      = `AWS4-HMAC-SHA256\n${ts}\n${credScope}\n${crypto.sha256(canonicalReq, 'hex')}`;
  const kDate          = sign(`AWS4${AWS_SECRET}`, date);
  const kRegion        = sign(kDate, REGION);
  const kService       = sign(kRegion, SERVICE);
  const kSigning       = sign(kService, 'aws4_request');
  const signature      = sign(kSigning, strToSign);
  return {
    'X-Amz-Date':    ts,
    Authorization:   `AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 Credential=${AWS_KEY}/${credScope}, SignedHeaders=${signedHeaders}, Signature=${signature}`,
  };
}

export default function () {
  const body    = JSON.stringify({ query: 'test' });
  const headers = { ...awsV4Headers('POST', '/v1/search', body), 'Content-Type': 'application/json' };
  const res     = http.post('https://api.example.com/v1/search', body, { headers });
  check(res, { 'signed request accepted': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Native xk6 extensions execute in Go and avoid the V8 JavaScript overhead of WebCrypto — HMAC throughput is roughly 10x faster — but the binary must be rebuilt via `xk6 build` every time you upgrade k6 or the extension, breaking Docker image caching and requiring a CI pipeline stage dedicated to binary compilation.

---

**Pattern 508** — `k6/net/grpc` bidirectional streaming with `Stream.on('data')` for chat/event protocols
```javascript
import grpc  from 'k6/net/grpc';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(['./proto'], 'chat.proto');

export const options = { vus: 5, duration: '2m' };

export default function () {
  client.connect('grpc.example.com:50051', { plaintext: false });

  const stream   = new grpc.Stream(client, 'chat.ChatService/Chat');
  const received = [];

  stream.on('data',  msg => received.push(msg.text));
  stream.on('error', err => console.error(`gRPC stream error: ${err.message}`));
  stream.on('end',   ()  => check(received, { 'got 3 replies': r => r.length === 3 }));

  stream.write({ text: 'hello',        user: `vu-${__VU}` });
  sleep(0.5);
  stream.write({ text: 'how are you?', user: `vu-${__VU}` });
  sleep(0.5);
  stream.write({ text: 'goodbye',      user: `vu-${__VU}` });

  stream.end();
  client.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: gRPC streams share a single HTTP/2 connection per `client.connect()` call — all VUs in the same JS execution context multiplex over one TCP connection — so a `client.close()` from one VU's finally block while another VU is mid-stream causes a `RST_STREAM` on all in-flight streams; call `connect()` inside `default()` (not at module scope) to get per-VU connections.

---

**Pattern 509** — `k6/timers` `setInterval` heartbeat keeping a WebSocket session alive during long soak tests
```javascript
import { WebSocket }              from 'k6/experimental/websockets';
import { setInterval, clearInterval, setTimeout } from 'k6/timers';
import { check }                  from 'k6';

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '10m' };

export function default_() {
  const ws = new WebSocket('wss://ws.example.com/events');
  let heartbeatHandle;
  let msgCount = 0;

  ws.onopen = () => {
    heartbeatHandle = setInterval(() => {
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'ping', ts: Date.now() }));
    }, 15000); // ping every 15s to prevent idle timeout
  };

  ws.onmessage = (evt) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(evt.data);
    if (msg.type !== 'pong') msgCount++;
  };

  ws.onerror = (e) => console.error(`WS error: ${e.error}`);

  ws.onclose = () => {
    clearInterval(heartbeatHandle);
    check(null, { 'received > 0 business events': () => msgCount > 0 });
  };

  // Close after 55s so the VU iteration completes before the 60s scenario timeout
  setTimeout(() => ws.close(), 55000);
}
```
Tradeoff: `setInterval` inside a WebSocket `onopen` handler creates a timer that fires on the VU's event loop — if the WebSocket closes before `clearInterval` is called (e.g., server-side disconnect), the interval fires into a closed socket and logs a stream of `WebSocket is not open` errors that flood stdout and increase log shipping costs.

---

**Pattern 510** — In-VU ES256 JWT minting with `k6/experimental/webcrypto` for OAuth-gated API load tests
```javascript
import { crypto } from 'k6/experimental/webcrypto';
import http       from 'k6/http';
import { check }  from 'k6';
import encoding   from 'k6/encoding';

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '5m' };

// Load PEM key from environment, strip headers, decode base64 to ArrayBuffer
const RAW_PRIVATE = encoding.b64decode(__ENV.ES256_PRIVATE_KEY_B64, 'std', 'rawBuffer');

async function mintJWT(subject) {
  const key = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
    'pkcs8', RAW_PRIVATE,
    { name: 'ECDSA', namedCurve: 'P-256' },
    false, ['sign']
  );
  const header  = encoding.b64encode(JSON.stringify({ alg: 'ES256', typ: 'JWT' }), 'rawurl');
  const payload = encoding.b64encode(JSON.stringify({
    sub: subject, iss: 'k6-load-test',
    iat: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000),
    exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 300,
  }), 'rawurl');
  const sigInput  = new TextEncoder().encode(`${header}.${payload}`);
  const sigBytes  = await crypto.subtle.sign({ name: 'ECDSA', hash: 'SHA-256' }, key, sigInput);
  const signature = encoding.b64encode(sigBytes, 'rawurl');
  return `${header}.${payload}.${signature}`;
}

export default async function () {
  const token = await mintJWT(`vu-${__VU}`);
  const res   = http.get('https://api.example.com/protected', {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
  check(res, { 'authorized': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `crypto.subtle.importKey` runs asynchronously with no caching — calling it every iteration for a 500-VU test mints 500 keys per second, adding ~3ms of ECDSA key-import overhead per iteration; import the key once in `setup()`, serialize via `exportKey`, and store in a `SharedArray` for VUs to re-import once per VU init, not per iteration.

### Community Gotchas

**G284** — `gracefulStop` not accounting for in-flight long-running iterations causes premature VU kills
A team runs a `ramping-vus` test against a reporting endpoint with a p99 response time of 45 seconds. They set `gracefulStop: '30s'` (the default). When the test ramp-down begins, k6 waits 30 seconds and then force-kills VUs mid-request. The result is a cluster of `http_req_failed` errors at the tail of the test that inflate the error rate metric above the 1% threshold, causing a false negative test result on every run.

Why this matters: `gracefulStop` is the window k6 gives VUs to finish their current iteration after the scenario's scheduled end. If any endpoint in your iteration can take longer than `gracefulStop`, k6 terminates the VU while the HTTP request is in-flight — the underlying TCP connection is reset, the server logs a broken-pipe error, and k6 records the request as failed. This is especially subtle with `ramping-vus` where the ramp-down phase begins at the end of the last stage, not after the last request completes.

Fix: Set `gracefulStop` to at least your p99.9 response time plus a 20% safety margin. For the reporting endpoint example: `gracefulStop: '60s'`. Additionally, add `gracefulRampDown` on `ramping-vus` scenarios to allow VUs being scaled down mid-ramp to finish their current iteration before being removed.

---

**G285** — `per-vu-iterations` with heterogeneous iteration duration causes misleading aggregated latency
A developer uses `per-vu-iterations` with `vus: 50` and `iterations: 200` per VU. The endpoint has bimodal response times: 80% respond in 50ms, 20% take 8 seconds (cache miss). Fast VUs complete all 200 iterations early and become idle; slow VUs keep running. The aggregated p95 latency looks fine at 120ms because most completed iterations are from fast VUs — but 20% of users are actually experiencing 8-second responses.

Why this matters: `per-vu-iterations` serializes each VU's iterations sequentially. A VU that hits a cache miss on iteration 1 is blocked for 8 seconds before starting iteration 2. Meanwhile, other VUs finish quickly and exit, reducing the VU count in the aggregation window. The final p95 is computed across all completed iterations regardless of timing, so the distribution is dominated by the fast path — the slow tail is real but statistically diluted.

Fix: Switch to `constant-arrival-rate` for open-model testing of endpoints with bimodal latency. Add a tagged threshold on the specific endpoint to surface the slow path: `'http_req_duration{name:slow-endpoint}': ['p(95)<500']`. Alternatively, add a `check` that asserts `r.timings.duration < 1000` and threshold on `checks` rate.

---

**G286** — `k6/browser` `page.goto()` with default `waitUntil: 'load'` misses async-rendered content in SPAs
A QA engineer writes a browser test for a React SPA. `page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard')` returns immediately after the `load` event fires, but the dashboard data is fetched via `fetch()` calls triggered by `useEffect` hooks that run after initial render. The `page.locator('[data-testid="user-table"]').waitFor()` call on the next line times out because the table is not in the DOM yet.

Why this matters: The browser `load` event fires when the initial HTML, CSS, and synchronous JavaScript have finished — but SPAs typically render a loading skeleton first and populate data asynchronously. `waitUntil: 'load'` (the default) resolves `page.goto()` at the skeleton state. Subsequent `locator().waitFor()` calls will then succeed or fail based on their own timeout budget, but if they are set too short (less than the actual data-fetch time), they will consistently time out even when the app is healthy.

Fix: Use `waitUntil: 'networkidle'` for SPAs that make API calls on mount, or use `waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded'` plus an explicit `locator().waitFor({ timeout: 15000 })` on the first meaningful element. For apps with infinite polling, `networkidle` will never fire — use `waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded'` and `locator().waitFor()` exclusively.

---

**G287** — Custom `Trend` metric `isTime` flag omitted, causing millisecond values to display as unit-less numbers in Grafana
A developer creates `new Trend('db_query_duration')` (without `true` as the second argument) and adds values in milliseconds. In Grafana, the panel auto-detects the metric as unit-less and displays `1234` instead of `1.23s`. When the team creates a dashboard alert at `> 500`, they do not realize the unit is ms not seconds, and set the alert threshold 1000x too high — the alert never fires despite 5-second query times.

Why this matters: The `isTime` boolean flag on `new Trend('name', true)` tells k6 to emit the metric with time-series metadata that downstream systems use to apply millisecond-to-second conversion and correct unit labels. Without it, Grafana treats the values as dimensionless counts. The flag has no effect on the raw number stored, but it affects the `__unit__` label in the JSON output and the Prometheus metric `_seconds` vs `_total` naming convention, causing unit mismatch in dashboards and alerts.

Fix: Always pass `true` as the second argument for duration metrics: `new Trend('db_query_duration', true)`. Audit existing custom metrics — any `Trend` metric where you `add()` millisecond values must have `isTime: true` to render correctly in Grafana and InfluxDB.

---

**G288** — `k6/experimental/csv` `Parser` created at module scope (init context) instead of inside `setup()` throws on import
A developer reads the `csv` module documentation and writes `const parser = new csv.Parser(await open('./data.csv'))` at module scope (outside any function). The `await` at module level is not supported in k6's CommonJS-style init context, causing a syntax error at startup. The developer then moves the `open()` call inside a regular (non-async) init block, but `csv.Parser` requires an `fs.File` handle from `k6/experimental/fs`, which can only be opened with `await open()` — trapping them in an async-in-init problem.

Why this matters: k6's init context is synchronous — module-level code runs before VUs start and cannot use `await`. The `k6/experimental/fs` `open()` function is async-only (returns a Promise), and `csv.Parser` requires an `fs.File` as its argument. This creates a mandatory async dependency chain that cannot be satisfied in the init context. The solution is non-obvious because `SharedArray` (the conventional init-context data loader) also cannot call `open()`.

Fix: Initialize `fs.File` and `csv.Parser` inside `setup()` (which supports `async/await`), return the parser state from `setup()`, and pass it into `default()` via the data parameter. Alternatively, use a pre-generated `SharedArray` from a pre-processed CSV loaded via the legacy synchronous `open()` from `k6` (not `k6/experimental/fs`) if your dataset is small enough to fit in memory.
