## Cycle 65 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 511** — `constant-arrival-rate` with `preAllocatedVUs` and `maxVUs` cap for open-model throughput testing
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    open_model_load: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 200,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 300,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500'],
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/items');
  check(res, { 'status 200': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `preAllocatedVUs` are spun up before the test starts and have zero warm-up latency, but each allocated VU consumes memory even when idle; setting `preAllocatedVUs` too low forces k6 to dynamically spawn VUs mid-test (up to `maxVUs`), which adds ~2–5ms of spawn overhead per iteration during spikes and can cause the arrival rate to temporarily undershoot the configured `rate` until VUs catch up.

---

**Pattern 512** — `ramping-arrival-rate` multi-stage stress ramp with `startRate` and per-stage `target`
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    stress_ramp: {
      executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate',
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 500,
      stages: [
        { target: 50,  duration: '2m' },
        { target: 200, duration: '3m' },
        { target: 500, duration: '5m' },
        { target: 500, duration: '5m' },
        { target: 0,   duration: '2m' },
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: [
      { threshold: 'p(99)<2000', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '30s' },
    ],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/catalog');
  check(res, { 'ok': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `startRate` prevents the default zero-to-target spike at test start, which would otherwise generate an artificial latency burst in the first few seconds that inflates the p99 for the entire test run; however, setting `startRate` above the system's cold-start capacity will still cause early-stage failures if the service has not fully initialized, so `startRate` should be validated against the service's idle warm-up throughput before running in CI.

---

**Pattern 513** — `per-vu-iterations` with `SharedArray` index mapping for deterministic per-VU data assignment
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';
import execution from 'k6/execution';

const users = new SharedArray('users', function () {
  return JSON.parse(open('./fixtures/users.json'));
});

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    deterministic: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 50,
      iterations: 10,
      maxDuration: '5m',
    },
  },
};

export default function () {
  const user = users[execution.vu.idInTest - 1];
  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/login', JSON.stringify(user), {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
  check(res, { 'logged in': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `execution.vu.idInTest` is stable within a scenario run and guarantees each VU reads a unique user record, eliminating credential collisions; however, `idInTest` is 1-based and not guaranteed to be contiguous if VUs are killed and respawned under `maxVUs` overflow, so always bounds-check the index with `% users.length` when the VU pool may exceed the fixture size.

---

**Pattern 514** — `shared-iterations` smoke test with `maxDuration` time-box and low VU count
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    smoke: {
      executor: 'shared-iterations',
      vus: 3,
      iterations: 30,
      maxDuration: '60s',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['max<1000'],
    http_req_failed: ['count<1'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/health');
  check(res, {
    'status 200': r => r.status === 200,
    'body not empty': r => r.body.length > 0,
  });
}
```
Tradeoff: `shared-iterations` distributes the 30 iterations across 3 VUs as fast as each can complete them, so fast VUs consume more iterations than slow ones — this is intentional for smoke tests where you want maximum throughput from minimal VUs, but it means you cannot guarantee uniform per-VU sample sizes, making it inappropriate for user-journey tests that require each VU to execute a full workflow exactly once.

---

**Pattern 515** — Multi-scenario parallel fan-out with `startTime` staggering and per-scenario `exec` functions
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    api_load: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 20,
      duration: '5m',
      exec: 'apiTest',
      tags: { service: 'api' },
    },
    db_load: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 10,
      duration: '5m',
      startTime: '30s',
      exec: 'dbTest',
      tags: { service: 'db' },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{service:api}': ['p(95)<300'],
    'http_req_duration{service:db}': ['p(95)<800'],
  },
};

export function apiTest() {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v2/items');
  check(res, { 'api ok': r => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(0.5);
}

export function dbTest() {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v2/reports');
  check(res, { 'db ok': r => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(1);
}
```
Tradeoff: Tag-scoped thresholds isolate SLO evaluation per service, but each threshold is evaluated independently — if `api` passes and `db` fails, the test exits with a non-zero status code even though the API is healthy; design CI gates that parse the threshold summary JSON to distinguish which service crossed its SLO rather than treating the binary exit code as a single aggregate pass/fail signal.

---

**Pattern 516** — `abortOnFail` threshold with `delayAbortEval` to avoid false-positive abort during ramp-up
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      startVUs: 0,
      stages: [
        { target: 100, duration: '2m' },
        { target: 100, duration: '8m' },
        { target: 0,   duration: '2m' },
      ],
      gracefulRampDown: '30s',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: [
      { threshold: 'p(95)<400', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '90s' },
    ],
    http_req_failed: [
      { threshold: 'rate<0.02', abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: '60s' },
    ],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/feed');
  check(res, { 'ok': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `delayAbortEval: '90s'` prevents threshold evaluation during ramp-up when a small sample of in-flight requests at low VU counts can produce misleadingly high p95 values; the tradeoff is that a genuine regression during ramp-up will not abort for 90 seconds, potentially wasting CI time — calibrate `delayAbortEval` to be at least as long as the ramp-up duration but no longer than the maximum cost-of-delay tolerable for your pipeline.

---

**Pattern 517** — Tag-scoped threshold per URL group using `name` tag for endpoint-level SLOs
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mixed: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 50,
      duration: '5m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{name:list-items}':   ['p(95)<200'],
    'http_req_duration{name:get-item}':     ['p(95)<300'],
    'http_req_duration{name:create-item}':  ['p(95)<600'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get('https://api.example.com/items',
    { tags: { name: 'list-items' } });

  const id = Math.floor(Math.random() * 1000) + 1;
  http.get(`https://api.example.com/items/${id}`,
    { tags: { name: 'get-item' } });

  http.post('https://api.example.com/items',
    JSON.stringify({ name: 'widget' }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      tags: { name: 'create-item' } });
}
```
Tradeoff: Assigning explicit `name` tags collapses all parameterized URLs (e.g., `/items/1`, `/items/2`) into a single metric series essential for threshold evaluation and Grafana aggregation; however, the tag must be set on every individual `http.*` call — omitting it on even one call causes that request to fall into the untagged `http_req_duration` series and miss its endpoint-level SLO, silently passing CI while the slow endpoint goes undetected.

---

**Pattern 518** — Custom `Trend`, `Counter`, and `Rate` metrics with `isTime` flag and typed thresholds
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Trend, Counter, Rate } from 'k6/metrics';

const dbQueryDuration = new Trend('db_query_duration', true);
const cacheHits        = new Counter('cache_hits');
const errorRate        = new Rate('business_error_rate');

export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    db_query_duration:    ['p(90)<250', 'p(99)<800'],
    cache_hits:           ['count>1000'],
    business_error_rate:  ['rate<0.005'],
  },
  vus: 30,
  duration: '3m',
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/search?q=test');
  check(res, { 'ok': r => r.status === 200 });

  const isCache = res.headers['X-Cache'] === 'HIT';
  if (isCache) cacheHits.add(1);

  const queryMs = parseFloat(res.headers['X-DB-Query-Ms'] || '0');
  if (queryMs > 0) dbQueryDuration.add(queryMs);

  errorRate.add(res.status >= 400 ? 1 : 0);
}
```
Tradeoff: Passing `true` as the second argument to `new Trend()` emits the metric with time-unit metadata so Grafana and InfluxDB apply millisecond-to-second conversion and display correct axis labels; omitting it makes the metric appear unit-less in dashboards, causing alert thresholds to be set in the wrong unit — a `>500` alert on a unit-less metric is 1000x looser than intended when values are in milliseconds.

---

**Pattern 519** — `k6/browser` `page.goto()` with `waitUntil: 'networkidle'` and Web Vitals thresholds
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browser_test: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 2,
      duration: '1m',
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    browser_web_vital_lcp:   ['p(75)<2500'],
    browser_web_vital_fid:   ['p(75)<100'],
    browser_web_vital_cls:   ['p(75)<0.1'],
    browser_http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://example.com/dashboard', {
      waitUntil: 'networkidle',
      timeout: 30000,
    });
    const title = await page.title();
    check(null, { 'page title set': () => title.length > 0 });
    await page.screenshot({ path: `screenshots/dash-${Date.now()}.png` });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `waitUntil: 'networkidle'` blocks `page.goto()` until no network activity occurs for 500ms, which correctly captures async-rendered SPA content but will hang indefinitely on pages with polling or WebSocket connections that continuously emit small requests — for such pages use `waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded'` with an explicit `locator().waitFor()` on the first meaningful element instead.

---

**Pattern 520** — `browser.newContext()` with device emulation for mobile-specific Web Vitals baseline
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mobile: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 3,
      iterations: 5,
      options: {
        browser: {
          type: 'chromium',
          args: ['--disable-gpu'],
        },
      },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    browser_web_vital_lcp: ['p(75)<4000'],
    browser_web_vital_fcp: ['p(75)<1800'],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const context = await browser.newContext({
    viewport: { width: 390, height: 844 },
    userAgent: 'Mozilla/5.0 (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 16_0 like Mac OS X)',
    isMobile: true,
    hasTouch: true,
    deviceScaleFactor: 3,
  });
  const page = await context.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://example.com/mobile', { waitUntil: 'load' });
    const lcp = await page.evaluate(() =>
      performance.getEntriesByType('largest-contentful-paint').pop()?.startTime ?? 0);
    check(null, { 'LCP under 4s': () => lcp < 4000 });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
    await context.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `deviceScaleFactor: 3` causes Chromium to request 3x resolution assets, increasing bytes transferred and rendering time relative to a desktop context — mobile LCP thresholds must be set 1.5–2x higher than desktop baselines to avoid false failures, and the CI agent must have sufficient CPU headroom to avoid throttling the simulated mobile rendering pipeline.

---

**Pattern 521** — `page.locator()` with `waitFor()` and `fill()` for resilient multi-step SPA form interaction
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    form_flow: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 2,
      iterations: 3,
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto('https://example.com/signup', { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' });

    const emailField = page.locator('input[name="email"]');
    await emailField.waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 10000 });
    await emailField.fill(`vu${Date.now()}@example.com`);

    await page.locator('input[name="password"]').fill('Test@1234!');
    await page.locator('button[type="submit"]').click();

    const success = page.locator('[data-testid="signup-success"]');
    await success.waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 15000 });
    const text = await success.textContent();
    check(null, { 'signup succeeded': () => text.includes('Welcome') });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Chaining `waitFor({ state: 'visible' })` before every interaction eliminates flaky `ElementNotInteractableError` failures caused by variable server-side rendering times, but each `waitFor` consumes up to its full `timeout` budget before throwing — setting all timeouts uniformly high (e.g., 15s) inflates the worst-case iteration duration to `n_interactions × timeout_ms`, so tune each `waitFor` timeout to the realistic maximum for that specific element rather than using a single global value.

---

**Pattern 522** — `k6/experimental/csv` `Parser` inside `setup()` with full row preload and VU-side random access
```javascript
import { open } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import csv from 'k6/experimental/csv';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export async function setup() {
  const fileHandle = await open('./fixtures/users.csv');
  const parser = new csv.Parser(fileHandle);
  const rows = [];
  let result;
  while (!(result = await parser.next()).done) {
    rows.push(result.value);
  }
  return { users: rows };
}

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: '2m',
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(95)<400'] },
};

export default function (data) {
  const user = data.users[Math.floor(Math.random() * data.users.length)];
  const res = http.post(
    'https://api.example.com/auth',
    JSON.stringify({ email: user[0], password: user[1] }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } },
  );
  check(res, { 'auth ok': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Parsing the CSV once in `setup()` and returning the full array avoids per-VU file I/O during the test run, but the entire dataset is serialized and broadcast to every VU via the `data` parameter — for datasets above ~50 MB, this serialization causes a noticeable startup delay and increased memory pressure; for large files use `k6/data` `SharedArray` with the synchronous `open()` from base `k6` to share the buffer across VUs without copying.

---

**Pattern 523** — `k6/experimental/fs` `seek()` with `SeekMode.Start` for random-access binary fixture reads
```javascript
import { open, SeekMode } from 'k6/experimental/fs';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

let imgFile;

export async function setup() {
  imgFile = await open('./fixtures/sample.jpg');
  const stat = await imgFile.stat();
  return { size: stat.size };
}

export const options = { vus: 10, duration: '1m' };

export default async function (data) {
  const chunkSize = 4096;
  const offset = Math.floor(Math.random() * Math.max(0, data.size - chunkSize));
  await imgFile.seek(offset, SeekMode.Start);
  const chunk = new Uint8Array(chunkSize);
  await imgFile.read(chunk);

  const res = http.post(
    'https://api.example.com/upload-chunk',
    chunk.buffer,
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/octet-stream',
                 'X-Chunk-Offset': String(offset) } },
  );
  check(res, { 'chunk accepted': r => r.status === 202 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `seek()` with `SeekMode.Start` provides random-access reads without loading the entire file into memory, making it ideal for simulating chunked upload clients against multi-gigabyte binaries; however, a module-level file handle is shared across all VUs in the same OS process, so concurrent `seek()` + `read()` calls from multiple VUs will interleave and produce corrupt chunks — each VU must open its own handle via `await open()` in VU scope (inside `default()`) to guarantee seek-position isolation.

---

**Pattern 524** — `execution.vu.metrics.tags.set()` for persistent per-VU region and environment tag propagation
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import execution from 'k6/execution';

const REGIONS = ['us-east-1', 'eu-west-1', 'ap-southeast-1'];

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    regional: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 30,
      duration: '5m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{region:us-east-1}':      ['p(95)<200'],
    'http_req_duration{region:eu-west-1}':      ['p(95)<350'],
    'http_req_duration{region:ap-southeast-1}': ['p(95)<500'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const region = REGIONS[(execution.vu.idInTest - 1) % REGIONS.length];
  execution.vu.metrics.tags.set('region', region);
  execution.vu.metrics.tags.set('env', __ENV.K6_ENV || 'staging');

  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/data');
  check(res, { 'ok': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `execution.vu.metrics.tags.set()` applies the tag persistently to all subsequent metrics emitted by that VU for all future iterations, eliminating the need to pass `{ tags: { region } }` on every individual request; however, the tag is sticky — if a VU's region assignment must change mid-test (e.g., to simulate a failover), you must call `tags.set()` again explicitly, or the stale tag value will silently mis-attribute subsequent metrics to the wrong region in Grafana dashboards.

---

**Pattern 525** — xk6 native Go extension for HMAC-SHA256 request signing compiled with `xk6 build`
```javascript
// Requires: k6 binary built with xk6-crypto extension
// Build:    xk6 build --with github.com/nicholasgasior/xk6-crypto
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import crypto from 'k6/x/crypto';

const SECRET_KEY = __ENV.SIGNING_KEY || 'test-secret';

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: '3m',
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(95)<400'] },
};

function hmacSign(method, path, body, timestamp) {
  const stringToSign = [method, path, body, timestamp].join('\n');
  return crypto.hmac('sha256', SECRET_KEY, stringToSign, 'hex');
}

export default function () {
  const ts   = String(Date.now());
  const body = JSON.stringify({ action: 'read', resource: 'orders' });
  const sig  = hmacSign('POST', '/api/orders', body, ts);

  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/orders', body, {
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'X-Timestamp': ts,
      'X-Signature': sig,
    },
  });
  check(res, { 'signed request accepted': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: A native Go xk6 extension performs HMAC-SHA256 signing in ~0.01ms versus ~3ms for the JavaScript `k6/experimental/webcrypto` equivalent, removing signing overhead as a latency floor for signed-API load tests; the tradeoff is that the k6 binary must be recompiled with `xk6 build` and the custom binary distributed to all CI agents and load generators, adding binary management overhead and breaking drop-in compatibility with the standard `k6` Docker image.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G289** — `ramping-vus` `gracefulRampDown` omitted causes mid-ramp VU kills that inflate error counters
Why this matters: When `ramping-vus` scales down VUs between stages (e.g., from 200 to 50), k6 immediately terminates excess VUs by default. Any VU executing an HTTP request at that moment has its TCP connection reset server-side and records an `http_req_failed` error. On a test with a long p99 response time (e.g., a report endpoint at 12 seconds), a ramp-down from 200 to 50 VUs will kill up to 150 in-flight requests simultaneously, spiking `http_req_failed` rate well above typical error thresholds and triggering false `abortOnFail` exits that terminate the test before steady-state data is collected.
Fix: Set `gracefulRampDown` on every `ramping-vus` scenario to at least your p99.9 response time: `gracefulRampDown: '15s'`. This gives VUs being scaled down a window to complete their current iteration before being killed. Also set `gracefulStop` to the same or greater value to cover the final scale-down to zero at test end, and validate both values against the actual p99.9 measured in a prior exploratory run.

---

**G290** — `constant-arrival-rate` `rate` exceeds `maxVUs` capacity, causing silent `dropped_iterations`
Why this matters: If `rate: 500` (500 iterations/s) requires more VUs than `maxVUs` allows (e.g., each iteration takes 800ms, requiring 400 concurrent VUs, but `maxVUs: 100`), k6 cannot spawn enough VUs to sustain the rate. Instead of throwing an error, k6 silently skips the iterations it cannot schedule — the `dropped_iterations` counter increments, but CI pipelines that only check `http_req_failed` rate or `http_req_duration` thresholds will see a "healthy" test result while the system actually handled 80% fewer requests than intended, making the load test invalid.
Fix: Add a threshold on `dropped_iterations`: `{ threshold: 'count<10', abortOnFail: true }`. Before running, calculate the required VU count as `ceil(rate × avg_iteration_duration_seconds)` and set `maxVUs` to at least 20% above that number. Monitor the JSON summary output for `dropped_iterations` in every local run before promoting the script to CI.

---

**G291** — `SharedArray` callback calling `JSON.parse(open(...))` on a 500 MB fixture causes OOM at init
Why this matters: `SharedArray` deserializes the callback's return value into a JavaScript object graph shared across all VUs. For a 500 MB JSON fixture, the raw buffer is 500 MB, but `JSON.parse` inflates it to 2–4 GB in V8's heap before the `SharedArray` can intern the result. A CI agent with 4 GB RAM will have k6 OOM-killed by the OS before the test starts. The failure mode is a silent `Killed` process exit with no k6 error message, making it appear as an infrastructure failure rather than a fixture size problem.
Fix: Split large fixtures into chunks of at most 50 MB each and load them in separate `SharedArray` instances. For CSV data, use `k6/experimental/csv` with streaming `Parser.next()` to avoid loading the full file at once. As a last resort, increase CI agent RAM and pre-process the fixture offline to extract only the columns actually needed by the test script.

---

**G292** — `page.evaluate()` returning a non-serializable DOM node silently resolves to `null`
Why this matters: `page.evaluate()` serializes the return value of the browser-side callback across the browser-to-k6 process boundary using structured clone. If the callback returns a DOM element (`document.querySelector('div')`), a function, or a Symbol, structured clone silently converts the result to `null` instead of throwing. The k6 test continues with `null` as the value, and any subsequent property access (e.g., `result.textContent`) throws a TypeError that k6 catches and records as a failed check — the root cause is invisible in the threshold summary because it looks like an assertion failure, not a serialization error.
Fix: Always return plain serializable values from `page.evaluate()`: strings, numbers, booleans, plain objects, and arrays. To extract text from a DOM element, return `el.textContent` inside the callback: `page.evaluate(() => document.querySelector('h1').textContent)`. Add an explicit null-guard check immediately after: `check(result, { 'result not null': v => v !== null })` before using the value downstream.

---

**G293** — `k6/net/grpc` client not closed in `finally` causes cumulative connection leak across CI runs
Why this matters: `new grpc.Client()` establishes a persistent HTTP/2 connection pool. If a VU's default function throws an uncaught exception mid-test (e.g., a malformed response causes a JavaScript error), the VU exits without reaching `client.close()`. Each leaked connection holds a goroutine on the gRPC server side. In a 500-VU test with a 10% error rate, 50 connections per test run accumulate across repeated CI pipeline runs, eventually exhausting the server's goroutine pool and causing `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` errors for subsequent test runs even from different machines.
Fix: Wrap all gRPC VU logic in a `try/finally` block and call `client.close()` in the `finally` clause to guarantee cleanup on both normal and error exit paths. Additionally, set `maxRecvMsgSize` and `maxSendMsgSize` options on `client.connect()` to prevent runaway large responses from causing JavaScript heap errors that bypass the `try/finally` entirely.

## Cycle 66 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 541** — `k6/websockets` global event loop with four concurrent connections per VU
```javascript
import { WebSocket } from 'k6/websockets';
import { sleep } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ws_fan_out: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 50,
      duration: '2m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'ws_msgs_received':    ['count>1000'],
    'ws_session_duration': ['p(95)<5000'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const sockets = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
    const ws = new WebSocket(`wss://api.example.com/stream/${i}`, null, {
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.WS_TOKEN}` },
    });
    ws.onopen    = () => ws.send(JSON.stringify({ subscribe: `channel-${i}` }));
    ws.onmessage = (e) => { /* process message */ };
    ws.onerror   = (e) => console.error(`socket ${i} error: ${e.error()}`);
    sockets.push(ws);
  }
  sleep(30);
  sockets.forEach(ws => ws.close());
}
```
Tradeoff: `k6/websockets`' global event loop allows a single VU to multiplex four concurrent connections with negligible scheduling overhead compared to `k6/ws`' local-loop model, but each open WebSocket occupies a file descriptor — running 50 VUs x 4 connections = 200 simultaneous FDs, so verify your OS `ulimit -n` is above 300 before running at scale or k6 will silently fail new connection attempts.

---

**Pattern 542** — `page.route()` network interception to stub third-party analytics in browser load tests
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browser_stub: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      options: { type: 'browser' },
      vus: 5,
      duration: '1m',
    },
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();

  // Block all analytics, ad, and CDN calls to isolate app performance
  await page.route(/\.(googletagmanager|hotjar|segment)\.com/, route => route.abort());
  await page.route(/\/api\/v1\/events$/, route =>
    route.fulfill({ status: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ ok: true }) })
  );

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard', { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' });
  const title = await page.title();
  check(title, { 'dashboard loaded': t => t.includes('Dashboard') });
  await page.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: Stubbing third-party analytics via `page.route()` eliminates ~150-400ms of external DNS + TLS overhead per page load, making browser VU timings reflect only your app's performance — but it also masks CDN-delivered first-party assets if your regex is too broad, and note that "the last registered handler wins," so registering a catch-all route after a specific route will silently override the specific one.

---

**Pattern 543** — `k6/secrets` async credential injection with `--secret-source` for vault-backed load tests
```javascript
import secrets from 'k6/secrets';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    authenticated_load: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 100,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '5m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 200,
    },
  },
  thresholds: { 'http_req_duration': ['p(95)<300'] },
};

export async function setup() {
  // Retrieve secret from HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager
  // configured via: k6 run --secret-source=vault=addr=http://vault:8200,token=s.xxx
  const apiKey = await secrets.get('API_LOAD_TEST_KEY');
  return { apiKey };
}

export default function (data) {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/v2/items', {
    headers: { 'X-API-Key': data.apiKey },
  });
  check(res, { '200 OK': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `k6/secrets` automatically redacts secret values from k6 logs and CI output (replaced with `***SECRET_REDACTED***`), preventing credential leakage in build artifacts, but `secrets.get()` is async-only and cannot be called at init/module scope — it must live in `setup()` or `default()`, and the returned value is a plain string with no rotation-aware cache invalidation, so long-running soak tests that outlive a secret's TTL will start returning 401s without warning.

---

**Pattern 544** — `k6/experimental/streams` `ReadableStream` for chunked NDJSON response processing
```javascript
import { ReadableStream } from 'k6/experimental/streams';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Counter } from 'k6/metrics';

export const options = {
  vus: 10,
  duration: '2m',
  thresholds: { 'stream_events_parsed': ['count>500'] },
};

const streamEvents = new Counter('stream_events_parsed');

export default async function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/events/stream');
  check(res, { 'stream started': r => r.status === 200 });

  // Process NDJSON payload line-by-line without buffering entire body
  const stream = new ReadableStream({
    start(controller) {
      const lines = res.body.split('\n').filter(l => l.trim());
      lines.forEach(line => controller.enqueue(line));
      controller.close();
    },
  });

  const reader = stream.getReader();
  let done = false;
  while (!done) {
    const { value, done: d } = await reader.read();
    done = d;
    if (value) {
      const event = JSON.parse(value);
      check(event, { 'has event_id': e => !!e.event_id });
      streamEvents.add(1);
    }
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `ReadableStream` processes large NDJSON payloads line-by-line without buffering the entire response body into a JS string, reducing peak heap allocation per VU by ~60% on 5MB streams — but the `k6/experimental/streams` module currently implements only `ReadableStream` (not `WritableStream` or `TransformStream`), is subject to breaking API changes before stable graduation, and adds ~2ms per VU per iteration of stream-setup overhead compared to a simple `res.body.split('\n')` approach.

---

**Pattern 545** — `BrowserContext` storage-state injection for pre-authenticated browser session reuse
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    auth_browse: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 10,
      iterations: 5,
      options: { type: 'browser' },
    },
  },
};

export async function setup() {
  // Log in once and capture cookies + localStorage
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/login');
  await page.locator('[name=username]').fill('load-test-user');
  await page.locator('[name=password]').fill(__ENV.TEST_PASSWORD);
  await page.locator('[type=submit]').click();
  await page.waitForNavigation();
  const storageState = await page.context().storageState();
  await page.close();
  return { storageState };
}

export default async function (data) {
  const ctx  = await browser.newContext({ storageState: data.storageState });
  const page = await ctx.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });
  check(await page.title(), { 'authenticated': t => !t.includes('Login') });
  await ctx.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: Injecting a `storageState` captured in `setup()` into each VU's `BrowserContext` eliminates the full login round-trip (~400-1200ms) from every iteration's timing, keeping test latency representative of authenticated user behavior — but all VUs share the same session token, so if the server enforces single-session semantics or token-per-device binding, concurrent VUs will invalidate each other's sessions and produce cascading 401 errors.

---

**Pattern 546** — `execution.test.abort()` for cascade-failure early termination with structured reason logging
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import execution from 'k6/execution';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    health_check: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 10,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '10m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_failed': [{ threshold: 'rate<0.05', abortOnFail: false }],
  },
};

let consecutiveFailures = 0;

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/health', { timeout: '5s' });
  const ok  = check(res, { 'healthy': r => r.status === 200 && r.json('status') === 'ok' });

  if (!ok) {
    consecutiveFailures++;
    if (consecutiveFailures >= 10) {
      console.error(`[ABORT] ${consecutiveFailures} consecutive failures detected`);
      execution.test.abort(`cascade-failure: ${consecutiveFailures} consecutive 5xx at ${new Date().toISOString()}`);
    }
  } else {
    consecutiveFailures = 0;
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: `execution.test.abort()` exits with code 108, signalling CI pipelines to fail the step immediately instead of waiting for the full `duration` to elapse — saving up to 9.5 minutes of wasted load against an already-down system — but abort is not instantaneous: in-flight HTTP requests continue until their individual `timeout` expires, so up to `preAllocatedVUs x timeout` worth of requests may still be logged after `abort()` is called, inflating the final error count in reports.

---

**Pattern 547** — `xk6-kafka` Avro message load testing against a Schema Registry-backed topic
```javascript
// Requires: xk6 build --with github.com/mostafa/xk6-kafka
import { Writer, SchemaRegistry, SCHEMA_TYPE_AVRO } from 'k6/x/kafka';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    kafka_produce: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate: 500,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '3m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 100,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'kafka_writer_error_count': ['count<10'],
    'kafka_writer_write_time':  ['p(95)<50'],
  },
};

const registry    = new SchemaRegistry({ url: 'http://schema-registry:8081' });
const valueSchema = registry.getLatestSchemaID('order-events-value');

const writer = new Writer({
  brokers: ['kafka-broker:9092'],
  topic:   'order-events',
});

export default function () {
  const messages = [{
    key:   { data: `order-${__VU}-${__ITER}` },
    value: {
      schemaID: valueSchema,
      schema:   '{"type":"record","name":"Order","fields":[{"name":"id","type":"string"},{"name":"amount","type":"double"}]}',
      data:     { id: `ord-${__VU}-${__ITER}`, amount: Math.random() * 1000 },
    },
  }];
  const err = writer.produce({ messages, schemaType: SCHEMA_TYPE_AVRO });
  check(err, { 'produced': e => e === undefined });
}

export function teardown() { writer.close(); }
```
Tradeoff: `xk6-kafka` with Avro schema validation catches schema-incompatible payloads at produce time — preventing silent deserialization failures on the consumer side — but fetching the schema ID from the registry on first produce adds ~5-15ms of latency that is amortized only if your VUs reuse the cached `valueSchema` variable across iterations; if you call `getLatestSchemaID()` inside `default()`, you add a registry round-trip to every message, multiplying your effective produce latency by 3-4x.

**Pattern 548** — `xk6-sse` server-sent events load test with event-type filtering and time-to-first-event tracking
```javascript
// Requires: xk6 build --with github.com/phymbert/xk6-sse
import sse from 'k6/x/sse';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { Counter, Trend } from 'k6/metrics';

export const options = {
  vus: 100,
  duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    'sse_events_received':     ['count>5000'],
    'sse_time_to_first_event': ['p(95)<2000'],
  },
};

const eventsReceived   = new Counter('sse_events_received');
const timeToFirstEvent = new Trend('sse_time_to_first_event', true);

export default function () {
  const startTime = Date.now();
  let firstEventReceived = false;

  const response = sse.open('https://api.example.com/v1/feed', {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.SSE_TOKEN}` },
    onopen(event)   { check(event, { 'connected': e => e.status === 200 }); },
    onmessage(event) {
      if (!firstEventReceived) {
        timeToFirstEvent.add(Date.now() - startTime);
        firstEventReceived = true;
      }
      if (event.type === 'order.created') {
        eventsReceived.add(1);
        check(JSON.parse(event.data), { 'has order_id': d => !!d.order_id });
      }
    },
    onerror(event) { console.error(`SSE error: ${event.error()}`); },
  });
  check(response, { 'SSE closed cleanly': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: `xk6-sse` holds an HTTP connection open for the full SSE session, so 100 VUs maintain 100 persistent connections to your server — accurately modeling real user behavior for event-driven UIs — but SSE connections bypass k6's built-in `http_req_duration` metric because they are long-lived; you must instrument custom `Trend` metrics (like `sse_time_to_first_event`) to capture meaningful latency signals, otherwise your k6 summary will show only connection setup time, not delivery latency.

---

**Pattern 549** — `page.keyboard.type()` + `press('Enter')` for keyboard-only form submission flows
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    keyboard_flow: {
      executor: 'per-vu-iterations',
      vus: 5,
      iterations: 10,
      options: { type: 'browser' },
    },
  },
  thresholds: { 'browser_web_vital_lcp': ['p(75)<2500'] },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/search', { waitUntil: 'domcontentloaded' });

  // Tab to search field, type query, submit via Enter key
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
  await page.keyboard.type('performance testing k6', { delay: 50 });
  await page.waitForTimeout(200); // allow autocomplete to populate
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');

  // Wait for results list to appear
  const results = page.locator('[data-testid="search-results"]');
  await results.waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 10000 });
  const count = await results.locator('li').count();

  check(count, { 'results returned': n => n > 0 });
  await page.screenshot({ path: `screenshots/search-${__VU}-${__ITER}.png` });
  await page.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `page.keyboard.type()` with a `delay` of 50ms per character accurately models a human typist's input cadence, triggering debounced autocomplete and input validation JavaScript that `page.fill()` or `locator.fill()` would bypass — revealing real-user-path rendering bottlenecks — but `type()` with delay adds `characters x delay` milliseconds to every iteration's wall time (e.g., a 22-character query adds 1.1s), skewing your LCP threshold comparisons unless you account for that floor in your `p(75)` budget.

---

**Pattern 550** — `ramping-arrival-rate` with `startRate: 0` + `preAllocatedVUs` warm-up to avoid cold-start spike
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ramp_and_soak: {
      executor:        'ramping-arrival-rate',
      startRate:       0,
      timeUnit:        '1s',
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs:          300,
      stages: [
        { target: 50,  duration: '2m' },  // ramp to 50 RPS
        { target: 200, duration: '5m' },  // stress to 200 RPS
        { target: 200, duration: '10m' }, // soak at 200 RPS
        { target: 0,   duration: '2m' },  // graceful ramp-down
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration':  ['p(95)<500', 'p(99)<1500'],
    'http_req_failed':    ['rate<0.01'],
    'dropped_iterations': [{ threshold: 'count<100', abortOnFail: false }],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.post(
    'https://api.example.com/v2/orders',
    JSON.stringify({ item: 'widget', qty: 1 }),
    { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } }
  );
  check(res, { 'order created': r => r.status === 201 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Setting `startRate: 0` and ramping from zero eliminates the "cold-start spike" where a constant-arrival-rate executor fires a burst of backlogged iterations when VU pools are not yet warm — keeping your p99 latency representative during ramp-up — but `preAllocatedVUs` must be sized to cover at least your peak `target` rate divided by your expected RPS-per-VU capacity; under-sizing forces k6 to provision VUs from `maxVUs` dynamically, adding ~50-100ms of goroutine-spawn overhead to iterations during rapid ramp stages.

---

**Pattern 551** — `page.emulateVisionDeficiency()` + Web Vitals for accessibility-aware performance baselining
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';
import execution from 'k6/execution';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    a11y_load: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 3,
      duration: '2m',
      options: { type: 'browser' },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'browser_web_vital_lcp{vision:protanopia}': ['p(75)<3000'],
    'browser_web_vital_cls{vision:protanopia}': ['p(75)<0.1'],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const ctx  = await browser.newContext();
  const page = await ctx.newPage();

  // Simulate red-green color blindness for accessibility regression testing
  await page.emulateVisionDeficiency('protanopia');
  execution.vu.metrics.tags.set('vision', 'protanopia');

  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/', { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });
  check(await page.title(), { 'page loaded': t => t.length > 0 });

  // Verify CTA is reachable without color differentiation
  const ctaButton = page.locator('[data-testid="cta-primary"]');
  await ctaButton.waitFor({ state: 'visible', timeout: 8000 });
  check(await ctaButton.isEnabled(), { 'CTA enabled': v => v === true });

  await ctx.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: `emulateVisionDeficiency()` applies Chromium-level CSS filter overrides that simulate color blindness rendering, enabling you to catch accessibility regressions (e.g., a red error banner invisible to protanopic users) as part of a load test without a separate accessibility audit tool — but the CSS filter does not affect JavaScript behavior or ARIA attributes, so it cannot replace a dedicated axe-core audit and adds ~15ms of Chromium GPU compositing overhead per page load.

---

**Pattern 552** — `execution.scenario.iterationsCompleted` for progress-proportional dynamic think time
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';
import execution from 'k6/execution';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    dynamic_think: {
      executor:   'per-vu-iterations',
      vus:        20,
      iterations: 100,
    },
  },
  thresholds: { 'http_req_duration': ['p(95)<400'] },
};

export default function () {
  const completed = execution.scenario.iterationsCompleted;
  const total     = 20 * 100; // vus x iterations
  const progress  = completed / total;

  // Increase think time as test progresses: 1s at start, up to 4s at end
  const dynamicWait = 1 + progress * 3;

  const res = http.get(`https://api.example.com/items?page=${execution.vu.iterationInScenario % 10}`);
  check(res, { 'items loaded': r => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(dynamicWait);
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `execution.scenario.iterationsCompleted` to scale think time models user fatigue patterns more realistically than a fixed `sleep()`, gradually shifting the test from peak throughput toward paced browsing — which better matches production traffic shapes for content-heavy pages — but `iterationsCompleted` is a scenario-level counter updated across all VUs, so in high-concurrency tests it creates a shared progress signal that may cause all VUs to synchronize their think-time increases simultaneously, producing an artificial throughput step-down rather than a smooth decay.

---

**Pattern 553** — `xk6-tcp` raw TCP smoke test for non-HTTP services (Redis, Memcached, custom protocols)
```javascript
// Requires: xk6 build --with github.com/szkiba/xk6-tcp
import tcp from 'k6/x/tcp';
import { check } from 'k6';
import encoding from 'k6/encoding';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    redis_ping: {
      executor: 'constant-arrival-rate',
      rate:     200,
      timeUnit: '1s',
      duration: '1m',
      preAllocatedVUs: 30,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'tcp_connect_duration': ['p(95)<5'],
    'tcp_req_duration':     ['p(95)<2'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const conn = tcp.connect('redis.internal:6379', { timeout: '2s' });
  check(conn, { 'connected': c => c !== null });

  // Send Redis PING inline command
  conn.write(encoding.b64encode('*1\r\n$4\r\nPING\r\n'));
  const response = conn.read(7); // "+PONG\r\n"

  check(response, { 'PONG received': r => r.includes('PONG') });
  conn.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: `xk6-tcp` measures raw TCP connect + round-trip latency below the HTTP abstraction layer, making it the correct tool for Redis, Memcached, or custom binary-protocol services that k6's HTTP client cannot address — but because the xk6-tcp module is community-maintained and not part of Grafana's official extension tier, its `tcp_connect_duration` and `tcp_req_duration` metrics are not guaranteed to follow the same naming conventions as k6 built-in metrics, so Grafana dashboard templates for k6 will not auto-discover them.

---

**Pattern 554** — `k6/net/grpc` client-side streaming with message batching for bulk ingestion load tests
```javascript
import grpc from 'k6/net/grpc';
import { check, sleep } from 'k6';
import { Counter } from 'k6/metrics';

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: '3m',
  thresholds: {
    'grpc_req_duration':   ['p(95)<200'],
    'grpc_streams_opened': ['count>100'],
  },
};

const streamsOpened = new Counter('grpc_streams_opened');
const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(['proto/'], 'ingest.proto');

export default function () {
  client.connect('ingest.example.com:443', { tls: true });

  const stream = new grpc.Stream(client, 'ingest.IngestionService/StreamEvents');
  streamsOpened.add(1);

  stream.on('data',  data => check(data, { 'ack received': d => d.ack === true }));
  stream.on('error', err  => console.error(`gRPC stream error: ${err.message}`));
  stream.on('end',   ()   => { /* stream completed cleanly */ });

  // Batch-send 50 events per stream before closing
  for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
    stream.write({
      event_id:  `${__VU}-${__ITER}-${i}`,
      timestamp: Date.now(),
      payload:   JSON.stringify({ value: Math.random() }),
    });
    if (i % 10 === 9) sleep(0.01); // yield every 10 messages
  }
  stream.end();
  client.close();
}
```
Tradeoff: Batching 50 messages per client-streaming gRPC call amortizes connection setup and TLS handshake cost (~20ms) across all 50 messages, reducing per-message overhead from ~22ms to ~0.4ms at 20 VUs — but calling `client.close()` inside `default()` instead of `teardown()` means a new TCP+TLS connection is established every iteration; move `client.connect()` to `setup()` and `client.close()` to `teardown()` when testing long-lived gRPC channel behavior to avoid measuring reconnect overhead.

---

**Pattern 555** — `handleSummary()` with custom JSON + HTML + status file for CI artifact integration
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { htmlReport }  from 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/benc-uk/k6-reporter/main/dist/bundle.js';
import { textSummary } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.0.2/index.js';

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration': ['p(95)<500'],
    'http_req_failed':   ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/catalog');
  check(res, { 'catalog OK': r => r.status === 200 });
}

export function handleSummary(data) {
  const passed = Object.values(data.metrics)
    .every(m => !m.thresholds || Object.values(m.thresholds).every(t => t.ok));

  return {
    'stdout':               textSummary(data, { indent: '-> ', enableColors: true }),
    'results/summary.json': JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
    'results/report.html':  htmlReport(data),
    'results/status.txt':   passed ? 'PASS\n' : 'FAIL\n',
  };
}
```
Tradeoff: `handleSummary()` runs once after all VUs finish, allowing you to emit multiple output formats (JSON for CI parsing, HTML for human review, a plain `status.txt` for `grep`-based pipeline gates) from a single test run without re-running k6 — but `handleSummary` receives only aggregated metric snapshots, not raw per-request data points; if you need per-request timing for tail-latency analysis, you must also use `--out json` or `--out influxdb` alongside `handleSummary`, as they are independent output channels.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G299** — `k6/secrets` called in init context (module scope) causes runtime panic, not a syntax error
A developer reads the `k6/secrets` documentation and writes `const apiKey = await secrets.get('API_KEY')` at module scope, outside any function, expecting it to behave like a top-level `const` initialized once. The test runner crashes with `GoError: cannot use async/await in init context` at startup — not at the line where `secrets.get` is called but at the awaited Promise resolution — making the stack trace confusing.

Why this matters: k6's init context is synchronous by design. Module-level code runs in a single-threaded init phase before VUs are spawned, and the event loop that processes Promises is not active during this phase. `secrets.get()` returns a Promise, and `await`-ing it in init context attempts to resume a Promise continuation that has no event loop to run on, causing a panic. The same restriction applies to `k6/experimental/fs`' `open()` — any async API called at module scope will fail.

Fix: Move all `secrets.get()` calls into `async function setup()`, which runs in a full async context with an active event loop. Return the resolved secret values from `setup()` and receive them in the `data` parameter of `default(data)`. Never use `await` at module scope in k6 scripts.

---

**G300** — `page.route()` last-registered-handler-wins ordering silently overrides specific routes with catch-all handlers
A developer registers a specific route stub first — `page.route('/api/user', r => r.fulfill({status:200,...}))` — and then registers a catch-all to block analytics — `page.route(/.*/, r => r.abort())`. Every request, including `/api/user`, is now aborted. The specific stub never fires, causing all API calls to return `net::ERR_ABORTED`, but the test still "passes" because the developer forgot to add `check()` assertions on those API responses.

Why this matters: The Grafana k6 documentation states explicitly: "When several routes match the given pattern, only the last registered route handler will run, and all others will be skipped." This is the opposite of most routing frameworks (Express, FastAPI) where first-match wins. The catch-all pattern `/.*/` matches every URL, so any route registered before it is dead code — but k6 provides no warning that an earlier route was superseded.

Fix: Register catch-all or broad routes first, then register specific overrides last. For the analytics-blocking pattern, register the analytics stub `page.route(/analytics\.com/, r => r.abort())` before any specific API stubs, so the specific stubs are evaluated last and take precedence. Always add `check()` assertions on critical API responses to detect silent abort-masking.

---

**G301** — `k6/websockets` VU `default()` returning without `sleep()` causes tight spin loop and thousands of open connections
A developer creates a WebSocket test using the new `k6/websockets` module. The `default()` function creates a `WebSocket`, attaches `onmessage`, and returns immediately — relying on the global event loop to process messages. Because `default()` completes instantly, k6 spawns a new iteration for the VU and calls `default()` again, creating thousands of open connections that the global event loop never gets CPU time to service.

Why this matters: Unlike `k6/ws`, which blocks inside a `ws.connect()` callback, `k6/websockets` returns control to `default()` immediately after the connection is initiated. If `default()` exits without a `sleep()` or explicit connection-close wait, k6 treats the iteration as complete and restarts it. With `constant-vus` and a 60-second duration, a single VU may open 10,000+ WebSocket connections in the first few seconds, exhausting the server's connection table and causing `ECONNREFUSED` at a fraction of the intended load.

Fix: Add `sleep(sessionDuration)` after attaching your event handlers, then explicitly call `ws.close()` before the sleep ends. For message-count-based termination, use a Promise-based sentinel: `await new Promise(resolve => { ws.onclose = resolve; ws.send('...'); })`.

---

**G302** — `execution.test.abort()` does not stop in-flight HTTP requests — they complete and inflate the post-abort error count
A developer writes a circuit-breaker pattern using `execution.test.abort()`: when 10 consecutive 5xx responses are detected, they call `abort()`. In their post-run report, they see 87 failed requests — far more than the expected 10 — and mistakenly conclude the circuit breaker did not trigger.

Why this matters: `execution.test.abort()` sends a stop signal to the k6 scheduler, which stops spawning new iterations, but it does not cancel in-flight HTTP requests. Any request already in flight at the moment of `abort()` will run to completion (or timeout), and k6 records all those responses. With `constant-arrival-rate` at 50 RPS and a 5-second timeout budget, up to `50 x 5 = 250` in-flight requests may complete after `abort()` is called. The test exit code is 108, not 99, so CI pipelines must check the exit code, not just the error count threshold.

Fix: Set a short `timeout` on HTTP requests in circuit-breaker scenarios to minimize in-flight completion time after abort. Log the abort timestamp and filter the post-run JSON output for requests that completed after `abort_time` to distinguish true failures from abort-tail noise. Use `execution.test.fail()` (exit code 110) when you want to mark the run as failed without stopping iteration dispatch.

---

**G303** — `xk6-kafka` `SchemaRegistry.getLatestSchemaID()` inside `default()` adds a registry round-trip to every produced message
A developer copies the xk6-kafka quickstart example that calls `registry.getLatestSchemaID('my-topic-value')` inside the `default()` function. At 500 messages/second across 50 VUs, this triggers 500 HTTP GET requests per second to the schema registry, saturating it within 30 seconds. The registry begins returning 429 responses, causing the Kafka writer to fail deserialization and silently drop messages — with no error surfaced in k6 metrics because `getLatestSchemaID` failures are swallowed by the extension.

Why this matters: `SchemaRegistry.getLatestSchemaID()` is a synchronous HTTP call to the schema registry's `/subjects/{subject}/versions/latest` endpoint. It is designed to be called once at test setup, not on every iteration. The xk6-kafka extension does not internally cache schema IDs between VU iterations, so placing the call in `default()` creates O(VU x RPS) registry requests — easily 10-100x more traffic to the registry than to the actual Kafka broker.

Fix: Call `getLatestSchemaID()` at module scope (it is synchronous and safe in init context unlike `k6/secrets`) or in `setup()`, store the numeric schema ID in a variable, and pass it to each `produce()` call. The schema ID is stable for the lifetime of a test run unless you explicitly publish a new schema version during the test.

**Pattern 526** — `k6/experimental/webcrypto` AES-GCM request payload encryption for end-to-end encrypted API tests
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { crypto } from 'k6/experimental/webcrypto';

const RAW_KEY = new Uint8Array([
  0x2b,0x7e,0x15,0x16,0x28,0xae,0xd2,0xa6,
  0xab,0xf7,0x15,0x88,0x09,0xcf,0x4f,0x3c,
]);

export const options = {
  vus: 10,
  duration: '2m',
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(95)<600'] },
};

let aesKey;

export async function setup() {
  aesKey = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
    'raw', RAW_KEY, { name: 'AES-GCM' }, false, ['encrypt', 'decrypt'],
  );
}

export default async function () {
  const iv = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(12));
  const plaintext = new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify({ user: 'load-test', ts: Date.now() }));
  const ciphertext = await crypto.subtle.encrypt({ name: 'AES-GCM', iv }, aesKey, plaintext);
  const body = JSON.stringify({
    iv: btoa(String.fromCharCode(...iv)),
    data: btoa(String.fromCharCode(...new Uint8Array(ciphertext))),
  });
  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/secure-ingest', body, {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
  check(res, { 'encrypted payload accepted': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `k6/experimental/webcrypto` AES-GCM keeps the test script portable across any standard k6 binary without a custom build, but each `crypto.subtle.encrypt()` call costs approximately 0.5–1 ms of CPU time per iteration in V8, which becomes the latency floor for tests targeting sub-5 ms iteration duration — for those cases, an xk6 Go extension doing AES-GCM in native code reduces per-call overhead to under 0.05 ms at the cost of requiring a custom binary distributed to all load generators.

**Pattern 527** — `k6/net/grpc` `Client.connect()` with TLS `plaintext: false` and custom root CA for mTLS load tests
```javascript
import grpc from 'k6/net/grpc';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { open } from 'k6/experimental/fs';

const client = new grpc.Client();
client.load(['./proto'], 'orders.proto');

let caCert;
export async function setup() {
  const f = await open('./certs/ca.pem');
  const buf = new Uint8Array(1024 * 64);
  await f.read(buf);
  caCert = new TextDecoder().decode(buf).replace(/\0+$/, '');
  return { caCert };
}

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    'grpc_req_duration': ['p(99)<500'],
    'grpc_req_failed':   ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

export default function (data) {
  client.connect('grpc.example.com:443', {
    plaintext: false,
    tls: {
      certificate: '/certs/client.crt',
      key:         '/certs/client.key',
      cacerts:     data.caCert,
    },
  });
  try {
    const response = client.invoke('orders.OrderService/GetOrder', { orderId: '12345' });
    check(response, { 'status OK': r => r && r.status === grpc.StatusOK });
  } finally {
    client.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Loading the CA certificate once in `setup()` and passing it through `data` avoids re-reading the file on every iteration, but the CA cert string is serialized and broadcast to every VU via the k6 data channel — for certificate chains above 64 KB (e.g., chains with intermediate CAs), this approach must be adapted to a `SharedArray` to avoid duplicating the cert string in every VU's heap; additionally, `client.connect()` called inside `default()` establishes a new TLS handshake per iteration, which adds 20–80 ms per connection to measured `grpc_req_duration` and must be moved to `setup()` or a VU-scoped init if handshake latency must be excluded from SLO measurements.

**Pattern 528** — Distributed tracing `traceparent` header injection with per-request trace ID for correlated APM analysis
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { uuidv4 } from 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-utils/1.4.0/index.js';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    traced: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 20,
      duration: '3m',
    },
  },
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(95)<300'] },
};

function makeTraceparent() {
  // W3C Trace Context v1: 00-<traceId>-<parentId>-01
  const traceId  = uuidv4().replace(/-/g, '');
  const parentId = uuidv4().replace(/-/g, '').slice(0, 16);
  return `00-${traceId}-${parentId}-01`;
}

export default function () {
  const traceparent = makeTraceparent();
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/catalog', {
    headers: {
      traceparent,
      'X-B3-TraceId':  traceparent.split('-')[1],
      'X-B3-SpanId':   traceparent.split('-')[2],
      'X-B3-Sampled':  '1',
    },
    tags: { trace_id: traceparent.split('-')[1] },
  });
  check(res, { 'catalog loaded': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Injecting `traceparent` enables precise correlation between k6 request timing and APM flame graphs (Jaeger, Tempo, Datadog), making it possible to attribute P95 latency spikes to specific service-internal spans; the tradeoff is that generating a cryptographically random UUID per request via `uuidv4()` adds approximately 0.2 ms per iteration and increases the tag cardinality in the k6 JSON summary — when exporting to Prometheus with the Prometheus Remote Write output, unique `trace_id` tag values cause unbounded metric cardinality and must be excluded from Prometheus labels using the `tagSet` filter in `k6 --out=experimental-prometheus-rw` configuration.

**Pattern 529** — `k6/timers` `setTimeout` for simulated user think-time with jitter to avoid thundering-herd synchronization
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { setTimeout } from 'k6/timers';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    realistic_users: {
      executor: 'ramping-vus',
      startVUs: 0,
      stages: [
        { duration: '2m', target: 100 },
        { duration: '5m', target: 100 },
        { duration: '2m', target: 0   },
      ],
      gracefulRampDown: '30s',
    },
  },
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(90)<500'] },
};

function jitteredDelay(baseMs, jitterMs) {
  return new Promise(resolve =>
    setTimeout(resolve, baseMs + Math.random() * jitterMs),
  );
}

export default async function () {
  let res = http.get('https://shop.example.com/homepage');
  check(res, { 'homepage ok': r => r.status === 200 });
  await jitteredDelay(500, 1000);  // 500–1500 ms think time

  res = http.get('https://shop.example.com/product/42');
  check(res, { 'product ok': r => r.status === 200 });
  await jitteredDelay(1000, 2000); // 1000–3000 ms browse time

  res = http.post('https://shop.example.com/cart', '{"productId":42,"qty":1}', {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
  check(res, { 'added to cart': r => r.status === 201 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Using `setTimeout` with random jitter desynchronizes VU request waves, preventing the artificial request-per-second spikes that occur when all VUs complete fixed `sleep()` intervals simultaneously (the "thundering herd" artifact that inflates measured P99 by 30–60% in synchronous tests); the tradeoff is that `async/await` VU functions require k6 v0.45+ and prevent use of `group()` calls that assume synchronous execution — any code inside the function that uses synchronous k6 APIs (like `check`) works normally, but mixing `await` with `group()` nested callbacks requires careful structuring to ensure groups are properly closed before the async boundary.

**Pattern 530** — `k6/browser` `page.screenshot()` on threshold breach for visual regression evidence capture
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/experimental/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browser_check: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 3,
      duration: '2m',
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    browser_web_vital_lcp: ['p(75)<2500'],
    browser_web_vital_fid: ['p(75)<100'],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    const resp = await page.goto('https://app.example.com/dashboard', {
      waitUntil: 'networkidle',
    });
    const lcp = await page.evaluate(() => {
      return new Promise(resolve => {
        new PerformanceObserver(list => {
          const entries = list.getEntries();
          resolve(entries[entries.length - 1].startTime);
        }).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });
      });
    });
    const breached = lcp > 2500;
    if (breached) {
      await page.screenshot({ path: `screenshots/lcp-breach-${Date.now()}.png` });
    }
    check(resp, { 'dashboard loaded': r => r && r.status() === 200 });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Capturing a screenshot only on threshold breach produces targeted visual evidence without the storage and performance cost of screenshotting every iteration (which at 3 VUs × 120 iterations adds ~180 PNG files per test run averaging 300 KB each = 54 MB); the tradeoff is that `PerformanceObserver` inside `page.evaluate()` is asynchronous and the Promise may never resolve if LCP fires before the observer is registered — to fix this, add `buffered: true` to the `observe()` call (shown above) and set a `setTimeout` fallback within the Promise to resolve with `Infinity` after 5 seconds, preventing a hung VU from blocking the scenario.

**Pattern 531** — `k6/experimental/redis` pipeline batching for cache-warming scenarios before load application
```javascript
import redis from 'k6/experimental/redis';
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';

const CACHE_KEYS = new SharedArray('cache-keys', () =>
  Array.from({ length: 1000 }, (_, i) => `product:${i + 1}`),
);

const redisClient = new redis.Client({
  addrs:    ['redis.example.com:6379'],
  password: __ENV.REDIS_PASSWORD || '',
});

export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: '30s', target: 50 },  // cache warm-up
    { duration: '3m',  target: 200 }, // full load
    { duration: '30s', target: 0   },
  ],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<200'],
    redis_cmd_duration: ['p(99)<5'],
  },
};

export async function setup() {
  // Prime 1000 product cache entries before VU ramp
  const pipeline = redisClient.pipeline();
  for (const key of CACHE_KEYS) {
    pipeline.set(key, JSON.stringify({ id: key, cached: true }), 300);
  }
  await pipeline.exec();
}

export default async function () {
  const key = CACHE_KEYS[Math.floor(Math.random() * CACHE_KEYS.length)];
  const cached = await redisClient.get(key);
  const res = http.get(`https://api.example.com/products/${key.split(':')[1]}`, {
    headers: cached ? { 'X-Cache-Hint': 'warm' } : {},
  });
  check(res, { 'product ok': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Using Redis pipeline batching in `setup()` pre-warms 1000 cache entries with a single TCP round-trip instead of 1000 individual SET commands, reducing cache warm-up time from ~5 s to ~50 ms at 100 Mbps network latency; the tradeoff is that `k6/experimental/redis` is an experimental module requiring k6 v0.49+ and the Redis client object is created at module scope (init context) — if the Redis server is unreachable at init time, k6 aborts before the test starts with an opaque connection-refused error rather than a clear threshold failure, so CI pipelines should include a pre-flight Redis connectivity check before invoking k6.

**Pattern 532** — `handleSummary()` with custom Markdown report generation for automated PR comment attachment
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  vus: 50,
  duration: '3m',
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ['p(95)<400', 'p(99)<800'],
    http_req_failed:   ['rate<0.005'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://api.example.com/health');
  check(res, { 'healthy': r => r.status === 200 });
}

export function handleSummary(data) {
  const p95 = data.metrics['http_req_duration']?.values?.['p(95)'] ?? 0;
  const p99 = data.metrics['http_req_duration']?.values?.['p(99)'] ?? 0;
  const errRate = (data.metrics['http_req_failed']?.values?.rate ?? 0) * 100;
  const passed = data.state.testRunDuration > 0 &&
    Object.values(data.thresholds ?? {}).every(t => !t.ok === false);

  const md = [
    `## k6 Load Test Summary`,
    `| Metric | Value | Threshold |`,
    `|--------|-------|-----------|`,
    `| P95 latency | ${p95.toFixed(1)} ms | < 400 ms |`,
    `| P99 latency | ${p99.toFixed(1)} ms | < 800 ms |`,
    `| Error rate  | ${errRate.toFixed(3)} % | < 0.5 % |`,
    `| Result | ${passed ? '✅ PASS' : '❌ FAIL'} | — |`,
  ].join('\n');

  return {
    'stdout': md + '\n',
    './k6-summary.md': md,
    './k6-summary.json': JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
  };
}
```
Tradeoff: `handleSummary()` runs synchronously in the k6 process after all VUs have stopped, making it the only place where final threshold pass/fail state is available for report generation — unlike `teardown()`, it cannot make HTTP requests, so CI pipelines that need to POST the summary to a Slack webhook or GitHub PR comment must shell out to `curl` after k6 exits using the generated `k6-summary.json` file; also, the `data.thresholds` map is `undefined` when no thresholds are defined, so the `?? {}` guard is required to prevent a runtime TypeError when the function is reused across scripts with varying options configurations.

**Pattern 534** — `k6/browser` `page.route()` request interception to mock slow third-party APIs during performance baselines
```javascript
import { browser } from 'k6/experimental/browser';
import { check } from 'k6';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    mocked_third_party: {
      executor: 'constant-vus',
      vus: 5,
      duration: '3m',
      options: { browser: { type: 'chromium' } },
    },
  },
  thresholds: { browser_web_vital_lcp: ['p(75)<1500'] },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    // Intercept analytics and third-party CDN calls to isolate first-party perf
    await page.route('**/analytics.js', route => route.abort());
    await page.route('**/cdn.thirdparty.com/**', async route => {
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 200,
        contentType: 'application/javascript',
        body: '/* mocked */',
      });
    });
    await page.route('**/slow-widget.example.com/**', async route => {
      // Simulate 50 ms third-party latency instead of real 2000 ms
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 50));
      await route.fulfill({ status: 200, body: '{}', contentType: 'application/json' });
    });

    const resp = await page.goto('https://app.example.com/checkout', {
      waitUntil: 'networkidle',
    });
    check(resp, { 'checkout loaded': r => r && r.status() === 200 });
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```
Tradeoff: Route interception with `page.route()` lets you establish first-party Web Vitals baselines that are independent of third-party SLA variability (analytics providers, tag managers, chat widgets that vary from 50 ms to 4 s depending on CDN PoP), producing stable, reproducible LCP measurements in CI; the tradeoff is that `page.route()` callbacks must be registered before `page.goto()` — routes registered after navigation has begun will not intercept requests already in flight — and the `abort()` call on analytics endpoints may cause JavaScript errors in the page's own error handling code that artificially increase the browser console error count, which some Web Vital scoring tools interpret as a signal for lower CLS scores.

**Pattern 535** — `k6/data` `SharedArray` with binary protocol fixture deserialization for Protobuf load tests
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
import { SharedArray } from 'k6/data';

// Pre-encoded Protobuf binary payloads serialized offline:
// `protoc --encode=orders.CreateOrderRequest orders.proto < fixture.txt | base64`
const PAYLOADS = new SharedArray('proto-payloads', () => {
  const raw = open('./fixtures/create-order-requests.json');
  return JSON.parse(raw).map(entry => ({
    b64: entry.proto_b64,
    label: entry.label,
  }));
});

export const options = {
  vus: 40,
  duration: '4m',
  thresholds: {
    'http_req_duration{endpoint:create-order}': ['p(95)<300'],
    http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'],
  },
};

function b64ToUint8Array(b64) {
  const binary = atob(b64);
  const arr = new Uint8Array(binary.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < binary.length; i++) arr[i] = binary.charCodeAt(i);
  return arr;
}

export default function () {
  const fixture = PAYLOADS[Math.floor(Math.random() * PAYLOADS.length)];
  const body = b64ToUint8Array(fixture.b64).buffer;
  const res = http.post('https://api.example.com/grpc-transcoder/orders.OrderService/CreateOrder', body, {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-protobuf' },
    tags: { endpoint: 'create-order', label: fixture.label },
  });
  check(res, { 'order created': r => r.status === 200 });
}
```
Tradeoff: Pre-encoding Protobuf payloads to base64 JSON offline and loading them via `SharedArray` avoids the need for a protobuf encoding library in the k6 script (which would require either an xk6 extension or a heavy pure-JS implementation), keeping the script dependency-free at the cost of a preprocessing step in the CI pipeline; the `atob()` + manual `Uint8Array` copy adds approximately 0.1 ms per payload decode per iteration, which is negligible for payloads under 10 KB but becomes measurable (>1 ms) for Protobuf messages above 100 KB — in those cases, pre-decode the base64 to a `SharedArray` of `ArrayBuffer` objects during `setup()` and index into them directly.

**Pattern 537** — `check()` with named group batching and `group()` for structured pass/fail reporting per user journey step
```javascript
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check, group } from 'k6';
import { Trend, Rate } from 'k6/metrics';

const loginLatency    = new Trend('journey_login_ms',    true);
const searchLatency   = new Trend('journey_search_ms',   true);
const checkoutLatency = new Trend('journey_checkout_ms', true);
const journeySuccess  = new Rate('journey_complete_rate');

export const options = {
  vus: 30,
  duration: '5m',
  thresholds: {
    journey_login_ms:      ['p(95)<200'],
    journey_search_ms:     ['p(95)<350'],
    journey_checkout_ms:   ['p(95)<600'],
    journey_complete_rate: ['rate>0.99'],
  },
};

export default function () {
  let token;
  let ok = true;

  group('01_login', () => {
    const res = http.post('https://shop.example.com/auth/login',
      JSON.stringify({ user: 'test@example.com', pass: 'pw' }),
      { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
    loginLatency.add(res.timings.duration);
    ok = ok && check(res, { 'login 200': r => r.status === 200 });
    if (ok) token = res.json('access_token');
  });

  group('02_search', () => {
    if (!token) { ok = false; return; }
    const res = http.get('https://shop.example.com/search?q=laptop', {
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
    });
    searchLatency.add(res.timings.duration);
    ok = ok && check(res, { 'search 200': r => r.status === 200 });
  });

  group('03_checkout', () => {
    if (!token) { ok = false; return; }
    const res = http.post('https://shop.example.com/orders',
      JSON.stringify({ items: [{ id: 1, qty: 1 }] }),
      { headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } });
    checkoutLatency.add(res.timings.duration);
    ok = ok && check(res, { 'order 201': r => r.status === 201 });
  });

  journeySuccess.add(ok);
}
```
Tradeoff: Structuring VU logic with `group()` and per-step custom `Trend` metrics provides granular journey-step latency SLOs that are impossible to enforce with the built-in `http_req_duration` metric (which aggregates all endpoints), enabling precise CI gate failures like "login step regressed by 40 ms in this PR"; the tradeoff is that custom `Trend` metrics double the cardinality of metrics exported to Prometheus Remote Write — with 30 VUs each emitting 3 Trend observations per iteration at 1 RPS, this generates ~90 new time series that must be budgeted in Prometheus TSDB retention and cardinality limits.
