## Migration / Conversion Tooling  [community]

### Pattern 571 — HAR → k6, Postman → k6, JMeter → k6 Conversion Workflow

The k6 ecosystem provides first-class converters that turn existing test assets into k6
scripts. This is the fastest path to k6 adoption when teams already have Postman collections,
browser HAR recordings, or legacy JMeter test plans.

#### har-to-k6 — Convert Browser HAR Recordings

`har-to-k6` converts an HTTP Archive (`.har`) file into a k6 script. HAR files can be
exported from Chrome DevTools, Firefox, or tools like `mitmproxy`.

```bash
# Install
npm install -g @nicholasgasior/har-to-k6
# Or via npx (no install required)

# Export a HAR from Chrome DevTools:
#   DevTools → Network tab → right-click → "Save all as HAR with content"
# Then convert:
npx har-to-k6 recording.har -o k6/scripts/from-har.js

# Run the generated script
k6 run k6/scripts/from-har.js
```

**Post-conversion checklist:**
1. Replace hardcoded hostnames with `__ENV.API_URL` or `options.hosts`
2. Extract authentication tokens into `setup()` — HAR captures static tokens
3. Add `check()` calls (HAR conversion does not add assertions by default)
4. Add `sleep()` for think time — converted scripts run at maximum speed
5. Replace sensitive query-string credentials with `k6/secrets` references
6. Tag requests with `http_req_name` or `name` for URL normalization

#### postman-to-k6 — Convert Postman Collections

`postman-to-k6` converts a Postman Collection JSON export (v2.0 or v2.1) into a k6
script, preserving pre-request and test scripts where possible.

```bash
# Export Postman collection:
#   Postman → Collection → Export → Collection v2.1

# Convert (Node.js tool)
npx postman-to-k6 my-collection.json -o k6/scripts/from-postman.js

# Pass Postman environment variables:
npx postman-to-k6 my-collection.json \
  -e my-environment.json \
  -o k6/scripts/from-postman.js

k6 run k6/scripts/from-postman.js
```

**What is preserved vs. lost:**
| Postman feature | Conversion result |
|-----------------|-------------------|
| Request URL, method, headers, body | Fully converted |
| Pre-request scripts (basic JS) | Partially converted |
| Test scripts (`pm.expect()`) | Converted to k6 `check()` |
| Postman variables (`{{base_url}}`) | Mapped to `__ENV` |
| Dynamic variables (`{{$randomEmail}}`) | NOT converted — replace manually |
| OAuth 2.0 flows | NOT converted — implement in `setup()` |

#### jmeter-to-k6 — Convert JMeter Test Plans

`jmeter-to-k6` reads a JMeter `.jmx` test plan and emits a k6 JavaScript script.
JMeter's Thread Groups map to k6 scenarios; HTTP Samplers map to `http.request()` calls.

```bash
# Convert a JMeter plan
npx jmeter-to-k6 jmeter/load-plan.jmx -o k6/scripts/from-jmeter.js

k6 run k6/scripts/from-jmeter.js
```

**JMeter → k6 concept mapping:**

| JMeter concept | k6 equivalent |
|---------------|---------------|
| Thread Group | `scenarios` executor |
| Ramp Up Period | `ramping-vus` stages |
| Throughput Controller | `constant-arrival-rate` |
| HTTP Sampler | `http.request()` |
| Regular Expression Extractor | `res.json()` / `res.html().find()` |
| Duration Assertion | `check()` on `res.timings.duration` |
| CSV Data Set | `SharedArray` + `open()` |
| BeanShell / JSR223 Sampler | Custom JS in VU code |
| Listeners (Summary, Aggregate) | `handleSummary()` |

> **[community]:** All three converters produce a working starting point, not a
> production-ready script. Treat the output as a scaffold — review it for hardcoded
> credentials, missing checks, missing URL normalization, and appropriate sleep/think time.
> Always run a smoke test (`vus: 1`, `iterations: 1`) immediately after conversion to
> confirm the script runs without errors before scaling up.

---

### Pattern 572 — `k6 new --template browser` CLI Scaffolding for Browser Tests  [official]

k6 v2.0.0+ ships a `--template` flag on `k6 new` for generating browser test scaffolds
without manually writing boilerplate. Three templates are available: `default`, `browser`,
and `extensions`.

```bash
# Scaffold a browser test (Chromium, async, basic Web Vitals threshold)
k6 new --template browser browser-script.js

# Scaffold a protocol-level (default) test
k6 new browser-script.js          # uses 'default' template implicitly

# Scaffold an extension development stub
k6 new --template extensions my-extension.js
```

The generated `browser-script.js` includes:
- Correct `options.scenarios` block with `browser: { type: 'chromium' }`
- `async export default function ()` with `browser.newPage()` / `page.close()` in `finally`
- Starter Web Vitals thresholds (`browser_web_vital_lcp`, `browser_web_vital_inp`)
- A `page.goto()` call pointing to `__ENV.APP_URL || 'http://localhost:3000'`

```javascript
// Typical output of: k6 new --template browser browser-script.js
import { browser } from 'k6/browser';

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ui: {
      executor: 'shared-iterations',
      options: {
        browser: { type: 'chromium' },
      },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    'browser_web_vital_lcp': ['p(75)<3000'],
    'browser_web_vital_inp': ['p(75)<200'],
  },
};

export default async function () {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  try {
    await page.goto(__ENV.APP_URL || 'http://localhost:3000');
  } finally {
    await page.close();
  }
}
```

Run the generated script immediately to verify the scaffold is correct:
```bash
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 k6 run browser-script.js
```

> **[official]:** Use `k6 new --template browser` as the canonical starting point for all new
> browser test files — the scaffold is maintained by the k6 team and updated when the
> browser module API changes. Avoid copying browser test boilerplate from older blog posts
> or tutorials; the `BrowserContext` and `browser.newPage()` APIs have changed across minor
> versions.

---

### Community Gotchas (continued)

**G309** — `http.get()` and `http.head()` called with a request body silently pass the wrong signature in k6 v1.x but emit a deprecation warning in v2.0.0  [official]

**What:** In k6 v1.x, calling `http.get(url, body, params)` (the three-argument `http.post()` signature) silently discards the `body` and `params` arguments — the GET request is made with no body and no extra params. In v2.0.0, k6 adds an explicit console warning: `"http.get() does not accept a body argument; it is ignored."` Teams that silently had broken tests in v1.x now see the warning, but the behavior (body discarded) is unchanged.

**Why this bites you:** A developer copies an `http.post()` call and changes the method to `http.get()` without removing the body argument. In v1.x, the test runs, checks pass (the server returns 200 to the body-less GET), and the misconfiguration is invisible. The test appears valid. In v2.0.0, the warning appears in CI logs, but if the CI pipeline treats all warnings as noise (no `--log-level=error` gate), the test continues to silently skip the body.

**Fix:**
```javascript
// WRONG — http.get() ignores the body in all k6 versions
const res = http.get(url, JSON.stringify({ id: 42 }), params);

// CORRECT — pass params (headers, tags) as the second argument only
const res = http.get(url, params);

// If you need to send a body, use http.post() or http.request('GET', ...)
// Note: RFC 7231 discourages GET request bodies; most servers ignore them
const res = http.request('GET', url, JSON.stringify({ id: 42 }), params);
```

Gate CI on warnings by piping k6 stderr through `grep` or by adding a log-format check:
```bash
# Fail CI if k6 emits any "ignored" warnings
k6 run script.js 2>&1 | tee /tmp/k6-output.txt
grep -i "ignored" /tmp/k6-output.txt && echo "Warning found — check script" && exit 1
k6_exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}
exit $k6_exit
```

---

**G310** — `k6 archive` does not embed runtime secrets — `--secret-source` configurations are NOT baked into the archive and must be re-supplied on each `k6 run archive.tar`  [official]

**What:** `k6 archive script.js` bundles the script, its dependencies, and extension
metadata into a `archive.tar` file. However, `--secret-source` values (whether from CLI flag
or `K6_SECRET_SOURCE` env var) are **not** included in the archive — secrets are a runtime
concern only and are intentionally excluded to prevent credential exposure in archive files.

**Why this bites you:** A developer runs `k6 archive script.js --secret-source=mock=default,api_key=test` thinking the secrets are baked in. When a CI job later runs `k6 run archive.tar`, the `secrets.get('api_key')` call throws because no secret source is configured in the new context. The error message references the secrets module rather than the missing `--secret-source` flag, leading to a confusing debugging session.

**Fix:** Always treat `--secret-source` as a deployment-time parameter, not a build-time parameter. Document the required secret keys in a `k6-secrets.example.env` file committed alongside the archive:
```bash
# k6-secrets.example.env — list expected secret names (no values)
# Provide via: K6_SECRET_SOURCE=file=./k6-secrets.actual.env k6 run archive.tar
api_key=
db_read_password=
payment_gateway_token=
```

In CI, pass secrets at runtime:
```bash
k6 archive script.js                              # build once
K6_SECRET_SOURCE="file=./secrets/ci-staging.env" k6 run archive.tar   # run with secrets
```

> **[official]:** Archive metadata (introduced in k6 v2.0.0) records extension dependencies so
> that auto-provisioning can resolve the correct binary version when running the archive —
> but this dependency metadata is separate from secrets and is stored in the archive manifest,
> not in a secrets vault. The distinction matters: extension versions are reproducible build
> artifacts; secret values are not.

### Pattern 573 — `xk6-client-tracing`: Load Testing Distributed Tracing Backends  [community]

`xk6-client-tracing` is the official Grafana extension for load testing distributed tracing
backends (Jaeger, Tempo, OTLP collectors). It provides two span-generation strategies:

- **Parameterized generator** — generates randomized spans at high volume with configurable attribute cardinality. Use for bulk throughput tests against the ingest pipeline.
- **Templated generator** — produces realistic trace trees following OpenTelemetry semantic conventions with defined parent-child hierarchies and fixed service names. Use for query-path tests and dashboards validation.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/tracing-backend-load.js
// Build: xk6 build --with github.com/grafana/xk6-client-tracing
import tracing from "k6/x/tracing";
import { sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    ingest_load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 500,          // 500 trace submissions per second
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 50,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    // xk6-client-tracing emits k6 metrics for each push call
    "tracing_push_duration": ["p(95)<200"],
    "tracing_push_errors":   ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};

// INIT CONTEXT — create client once per VU
const client = new tracing.Client({
  endpoint: __ENV.TRACING_ENDPOINT || "localhost:4317",  // OTLP gRPC
  exporter: "otlp",  // "otlp" | "jaeger"
  tls: { insecure: true },
});

// Parameterized generator — randomised spans, high cardinality
const paramGen = new tracing.ParameterizedGenerator({
  randomAttributes: { count: 10, minLength: 5, maxLength: 20 },
  randomResources:  { count: 5,  minLength: 3, maxLength: 15 },
});

export default function () {
  client.push(paramGen.traces({ count: 10, minDuration: "50ms", maxDuration: "500ms" }));
  sleep(0); // yielding not required — arrivals are rate-controlled
}
```

**Templated generator for realistic service-map traces:**

```javascript
// k6/scripts/tracing-templated.js
import tracing from "k6/x/tracing";

const client = new tracing.Client({
  endpoint: __ENV.TRACING_ENDPOINT || "localhost:4317",
  exporter: "otlp",
  tls: { insecure: true },
});

// Templated generator — realistic span hierarchies with fixed service topology
const tmplGen = new tracing.TemplatedGenerator({
  defaults: {
    attributeSemantics: "http",  // apply HTTP semantic conventions to spans
    randomAttributes:   { count: 3 },
  },
  // Define the service call graph (parent → children)
  topology: {
    "frontend": ["api-gateway"],
    "api-gateway": ["auth-service", "product-service"],
    "product-service": ["db-service"],
  },
  services: [
    { name: "frontend",        type: "http_server", resourceAttributes: { "service.version": "1.0" } },
    { name: "api-gateway",     type: "http_server" },
    { name: "auth-service",    type: "http_client" },
    { name: "product-service", type: "http_server" },
    { name: "db-service",      type: "db",
      spanAttributes: { "db.system": "postgresql", "db.name": "products" } },
  ],
});

export default function () {
  // Each push generates one root trace spanning the full topology
  client.push(tmplGen.traces({ count: 1, minDuration: "100ms", maxDuration: "800ms" }));
}
```

> **[community]:** Use the templated generator when testing Tempo's or Jaeger's service-map
> feature — fixed service names produce stable nodes in the UI, enabling you to detect
> graph-rendering regressions under load. The parameterized generator is better for raw ingest
> throughput benchmarks where topology fidelity is irrelevant.

> **Build note:** v0.0.9 (October 2025) is the latest release. Build with:
> `xk6 build --with github.com/grafana/xk6-client-tracing@latest`
> Docker: `grafana/xk6-client-tracing` image pre-builds the extension.

### Pattern 574 — `xk6-loki`: Load Testing Loki Log Ingestion and Query Paths  [community]

`xk6-loki` is the official Grafana extension for push-and-query load testing of Loki.
It supports configurable label cardinality, mixed JSON/Protobuf encoding, and both write
and query workloads in a single k6 script.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/loki-load.js
// Build: xk6 build --with github.com/grafana/xk6-loki
import loki from "k6/x/loki";
import { sleep } from "k6";

// INIT CONTEXT — configure client once, shared across VUs via SharedArray pattern
const conf = new loki.Config(
  __ENV.LOKI_URL || "http://localhost:3100",
  10000,         // timeout ms
  0.9,           // 90% protobuf / 10% JSON encoding ratio
  {
    // Label cardinality: k Cartesian-product streams
    "app":    ["checkout", "catalog", "cart", "auth"],
    "region": ["us-east-1", "eu-west-1", "ap-southeast-1"],
    "level":  ["info", "warn", "error"],
  }
);

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    // Write scenario: constant-arrival-rate push
    loki_write: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 200,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "3m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 50,
      exec: "writeScenario",
      tags: { scenario: "write" },
    },
    // Read scenario: lightweight query load, starts after 30s
    loki_read: {
      executor: "constant-vus",
      vus: 5,
      duration: "2m30s",
      startTime: "30s",
      exec: "readScenario",
      tags: { scenario: "read" },
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "loki_client_lines_sent_total{scenario:write}":         ["count>10000"],
    "http_req_duration{scenario:read}":                     ["p(95)<500"],
    "http_req_failed{scenario:read}":                       ["rate<0.02"],
  },
};

const client = new loki.Client(conf);

export function writeScenario() {
  // pushParameterized: configurable stream count + payload size
  const streams = 5;
  client.pushParameterized(streams, 512, 4096);  // 5 streams, 512–4096 bytes each
  sleep(0);
}

export function readScenario() {
  const now   = Date.now();
  const start = new Date(now - 5 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();  // last 5 minutes
  const end   = new Date(now).toISOString();

  // Range query — retrieves logs matching any "error" level stream
  client.rangeQuery('{level="error"}', start, end, 100);
  sleep(1);
}
```

**Key `xk6-loki` metrics:**

| Metric | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `loki_client_lines_sent_total` | Total log lines pushed across all streams |
| `loki_client_bytes_processed_total` | Uncompressed bytes pushed |
| `loki_client_compressed_bytes_total` | On-wire compressed bytes pushed |
| `loki_client_sent_bytes_total` | Total bytes (per request) |

> **[community]:** Set the Protobuf encoding ratio to `≥0.9` for production-representative
> ingest tests — Promtail and the Grafana Alloy agent default to Protobuf. A ratio of `0.0`
> (pure JSON) benchmarks the overhead of the uncompressed path, which is useful for sizing
> Loki CPU budgets for legacy clients. Combine both in one test by running two scenarios with
> different `conf` objects pointing at the same Loki instance.

> **[community]:** `pushParameterized` generates the Cartesian product of your label sets
> to determine available streams, then randomly selects `stream_count` streams per call.
> With 4 app × 3 region × 3 level labels, there are 36 possible streams — `pushParameterized(36, ...)`
> exercises every stream simultaneously, which is the worst-case ingest cardinality scenario
> for Loki's chunk store.

---

### Pattern 575 — `xk6-kubernetes`: Kubernetes Resource Lifecycle Management Inside Load Tests  [community]

`xk6-kubernetes` allows k6 VUs to create, inspect, and delete Kubernetes resources during a
test run. This is useful for testing Kubernetes controllers (operators, admission webhooks,
CRDs) under concurrent resource creation pressure.

```javascript
// k6/scripts/k8s-operator-load.js
// Build: xk6 build --with github.com/grafana/xk6-kubernetes
import { Kubernetes } from "k6/x/kubernetes";
import { sleep, check } from "k6";
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    operator_load: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate",
      rate: 10,         // 10 resource creation requests per second
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "2m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 20,
      maxVUs: 40,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    "k8s_resource_create_duration": ["p(95)<2000"],  // custom metric from extension
    "checks":                       ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

// INIT CONTEXT — one Kubernetes client per VU
// Uses $KUBECONFIG or ~/.kube/config by default
const k8s = new Kubernetes({
  // server: "https://my-cluster:6443",
  // token:  __ENV.K8S_TOKEN,
  // config: "/path/to/kubeconfig",
});

const NAMESPACE = __ENV.K8S_NAMESPACE || "k6-load-test";

export default function () {
  const resourceName = `load-test-job-${__VU}-${__ITER}`;

  // Create a Kubernetes Job resource
  const job = k8s.apply(`
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: ${resourceName}
  namespace: ${NAMESPACE}
  labels:
    test-run: k6-load
spec:
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 30
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: busybox:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "echo load-test && sleep 1"]
`);

  check(job, { "job created": (j) => j !== null });

  // Wait for the pod to become running (with timeout)
  const podRunning = k8s.helpers(NAMESPACE).waitPodRunning(resourceName, 15000);
  check(podRunning, { "pod became running": (r) => r === true });

  // Clean up immediately after verification — prevent resource accumulation
  k8s.delete("Job", resourceName, NAMESPACE);

  sleep(0.1);
}

export function teardown() {
  // Clean up any orphaned resources from failed iterations
  const jobs = k8s.list("Job", NAMESPACE);
  jobs.forEach((job) => {
    if (job.metadata.labels?.["test-run"] === "k6-load") {
      k8s.delete("Job", job.metadata.name, NAMESPACE);
      console.log(`Cleaned up orphaned job: ${job.metadata.name}`);
    }
  });
}
```

**Testing admission webhooks with `xk6-kubernetes`:**

```javascript
// Test that a ValidatingAdmissionWebhook rejects invalid resources correctly under load
export default function () {
  const invalidResource = {
    apiVersion: "v1",
    kind: "ConfigMap",
    metadata: { name: `cm-${__VU}-${__ITER}`, namespace: NAMESPACE },
    data: { forbidden_key: "value" },  // webhook rejects this key
  };

  try {
    k8s.create(invalidResource);
    // If creation succeeds, the webhook failed to reject — fail the check
    check(false, { "webhook rejected invalid resource": () => false });
  } catch (e) {
    // Expected: webhook returns 403/422 — admission denied
    check(true, { "webhook rejected invalid resource": () => e.message.includes("denied") });
  }
}
```

> **[community]:** Always create resources in a **dedicated test namespace** and label them
> with a unique `test-run` identifier. This allows `teardown()` to bulk-delete any orphans
> even if VU iterations are interrupted. Without a teardown cleanup, failed load tests leave
> hundreds of zombie resources in the cluster, which can trigger resource-quota exhaustion
> on the next run.

> **[community]:** `waitPodRunning()` uses a polling loop inside the extension Go code —
> the timeout is in milliseconds and defaults to 30000ms. Set it conservatively (15000ms or
> less) in load tests to prevent VUs from blocking on slow schedulers and inflating your
> `preAllocatedVUs` requirement. If >20% of VUs time out on `waitPodRunning`, your cluster's
> scheduling latency under load is your actual SLO bottleneck.

### Community Gotchas (continued)

**G311** — `k6 cloud` commands in v2.0.0 require an explicit stack configuration — omitting `--stack-id` (or `K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID` / running `k6 cloud login` first) produces an opaque authentication error that doesn't mention the missing stack  [official]

**What:** In k6 v2.0.0 every `k6 cloud` subcommand (`run`, `upload`, `project list`) requires
a Grafana Cloud stack to be configured. This is provided via:
1. `k6 cloud login` (interactive, stores token + stack ID)
2. `K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID` environment variable + `K6_CLOUD_TOKEN`
3. `--stack-id` flag

When no stack is configured, the error message references authentication ("unauthenticated
request" or "missing API token") rather than the missing stack ID, which leads to debugging
the wrong thing — teams check their API token rather than the stack ID configuration.

**Why this bites you:** Teams that previously used `k6 login cloud` (removed in v2.0.0) and
relied on cached credentials now get unauthenticated errors on first run after upgrade. The
v1.x command `k6 login cloud --token=$TOKEN` no longer exists; the v2.0.0 replacement is
`k6 cloud login` (subcommand syntax changed).

**Fix:**
```bash
# v1.x (removed in v2.0.0)
k6 login cloud --token=$GRAFANA_CLOUD_TOKEN

# v2.0.0+ — interactive login (persists to ~/.config/k6)
k6 cloud login

# v2.0.0+ — CI/CD: env vars, no interactive prompt required
export K6_CLOUD_TOKEN="your-grafana-cloud-token"
export K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID="12345"
k6 cloud run script.js

# v2.0.0+ — single-run override
k6 cloud run --stack-id=12345 script.js
```

Verify your configured stack:
```bash
k6 cloud project list         # lists projects; confirms stack is reachable
k6 cloud project list --format=json | jq '.[].id'   # extract project IDs for scripting
```

> **[official]:** The `k6 cloud login` command stores credentials in `~/.config/k6/config.json`
> on Linux/macOS and `%APPDATA%\k6\config.json` on Windows. In containerised CI, mount this
> file as a secret volume or use environment variables exclusively — never bake credentials
> into the Docker image.

---

**G312** — k6 v2.0.0 cloud run exit code `97` is new — CI pipelines that check only for exit
code `0` or `1` will silently pass on system aborts, timeouts, and user cancellations  [official]

**What:** In k6 v1.x, a `k6 cloud run` that was aborted by the system (server-side error,
network timeout, test cancelled via UI) returned exit code `0` — making it indistinguishable
from a successful run that passed all thresholds. k6 v2.0.0 introduces a new exit code:

| Exit code | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `0`       | Test ran to completion; all thresholds passed |
| `1`       | Test ran; at least one threshold failed |
| `97`      | Test aborted for non-threshold reason (system error, timeout, user cancellation) |
| `99`      | Test configuration error (script parse failure, invalid options) |

**Why this bites you:** A CI pipeline that gates on `exit_code != 0` now correctly catches
code `97` aborts. But a pipeline written as `if k6_exit -eq 1; then fail; fi` (only catching
threshold failures) still silently passes on code `97`. Teams that upgraded from v1.x
without updating their CI exit-code handling now have tests that appear green when the cloud
run was actually aborted.

**Fix:** Update all CI pipeline exit-code checks to handle the full exit-code matrix:
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/run-cloud-test.sh — v2.0.0 exit code handling
set -e

k6 cloud run "$@"
EXIT_CODE=$?

case $EXIT_CODE in
  0)  echo "PASS: all thresholds met"; exit 0 ;;
  1)  echo "FAIL: one or more thresholds failed"; exit 1 ;;
  97) echo "ABORT: cloud run was aborted (system error / timeout / cancellation)"; exit 1 ;;
  99) echo "ERROR: script configuration error (parse failure or invalid options)"; exit 1 ;;
  *)  echo "UNKNOWN exit code $EXIT_CODE"; exit 1 ;;
esac
```

GitHub Actions example:
```yaml
- name: Run k6 cloud load test
  run: |
    k6 cloud run k6/scripts/api-load.js
  env:
    K6_CLOUD_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.K6_CLOUD_TOKEN }}
    K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID: ${{ vars.K6_CLOUD_STACK_ID }}
  # GitHub Actions: any non-zero exit code from the step marks it failed,
  # so exit code 97 will correctly fail the workflow step without extra handling.
  # Explicit handling above is needed only when you want different behavior per code.
```

> **[official]:** This exit-code change is part of the k6 v2.0.0 release. Verify your
> current k6 binary's exit-code behavior with: `k6 run --help | grep "exit code"` or consult
> https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/k6-options/reference/#results-output
